DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

12 CFR Parts 3, 6, 8, 15, and 19

[Docket ID OCC-2025-0372]
RIN 1557-AF41

Implementing the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for 
U.S. Stablecoins Act for the Issuance of Stablecoins by Entities 
Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Office of the Comptroller of the 
Currency

AGENCY: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Treasury.

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is issuing 
regulations implementing the Guiding and Establishing National 
Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act regarding the issuance of payment 
stablecoins and certain related activities by entities subject to the 
OCC's jurisdiction.

DATES: The final rule is effective on January 18, 2027.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Sarah Turney, Assistant Director, 
Henry Barkhausen, Special Counsel, Kevin Korzeniewski, Special Counsel, 
Mark O'Horo, Special Counsel, Daniel Borman, Counsel, or Collin Berger, 
Attorney, Chief Counsel's Office, 202-649-5490, Office of the 
Comptroller of the Currency, 400 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20219. 
If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please 
dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background and Summary of the Final Rule

    The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. 
Stablecoins Act (12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.) (GENIUS Act or the Act) was 
enacted on July 18, 2025. The Act establishes a regulatory framework 
for payment stablecoin activities.\1\ Stablecoins are digital assets, 
i.e., digital representations of value recorded on a cryptographically 
secured distributed ledger,\2\ such as a blockchain.\3\ The Act sets 
forth various regulatory and licensing requirements for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers. In 
many instances, the Act states that the specific requirements 
applicable to these entities (e.g., those related to capital, 
liquidity, or operational risk management) will be established by 
regulations issued by the relevant primary Federal payment stablecoin 
regulator, in coordination with other relevant agencies, as 
appropriate.\4\ On March 2, 2026, the OCC issued a notice of proposed 
rulemaking (proposal or proposed rule) proposing, and seeking comment 
on, the regulations that would apply to permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers under the OCC's 
jurisdiction (including subsidiaries of insured national banks or 
Federal savings associations, Federal qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers, certain nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, 
and foreign payment stablecoin issuers) as well as certain custody 
activities conducted by OCC-supervised entities.\5\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Under section 2(22) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(22)), 
``payment stablecoin'' means ``a digital asset--(i) that is, or is 
designed to be, used as a means of payment or settlement; and (ii) 
the issuer of which--(I) is obligated to convert, redeem, or 
repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value, not including a 
digital asset denominated in a fixed amount of monetary value; and 
(II) represents that such issuer will maintain, or create the 
reasonable expectation that it will maintain, a stable value 
relative to the value of a fixed amount of monetary value[.]'' The 
term does not include a digital asset that is (i) a national 
currency; (ii) a deposit (as defined in 12 U.S.C. 1813), including a 
deposit recorded using distributed ledger technology; or (iii) a 
security, as defined in 15 U.S.C. 77b, 78c, or 80a-2.
    \2\ 12 U.S.C. 5901(6).
    \3\ White House, ``Strengthening American Leadership in Digital 
Financial Technology,'' at 15 (July 17, 2025), (hereinafter, Digital 
Financial Technology Report), https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Digital-Assets-Report-EO14178.pdf. A 
cryptographically secured ledger uses cryptography to maintain the 
integrity of the ledger. See also E.O. No. 14178, Strengthening 
American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology, 90 FR 8647 
(January 31, 2025) (defining blockchain to mean ``any technology 
where data is: (i) shared across a network to create a public ledger 
of verified transactions or information among network participants; 
(ii) linked using cryptography to maintain the integrity of the 
public ledger and to execute other functions; (iii) distributed 
among network participants in an automated fashion to concurrently 
update network participants on the state of the public ledger and 
any other functions; and (iv) composed of source code that is 
publicly available'').
    \4\ See, e.g., 12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4), (b), (h).
    \5\ See Implementing the Guiding and Establishing National 
Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act for the Issuance of Stablecoins 
by Entities Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Office of the 
Comptroller of the Currency, 91 FR 10202 (March 2, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received approximately 328 comments in response to the 
proposal from a wide variety of commenters, including crypto-focused 
companies, trade groups, banks, non-profit organizations, academics, 
and individuals.\6\ Commenters had diverging views on several of the 
proposal's key provisions. The final rule addresses these comments, as 
discussed below. However, as discussed in the proposal, the OCC 
anticipates that these implementing regulations will be updated, as 
necessary, in the years following the effective date of the GENIUS Act 
as the business practices of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers continue to evolve and develop and 
the OCC gains experience regulating and supervising permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. Likewise, the OCC will supplement this final rule 
with guidance documents, as appropriate. As is its practice in other 
areas, the OCC will continue to track market developments and meet with 
interested parties to discuss the regulation and supervision of 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers, foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers, national banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal 
branches under the final rule in the coming years to understand the 
application of the rule in practice. At a high level, many commenters 
held differing views with respect to the proposal's approach concerning 
reserve asset management, liquidity, and diversification; the 
prohibition against a permitted payment stablecoin issuer paying 
interest or yield to a payment stablecoin holder solely in connection 
with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin (yield 
prohibition); redemption; and the proposal's capital requirements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ Although the comment period closed on May 1, 2026, the OCC 
continued to accept and consider late comments until July 1, 2026.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to reserve asset management, liquidity, and 
diversification, commenters differed as to how prescriptive the final 
rule should be. Several commenters advocated setting principles-based 
requirements, either with or without a quantitative safe harbor 
concerning diversification requirements, and making certain changes to 
the proposed quantitative diversification safe harbor. Other commenters 
advocated for more prescriptive and quantitative reserve asset 
management, liquidity, and diversification requirements.
    Many commenters opposed the proposal's approach with respect to the 
yield prohibition. The proposal included a rebuttable presumption that 
would have presumed certain transactions with affiliates and related 
third parties violated the prohibition. Many commenters generally 
favored a strong prohibition that would address a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer using a third party to pay interest or yield. Of 
these commenters, several favored broadening the rebuttable 
presumption. Others said that a presumption was inadequate, and certain 
transactions that implicated indirect payments should be

[[Page 67001]]

conclusively prohibited. In contrast, many commenters advocated for a 
narrow prohibition and either eliminating or narrowing the rebuttable 
presumption. Many of these commenters voiced concerns that the proposed 
rebuttable presumption could capture certain payments to related third 
parties that were not made solely in connection with the holding, use, 
or retention of payment stablecoin.
    Concerning redemption, many commenters argued against imposing a 
freeze on (or extension of) redemption when there is a spike in 
redemption requests. Commenters argued that including these types of 
provisions could accelerate a run. With respect to capital, many 
commenters generally favored the flexible approach afforded by the 
proposed rule. Nevertheless, other commenters advocated a more 
quantitative and standardized approach. Commenters also addressed 
several other issues, including definitions; permitted activities; 
redemption; risk management; audits, reports, and supervision; State 
issuers; custody; foreign issuers; applications and registration 
requirements, among other issues. Each of these subjects is addressed 
in greater detail below.
    Commenters also provided input concerning requirements relating to 
Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) and sanctions evasion. 
These comments will be addressed in a separate rulemaking.\7\ Likewise, 
some comments on that separate rulemaking are best addressed in this 
final rule. Some commenters stated that the OCC should delay finalizing 
the rule due to uncertainties in stablecoin markets, ongoing 
legislative efforts, the complexity of the Act and rule, or to 
facilitate issuance of a joint rule.\8\ Some commenters requested that 
the OCC re-propose any aspects that are inconsistent with the proposals 
of other agencies that issue rules under the GENIUS Act. The GENIUS Act 
will be effective on January 18, 2027, and it is important that the 
OCC's implementing regulations be effective as of that date. With 
respect to legislation, the OCC will revise the final rule, as 
appropriate, in response to any enacted legislation impacting the OCC's 
implementation of the GENIUS Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \7\ See Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuer Anti-Money 
Laundering/Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Sanctions 
Compliance Risk Management, 91 FR 37840 (June 24, 2026). On December 
8, 2025, the OCC received a petition for regulatory action from 
Peter Tang at Stablecoin Standards Authority requesting (1) clear, 
risk-based supervisory expectations for national banks that 
participate in payment stablecoin activities with the GENIUS 
framework, (2) consistent application of Federal standards to large 
offshore U.S.-dollar referenced stablecoin arrangements with a 
material United States nexus, and (3) a targeted rulemaking to 
ensure that stablecoin settlement infrastructure is identifiable and 
subject to ongoing compliance accountability through on-chain node 
KYC and a Federally administered node registry. The OCC is 
addressing BSA/AML provisions of the GENIUS Act in a separate 
rulemaking, and the proposal related to that separate rulemaking was 
published in the Federal Register on June 24, 2026. The OCC is 
issuing the final rule consistent with the GENIUS Act and denies 
Stablecoin Standards Authority's petition for a separate rulemaking 
given the BSA/AML proposal.
    \8\ On September 9, 2024, the OCC received a petition for 
rulemaking from Dmitry Shkipin at HomeOpenly.com requesting that the 
OCC repeal OCC Interpretive Letters 1170 (July 22, 2020), 1172 
(September 21, 2020), and 1174 (January 4, 2021). The petition 
asserts that virtual currencies are unlawful. The OCC is issuing the 
final rule consistent with the GENIUS Act and denies 
HomeOpenly.com's petition for a rulemaking because these activities 
are lawful, as explained in the letters, and because many of the 
stablecoin activities permissible under OCC Interpretive Letters 
1170, 1172, and 1174 were expressly affirmed by the GENIUS Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

In addition, several commenters requested an extension of the 
comment period or to avoid finalizing the rule until certain 
legislative clarity was provided or to ensure that the effective date 
of the Act would be no sooner than January 18, 2027. Commenters also 
raised concerns regarding interagency coordination and advocated for 
ensuring that there is alignment among the rules issued by the agencies 
tasked with implementing the GENIUS Act. Balancing the need to have 
final rules implementing the GENIUS Act in advance of the statutory 
effective date against commenters' desire for additional time to 
comment on the proposal, the OCC elected not to extend the comment 
period but did accept and consider comments submitted after the close 
of the formal comment period. With respect to interagency coordination, 
the OCC has coordinated closely with the other Federal agencies 
consistent with section 13 of the GENIUS Act. The OCC has taken 
seriously its obligation to coordinate with other agencies, as 
appropriate, and does not believe that it is necessary to do so through 
a joint rule. The OCC will continue to coordinate appropriately.
    Commenters provided suggestions on amendments to regulations that 
should be made in coordination with the GENIUS Act rulemaking. For 
example, a few commenters noted that the OCC should coordinate with the 
other Federal banking agencies to amend the standardized bank capital 
and liquidity requirements to provide for appropriate treatment for 
payment stablecoins and reserve assets, including that because reserve 
assets are not available to meet the obligations of a parent entity of 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, they should not be included in 
parent-level capital and liquidity requirements. Other commenters 
stated that the agencies implementing the GENIUS Act should revise 
their liquidity rules to accommodate the GENIUS Act framework, 
including the liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio. 
These comments are beyond the scope of this rulemaking, and the final 
rule therefore does not revise existing regulations to address them.
    Several commenters raised other issues that are also beyond the 
scope of this rulemaking. Some commenters requested that the OCC apply 
certain other statutes to permitted payment stablecoin issuers by rule. 
The OCC has not done so in this final rule. The scope of statutes that 
apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers cannot change by 
regulation. Thus, the final rule neither subjects permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to statutes that would not otherwise apply nor 
excludes them from the scope of statutes that do apply to their 
activities. Some commenters stated that the OCC should coordinate with 
the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Federal Reserve) 
concerning designation of certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
as systemically important. Such designation is beyond the scope of this 
rulemaking, and therefore the final rule does not address such 
designations. In addition, one commenter requested that the OCC address 
the tax treatment of payment stablecoins. This issue is outside the 
scope of this rule and the OCC's authority and is not addressed in the 
final rule. Likewise, some commenters brought up antitrust concerns 
that are outside the scope of this rulemaking. Some commenters raised 
issues concerning non-payment stablecoins, decentralized finance 
(DeFi),\9\ and crypto-assets more broadly that also fall outside the 
scope of this rulemaking.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \9\ DeFi generally refers to the use of blockchain technology to 
provide financial services on a peer-to-peer basis. Digital 
Financial Technology Report at 20.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Many commenters suggested that the OCC apply various existing 
consumer protection laws and regulations to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. For example, several commenters pointed to Unfair, 
Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices (UDAAP) pursuant to section 
1031 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5531), Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices (UDAP) under 
section 5 of the Federal Trade

[[Page 67002]]

Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 45), the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978 
(15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq.) (EFTA), the Truth in Lending Act of 1968 (15 
U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) (TILA), and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (15 U.S.C. 
6801 et seq.) (GLBA) as existing consumer protection laws that should 
apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Commenters argued that 
consumers should not receive different protections based solely on the 
technological form of a payment instrument. Some commenters suggested 
that new consumer protection requirements for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should be drafted rather than simply applying 
existing statutes and regulations. For example, a few commenters 
suggested that consumer protection should be addressed in the 
application and supervisory framework under the GENIUS Act. A few 
commenters suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should 
be required to maintain frameworks for managing risks arising from 
redemption failures, misleading disclosures, or inadequate customer 
communication. Other commenters suggested that, in addition to 
traditional fraud risks, specific operational risks such as transaction 
delays, rejections, and account restrictions should be addressed in the 
case of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. In contrast, a few 
commenters argued that consumer protection currently has its own 
regulatory framework and should not be duplicated. It would be outside 
the scope of this rulemaking to opine on all the statutes that may be 
applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC's final 
rule does not alter the scope of the consumer protection laws that 
apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
    Several commenters also requested that the OCC take additional 
action to clarify the treatment of reserve assets upon an issuer's 
insolvency. For example, commenters suggested that the rule clarify 
that reserve assets are held for the benefit of the holders of the 
issuer's payment stablecoin or that the assets are not assets of the 
issuer's estate. Another commenter suggested that the OCC rely on its 
fiduciary rulemaking powers to require that reserve assets be held in a 
statutory trust or other equivalent legal structure. As discussed in 
greater detail below, the OCC has made changes in the final rule to 
accommodate certain structures, including the use of special purpose 
vehicle (SPV) issuers designed to protect the rights of payment 
stablecoin holders.
    One commenter emphasized that it is appropriate to recognize the 
United States Federal framework already applicable to foreign banks' 
United States presence when operationalizing the permitted payment 
stablecoin framework. Although the International Banking Act of 1978 
(12 U.S.C. 3101 et seq.) applies to the United States operations of 
foreign banks, the GENIUS Act includes additional, specific 
requirements related to foreign issuers of payment stablecoins in the 
United States.
    The OCC is adopting this final rule with certain modifications from 
the proposal in light of the comments received. At a high level, the 
final rule makes several changes to the provisions concerning reserve 
asset management. These changes provide more flexibility to permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers while still maintaining core liquidity, 
diversification, and concentration requirements to ensure that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers remain sufficiently reserved and 
capable of meeting redemption requests in a timely manner. The final 
rule provides additional clarity with respect to a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's permitted activities, redemption requirements, and 
risk management obligations. It also includes clarifications concerning 
the OCC's supervision of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, custody, 
and licensing and registration. In addition, the final rule includes 
capital and operational backstop requirements that are more detailed 
than, but consistent with, the proposal. The capital elements have also 
been simplified relative to the proposal. The final rule, like the 
proposal, imposes requirements consistent with the GENIUS Act that are 
tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. For example, as described below, the agency is 
implementing flexible risk management standards in Sec.  15.13 that 
scale based on the nature, scope, and risk of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's activities. Consistent with certain comments 
received on the proposal, the final rule facilitates an approach to 
supervision that focuses on activities over institution type.
    In addition, other regulations beyond those addressed in this 
rulemaking may need to be updated in light of the passage of the GENIUS 
Act. For example, the OCC intends to incorporate references to 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers, as appropriate, into 12 CFR part 4 \10\ and is considering 
updates to 12 CFR part 28.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ See OCC Rules Regarding the Availability of OCC 
Information, 91 FR 50610 (August 5, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    These implementing regulations will be effective on January 18, 
2027.

A. Self-Executing Provisions

    The proposal discussed certain self-executing provisions of the 
GENIUS Act but did not propose rule text for these self-executing 
provisions.\11\ For example, the Act includes several provisions 
addressing the applicability of State law to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. Specifically, section 4(b)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(b)(1)) states that, notwithstanding certain Federal law 
addressing preemption standards for OCC-regulated institutions,\12\ and 
certain State laws, a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
``shall be licensed, regulated, examined, and supervised exclusively by 
the Comptroller.'' This provision provides the OCC with the exclusive 
authority to exercise visitorial powers with respect to Federal 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers, consistent with the agency's 
authority in 12 U.S.C. 484.\13\ This exclusivity generally prevents 
other regulators from subjecting these entities to additional 
oversight, which can be unduly burdensome, duplicative, or 
inconsistent.\14\ In addition, based on the exclusivity granted to the 
OCC, section 4(b) of the Act preempts certain State laws with respect 
to Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \11\ 91 FR at 10203-04.
    \12\ Specifically, 12 U.S.C. 25b and 1465 respectively address 
the preemption standards applicable to national banks and Federal 
savings associations and their subsidiaries.
    \13\ Although the GENIUS Act does not specifically use the term 
``visitorial powers,'' its plain language is consistent with the 
Supreme Court's description of visitorial authority. See Cuomo v. 
Clearing House Ass'n, L.L.C., 557 U.S. 519, 526 (2009) (describing 
visitation as the exercise of ``general supervision'') (emphasis 
added); see also 12 CFR 7.4000(a)(2) (describing the OCC's 
visitorial powers with respect to national banks).
    \14\ Twelve U.S.C. 484 would also continue to apply to uninsured 
national banks and Federal branches that become permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Section 5(h) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(h)) expressly 
preempts ``any State requirement for a charter, license, or other 
authorization to do business with respect to a Federal qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer or [a] subsidiary of an [OCC-regulated] 
insured depository institution . . . that is approved . . . to be a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer.'' As a result, these entities are 
only required to obtain authorization to do business from the OCC, 
which reduces the complexity that

[[Page 67003]]

would result from requiring these entities to also obtain a charter, 
license, or other authorization from one or more States.\15\ Finally, 
section 7(f)(4) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(f)(4)) provides that 
nothing in the GENIUS Act preempts State consumer protection laws.\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \15\ See also Section 4(b)(1) (12 U.S.C. 5903(b)(1)).
    \16\ Depending on the circumstances, other Federal law, such as 
the National Bank Act and the Home Owners' Loan Act, may also be 
relevant in assessing the applicability of State law, including a 
State consumer protection law, to certain permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, such as uninsured national banks.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Together, these GENIUS Act provisions establish a framework for 
assessing the applicability of State law to a Federal qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer or a subsidiary of an OCC-regulated insured 
depository institution approved to be a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.\17\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ The GENIUS Act also addresses the applicability of State 
law to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. See, e.g., 
section 7(f) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(f)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received several comments on these self-executing 
provisions. Some commenters requested that the OCC more specifically 
address whether the GENIUS Act preempts licensing requirements in 
certain circumstances (e.g., when third parties provide services to 
certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers, when a foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer is authorized to issue stablecoins in the U.S., or 
when a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer or subsidiary of an 
OCC-regulated insured depository institution engages in activities 
other than those addressed in section 4(a)(7)(A) (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(7)(A)). Commenters also recommended that the OCC state that it 
has exclusive visitorial powers over subsidiaries of insured national 
banks that are permitted payment stablecoin issuers, similar to the 
proposal's statement regarding the OCC's exclusive visitorial powers 
for Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers. With respect to State 
consumer protection laws, commenters had several suggestions, including 
that the OCC specifically address compliance with applicable State 
consumer protection laws in its final regulation. Commenters also 
recommended that the OCC further explain how it will approach certain 
preemption issues.
    After carefully considering the comments received, the OCC 
determined that the issues raised by commenters do not require 
regulatory changes, are outside the scope of this rulemaking, or are 
better evaluated on an individualized basis. The section of the 
preamble to the proposal discussing these self-executing provisions was 
intended to provide stakeholders with a general understanding of the 
GENIUS Act's preemption and visitation framework. Because this 
framework is self-executing, however, the OCC did not propose any 
implementing regulation text, nor is it including any in the final 
rule. While commenters raised several interpretive issues that may 
warrant clarification at the appropriate time, the OCC has concluded 
that the agency should retain the flexibility to address such issues as 
they arise. This will ensure that the OCC's analysis is appropriately 
informed by, and tailored to, the relevant facts and circumstances. 
Stakeholders may contact the OCC with questions as they arise, and the 
OCC will provide additional clarification if appropriate.\18\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \18\ At least one commenter observed that the proposal did not 
explain how the OCC will comply with 12 U.S.C. 25b, which imposes 
procedural requirements on certain OCC preemption actions. The OCC 
has complied, and will continue to comply, with all applicable legal 
requirements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Among other self-executing provisions, section 4(g) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(g)) provides that a Federal savings association 
established under the Home Owners' Loan Act (12 U.S.C. 1461 et seq.) 
that holds a reserve that satisfies the requirements of section 4(a)(1) 
of the GENIUS Act shall not be required to satisfy the qualified thrift 
lender test under section 10(m) of the Home Owners' Loan Act (12 U.S.C. 
1467a(m)) \19\ with respect to such reserve assets. Because this 
provision is self-executing, the OCC did not propose regulatory text to 
implement section 4(g). The OCC received no comments on this aspect of 
the Act and, consistent with the proposal, is not including any 
regulatory text to implement section 4(g) of the Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \19\ A Federal savings association is generally required to be a 
qualified thrift lender. A Federal savings association is a 
qualified thrift lender if it meets one of the following qualified 
thrift lender tests: (1) it qualifies as a domestic building and 
loan association as defined in 26 U.S.C. 7701(a)(19); or (2) its 
qualified thrift investments equal or exceed 65 percent of its 
portfolio assets, and its qualified thrift investments continue to 
equal or exceed 65 percent of its portfolio assets on a monthly 
average basis in nine out of every 12 months.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

II. Description of the Final Rule

    The final rule, like the proposal, addresses the majority of the 
OCC's implementation of the GENIUS Act through new 12 CFR part 15. In 
addition, like the proposal, the final rule makes updates to 12 CFR 
parts 3 (Capital Adequacy Standards), 6 (Prompt Corrective Action), 8 
(Assessment of Fees), and 19 (Rules of Practice and Procedure). For 
each subpart, or substantive subsection, of 12 CFR part 15, an overview 
of the changes from the proposed rule to the final rule is provided, 
followed by a detailed description of the proposed rule, relevant 
comments, and final rule.

A. Subpart A--Purpose, Scope, Definitions, Severability, and 
Reservation of Authority

    Consistent with the proposal, subpart A of 12 CFR part 15 provides 
the purpose and scope and defines terms used throughout the final rule.
1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart A
    As described below, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.1, which provides 
the scope and purpose of part 15, as proposed.
    The OCC is adopting many of the part 15 definitions in Sec.  15.2 
as proposed, but several definitions are being added, removed, or 
changed. The agency is adopting the following definitions as proposed: 
affiliate, Bank Secrecy Act, control, deposit, digital asset, director, 
distributed ledger, executive officer, fair value, FDIC, Federal 
branch, Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer, Federal Reserve, 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer, GAAP, immediate family, insider, 
insured credit union, insured depository institution, monetary value, 
money, national currency, nonbank entity, OCC, payment stablecoin, 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer, person, principal shareholder, 
publicly available information, registered public accounting firm, 
related interest, reserve asset, Stablecoin Certification Review 
Committee, State, State payment stablecoin regulator, and subsidiary. 
The agency is adding to Sec.  15.2 new definitions for business day, 
payment stablecoin holder, reserve asset value, sensitive customer 
information, share account, and tokenized form. Additionally, the 
agency is removing from Sec.  15.2 the definitions of distributed 
ledger protocol, State-chartered depository institution, and trading 
volume.
    The agency is finalizing the following Sec.  15.2 definitions with 
differences from the proposed definitions: board of directors, 
customer, depository institution, eligible financial institution, 
nonpublic personal information, outstanding issuance value, private 
key, State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, and United States 
customer.
    As described below, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.3, providing for 
the severability of part 15 provisions, as proposed.

[[Page 67004]]

    The OCC is adding Sec.  15.4 on the reservation of authority that 
was not in the proposed rule.
2. Purpose and Scope (Sec.  15.1)
    Proposed Sec.  15.1 set forth the purpose and scope of the 
stablecoin-related regulations. Paragraph (a) described the purpose, 
which is to implement the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq., with 
respect to entities for which the OCC is authorized to issue 
regulations or exercise its enforcement authority under the Act. These 
entities were listed in the proposed scope provision in paragraph (b), 
which provided that proposed part 15 would apply to activities related 
to payment stablecoins and certain custody activities of (1) national 
banks and their subsidiaries; (2) Federal savings associations and 
their subsidiaries; (3) Federal branches and their subsidiaries; (4) 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers; (5) nonbank entities that seek to 
be or are approved as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; and 
(6) State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for whom the OCC has 
regulatory or enforcement authority pursuant to proposed Sec.  15.15 or 
Sec.  15.16. Thus, except where otherwise noted, references in part 15 
to permitted payment stablecoin issuers would only apply to these types 
of listed entities despite the broader scope of the term in the GENIUS 
Act.
    As described in the section-by-section analysis below, proposed 
subparts B and E would apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
that are subsidiaries of insured national banks, subsidiaries of 
Federal savings associations, uninsured national banks, Federal 
branches or subsidiaries thereof, nonbank entities that are not State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has regulatory or enforcement 
authority. Proposed subpart C would apply to national banks, Federal 
savings associations, Federal branches, Federal qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with 
a total consolidated outstanding issuance value of more than $10 
billion subject to supervision and regulation by the OCC that provide 
custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins, reserve 
assets, and other ``covered assets'' (described in detail in subpart 
C). The application and registration sections in proposed subpart D 
would apply to insured national banks, Federal savings associations, or 
Federal branches that seek to issue payment stablecoins through a 
subsidiary; nonbank entities that seek to be Federal qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers, uninsured national banks, and uninsured Federal 
branches that seek to be Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; 
and entities that seek to register as foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers. The capital requirements detailed in proposed subpart E would 
apply to subsidiaries of insured national banks, subsidiaries of 
Federal savings associations, uninsured national banks, Federal 
branches or subsidiaries thereof, nonbank entities that are not State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has regulatory authority.
    Several commenters sought greater clarity about which entities 
would become subject to the proposed regulation because of their 
activities. These commenters were concerned that a broad scoping of 
stablecoin issuer activities and digital asset service provider 
activities might result in an overly broad set of entities becoming 
subject to the OCC's regulations, including entities engaged in 
blockchain infrastructure, technology-service providers, vendor support 
function providers, and companies that facilitate businesses' adoption 
of stablecoin technology. Related to this scope issue, one commenter 
suggested that the rule should require a standardized certification 
under Federal oversight for core service providers, which would alter 
the scope of entities affected by the rule. Several commenters 
suggested the OCC follow a regulatory approach based on the activity 
type and not the institution type. Commenters suggested such an 
approach increases fair competition and decreases the risk of 
regulatory arbitrage.
    The scope of the final rule is consistent with the text of the 
GENIUS Act and the OCC's jurisdiction. The OCC's part 15 applies to 
national banks and their subsidiaries, Federal savings associations and 
their subsidiaries, Federal branches and their subsidiaries, foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers, nonbank entities that seek to be or are 
approved as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers over which the OCC has regulatory 
or enforcement authority. To the extent that an entity falls under one 
of these categories, it is subject to part 15. Otherwise, the entity is 
not captured by the rule. Therefore, to the extent a blockchain 
infrastructure or technology service-provider issues a payment 
stablecoin and is a type of entity subject to the OCC's jurisdiction, 
it is covered under part 15. Additionally, entities that are covered 
custodians as that term is defined in subpart C of part 15 are also 
subject to part 15. Otherwise, part 15 does not apply.
    The OCC received no additional comments concerning proposed Sec.  
15.1 and is adopting Sec.  15.1, with one technical change. Paragraph 
(b)(6) of the proposed rule referred to State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers for whom the OCC has regulatory or enforcement 
authority. The final rule replaces ``for whom'' with ``for which.''
3. Definitions (Sec.  15.2)
    Section 15.2 contains the following definitions of terms used 
throughout part 15, many of which are included in or based on the 
definitions in the GENIUS Act.\20\ A description of the proposed 
definitions, comments received, and final definitions is below.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\20\ The definitions in Sec.  15.2 describe only terms used in 
part 15. These definitions do not interpret terms for purposes of 
any other statute or regulation and are not issued pursuant to 
section 3(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(d)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Acting in concert. The OCC did not propose to define ``acting in 
concert'' but requested comment on whether to do so, including whether 
to incorporate any of the presumptions for acting in concert under 12 
CFR 5.50. One commenter stated that the term did not need to be 
defined. Another recommended defining the term in a manner based on 12 
CFR 5.50. Another commenter stated that the definition should not be so 
broad as to inadvertently capture arm's-length commercial relationships 
between stablecoin issuers and their technology, custody, clearing, or 
compliance providers. Another commenter recommended adapting the 
definition in 12 CFR 5.50 to require knowing and purposeful 
coordination. The definition of ``acting in concert'' is pertinent to 
the definition of ``principal shareholder,'' which, in turn, is 
relevant to the definition of ``insider'' and to certain application 
requirements. The definition of ``principal shareholder'' is based on 
the definition in 12 CFR 5.20. The definition of ``insider'' is based 
on the definition in Regulation O (12 CFR 215). Both 12 CFR 5.20 and 
Regulation O use the terms ``acting in concert'' or ``acting through or 
in concert'' but do not define the terms. After considering the 
comments received, the OCC has concluded that it is unnecessary to 
define the term for purposes of 12 CFR part 15 because the term would 
serve the same purpose as in 12 CFR 5.20 and Regulation O, and the 
existing regulations are well established and understood. While the OCC 
is not defining the term for purposes of 12 CFR part 15, the OCC 
expects that any

[[Page 67005]]

person that would be deemed to be acting in concert for purposes of 12 
CFR 5.50 would also be acting in concert for purposes of Sec.  
15.14(m), which applies the requirements of 12 CFR 5.50 in the context 
of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Because the term ``acting in 
concert'' serves a different purpose in 12 CFR part 15 than in 12 CFR 
5.50, the OCC has not, however, incorporated the definition in 12 CFR 
5.50 or incorporated any of the presumptions therein.
    Affiliate. The OCC proposed to define the term ``affiliate'' 
consistent with the definition in the Bank Holding Company Act, 12 
U.S.C. 1841(k), but modified to use the defined term ``person'' in 
place of the term ``company.'' Under the proposed rule, the term 
``affiliate'' would have meant a person that controls, is controlled 
by, or is under common control with another person.
    Commenters generally supported or did not opine on the definition 
of ``affiliate'' (but, as discussed below, the OCC did receive comments 
concerning the definition of control, which has implications for the 
definition of affiliate). The OCC is adopting the definition of 
affiliate as proposed. This approach aligns the definition with the 
definition in the Bank Holding Company Act with which market 
participants are generally familiar. As discussed in the proposal, the 
definition of ``affiliate'' is consistent with the definition in the 
Bank Holding Company Act, and the OCC generally expects that it will 
interpret questions regarding the definition of ``affiliate'' 
consistent with the provisions of 12 CFR part 225 as of the date of the 
issuance of this final rule.
    Bank Secrecy Act. The OCC proposed to define the term ``Bank 
Secrecy Act'' consistent with the definition provided in the GENIUS 
Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(2). Under the proposal, the term ``Bank Secrecy 
Act'' would have meant: (1) section 21 of the Federal Deposit Insurance 
Act (12 U.S.C. 1829b); (2) chapter 2 of title I of Public Law 91-508 
(12 U.S.C. 1951 et seq.); and (3) subchapter II of chapter 53 of title 
31, United States Code and notes thereto (31 U.S.C. 5311 et seq.). The 
proposal added the phrase ``and notes thereto'' as a clarification. The 
OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``Bank Secrecy 
Act.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Board of directors. Under the proposed rule, ``board of directors'' 
would have meant a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's or applicant's 
board of directors or the group of individuals that serve the nearest 
equivalent function of acting as the governing body of the issuer or 
applicant. The proposed definition captured the persons responsible for 
certain requirements under proposed part 15, including for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers that do not have a board of directors as 
that term is commonly understood. The OCC received no comments 
addressing the definition of ``board of directors.'' The OCC is 
adopting the definition with one technical change replacing ``serve'' 
with ``serves.''
    Business day. One commenter requested that the OCC clarify the 
meaning of ``business day,'' including whether Saturdays, Sundays, and 
national holidays are excluded, for purposes of the timely redemption 
requirement in Sec.  15.12. Alternatively, the commenter stated that 
the OCC could impose a requirement that issuers disclose how they 
calculate the two-business-day period under Sec.  15.12. To provide 
clarity, the OCC is defining ``business day'' to mean any day other 
than a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday.
    Conspicuous. One commenter requested that the OCC define 
``conspicuous'' for purposes of relevant disclosures. The OCC declines 
to do so in this final rule because whether disclosures are conspicuous 
depends heavily on context. The OCC generally expects that disclosures 
that would be considered conspicuous under 12 CFR part 328 would 
generally be considered conspicuous under 12 CFR part 15.
    Control. The OCC proposed to define ``control'' such that a person 
would have controlled another person if: (1) the person directly or 
indirectly or acting through one or more other persons owns, controls, 
or has power to vote 25 percent or more of any class of voting 
securities of the other person; (2) the person controls in any manner 
the election of a majority of the directors or trustees of the other 
person; or (3) the OCC determines, after notice and opportunity for 
hearing, that the person directly or indirectly exercises a controlling 
influence over the management or policies of the other person. Like the 
definition of ``affiliate,'' the proposed definition of ``control'' was 
generally consistent with the Bank Holding Company Act. The OCC noted 
that proposed Sec.  15.14 included certain provisions regarding changes 
in control that would refer to the use of that term under 12 CFR 5.50, 
rather than under the Bank Holding Company Act. Thus, for purposes of 
those provisions, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would refer to 
12 CFR 5.50.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``control.'' Several commenters requested that the OCC clarify the 
definition of control, including by expressly incorporating the 
presumptions of control in the Bank Holding Company Act and the Federal 
Reserve's Regulation Y. Other commenters argued for narrowing the 
definition of control by providing that ``controlling influence'' 
should be assessed based on actual decision-making authority and 
economic control, rather than formal or theoretical influence. One 
commenter advocated for a blend of Bank Holding Company Act and Change 
in Bank Control Act concepts. Some stated that a framework based on the 
Bank Holding Company Act is useful but should be adapted or clarified. 
Some commenters advocated for a narrower definition and for assessing 
controlling influence based on actual economic and legal control, 
rather than theoretical influence. Another stated that control 
encompasses not only ownership and voting power, but also the ability 
to direct or materially influence governance, operational decision-
making, or risk-bearing functions, whether exercised directly or 
indirectly.
    After considering the comments received, the OCC is adopting the 
definition as proposed. This approach aligns with the definition in the 
Bank Holding Company Act, with which market participants are generally 
familiar. Consistent with a statement in the proposal, the OCC 
generally expects that it will interpret questions regarding the 
definition of ``control'' consistent with the provisions of 12 CFR part 
225, including those relating to controlling influences and to the 
presumption of control, as of the date of the issuance of this final 
rule. The interpretations of control under the Bank Holding Company 
Act, including 12 CFR part 225, generally have been developed after 
consideration of the same or similar comments received in response to 
the proposal. Moreover, the OCC may provide additional clarity through 
guidance and interpretations, as necessary. The OCC believes that this 
approach will provide clarity to market participants.
    Customer. The OCC proposed to define the term ``customer'' to mean 
a person that purchases (through any consideration) the products or 
services of another person. Among other provisions, the definition of 
``customer'' was relevant to certain information protection and 
notification requirements.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``customer.'' Several commenters regarded the proposed definition of 
``customer'' as

[[Page 67006]]

overly broad because it could capture indirect relationships between 
stablecoin holders and permitted payment stablecoin issuers. These 
commenters generally argued in favor of requiring a contractual 
relationship between a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and a 
counterparty for the counterparty to be covered by the definition of 
customer. Other commenters generally favored a broad definition that 
would include persons who acquired payment stablecoins in the secondary 
market. One commenter advocated not defining the term.
    The final rule modifies the definition by defining customer (except 
in the context of the custody provisions, where the term ``covered 
customer'' is used) to mean a person that purchases (through any 
consideration) the products or services of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer directly from 
the issuer or that makes a request directly to the issuer that the 
issuer convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin. This 
definition focuses on the relationship between the issuer and its 
direct counterparties. Thus, for example, if a payment stablecoin 
holder acquired its payment stablecoin from a third-party distributor 
(including a distributor that is associated with the payment 
stablecoin, for example, as part of a white-label arrangement) that did 
not act as agent for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the 
payment stablecoin holder would not be a customer of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer unless and until the holder sought to redeem 
the payment stablecoin from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (or 
otherwise purchased products or services directly from the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer).
    The OCC believes that this narrower definition is appropriate in 
light of additional changes, described below, including adopting a 
definition of ``payment stablecoin holder'' and clarifying how certain 
notification requirements in the final rule apply to customers. The OCC 
believes that these changes will help ensure that the term is neither 
overly broad nor overly narrow. The OCC believes that this revised 
definition will result in a set of customers that is easily 
identifiable by permitted payment stablecoin issuers. This definition 
does not affect the definition of customer for purposes of other laws 
and regulations, including privacy laws and the Bank Secrecy Act and 
its implementing regulations.\21\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\21\ See generally 91 FR 37840; Permitted Payment Stablecoin 
Issuer Customer Identification Program, 91 FR 37234 (June 22, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Deposit. The OCC proposed to define the term ``deposit'' to have 
the same meaning as deposit in section 3 of the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(l)). The OCC received no comments 
addressing the definition of ``deposit.'' The OCC is adopting the 
definition as proposed.
    Depository institution. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``depository institution'' to mean a depository institution as that 
term is defined in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 
U.S.C. 1813(c)(1)) or a credit union. The OCC proposed this definition 
because, although the GENIUS Act uses the term ``depository 
institution,'' it is not defined in section 2 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901). Section 11(g) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5910(g)) does, however, 
refer to the Federal Deposit Insurance Act's definition.\22\ Under the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act, the term ``depository institution'' 
means any bank or savings association, both of which are defined terms 
under that statute and would be incorporated to determine whether an 
institution is a depository institution for purposes of proposed part 
15. The OCC also proposed to include a reference to credit unions 
consistent with the approach that the GENIUS Act took with respect to 
the definition of ``insured depository institution,'' defined below, 
and which explicitly includes insured credit unions. This term is 
particularly relevant with respect to the OCC's jurisdiction over 
certain nonbank entities under sections 2(25), 4(d), and 7(e) of the 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(25), 5903(d), and 5906(e)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \22\ The proposed definition of ``depository institution'' for 
purposes of part 15 would not affect the meaning of the term under 
section 11(g) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5911).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``depository institution.'' Some commenters stated that privately 
insured credit unions should be excluded from the definition so that 
they could apply to be Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC clarify whether ``depository 
institution'' refers strictly to FDIC-insured institutions or extends 
to other charter types with deposit-like authorities. One commenter 
suggested that the OCC should make clear that the term ``depository 
institution'' also includes the uninsured State branches of foreign 
banks.
    The final rule includes certain modifications to the definition. 
Under the final rule, the term ``depository institution'' would mean a 
depository institution, as that term is defined in section 3 of the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(c)(1)), or an insured 
credit union as defined in section 101 of the Federal Credit Union Act 
(12 U.S.C. 1752) (i.e., a credit union that is not an insured credit 
union under section 101 of the Federal Credit Union Act would not be 
included in the definition of depository institution). Absent this 
change, there could have been ambiguity as to which agency is the 
primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator for a non-Federally 
insured credit union. Such a credit union would not meet the definition 
of ``State depository institution'' under section 2(29) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(29)) but, if the credit union were a depository 
institution, it would not be a nonbank entity. In other words, the 
proposed definition could have the effect of excluding non-Federally 
insured credit unions from being regulated by the OCC as permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers. The amended definition makes clear that a 
non-Federally insured credit union is a nonbank entity and that the OCC 
is the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator for such entities. 
In response to other comments, the OCC does not believe that it is 
appropriate to limit the definition of ``depository institution'' 
strictly to insured depository institutions. The statute uses both 
terms, and it is appropriate to regard each term as having a separate 
meaning. In light of the GENIUS Act's frequent references to the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act, the most faithful reading of the statute 
would incorporate the Federal Deposit Insurance Act's definition, with 
the modification described above to address the fact that the GENIUS 
Act addresses credit unions while the Federal Deposit Insurance Act 
does not. Thus, institutions that are depository institutions under the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act (i.e., national banks, savings 
associations, State banks, Federal branches, and insured branches) 
would be depository institutions for purposes of 12 CFR part 15. The 
OCC further notes that ``insured depository institution'' is defined 
separately (discussed below).
    Digital asset. The OCC proposed to define the term ``digital 
asset'' as provided in section 2(6) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901(6)). Under the proposed rule, the term ``digital asset'' would 
have meant any digital representation of value that is recorded

[[Page 67007]]

on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``digital asset.'' Several commenters supported the proposed definition 
but asked the OCC to clarify that application of this definition within 
the proposed rule remains limited to the activities and obligations 
expressly contemplated by the GENIUS Act. Some commenters suggested 
that the OCC ensure that the definition clearly distinguishes between 
(i) payment stablecoins covered by the rule, (ii) tokenized deposits 
and certain other bank liabilities, and (iii) digital representations 
of traditional financial assets that do not function as standalone 
mediums of exchange. One commenter stated that the definition does not 
cover non-fungible loyalty points, to the extent they are not recorded 
on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The regulatory 
definition matches the statutory definition. In response to comments, 
other definitions, including the definition of ``payment stablecoin,'' 
appropriately distinguish different types of digital assets from one 
another. The definition of ``payment stablecoin'' distinguishes a 
payment stablecoin from a deposit, including a tokenized deposit, 
without any need to revise the broader definition of ``digital asset.'' 
In addition, the OCC confirms that the definition applies for purposes 
of implementing the GENIUS Act under part 15 and does not necessarily 
apply in other contexts. The OCC also confirms that, under the 
definition in part 15, a representation of value that is not recorded 
on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger is not a digital 
asset.
    Digital asset service provider. The proposed rule did not include 
the term ``digital asset service provider'' but sought comment on 
whether to include such a term. The OCC received several comments on 
the term. Many of these comments sought clarifications around the scope 
of the term. Some sought to distinguish digital asset service providers 
from permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Others requested that the 
OCC clarify that the term does not include providers of blockchain 
infrastructure or DeFi activities. Others stated that the statutory 
definition was sufficiently clear or that the OCC had no authority to 
interpret the term.
    The final rule, like the proposal, does not use the term, which is 
generally more relevant to section 3 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5902) 
than the sections that part 15 implements. The OCC therefore found it 
unnecessary to define the term for purposes of part 15. The OCC does 
note that certain provisions of the GENIUS Act (e.g., 12 U.S.C. 5902) 
apply to digital asset service providers and that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may also be considered digital asset service 
providers. Accordingly, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should 
ensure compliance both with the rules that apply to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers and the rules that apply to digital asset service 
providers, as applicable.\23\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \23\ See Department of the Treasury, GENIUS Act Regulations on 
Payment Stablecoin Issuance, Offer, and Sale, 91 FR 53368, 53371 
(August 18, 2026) (stating that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
are also digital asset service providers under the GENIUS Act).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Director. The OCC proposed to define the term ``director'' for 
purposes of proposed part 15 to mean an individual who serves on the 
board of directors of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or 
applicant, except an advisory director who does not have the authority 
to vote on matters before the board of directors or any committee of 
the board of directors and provides solely general policy advice to the 
board of directors or any committee. The OCC based the proposed 
definition on the definition included in 12 CFR 5.51. The proposed 
definition was modified from that in 12 CFR 5.51 to remove the 
exclusion for a director of a foreign bank that operates a Federal 
branch. The OCC determined that this language was unnecessary in light 
of the proposed definition of the term ``board of directors.'' As 
described above, to address the various organizational forms used by 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers and applicants, including those 
that do not have a traditional board of directors, the OCC proposed to 
define the term ``board of directors'' in proposed part 15 to include a 
group of individuals that serve the nearest equivalent function of 
acting as the governing body of the issuer or applicant. For a Federal 
branch, individuals who would meet the proposed definition of 
``director'' would include individuals that are part of that group. 
Further, a director of a foreign bank is not a director of the branch 
unless the director serves on the board of a Federal branch (or serves 
in an equivalent capacity with respect to the branch).
    The OCC received a few comments addressing the definition of 
``director.'' A commenter suggested that: (i) branch-level senior 
officers should not automatically be considered ``directors'' solely 
because they exercise local management authority and (ii) for Federal 
branches seeking to issue stablecoins through a subsidiary, 
``director'' should mean members of the subsidiary's board with binding 
governance authority, not the branch's country officer or regional 
manager.\24\ The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The OCC 
believes the proposed definition was appropriately scoped in light of 
the definition of ``board of directors,'' which includes the group of 
individuals that serves the nearest equivalent function of acting as 
the governing body of the issuer or applicant. This definition focuses 
on persons with actual authority with respect to an entity. This 
functional definition of ``director'' appropriately captures persons 
serving the actual governance function associated with serving on the 
board of directors, regardless of formal structure or title.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \24\ The commenter also stated that independent directors 
required for audit and risk committees should not need to be United 
States citizens but must be subject to United States jurisdiction 
for enforcement purposes. The OCC confirms that a director need not 
be a United States citizen but is subject to the enforcement 
provisions of the GENIUS Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Distributed ledger. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``distributed ledger'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 
5901(8), with certain technical edits. The proposed rule defined the 
term ``distributed ledger'' to mean technology in which (1) data is 
shared across a network that creates a public digital ledger of 
verified transactions or information among network participants and (2) 
cryptography is used to link the data to maintain the integrity of the 
public ledger and execute other functions. The proposed definition 
reformatted the definition in the GENIUS Act by using numbering to 
distinguish between the two components of the definition. The 
formatting changes were technical and did not substantively affect the 
definition.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``distributed ledger.'' Commenters generally supported the proposed 
definition but suggested making clarifications or including definitions 
of additional terms. For example, commenters had varying views on 
whether the term should include or exclude public ledgers, private 
ledgers, or semi-private ledgers.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. This approach 
aligns with the statute. The OCC may address future innovations and 
developments through interpretations or additional rulemaking, as 
appropriate.
    Distributed ledger protocol. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``distributed

[[Page 67008]]

ledger protocol'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(9). The 
term ``distributed ledger protocol'' would have meant publicly 
available and accessible executable software deployed to a distributed 
ledger, including smart contracts or networks of smart contracts. The 
OCC received no comments separately addressing the definition of 
``distributed ledger protocol.'' The final rule, however, does not use 
the term. Accordingly, the OCC is not including a definition of the 
term in the final rule.
    Eligible financial institution. The OCC proposed to define 
``eligible financial institution'' to mean (1) a person that (a) is 
eligible to hold reserve assets in custody under section 10(a) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(a)); (b) complies with the applicable 
requirements in section 10(b), (c), and (d) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5909(b), (c) and (d)), including with applicable implementing 
regulations issued by a relevant primary Federal payment stablecoin 
regulator as defined in 12 U.S.C. 5901(25), primary financial 
regulatory agency described in 12 U.S.C. 5301(12)(B) or (C), State bank 
supervisor, or State credit union supervisor; and (c), if applicable, 
enters into a custody agreement with a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer documenting the person's compliance with paragraph (2) of the 
definition of eligible financial institution; or (2) a Federal Reserve 
Bank.
    The term ``eligible financial institution'' is relevant to the 
reserve asset diversification and concentration requirements in Sec.  
15.11(c) of the rule. Under section 10(a) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5909(a)), a person may only engage in the business of providing 
custodial or safekeeping services for the payment stablecoin reserve, 
the payment stablecoins used as collateral, or the private keys used to 
issue payment stablecoins if the person meets certain requirements, 
including being subject to supervision or regulation by a primary 
Federal payment stablecoin regulator, primary financial regulatory 
agency, or supervision by a State bank supervisor or a State credit 
union supervisor if such State bank supervisor or State credit union 
supervisor makes available to the Federal Reserve certain information. 
Such a person must also comply with the requirements under section 
10(b) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(b)), unless the person holds 
such property in accordance with similar requirements as required by a 
primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator, the Securities and 
Exchange Commission, or the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
    Eligible financial institutions would have included insured 
depository institutions and national banks regardless of whether the 
entities engaged in stablecoin activities or provided custody services 
to permitted payment stablecoin issuers because these entities are 
subject to supervision or regulation by a primary Federal payment 
stablecoin regulator. Thus, for example, under proposed Sec.  15.11(c) 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer could hold reserves as deposits 
at a national bank regardless of whether the national bank acted as 
custodian for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's other reserve 
assets.
    To meet the proposed definition, a financial institution would have 
also needed to comply with the applicable requirements of section 10 of 
the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909), and the relevant custody agreement would have 
needed to reflect compliance with section 10 as well as policies and 
procedures to ensure such compliance.\25\ These criteria help ensure 
compliance with section 10 of the Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \25\ As discussed above, to the extent that an eligible 
financial institution does not engage in custody of covered assets, 
section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) would not apply.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC recognized that multiple agencies will regulate permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers and the entities that may permissibly 
custody reserve assets. The proposed rule would have imposed 
requirements on where and how OCC-regulated permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may hold reserve assets in Sec.  15.11. Proposed 
subpart C would have separately imposed the requirements of section 10 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) on OCC-regulated institutions that 
hold reserve assets on behalf of payment stablecoin issuers, including 
on behalf of payment stablecoin issuers not regulated by the OCC. 
Proposed Sec.  15.11 did not mandate that OCC-regulated permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers only hold their reserve assets in the 
custody of OCC-regulated custodians. Accordingly, the proposal 
acknowledged that there could be overlap between the requirements 
imposed by different regulators with different requirements 
implementing section 10 of the GENIUS Act. The OCC invited comment on 
the best ways to manage potentially overlapping requirements. The 
proposed rule would have required that an ``eligible financial 
institution'' comply with the requirements in section 10(b), (c), and 
(d) of the GENIUS Act, including applicable implementing regulations. 
Accordingly, even if different types of eligible financial institutions 
were subject to different regulations on the safe handling of 
stablecoin reserve assets, an OCC-regulated permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer could still custody reserve assets at any entity that 
met the requirements in the definition of ``eligible financial 
institution.''
    The proposed rule would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to enter into a custody agreement with an eligible 
financial institution, which would have required that the eligible 
financial institution adhere to the requirements in section 10(b), (c), 
and (d), along with any applicable implementing regulations. This 
requirement would have helped ensure that the eligible financial 
institution knows that it is subject to the requirements of the GENIUS 
Act and would have provided permitted payment stablecoin issuers a 
contractual means of enforcing compliance with applicable provisions of 
the Act.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``eligible financial institution.'' Commenters generally supported the 
proposed definition but made suggestions that the OCC make certain 
clarifications. One commenter suggested publishing and maintaining a 
list of institution types that qualify as eligible financial 
institutions, rather than leaving payment stablecoin holders to 
determine what may be an eligible financial institution. The OCC will 
not provide a list of eligible financial institutions or eligible 
financial institution types as that list may become stale as new types 
of entities become eligible to hold reserve assets in custody under 
section 10 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) and it would be resource-
intensive for the OCC to identify all eligible financial institutions 
regulated by different States. Rather than updating the list every time 
a new entity type becomes eligible, the OCC believes that a definition 
that relates back to the statutory requirements in section 10 (12 
U.S.C. 5909) is appropriate.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC confirm the eligibility of 
foreign branches and agencies as eligible financial institutions for 
reserve custody purposes. The OCC confirms that foreign branches and 
agencies may hold reserve assets in custody, provided that they meet 
the requirements in section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909). 
However, as discussed below, deposit liabilities of institutions that 
are not insured depository institutions do not qualify as reserve 
assets under section

[[Page 67009]]

4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)).\26\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \26\ Uninsured deposits of insured banks are, however, 
permissible reserve assets under section 4(a)(1)(ii) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(ii)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    To be clear, section 10 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) would not apply 
to a foreign custodian holding payment stablecoin reserves where there 
is no nexus to the United States. This approach ensures that the Act 
does not have an overly broad extraterritorial effect. However, holding 
payment stablecoin reserves for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
is clearly within the scope of section 10 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909). 
Moreover, because the definition of permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
is limited to persons formed in the United States, holding reserve 
assets for such persons entails a clear nexus to the United States.
    A few commenters stated that eligibility should be based more on 
the activities performed and the institution's ability to satisfy 
segregation, custody, and operational standards than on balance sheet 
size or charter type, so that institutions of varying sizes and charter 
types can participate if they meet the relevant standards. The OCC's 
proposed definition would not have been inconsistent with these 
comments. The proposed definition did not impose any limitations for 
eligible financial institutions based on size. Moreover, the proposed 
rule did not limit eligible financial institutions to any particular 
charter type. Rather, the proposed rule imported the requirement in 
section 10 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) that the institution be subject 
to supervision by certain State or Federal regulators.
    Another commenter suggested that the OCC align the definition with 
established statutory and regulatory frameworks, such as the Bank 
Holding Company Act and State money transmitter laws, to promote 
consistency and reduce ambiguity. The OCC does not believe that further 
alignment is necessary or appropriate. Section 10 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5909) sets forth the supervisory framework that applies to custodians 
of reserve assets, and the proposed rule merely ensures that such 
custodians comply with section 10. Any further changes to the 
definition could result in narrowing or broadening the types of 
institutions that may hold reserve assets in custody in a manner 
inconsistent with the statute.
    One commenter stated that the definition of ``eligible financial 
institution'' should not be conditioned on complying with sections 
10(b), (c), and (d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(b)-(d)). The OCC 
disagrees. Sections 10(b), (c), and (d) each cross-reference to persons 
described in section 10(a) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(a)). Thus, a 
person that is eligible to hold payment stablecoin reserve assets in 
custody under section 10(a) (12 U.S.C. 5909(a)) is subject to the 
requirements of sections 10(b), (c), and (d) of the Act, as 
applicable.\27\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\27\ Under section 10(a)(2) of the Act, 12 U.S.C. 5909(a)(2), a 
custodian of reserve assets must comply with the requirements of 
section 10(b) of the Act unless the custodian holds the reserve 
assets (or other covered assets) in accordance with similar 
requirements as required by a primary Federal payment stablecoin 
regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission, or the Commodity 
Futures Trading Commission.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC is adopting the definition, with technical changes. The 
final rule renumbers paragraphs (1)(a) through (c) as (1)(i) through 
(iii) and replaces in paragraph (iii) a reference to paragraph (2) with 
a reference to paragraph (1)(ii). The final rule also includes 
additional clarifying language stating that a person must have in place 
policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with paragraph 
(ii) (whereas the proposal referred to policies and procedures without 
explicit language clarifying that the person must have such policies 
and procedures in place). The definition appropriately encompasses the 
institutions that may hold reserve assets under section 10 of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909).
    Excessive. The OCC received a few comments recommending the OCC 
define ``excessive'' both for purposes of affiliate transactions and 
for purposes of relevant capital requirements. The OCC is not adding a 
definition of ``excessive'' because the final rule does not use the 
term. The OCC has revised the provisions of the rule that used the word 
``excessive'' in the proposal to provide additional clarity.
    Executive officer. The OCC proposed a definition for the term 
``executive officer,'' which is used in connection with the proposed 
application process in Sec.  15.30. Under the proposal, the term 
``executive officer'' would have been defined to mean the president, 
chairman, chief executive officer, chief operating officer, chief 
financial officer, chief investment officer, chief risk officer, chief 
technology officer, and Bank Secrecy Act officer. The term would have 
included any individual serving in the functional capacity of the 
listed titles or their equivalent, without regard to title, salary, or 
compensation. The OCC based the proposed ``executive officer'' 
definition on the definition of ``Senior executive officer'' in 12 CFR 
5.51(c)(4) with certain modifications to conform the language and 
format to apply to the relevant individuals and entities under this 
part and to streamline the definition to the positions most likely to 
be relevant for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC received 
no comments addressing the definition of ``executive officer.'' The OCC 
is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Fair value. The OCC proposed to include a definition of the term 
``fair value'' in the rule. As proposed, the term ``fair value'' would 
mean the fair value as determined under GAAP.\28\ Fair value is used in 
the definition of ``reserve asset value,'' which pertains to the 
reserve asset requirements in Sec.  15.11. The OCC received no comments 
addressing the definition of ``fair value.'' The OCC is adopting the 
definition as proposed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \28\ See discussion of the definition of ``GAAP,'' infra.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    FDIC. The OCC proposed to define FDIC to mean the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Corporation. This accords with the definition of 
``Corporation'' in section 2(5) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(5)). 
The OCC opted not to use the term ``Corporation'' to describe the FDIC 
because that term is used more broadly in the definition of person,
