discussed below. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition 
of ``FDIC.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Federal branch. The OCC proposed to define the term ``Federal 
branch'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(10). 
Specifically, the proposed rule provided that the term ``Federal 
branch'' would have the meaning set forth in section 3 of the Federal 
Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(s)(2)). The OCC received no 
comments addressing the definition of ``Federal branch.'' The OCC is 
adopting the definition as proposed.
    Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC proposed to 
define the term ``Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer'' 
consistent with the definition of that term in the GENIUS Act, 12 
U.S.C. 5901(11), with certain technical and conforming changes. 
Specifically, the proposed rule defined the term ``Federal qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer'' to mean the following entities that are 
approved by the OCC, pursuant to proposed Sec.  15.30, to issue payment 
stablecoins: (1) a nonbank entity, other than a State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer; (2) an uninsured national bank that is chartered by 
the OCC, pursuant to title LXII of the Revised Statutes; or (3) a

[[Page 67010]]

Federal branch.\29\ The proposed definition modified the definition 
provided in the GENIUS Act by reformatting it to reduce repetition and 
replacing the statutory term ``Comptroller'' with the proposed defined 
term ``OCC.'' In addition, the proposed definition replaced cross 
references to section 5 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904) with a cross 
reference to the proposed implementing provisions in proposed Sec.  
15.30. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of 
``Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer.'' The OCC is adopting 
the definition as proposed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \29\ Certain Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers may be 
subsidiaries of national banks. For example, an uninsured national 
trust bank may be a subsidiary of a national bank. An insured 
national bank or Federal savings association seeking to issue a 
payment stablecoin would, however, need to do so through a 
subsidiary, as required under the GENIUS Act. See 12 U.S.C. 5901(23) 
(defining ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Federal Reserve. The proposed rule defined the term ``Federal 
Reserve'' to mean the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. 
This accords with the definition of ``Board'' in section 2(3) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(3)). The OCC proposed to use the term 
``Federal Reserve'' in place of ``Board'' for greater clarity because 
the proposed rule refers separately to boards of directors in various 
sections. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of 
``Federal Reserve.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Foreign payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC proposed to define the 
term ``foreign payment stablecoin issuer'' consistent with the 
definition of that term in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(12), with 
certain clarifying changes. Under the proposed rule, the term ``foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer'' would have meant an issuer of a payment 
stablecoin that is (1) organized under the laws of or domiciled in a 
foreign country or a territory of the United States; and (2) not a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer as defined in 12 U.S.C. 5901(23). 
The proposed definition of foreign payment stablecoin issuer referred 
to the statutory definition of ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' 
because the proposed rule generally limits the definition of that term 
to entities subject to the OCC's jurisdiction.
    Although included in the statutory definition, the proposed 
definition did not include the phrase ``Puerto Rico, Guam, American 
Samoa, or the Virgin Islands.'' The OCC determined that the omitted 
phrase was redundant and may lead to confusion. Under the proposed 
definition, a foreign payment stablecoin issuer may be organized under 
the laws of, or domiciled in, any territory of the United States. The 
United States currently has five permanently inhabited territories: the 
four listed above and the Northern Mariana Islands. The OCC received no 
comments addressing the definition of ``foreign payment stablecoin 
issuer.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed with a 
technical modification to add commas.
    Freeze and seize. The OCC received one comment stating that the OCC 
should separately define ``freeze'' and ``seize.'' The final rule does 
not use these terms. Therefore, the OCC has elected not to define them. 
To the extent they are used in the forthcoming rule considering BSA/AML 
and sanctions, the OCC may consider defining these terms.
    GAAP. The OCC proposed to include a definition of the term GAAP in 
the rule. The proposed rule defined the term ``GAAP'' to mean generally 
accepted accounting principles as used in the United States. GAAP is 
used in the definition of fair value and proposed subparts B and E. The 
OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``GAAP.'' The OCC 
is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Immediate family. The OCC proposed to define the term ``immediate 
family'' to mean the spouse of an individual, the individual's minor 
children, and any of the individual's children (including adults) 
residing in the individual's home. This term is relevant to the risk 
management standards concerning insider and affiliate transactions and 
is consistent with the definition in Regulation O (12 CFR part 215). 
The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``immediate 
family.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Insider. The OCC proposed to define the term ``insider'' to mean a 
principal shareholder, an executive officer, a director, or a related 
interest of, or the immediate family member of, any of these persons. 
This term is relevant to the risk management standards concerning 
insider and affiliate transactions and is adapted from the definition 
in Regulation O (12 CFR part 215). The term was adapted to make direct 
reference to the immediate family of a principal shareholder, executive 
officer, or director to mitigate the risk of an insider engaging in 
inappropriate transactions to benefit immediate family members. The OCC 
received no comments addressing the definition of ``insider.'' The OCC 
is adopting the definition as proposed with a technical modification to 
add commas.
    Insured credit union. The OCC proposed to define the term ``insured 
credit union'' consistent with the definition of the term in the GENIUS 
Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(14). As proposed, the term ``insured credit union'' 
would have the meaning given to that term in section 101 of the Federal 
Credit Union Act (12 U.S.C. 1752). The OCC received no comments 
addressing the definition of ``insured credit union.'' The OCC is 
adopting the definition as proposed.
    Insured depository institution. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``insured depository institution'' consistent with the definition of 
the term in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(15). As proposed, the term 
``insured depository institution'' would have been defined to mean an 
insured depository institution, as defined in section 3 of the Federal 
Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(c)(2)) and an insured credit 
union.
    The OCC received a number of comments addressing the definition of 
``insured depository institution.'' Some commenters stated that the OCC 
should define ``insured depository institution'' by reference to 
section 3(c)(3) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act rather than the 
generally applicable definition in section 3(c)(2) of the same Act. 
Commenters stated that excluding uninsured branches from the definition 
distorts markets and contradicts the GENIUS Act's intent to decouple 
payment stablecoins from deposit insurance and to promote competitive 
equity among United States banks and foreign banks and would be 
inconsistent with generally applicable principles of national 
treatment. Commenters also stated that using the broader definition in 
section 3(c)(3) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act would be 
consistent with longstanding principles concerning national treatment. 
Commenters stated that the term ``insured depository institution'' 
should not depend on actual FDIC insurance coverage (per section 
3(c)(2) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act) but rather on 
comprehensive regulation and enforcement (per section 3(c)(3) of the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act). A few commenters stated that 
legislative history supports treating foreign banking organizations the 
same as United States banks and indicates that reserve demand deposits 
need not be insured so long as they are held at regulated institutions. 
Some commenters pointed to prior Federal Reserve interpretations under 
section 716 of the Dodd-Frank Act as support for reading ambiguous 
statutory

[[Page 67011]]

language to include branches and agencies of foreign banks. One 
commenter also stated that, while reserve balances generally should be 
held onshore to support onshore redemption, issuers should be able to 
hold a portion of reserves offshore to facilitate minting and burning 
for non-U.S. holders outside United States banking hours. Another 
commenter argued that using the broader definition would be consistent 
with the goals of the statute and would not create undue risk given the 
applicable prudential regulations.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. Under section 
3(c)(2) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, ``insured depository 
institution'' means any bank or savings association the deposits of 
which are insured by the FDIC. This is the definition that generally 
applies under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. Section 3(c)(3) 
provides that the term ``insured depository institution'' also includes 
any uninsured branch or agency of a foreign bank or a commercial 
lending company owned or controlled by a foreign bank for purposes of 
12 U.S.C. 1818. As this provision is clearly limited to section 8 of 
the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, it would not be a permissible 
interpretation of the Act to extend the provision beyond section 8 of 
the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. Therefore, uninsured branches and 
agencies of foreign banks or commercial lending companies owned or 
controlled by foreign banks are not insured depository institutions 
under the Act based on a plain reading of the Act. Because the statute 
is clear that uninsured branches and agencies of foreign banks are not 
insured depository institutions, the OCC is not amending the 
definition.
    Monetary value. The OCC proposed to define the term ``monetary 
value'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(17). The proposal 
defined ``monetary value'' to mean a national currency or deposit 
(which, as discussed above, would have the same meaning as in section 3 
of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(l)) denominated in 
a national currency. The OCC received no comments addressing the 
definition of ``monetary value.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as 
proposed.
    Money. Section 2(18) of the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(18), defines 
``money'' to mean a medium of exchange currently authorized or adopted 
by a domestic or foreign government, including a monetary unit of 
account established by an intergovernmental organization or by 
agreement between two or more countries. This definition is relevant to 
the definition of national currency (discussed below) and certain 
reserve assets described in section 4(a)(1)(A)(i) and (iv) of the Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(i) and (iv)). Section 4(a)(1)(A)(i) refers to 
money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank. 
Section 4(a)(1)(A)(iv) refers to money received under a repurchase 
agreement that meets certain requirements. Although the statutory 
definition of money clearly includes monetary value, it may be unclear 
at any point in time whether other mediums of exchange have been 
authorized or adopted by a domestic or foreign government. Moreover, 
whether a medium of exchange meets this definition may change based on 
actions of foreign governments or intergovernmental organizations. 
While it may be relatively clear whether an asset is money standing to 
the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, there could be 
ambiguity as to whether a particular asset is money received under a 
repurchase agreement. Therefore, to promote clarity and uniformity for 
purposes of determining whether certain assets would qualify as money, 
the OCC proposed that it would provide prior confirmation publicly that 
a medium of exchange (other than those defined as monetary value) meets 
the definition of ``money'' under the GENIUS Act. Specifically, the OCC 
proposed to define ``money'' for the purposes of part 15 to mean 
monetary value and any other medium of exchange that the OCC has 
determined is currently authorized or adopted by a domestic or foreign 
government, including a monetary unit of account established by an 
intergovernmental organization or by agreement between two or more 
countries.
    The OCC received a few comments addressing the definition of 
``money.'' Commenters generally supported the proposed definition but 
suggested that the OCC incorporate certain additions. One commenter 
suggested that the OCC confirm that ``money'' does not include 
particular crypto-assets. Another commenter suggested that the OCC 
should not rely solely on the statutory language and should clarify 
that determinations issued are binding on all primary Federal payment 
stablecoin regulators to prevent interagency inconsistency. Another 
commenter suggested that the OCC should explicitly state that any OCC 
determination must remain grounded in whether the instrument functions 
as a government-authorized medium of exchange, consistent with the 
GENIUS Act's structure and purpose.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The OCC believes 
that this definition will provide sufficient clarity as to what 
constitutes money and will allow the OCC to assess the facts presented 
by any particular medium of exchange. The OCC declines to confirm in 
regulation text whether any particular asset that is not monetary value 
is money because such regulation text may become dated quickly as 
governments may authorize or deauthorize such assets. To promote 
clarity and consistency, the OCC intends to publish any determinations 
it makes as to whether an asset constitutes ``money'' for purposes of 
part 15.
    National currency. The OCC proposed to define the term ``national 
currency'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(19). Under the 
proposed rule, the term ``national currency'' would have meant (1) a 
Federal Reserve note (as the term is used in the first undesignated 
paragraph of section 16 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 411)); 
(2) money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve 
Bank; (3) money issued by a foreign central bank; or (4) money issued 
by an intergovernmental organization pursuant to an agreement by two or 
more governments. The OCC received no comments addressing the 
definition of ``national currency.'' The OCC is adopting the definition 
as proposed.
    Nonbank entity. The OCC proposed to define the term ``nonbank 
entity'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(20). 
Specifically, under the proposed rule, the term ``nonbank entity'' 
would have meant a person that is not a depository institution or 
subsidiary of a depository institution. Consistent with the statutory 
definition, a nonbank entity could include a non-subsidiary affiliate 
of a depository institution.
    One commenter requested that the OCC confirm that the definition of 
nonbank entity can include certain FinCEN-registered money services 
businesses. The OCC confirms that any person that is not a depository 
institution or a subsidiary of a depository institution is a nonbank 
entity. Thus, money services businesses that are not depository 
institutions (or subsidiaries of depository institutions) are nonbank 
entities and may apply to become Federal qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers. In addition, as described above, under the final rule, an 
uninsured credit union would constitute a nonbank entity due to 
revisions to the definition of depository

[[Page 67012]]

institution. The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Nonpublic personal information. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``nonpublic personal information'' to mean information (1) provided by 
a customer to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to obtain a 
financial product or service, (2) about a customer resulting from any 
transaction involving a financial product or service between the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer and a customer, or (3) otherwise 
obtained by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in connection with 
providing a financial product or service to a customer. The proposed 
definition did not include publicly available information, unless such 
publicly available information, when combined with other information, 
would reveal the identity of a customer or would enable access to the 
customer's account.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
nonpublic personal information. Commenters generally argued that the 
proposed definition is overbroad and should better distinguish between 
nonpublic customer information and information associated with public 
blockchain activity or institutional transactions. Some commenters 
suggested that the OCC should limit the definition to information that 
is not publicly available and that an issuer receives in confidence 
through a direct customer relationship. Several commenters suggested 
that the OCC clarify that information recorded on a public blockchain 
is not nonpublic personal information for purposes of the rule. One 
commenter suggested that Travel Rule data transmitted as part of 
interbank settlement merits special treatment and should be dealt with 
under BSA/AML confidentiality frameworks rather than consumer privacy 
frameworks.
    The OCC is adopting the proposed definition, with certain 
modifications to the proposed exclusion for publicly available 
information. Under the final rule, nonpublic personal information does 
not include publicly available information, including information 
broadly accessible through a distributed ledger. The final rule 
eliminates language concerning the use of publicly available 
information that, when combined with other information, would reveal 
the identity of a customer or would enable access to the customer's 
account. The OCC determined that this language was unnecessary because 
the reference to ``other information'' concerned nonpublic information. 
Under the final rule, for example, public wallet addresses would not be 
considered nonpublic information, but certain additional private 
information that could tie a customer's identity to the address would 
be considered nonpublic information. Nonpublic information would also 
generally include sensitive customer information, described in greater 
detail below. The OCC believes that the revisions to the definitions of 
nonpublic personal information and customer combined with revisions to 
the final rule's risk management requirements will provide greater 
clarity for permitted payment stablecoin issuers while ensuring that 
customer information is appropriately protected. With respect to the 
comment concerning Travel Rule data, the comment is outside the scope 
of this final rule. The OCC is clarifying that the provisions of 12 CFR 
part 15 relating to nonpublic personal information do not alter any 
obligations under BSA/AML frameworks.
    OCC. The OCC proposed to substitute the term ``OCC'' for the term 
``Comptroller'' as defined in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(4). 
Specifically, the proposed rule defined the term ``OCC'' to mean the 
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The proposed definition 
would refer to the organization as opposed to the individual who 
occupies the office. Using the term OCC is consistent with the agency's 
terminology in other regulations for which it has rulemaking authority. 
The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``OCC.'' The 
OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Outstanding issuance value. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``outstanding issuance value'' to mean the total consolidated par value 
of all of a payment stablecoin issuer's payment stablecoins. This would 
have included the combined total par value of different brands of 
payment stablecoin issued by the payment stablecoin issuer (e.g., under 
a white-label arrangement) to the extent that such an arrangement 
complies with proposed 12 CFR part 15. The OCC sought comment on the 
proposed definition, including whether it should include the par value 
of the issuance of non-consolidated affiliates. The OCC received 
several comments addressing the definition of ``outstanding issuance 
value.'' Commenters generally suggested that the OCC adopt a definition 
that is clear, operationally workable, and aligned with reserve backing 
and accurate measurement of circulating supply. Commenters urged the 
OCC to clarify the scope of ``outstanding issuance value.'' Commenters 
also asked the OCC to clarify the treatment of repurchased but not yet 
permanently retired tokens, temporary discrepancies caused by technical 
or legal compliance processes, and the application of the definition in 
multi-issuer or branded stablecoin arrangements.
    The OCC is adopting the definition with certain clarifications. 
Under the final rule, ``outstanding issuance value'' means the total 
par value of all the payment stablecoins issued by a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer. The final rule's definition is consistent with the 
statute's focus on the issuer, rather than the issuer's affiliates. 
Absent conduct suggesting an attempt to evade the GENIUS Act or an 
arrangement that suggests that reserve assets may be inadequate or 
misallocated relative to outstanding issuance value, the OCC does not 
believe that it is generally necessary to include payment stablecoins 
issued by affiliates that are not consolidated into a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer in the outstanding issuance value of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer.\30\ Not including non-consolidated 
affiliates will also help ensure that business models that rely on 
multiple SPV issuers are not penalized relative to other business 
models. Such SPV issuers would only need to hold reserve assets against 
the payment stablecoins that they issue, rather than also needing to 
hold reserves against an affiliate's payment stablecoins. In response 
to commenters, the OCC reiterates that, to be included within 
outstanding issuance value, an instrument must be a payment stablecoin, 
which means that the issuer must have incurred the obligation to 
convert, redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin. Thus, for 
purposes of calculating the outstanding issuance value, a digital asset 
that is, or is designed to be, used as a means of payment or settlement 
but for which there is not yet an obligation to convert, redeem, or 
repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value would not be included 
in the calculation. A digital asset minted (i.e., created on a 
blockchain) by an issuer to be a payment stablecoin would not be 
included in the calculation of outstanding issuance value until the

[[Page 67013]]

obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase the digital asset for a 
fixed amount of monetary value is incurred. For example, an issuer may 
mint a digital asset that it keeps in treasury, but it would not be 
considered a payment stablecoin or included in the calculation of the 
issuer's outstanding issuance value until the digital asset was 
transferred to a third party or the issuer was otherwise obligated to 
convert, redeem, or repurchase the digital asset. Similarly, once an 
issuer permanently removes a payment stablecoin from circulation (e.g., 
burns the payment stablecoin), the digital asset would cease to be 
included in the calculation of outstanding issuance value.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \30\ The OCC notes, however, that in certain situations, the OCC 
may consider a non-consolidated affiliate's issuance. For example, 
if a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer treats affiliate-
issued stablecoins as fungible with its own and appears to use 
affiliates to stay under the $10 billion threshold for transition to 
the Federal framework, such behavior could indicate an attempt to 
evade the GENIUS Act or could, depending on the facts and 
circumstances, indicate unusual and exigent circumstances within the 
meaning of section 7 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Payment stablecoins for which holder access has been restricted 
pursuant to applicable law, regulation, or court order would remain 
payment stablecoins, as the issuer's obligation to convert, redeem, or 
repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value continues and the 
associated reserves are maintained in segregated accounts pending 
resolution of the restriction. Likewise, if an issuer repurchased a 
payment stablecoin but did not burn the payment stablecoin, the 
stablecoin in the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's inventory would 
not be part of the issuer's outstanding issuance value because the 
issuer has no obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase the 
stablecoin when it is in the issuer's inventory (but would become part 
of the outstanding issuance value if the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer subsequently put the payment stablecoin back into circulation). 
Therefore, the definition of ``outstanding issuance value'' only 
includes payment stablecoins for which the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed 
amount of monetary value (i.e., generally the issued payment 
stablecoins in circulation). The final rule also excludes the word 
``consolidated'' from the definition of outstanding issuance value. 
This is to better facilitate the use of SPV issuers under part 15. This 
revision makes clear that each SPV issuer only needs to have reserve 
assets backing the payment stablecoins that it issues. The OCC is 
adding the word ``consolidated'' to certain other provisions of part 15 
(relating to certain non-financial companies and nonbank State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers) in light of this change and to 
maintain consistency with the requirements of the GENIUS Act.
    Payment stablecoin. The OCC proposed to define the term ``payment 
stablecoin'' consistent with the definition of the term in the GENIUS 
Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(22), with certain technical changes. Under the 
proposal, the term ``payment stablecoin'' would have meant a digital 
asset (i) that is, or is designed to be, used as a means of payment or 
settlement; and (ii) the issuer of which (A) is obligated to convert, 
redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value, not 
including a digital asset denominated in a fixed amount of monetary 
value; and (B) represents that such issuer will maintain, or creates 
the reasonable expectation that it will maintain, a stable value 
relative to the value of a fixed amount of monetary value.\31\ For a 
digital asset to be a payment stablecoin under proposed part 15, the 
issuer must be obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase the digital 
asset for a fixed amount of monetary value.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \31\ The OCC interprets the statutory language in 12 U.S.C. 
5901(22) to mean that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would 
be obligated to meet redemption requests at par.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The proposed definition also provided that a ``payment stablecoin'' 
does not include a digital asset that is a (i) national currency; (ii) 
deposit (as defined in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act 
(12 U.S.C. 1813)), including a deposit recorded using distributed 
ledger technology; or (iii) security, as defined in section 2 of the 
Securities Act of 1933 (15 U.S.C. 77b), section 3 of the Securities 
Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78c), or section 2 of the Investment 
Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-2). The GENIUS Act's definition of 
``payment stablecoin'' also contains language clarifying that ``no 
bond, note, evidence of indebtedness, or investment contract that was 
issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall qualify as a 
security solely [because the issuer satisfies] the conditions in 
[paragraph (1) of the proposed ``payment stablecoin'' definition], 
consistent with section 17 of the Act.'' The GENIUS Act provides that 
this language was included ``for the avoidance of doubt.'' The OCC 
determined that it was not necessary to include this language in the 
proposed ``payment stablecoin'' definition because section 17 of the 
GENIUS Act includes amendments to the cited Federal statutes that 
clarify that payment stablecoins are not securities.
    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``payment stablecoin.'' Commenters generally sought a definition that 
more clearly distinguished payment stablecoins covered by the Act from 
other digital instruments. Commenters suggested that the OCC clarify 
the scope of the definition so that it captures instruments primarily 
designed and used for payment or settlement and excludes products that 
function instead as securities, investment instruments, tokenized 
deposits, closed-loop or community tokens, algorithmic tokens, or other 
nonpayment digital assets. Other commenters asked the OCC to clarify 
certain definitional boundaries (e.g., payment or settlement use, 
redemption obligations, reserve backing, and instruments structured 
under United States or foreign securities laws). One commenter stated 
that the definition should include products designed to circumvent the 
GENIUS Act. Some commenters stated that the term was appropriately 
defined.
    Commenters requested clarity regarding potential disclosures 
relating to the definition of payment stablecoin, with one commenter 
stating that the OCC should treat the core properties of a payment 
stablecoin--that it represents stable value and that it creates a 
reasonable appearance or expectation of redemption at or near par--
disjunctively in order to assess violations of marketing restrictions. 
The commenter further stated that, by treating either condition as 
sufficient, the OCC would prevent regulatory arbitrage, ensure 
consistent application of core protections, and maintain competitive 
neutrality. A different commenter stated that unregistered foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers of dollar-denominated crypto-assets 
purporting to hold a stable dollar-referenced value cannot use the term 
``payment stablecoin'' to describe such instruments. Section 4(e)(3) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(e)(3)) prohibits the marketing of 
products as payment stablecoins when they are not issued pursuant to 
the GENIUS Act. The Department of the Treasury has enforcement 
authority with respect to that provision of the Act, so the OCC is not 
addressing that marketing prohibition in this final rule.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The proposed 
definition aligns with the statutory definition and thus appropriately 
captures the scope of instruments that are payment stablecoins under 
the GENIUS Act. As in the proposed definition, the OCC does not believe 
that it is necessary to separately specify that ``no bond, note, 
evidence of indebtedness, or investment contract that was issued by a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall qualify as a security solely 
[because the issuer satisfies] the conditions in [paragraph (1) of the 
``payment stablecoin'' definition], consistent with section 17 of the 
Act'' because the GENIUS Act

[[Page 67014]]

amended the pertinent securities laws to specify that a payment 
stablecoin is not a security. Thus, including this language from 
section 2(22)(B)(iii) would be redundant. The OCC believes that other 
changes to the definition may risk deviating from the scope of 
instruments intended to be captured by the GENIUS Act's definitions. In 
response to specific comments, the OCC notes that instruments for which 
an issuer is not obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a 
fixed amount of monetary value are outside the scope of the definition 
of ``payment stablecoin'' for purposes of part 15. Redefining ``payment 
stablecoin'' based on the characteristics noted by certain commenters 
would be inconsistent with the statutory definition. Because the 
definition of monetary value does not include payment stablecoins, a 
stablecoin that is redeemable for a payment stablecoin is not itself a 
payment stablecoin. Thus, for purposes of the OCC's implementation of 
the Act, a ``wrapped'' stablecoin generally would not be a payment 
stablecoin. The OCC does not believe that it is necessary to define 
payment or settlement. The statute merely requires that a payment 
stablecoin be, or be designed to be, used as a means of payment or 
settlement. It does not require that the primary purpose of the payment 
stablecoin be payment or settlement. In light of this fact, and the 
broad scope of what is generally included within payment or settlement, 
the OCC expects that most stablecoins could meet this prong of the 
definition of payment stablecoin. Accordingly, the OCC does not believe 
that it is necessary to further define ``payment'' or ``settlement'' 
for purposes of the definition of payment stablecoin. The OCC also 
believes that the definition appropriately and clearly excludes 
deposits, including deposits in tokenized form, and that additional 
revisions are not necessary to distinguish payment stablecoins from 
deposits.
    Payment stablecoin holder. The proposed rule did not define the 
term ``payment stablecoin holder'' but used the term in several 
sections and requested comment on whether to define ``stablecoin 
holder.'' The OCC received several comments concerning the definition 
of customer and payment stablecoin holder. Several comments recommended 
distinguishing the two terms, with ``customer'' referring to persons 
that interact directly with an issuer and ``payment stablecoin holder'' 
referring to beneficial owners of payment stablecoins (or, in some 
cases, beneficial and legal owners of payment stablecoins). One comment 
stated that the OCC should not define the term ``stablecoin holder.'' 
This commenter asserted that the GENIUS Act does not use the term (but 
rather uses the term ``holder of any payment stablecoin'') and stated 
that defining a new term would exceed the authority delegated to the 
OCC. This commenter also stated that the GENIUS Act concerns payment 
stablecoins only, so the term would be overbroad. Others stated that 
the OCC should define the term to include both legal and beneficial 
owners of payment stablecoins. These commenters stated that 
interpreting the term was within the OCC's interpretive authority.
    In response to these comments, the OCC is defining the term 
``payment stablecoin holder'' rather than ``stablecoin holder.'' This 
will clarify that the scope is limited to holders of payment 
stablecoins that are issued or held in custody by entities engaged in 
activities that are subject to the GENIUS Act. The final rule defines 
payment stablecoin holder to mean the beneficial owner of a payment 
stablecoin. The OCC is defining this term solely for purposes of the 
OCC's implementing regulations and doing so does not exceed the OCC's 
authority. The definition in the final rule does not affect, for 
example, the insolvency provisions in section 11 of the GENIUS Act. The 
definition will appropriately distinguish persons that merely control a 
payment stablecoin on another's behalf (e.g., custodians) from persons 
that would benefit economically from a payment of interest or yield on 
a payment stablecoin. This definition, combined with the change to the 
definition of customer, will help ensure that part 15 is not unduly 
burdensome and that the requirements with respect to payment stablecoin 
holders and customers are appropriately scoped. The OCC notes that the 
GENIUS Act uses the term ``payment stablecoin holder'' six times in 
other contexts in addition to the substantially similar phrase ``holder 
of any payment stablecoin'' in the context of the yield prohibition. 
The statute is unclear as to whether the term refers to any person that 
controls a payment stablecoin or rather the beneficial owner of a 
payment stablecoin. Clarifying this point is important to implementing 
the statutory prohibition against paying interest or yield solely in 
connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin 
in section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)).
    Permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC proposed to define the 
term ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' consistent with the 
definition of the term in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(23), with 
certain modifications. Specifically, the proposed definition would have 
limited the definition to the entities that are subject to the OCC's 
jurisdiction, including State qualified payment stablecoin issuers 
subject to the OCC's regulatory authority under section 4 of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903).\32\ In addition, the proposed definition cross-
referenced the relevant proposed implementing provision in place of the 
statutory provision included in the GENIUS Act's definition. Under the 
proposed rule, the term ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' would 
have meant a person formed in the United States that is a (1) 
subsidiary of an insured national bank or Federal savings association 
that has been approved to issue payment stablecoins under Sec.  15.30; 
(2) Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer; or (3) State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer subject to the OCC's regulatory or 
enforcement authority under section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903).\33\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\32\ See Scope section-by-section analysis, supra.
    \33\ In addition, the OCC has enforcement authority pursuant to 
section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)) with 
respect to certain nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers in unusual and exigent circumstances. Proposed Sec.  15.16 
would address the requirements applicable to certain State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuers under unusual and exigent circumstances, 
but the OCC is not proposing to include State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers that come within the OCC's jurisdiction solely as 
a result of section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act within the definition 
of permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of 
``permitted payment stablecoin issuer.'' Comments generally supported 
the definition but suggested clarifications to identify the responsible 
issuing entity while avoiding overinclusion of affiliated parties or 
service providers. Commenters also suggested that the OCC clarify which 
entities qualify as issuers (e.g., uninsured Federal branches, 
agencies, and multi-issuer payment stablecoin structures). Other 
commenters asked the OCC to distinguish between entities with primary 
legal and economic responsibility for issuing, redeeming, and backing 
payment stablecoins and service providers or intermediaries that 
perform ancillary technical, distribution, or support functions.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The definition 
closely matches the statutory definition, with minor changes to reflect 
the OCC's jurisdiction. In response to comments, the OCC confirms that, 
consistent with the definition of payment stablecoin in section 2 of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C.

[[Page 67015]]

5901(22)), for the purposes of part 15, the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer is the entity that is obligated to convert, redeem, 
or repurchase a tendered payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of 
monetary value (not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed 
amount of monetary value). A service provider that is not obligated to 
convert, redeem, or repurchase is not a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. Under the statute, a variety of entities may be permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers subject to the OCC's jurisdiction, including 
subsidiaries of insured national banks or Federal savings associations; 
Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers that are approved by the 
OCC, comprising uninsured national banks, Federal branches, or nonbank 
entities; or State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that transition 
to the OCC's regulatory framework. As discussed above, due to changes 
in the definition of ``depository institution,'' an uninsured credit 
union would qualify as a nonbank and could seek to be a Federal 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
    Person. The OCC proposed to define the term ``person'' as the term 
is defined in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(24). As proposed, the term 
``person'' would have meant an individual, partnership, company, 
corporation, association, trust, estate, cooperative organization, or 
other business entity, incorporated or unincorporated.
    The OCC received a few comments addressing the definition of 
``person.'' Commenters generally agreed with the definition but sought 
clearer boundaries around which collective arrangements would be 
treated as associations. Commenters suggested that the OCC clarify that 
the definition applies to legally identifiable entities or organized 
groups capable of exercising governance or control. Other commenters 
also urged the OCC to address how the definition applies in 
decentralized or algorithmically governed structures, while another 
commenter supported keeping the definition broad.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The statutory 
definition of ``person'' in section 2(24) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901(24)) is broad and expressly includes individuals, partnerships, 
and both incorporated and unincorporated business entities. 
Accordingly, the OCC declines to exclude arrangements that are not 
legally identifiable as such arrangements may be included within the 
statutory definition. The OCC also declines to opine as to whether 
decentralized arrangements generally would constitute a person, as the 
determination would depend on the facts and circumstances of the 
arrangement. As with its other regulations, interested parties may 
request that the OCC provide interpretive guidance, as necessary.
    Principal shareholder. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``principal shareholder'' to mean a person who directly or indirectly 
or acting in concert with one or more persons, or together with members 
of their immediate family, will own, control, or hold 10 percent or 
more of the voting stock of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or 
applicant. This definition is substantially similar to the definition 
used in the OCC's general licensing regulations in 12 CFR 5.20(d)(10).
    The OCC received a few comments addressing the definition of 
``principal shareholder.'' Commenters generally agreed with the 
definition but requested additional clarity regarding identifying 
control and significant ownership interests. Commenters suggested that 
the OCC clarify how the definition applies to governance rights and 
influences that may not take the form of traditional securities 
ownership. Other commenters suggested that the OCC clarify the meaning 
of ``acting in concert'' and align the definition with existing banking 
law concepts.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. As discussed above, 
the OCC believes that it is unnecessary to define ``acting in concert'' 
for purposes of 12 CFR part 15 at this time. The OCC also believes that 
it is unnecessary to change the definition of principal shareholder. 
Retaining the proposed definition would maintain parity between the 
treatment of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and national banks 
and Federal savings associations.
    Private key. The OCC proposed to define the term ``private key'' to 
mean the unique alphanumeric string that allows an individual to 
transfer a particular unit of a digital asset using a distributed 
ledger. While the preamble to the proposal noted that this definition 
was intended to include shards of a private key,\34\ several commenters 
noted that the definition in the regulatory text nonetheless implies a 
static single-key architecture and does not easily fit with a 
distributed-key architecture, wherein cryptographic key shares are 
distributed across independent parties or hardware environments such 
that the full key material is not held in any one place and exists only 
as a mathematical construct realized at the moment of signing. The OCC 
has decided to modify the definition to more expressly address 
sharding. Under the final rule, private key means the cryptographic 
material, whether held in whole, in shares, or reconstructed 
ephemerally, that confers the ability to authorize a transaction on a 
distributed ledger.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \34\ Sharding refers to dividing a private key into distinct 
pieces for enhanced security.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Publicly available information. The OCC proposed to define the term 
``publicly available information'' to mean any information that a 
person has a reasonable basis to believe is lawfully made available to 
the general public from: (1) Federal, State, or local government 
records; (2) widely distributed media; (3) disclosures to the general 
public that are required to be made by Federal, State, or local law; or 
(4) a distributed ledger.\35\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ As noted above, the term ``distributed ledger'' is limited 
to publicly available and accessible ledgers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received a few comments addressing the definition of 
``publicly available information.'' Commenters generally suggested that 
the OCC provide clearer treatment of blockchain-based information 
within the privacy framework. Some commenters suggested that the 
definition should apply to distributed ledger or on-chain transaction 
data. Other commenters suggested that privacy protections should not be 
eliminated where issuers can control disclosure or where transaction 
data can be linked to identifiable individuals. Other commenters 
suggested that certain transaction-level data should be treated as 
protected financial records rather than excluded from coverage 
altogether.
    The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. The OCC believes 
that this approach, combined with revisions to Sec.  15.13 and to the 
definitions of customer and nonpublic personal information, 
appropriately provides a robust data protection requirement with 
respect to customers of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. As 
discussed in greater detail above, in response to commenters, the 
revisions to the definition of nonpublic personal information discussed 
above further emphasize that information broadly available through a 
distributed ledger would generally be outside the scope of nonpublic 
personal information.
    Registered public accounting firm. The OCC proposed to define the 
term ``registered public accounting firm'' as provided in the GENIUS 
Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(26). Under the proposal, the term ``registered 
public accounting firm'' would have meant a registered public 
accounting firm set forth in section 2 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 
2002 (15 U.S.C. 7201). The OCC received no

[[Page 67016]]

comments addressing the definition of ``registered public accounting 
firm.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
    Related interest. The OCC proposed to define the term ``related 
interest'' of a person to mean (1) a company that is controlled by that 
person; or (2) a political or campaign committee that is controlled by 
that person or the funds or services of which will benefit that person. 
This term is relevant to the risk management standards for insider and 
affiliate transactions and is derived from the definition in Regulation 
O (12 CFR part 215). The OCC received no comments addressing the 
definition of ``related interest.'' The OCC is adopting the definition 
as proposed.
    Reserve asset. The OCC proposed to define the term ``reserve 
asset'' to mean an asset maintained by a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer of a type enumerated in Sec.  15.11(b).\36\ The OCC received no 
comments addressing the definition of ``reserve asset.'' The OCC is 
adopting the definition as proposed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \36\ A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may maintain reserve 
assets at a custodian.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Reserve asset value. The final rule defines reserve asset value to 
mean the sum of: (1) the total fair value of reserve assets, net of any 
associated liabilities, other than United States coins and currency; 
and (2) the total face value of reserve assets comprising United States 
coins and currency. The proposed rule did not include this term. 
Rather, it required all reserve assets to be valued at fair value for 
the purpose of ensuring that the total outstanding issuance value is 
backed on at least a 1 to 1 basis by reserve assets. The OCC is 
adopting this new term because, in the case of United States coins and 
currency, it is more appropriate to value these items based on face 
value. This confirms, for instance, that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may not back a payment stablecoin based on the metallic or 
collector value associated with a particular coin (which may be 
volatile). The OCC acknowledges that the use of coins or currency to 
back a payment stablecoin is likely to be rare. Thus, in most 
instances, reserve asset value will be determined purely by the fair 
value of reserve assets. The final rule also clarifies that reserve 
asset value is calculated net of associated liabilities. Notably, this 
makes clear that assets that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
obligated to repurchase under a repurchase agreement may not be 
essentially double counted when determining the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's reserve asset value. If, for example, an issuer 
holds a Treasury security as a reserve asset and pledges the security 
pursuant to a repurchase agreement, the issuer would include the cash 
received under the repurchase agreement in its reserve asset value but 
must also subtract its obligation to repurchase the Treasury security.
    Senior management. Proposed Sec. Sec.  15.14(i) and 15.42(a)(5) 
referred to the senior management of a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. The proposal did not define the term but sought comment on 
whether to do so. The OCC received a few comments stating that the term 
should align with ``executive officers'' or a subset thereof. One 
commenter said that a formal definition was not necessary, but the term 
should be read to include the individuals responsible for day-to-day 
management, rather than looking to titles alone. Section 15.42 refers 
to senior management only in a list of examples of factors the OCC may 
consider. Accordingly, the OCC does not believe that a definition is 
necessary for senior management in Sec.  15.42. With respect to Sec.  
15.14, as discussed in greater detail below, the OCC is providing 
additional specificity as to which executive officers must attest to 
each quarterly report. The final rule, like the proposal, does not 
define ``senior management.''
    Sensitive customer information. One commenter requested that the 
OCC either define ``sensitive customer information'' or else replace 
the term with customer nonpublic information. To provide greater 
clarity, under the final rule, ``sensitive customer information'' means 
any combination of components of customer information that would reveal 
the identity of the customer or allow someone access to the customer's 
account, including a customer's public key in conjunction with the 
customer's private key.
    Share account. The final rule includes the new term ``share 
account.'' Under the final rule, this term means an ``account'' as 
defined in section 101 of the Federal Credit Union Act (12 U.S.C. 
1752(5)). The term is relevant to the reserve asset provisions in Sec.  
15.11 and the operational backstop provisions in Sec.  15.41.
    Stablecoin Certification Review Committee. The OCC proposed to 
define the term ``Stablecoin Certification Review Committee'' 
consistent with the definition in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(27) by 
incorporating the statutory definition. The proposed rule defined the 
term ``Stablecoin Certification Review Committee'' as having the 
meaning set forth in section 2 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(27)). 
The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``Stablecoin 
Certification Review Committee.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as 
proposed.
    State. The OCC proposed to define the term ``State'' as provided in 
the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(28). The proposed rule defined the term 
``State'' to mean each of the several States of the United States, the 
District of Columbia, and each territory of the United States.\37\ The 
OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``State.'' The 
OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\37\ United States territories are also referenced in the proposed definition of ``foreign payment stablecoin issuers.'' The GENIUS Act and the proposed and final rules address the potential overlap created by the inclusion of territories in both definitions by defining ``foreign payment stablecoin issuers'' to exclude ``permitted payment stablecoin issuers.'' Therefore, if a payment stablecoin issuer is a ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' because it is a ``State qualified payment stablecoin issuer'' that is legally established under the laws of a territory of the United States then by definition it cannot be a ``foreign payment stablecoin issuer.'' --------------------------------------------------------------------------- State-chartered depository institution. The OCC proposed to define the term ``State-chartered depository institution'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(29). Specifically, the proposed rule would have defined the term ``State-chartered depository institution'' as having the meaning as set forth for ``State depository institution'' in section 3(c) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(c)(5)). The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``State-chartered depository institution.'' The final rule, however, does not use the term. The final rule therefore does not adopt the term. State payment stablecoin regulator. The OCC proposed to define the term ``State payment stablecoin regulator'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(30). As such, the OCC proposed to define ``State payment stablecoin regulator'' to mean a State agency that has primary regulatory and supervisory authority in such State over entities that issue payment stablecoins. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``State payment stablecoin regulator.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. State qualified payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC proposed to define the term ``State qualified payment stablecoin issuer'' consistent with the definition of that term in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(31), with a non-substantive, clarifying change. Under the proposed rule, the term ``State qualified payment stablecoin issuer'' would have meant an entity that is (1) legally established under the laws of a [[Page 67017]] State and approved to issue payment stablecoins by a State payment stablecoin regulator; and (2) not an uninsured national bank chartered by the OCC pursuant to title LXII of the Revised Statutes, a Federal branch, an insured depository institution, or a subsidiary of such an uninsured national bank, Federal branch, or insured depository institution. The proposed definition clarified the definition of ``State qualified payment stablecoin issuer'' provided in the GENIUS Act by adding the phrase ``an uninsured'' before the term ``national bank'' in the list of excluded subsidiaries to parallel the description of excluded entities in the preceding list. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.'' The OCC is making one clarifying edit, replacing the term ``entity'' with the term ``person,'' because ``person'' is a defined term in the final rule. Otherwise, the OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. Subsidiary. The OCC proposed to define the term ``subsidiary'' as provided in the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5901(32). Specifically, the proposed rule would have defined the term ``subsidiary'' as having the meaning set forth in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1813(w)(4)). Because the term in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act relies on the definitions of ``company'' and ``control'' in section 2 of the Bank Holding Company Act, the OCC proposed to incorporate those definitions in proposed part 15, tailored to the extent necessary, as described above. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of ``subsidiary.'' The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed. Tokenized form. The proposed rule did not define ``tokenized form'' but used the term in Sec. 15.11 and Sec. 15.32. The OCC received several comments requesting that the OCC clarify the meaning of the term ``tokenized form.'' Under section 4(a)(1)(A)(viii) (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(viii)) of the GENIUS Act, certain reserve assets may be in tokenized form, but the Act does not define what constitutes tokenized form. Commenters generally agreed that any definition should ensure that a reserve asset in tokenized form provides the same legal rights as a reserve asset in non-tokenized form. Several commenters urged the OCC to provide clearer and more coordinated standards for tokenized reserve assets, including through coordination with the SEC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, CFTC, FinCEN, and Treasury and, in some cases, a joint policy statement or standardized supervisory assessment framework. Some commenters stated that tokenized forms of otherwise eligible reserve assets should be presumptively permissible and evaluated under a principles-based approach focused on economic substance, legal certainty, enforceable and bankruptcy-remote claims to the underlying assets, custody and segregation protections, and the issuer's ability to promptly monetize the assets to meet redemptions. Several commenters suggested that eligibility should not depend on the technology used to record ownership. Some commenters urged the OCC to provide a transparent approval process or public list of permissible tokenized reserve assets. Other commenters suggested that case-by-case approval should not be required and that assets approved in conventional form should automatically be permitted in tokenized form. The OCC agrees with commenters that it is important to define ``tokenized form'' and to ensure that reserve assets in tokenized form provide the same rights as reserves in non-tokenized form. The final rule defines ``tokenized form'' to mean, with respect to an asset, that: (1) the authoritative record of the asset is maintained using distributed ledger technology, regardless of whether a corresponding non-tokenized instrument or account entry also exists; and (2) the legal rights conferred by the asset are identical to those that would be conferred by a non-tokenized form of the asset under applicable law. This definition is generally consistent with the scope of the term ``tokenized security'' in the Federal Banking Agencies FAQ concerning tokenized securities.\38\ The definition includes a digital asset that represents, and provides identical legal rights as, a traditionally issued asset as well as a digitally native asset that provides the identical legal rights as a non-tokenized version of the same asset. For example, a money market fund that qualified as a permissible reserve asset under section 4(a)(1)(A)(vi) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(vi)) could be held in tokenized form if the fund was issued directly on a distributed ledger. Alternatively, a token representing ownership of a traditionally issued money market fund could also be a reserve in tokenized form, depending on how the tokenization was implemented and which rights would be conferred on the holder. In such instances, the tokens would need to provide identical rights to those associated with owning the asset held in custody. The OCC encourages any permitted payment stablecoin issuer that seeks clarity on whether a specific asset is an asset in tokenized form and whether such asset qualifies as a permissible reserve asset under Sec. 15.11(b) to consult with the OCC as to whether the asset qualifies. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \38\ See OCC Bulletin 2026-7, ``Regulatory Capital: Interagency FAQs on Tokenized Securities'' (March 5, 2026), https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-7.html. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Trading volume. The OCC proposed to define the term ``trading volume'' to mean the aggregate number of payment stablecoins issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that were purchased or sold on exchanges during a specified period of time. In the proposal, the term was to be used as a metric to determine a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's examination schedule. The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of ``trading volume.'' Commenters suggested that the definition be revised to be more analytically useful, operationally feasible, and tailored to the realities of digital asset markets. Commenters suggested that the OCC distinguish trading activity from settlement activity. Other commenters suggested that the OCC clarify the scope of ``exchange,'' particularly how it applies to centralized and decentralized platforms, while limiting reporting expectations to data reasonably available to issuers. The final rule eliminates the term ``trading volume'' because, as described below, the final rule does not use trading volume as a metric to determine a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's examination schedule. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers would be required to provide certain information concerning trading volume as part of the reports required under Sec. 15.14 of the final rule, but the OCC has concluded that the instructions for the reporting form are the more appropriate place to define ``trading volume'' for those purposes. United States customer. The OCC proposed to define the term ``United States customer'' to mean a customer that resides in the United States. The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of ``United States customer.'' Commenters suggested that the OCC adopt a clearer and more administrable standard for identifying United States customers. Commenters generally supported further clarification of the term. Some commenters sought clarification on how United States residence or location should be determined, whether the definition should be tied to direct customer relationships, and how it [[Page 67018]] should apply to institutional customers, foreign intermediaries, and secondary-market activity. Some commenters suggested that the OCC adopt an approach that is more operationally workable and aligned with jurisdictional boundaries. Other commenters cautioned against creating a definition that assumes a level of precision issuers may not be able to achieve. To provide additional clarity, the final rule revises Sec. 15.31(a)(3) (discussed in greater detail below) and redefines ``United States customer'' to mean a customer that, at the time of onboarding: (1) is an individual and resides in the United States,\39\ (2) is incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State; or (3) has its principal place of business in the United States.\40\ Specifying both when and how a person is determined to be a United States customer will enhance the operability of this provision of the final rule and provide clear lines for foreign payment stablecoin issuers and customers. This definition does not affect the definition of ``customer'' for purposes of other laws and regulations, including privacy laws and the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \39\ For the purposes of determining residence in the United States, United States citizens are considered to be residents. For non-United States citizens, residence is determined by the test in 26 CFR 301.7701(b)-1. Pursuant to that test, an individual will be considered to be residing in the United States if he or she is a lawful permanent resident (i.e., has a green card) or meets the substantial presence test. 26 CFR 301.7701(b)-1(b) and (c). \40\ See Hertz Corp. v Friend, 559 U.S. 77 (2010) (describing the test for what constitutes a corporation's principal place of business). ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

4. Severability (Sec.  15.3)
    Proposed Sec.  15.3 provided that the provisions of the proposed 
rule were separate and severable from one another. If any provision is 
stayed or determined to be invalid, it was the OCC's intention that the 
remaining provisions would have continued in effect.
    As noted in the proposal,\41\ the OCC generally intends all of its 
rulemakings to be severable to the extent portions of the rule are 
determined to be invalid regardless of the presence of a severability 
clause. The OCC proposed to include an explicit severability clause 
because of the novelty and scope of the GENIUS Act and the importance 
of ensuring as much certainty as possible for the regulatory framework 
for payment stablecoins.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \41\ 91 FR 10210.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC received no comments addressing Sec.  15.3 and is 
finalizing Sec.  15.3 as proposed.
5. Reservation of Authority (Sec.  15.4)
    The OCC is adding, in the final rule, a general reservation of 
authority provision. Section 15.4 provides that the OCC may waive or 
modify the requirements of part 15 or adopt different procedures 
implementing this part, as necessary, to administer and carry out the 
requirements of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.), including with 
respect to ensuring financial stability, ensuring timely redemption of 
payment stablecoins, and protecting the claims of payment stablecoin 
holders. The OCC is adopting this provision in recognition of the 
nascent nature of the stablecoin industry and the novelty of the GENIUS 
Act framework. The OCC will only exercise this reservation of authority 
where consistent with the GENIUS Act and where circumstances justify 
its use. The OCC generally uses reservations sparingly to address 
unanticipated circumstances for which a rulemaking is not appropriate.

B. Subpart B--Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers and State Qualified 
Payment Stablecoin Issuers

1. Activities (Sec.  15.10)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Sec.  15.10
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10 as proposed with modifications, as 
described below.
    The OCC is modifying the language in paragraph (a) for clarity and 
replacing the word ``only'' with ``not engage in any activity other 
than the following:'' to make clear that the list of activities in 
final Sec.  15.10(a) is an exclusive list of activities that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers may engage in. Within the Sec.  15.10(a) 
list of permitted activities for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, 
the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (7) as proposed.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10(a)(8), renumbered as Sec.  
15.10(a)(11), as proposed except for a clarification that other 
activities include the hiring of third parties.
    The OCC is adding three new activities to the list of permitted 
activities. First, in new Sec.  15.10(a)(8) of the final rule, the 
agency allows permitted payment stablecoin issuers to hold as principal 
non-payment stablecoin digital assets as necessary to pay fees, 
including customer fees and network fees, or to conduct necessary 
testing on distributed ledger-based platforms, provided that such 
principal holdings shall not exceed quantities necessary for the 
reasonably foreseeable conduct of such activities. Second, in Sec.  
15.10(a)(9) of the final rule, the OCC allows permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to establish a trust arrangement under applicable 
law for reserve assets, including the granting of a security interest 
in reserve assets, provided that any security interest in reserve 
assets granted to the trustee is for the sole benefit of payment 
stablecoin holders, the arrangement with the trustee does not impair 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to timely redeem 
payment stablecoins in the normal course of business prior to default, 
the arrangement does not introduce claims that would compete with the 
claims of payment stablecoin holders of payment stablecoins issued by 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in the event of the insolvency 
of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, and the arrangement with 
the trustee does not impair the ability of a receiver of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to direct the prompt transfer or liquidation 
of the reserve assets in order to pay claims to payment stablecoin 
holders. Third, the OCC is adding the management of foreign exchange 
risk, subject to the requirements of Sec.  15.13(a)(10) of the final 
rule, as a permitted activity. Section 15.13(a)(10) of the final rule 
provides the relevant risk management principles for foreign exchange 
risk.
    The OCC is adopting the rule of construction in Sec.  15.10(b) as 
proposed, renumbered as Sec.  15.10(b)(1). Additionally, the OCC is 
adopting an additional provision in final Sec.  15.10(b)(2) that 
provides that nothing in Sec.  15.10(a) limits the authority of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to engage in an activity consistent 
with section 4(a)(7)(B) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(B)). This 
change is made to clarify that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may 
engage in digital asset service provider activities specified by the 
Act, and activities incidental thereto, that are authorized by the OCC 
and independently authorized by applicable Federal or State law, to the 
extent that any such State law is not inconsistent with Federal law.
    Within the list of prohibitions listed in Sec.  15.10(c), the OCC 
is adopting Sec.  15.10(c)(1) through (3), and (c)(6) as proposed. The 
agency is modifying Sec.  15.10(c)(4) to eliminate the rebuttable 
presumption in Sec.  15.10(c)(4)(i) through (iii) and to replace the 
use of ``holder of any payment stablecoin'' with ``payment stablecoin 
holder,'' which is now a defined term, in Sec.  15.10(c)(4).

[[Page 67019]]

Additionally, the OCC is making clarifying edits to Sec.  15.10(c)(5) 
to remove paragraph (c)(5)(iii)(C) and add new Sec.  15.10(d), which 
provides that pursuant to section 4(a)(2)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(ii)) and Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii)(B), the OCC approves, 
for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, repurchase agreements 
wherein the Treasury bills that are sold as purchased securities have a 
maturity of 93 days or less. The OCC is also modifying paragraph 
(c)(5)(iii)(B) to provide that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
may receive approval of a repurchase agreement by order or pursuant to 
final Sec.  15.10(d).
b. Description of Proposed Rule, Comments, and Final Rule
    Enumerated Permissible Activities in Sec.  15.10(a)(1) Through (4): 
Core Statutory Activities
    Consistent with the statute, the OCC proposed to mirror the 
permitted activities set forth in section 4(a)(7)(A) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)) in proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (4), 
which include: (1) issuing payment stablecoins; (2) redeeming payment 
stablecoins; (3) managing reserves related to the issuance or 
redemption of payment stablecoins, including purchasing, selling, and 
holding reserve assets or providing custodial services for reserve 
assets, consistent with applicable State and Federal law; and (4) 
providing custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins, 
required reserves, or private keys of stablecoins consistent with the 
GENIUS Act, as implemented in proposed subpart C. Additionally, 
consistent with section 4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(7)(A)(v)), proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8) provided that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer may undertake any other activities that 
directly support any of the activities in proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(1) 
through (4).
    With respect to the activities enumerated in proposed Sec.  
15.10(a)(1) through (4) as implementations of section 4(a)(7)(A)(i) 
through (iv), commenters did not express substantive concerns. Two 
commenters offered suggestions about how the agency should list or 
otherwise recognize additional permissible activities, including 
integration with payment networks and development of compliance tools. 
One comment suggested the regulation remain narrowly focused such that 
stablecoin issuers may engage in necessary activities, but any 
additional activities should be closely connected to stablecoin 
issuance.
    With respect to integration with payment networks and development 
of compliance tools, without more information, the OCC cannot determine 
whether such activities are permissible. While these activities might 
qualify as directly supporting activities pursuant to final Sec.  
15.10(a)(11), the OCC would need to assess the facts underlying these 
activities prior to making such a determination. The OCC invites 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification from the OCC 
as to whether a particular activity is permissible. For the list of 
enumerated permissible activities in Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (4), the 
agency declines to focus only on necessary activities and activities 
closely connected to stablecoin issuance. The commenter's requirement 
of a close connection to stablecoin issuance alters the statutory test 
and does not account for activities that are authorized, such as 
redemption of payment stablecoins, managing related reserves, and 
providing custodial or safekeeping services. Accordingly, the OCC is 
adopting Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (4) as proposed, with a clarifying 
edit in paragraph (a) to replace the word ``only'' with ``not engage in 
any activity other than the following:'' to make clear that the list of 
activities in final Sec.  15.10(a) is an exclusive list of activities 
that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may engage in.
Activities that Directly Support: Proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8), 
Renumbered as Final Sec.  15.10(a)(11)
    In proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8), consistent with section 
4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)(v)), the OCC 
included a provision that would have provided that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may undertake any other activities that directly 
support the issuance of payment stablecoins, redemption of payment 
stablecoins, managing reserves related to the issuance or redemption of 
payment stablecoins, or providing custodial or safekeeping services for 
payment stablecoins. One such example of an activity that would qualify 
under proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8) because it directly supports both 
issuance and redemption of payment stablecoins would be the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's holding of non-payment stablecoin digital 
assets as principal necessary for testing a distributed ledger, whether 
internally developed or acquired from a third party. Such an activity 
may be necessary to ensure that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
may operate safely and effectively on a distributed ledger.\42\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \42\ As discussed infra, this activity is enumerated as a 
permissible activity, subject to certain conditions in final rule 
Sec.  15.10(a)(8).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Several commenters suggested the OCC provide additional examples of 
activities that directly support such activities or otherwise indicate 
that such activities are broader than what the proposed rule 
illustrated. Among these commenters, one argued that the above example 
(holding non-payment stablecoin digital assets as principal for testing 
a distributed ledger) could imply the agency would limit permissible 
activities that directly support to those that are necessary. This 
commenter suggested a broader definition. Various commenters suggested 
the agency provide specific examples of directly supporting activities, 
and some commenters offered examples. Such examples included, among 
other things, the operation of distributed ledger nodes, smart contract 
deployment, wallet infrastructure and key management, blockchain 
transaction monitoring, and settlement and liquidity services.
    As an alternative to listing examples, one commenter suggested that 
the agency publish separate interpretive guidance specifically on the 
scope of proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8) activities. Several commenters 
suggested the agency take a narrow understanding of ``directly 
support'' in section 4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(7)(A)(v)). These commenters suggested a broad interpretation 
could allow such activities to expand over time or overlap with 
activities that generally require State licensing. One commenter 
recommended that activities permissible under the ``directly support'' 
prong should only be those that materially facilitate certain other 
permitted activities or are operationally necessary for those 
activities.
    Congress's use of ``directly support'' demonstrates the statute 
does not limit permitted activities to those that are necessary for one 
of the statute's enumerated activities.\43\ Such a reading would add a 
substantive limitation--namely, that the activities be strictly
