necessary--that is absent from the text of the statute. Given the 
innovation in the payment stablecoin industry, a limitation of 
``directly support'' to what

[[Page 67020]]

is strictly necessary for one current operational model could also 
stifle innovation. The above example of holding crypto-assets as 
principal for testing does not necessarily illustrate the outer 
perimeter of activities that fit under the ``directly support'' prong; 
it is only intended to be a clarifying example.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \43\ In addition, Congress uses the word ``necessary'' in other 
sections of the Act. See, e.g., sections 4(a)(4)(A)(i)(III) and 
7(e)(1)(C) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(i)(III) and 
5906(3)(1)(C)). This is important because ``Congress generally acts 
intentionally when it uses particular language in one section of a 
statute but omits it in another.'' Dep't of Homeland Sec. v. 
MacLean, 574 U.S. 383, 391 (2015) (citation modified).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to the examples for which commenters requested 
clarification, the OCC declines to opine on the permissibility of such 
activities in the final rule without additional information. The OCC 
encourages permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification 
from the OCC regarding the permissibility of such activities.
    One commenter suggested the agency adopt a brand- and technology-
neutral interpretation of the Act's ``directly support'' language. As 
indicated above, the agency is aware technology and business models may 
change substantially. To avoid locking industry participants into the 
current standards that may quickly become outdated and run counter to 
the Act's goals, the OCC plans to, consistent with its general 
technology-neutral approach, follow a brand- and technology-neutral 
understanding of the ``directly support'' language in the statute and 
rule.
    Some comments combined discussion of the scope of proposed Sec.  
15.10(a)(8) permissible activities with discussion of the appropriate 
risk management practices. One such commenter stated that some of the 
activities under proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8) may entail novel risks. 
Refer to the discussion below on Sec.  15.13 for more about appropriate 
risk management practices.
    One commenter stated that the list of enumerated activities in 
proposed Sec.  15.10(a) is incomplete and risks being read as an 
exclusive list. The commenter suggested other activities that should 
qualify, including the facilitation of independently provided customer 
rewards and benefits, liquidity management, and interaction with third-
party protocols or distributed ledger infrastructure.
    Without additional information, the OCC declines to add the 
facilitation of independently provided customer rewards as an 
enumerated activity. The OCC expects liquidity management generally to 
be permissible as an activity that directly supports issuance, 
redemption, and the management of reserves. With respect to interaction 
with third-party protocols or distributed ledger infrastructure, 
without additional information, the OCC cannot categorically determine 
whether such activities are permissible in the final rule. However, 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers may seek additional clarity from 
the OCC to the extent issuers have questions on the permissibility of 
an activity. With respect to the list in Sec.  15.10(a) being 
incomplete, the OCC may amend these regulations over time, including 
the list of enumerated activities.
    As discussed in more detail below, in the final rule, the OCC is 
adopting proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8), renumbered as Sec.  15.10(a)(11), 
with a change to explicitly permit the hiring of third parties to 
engage in certain activities.
Third-Party Investment Advisers, Asset Managers, and Separately Managed 
Accounts
    Several comments spoke to the permissibility of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers hiring third-party investment advisers or asset 
managers of separately managed accounts, where a custodian controls 
investment decisions within parameters set by the owner. Some 
commenters stated that separately managed accounts can be an 
operationally prudent tool because they allow reserve assets to remain 
legally owned and controlled by the issuer while improving transparency 
and reducing operational risk. Some of these commenters argued these 
investment advisers and asset managers would directly support the 
management of reserves and reserves' liquidity under Sec.  15.10(a)(3) 
of the proposed rule. Thus, these commenters argued that a stablecoin 
issuer may hire investment advisers or asset managers under proposed 
Sec.  15.10(a)(8). One prospective stablecoin issuer asked for 
confirmation that its particular structure with a third-party reserve 
manager would be permissible.
    The OCC agrees that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may use 
an investment adviser or asset manager and may use a separately managed 
account for reserve assets because such arrangements directly support 
stablecoin issuance and reserve management. Accordingly, the OCC is 
clarifying in final Sec.  15.10(a)(11) that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer may undertake any other activities, including the 
hiring of third parties, that directly support any of the activities 
described in Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (a)(4). The hiring of third-
party investment advisers or asset managers is an example of an 
activity that is permissible under Sec.  15.10(a)(11) of the final 
rule. However, such activities should be designed to ensure compliance 
with the GENIUS Act, 12 CFR part 15, and other applicable laws and 
regulations.
Collateral Trustee Arrangements
    A few commenters addressed the topic of collateral trustee 
arrangements. As explained in the preamble to the proposed rule, a 
collateral trustee arrangement involves a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer granting a first-priority security interest in reserve assets to 
the collateral trustee for the benefit of stablecoin holders. The 
proposal asked for comments on whether collateral trustee arrangements 
would protect the reserve assets.
    Many commenters responded that the OCC should expressly permit 
collateral trustee arrangements used solely for the benefit of 
stablecoin holders. Several of those commenters stated that the 
rehypothecation prohibition applies to issuer self-dealing in which 
issuers exploit reserve assets for their own benefit. Those commenters 
noted that a collateral trustee arrangement is intended to further the 
purposes behind the prohibition against rehypothecation, in that it 
exists to ensure that reserves remain available to back outstanding 
payment stablecoins, protect stablecoin holders, and promote financial 
stability. Several commenters supported requirements for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to include disclosures for holders related 
to a collateral trustee arrangement. Commenters advocated for 
disclosures involving the identity and regulatory status of the 
trustee, the nature and scope of the security interest, the 
circumstances in which the trustee may enforce its rights, and any 
limitations on the issuer's ability to access or substitute reserve 
assets. Some commenters also advocated for requirements that issuers 
obtain express and affirmative consent from holders regarding the 
collateral trustee structure before purchasing to ensure holders can 
understand and evaluate the arrangement.
    The OCC agrees that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may 
establish such collateral trustee arrangements. These arrangements may 
have the benefit of protecting payment stablecoin holders by providing 
a potential mechanism for administration of the reserve assets prior to 
bankruptcy or receivership. It is possible that such arrangements can 
facilitate redemptions more quickly than would occur in insolvency or 
bankruptcy. The OCC plans to continue to evaluate such arrangements to 
ensure they are serving their intended purpose of protecting payment 
stablecoin holders. To the extent it becomes clear that such 
arrangements add uncertainty or do not adequately protect payment 
stablecoin holders, the OCC will consider whether

[[Page 67021]]

such arrangements should continue to be permissible.
    To effectuate the use of collateral trustee arrangements, the OCC 
is adding a new Sec.  15.10(a)(9) clarifying that it is permissible for 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to establish a trust arrangement 
under applicable law for reserve assets, including the granting of a 
security interest in reserve assets, provided that: (i) any security 
interest in reserve assets granted to the trustee is for the sole 
benefit of payment stablecoin holders; (ii) the arrangement with the 
trustee does not impair the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
ability to timely redeem payment stablecoins in the normal course of 
business prior to default; (iii) the arrangement does not introduce 
claims that would compete with the claims of payment stablecoin holders 
of payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer in the event of the insolvency of the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer; and (iv) the arrangement with the trustee does not 
impair the ability of a receiver of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to direct the prompt transfer or liquidation of the reserve 
assets in order to pay claims to payment stablecoin holders.\44\ These 
conditions are designed to ensure that such arrangements do not compete 
with the claims of payment stablecoin holders both prior to default as 
well as following default and that such arrangements are not used to 
grant security interests on behalf of parties that are not payment 
stablecoin holders. The OCC is considering whether to issue a separate 
rulemaking providing further clarity regarding this activity. As part 
of such a rulemaking, the OCC may consider including additional 
conditions, such as conditions to clarify the rights that the trust 
agreement must expressly provide to the receiver of, or bankruptcy 
trustee for, an insolvent permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \44\ To the extent a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
utilizes a collateral trustee arrangement but maintains ownership 
and control over the reserve assets, the OCC expects that the 
reserve assets would continue to be reflected on the issuer's 
balance sheet rather than on that of the collateral trustee.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to the payment of the trustee in collateral trustee 
arrangements, it would be a violation of the condition in Sec.  
15.10(a)(9)(i) if the trustee were paid from the proceeds of the 
reserve asset collateral because the trustee holds a security interest 
in such collateral.
    The OCC declines to require a disclosure regime for collateral 
trustee arrangements at this time. Mandating a disclosure regime will 
not be effective at this point as the practice is nascent and the 
arrangements may vary extensively, such that mandatory disclosure may 
not capture the important aspects of such arrangements and could lead 
to customer confusion or a lack of relevant information. The OCC is 
also not requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to obtain 
express consent from payment stablecoin holders prior to entering into 
such arrangements. The OCC believes that the conditions set forth in 
Sec.  15.10(a)(9)(i) through (iii) are designed to protect payment 
stablecoin holders and obviate the need to require affirmative consent.
Fees Associated With Purchasing or Redeeming
    In addition to the activities outlined in section 4(a)(7) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)), for the sake of clarification, 
proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(5) would have provided that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may assess fees that are associated with the 
purchasing or redeeming of payment stablecoins. This power is inherent 
in the activities described above and is explicitly recognized in 
section 4(a)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(ii)).
    One commenter recommended that the OCC confirm expressly that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers may charge certain fees to 
generate revenue, including fees for minting and burning stablecoins 
and fees to collect a share of network transaction fees. The commenter 
recommended that the final rule permit alternate fee structures subject 
to supervisory review and that the final rule require disclosure of all 
fee structures.
    With respect to the commenter's suggestion about the inclusion of 
fees, the OCC does not believe further elucidation of this provision is 
necessary as it is intended to encompass a broad set of fees. The OCC 
addresses the assessment of fees in non-payment stablecoin digital 
assets in more detail below. To the extent an issuer has questions 
regarding whether a fee structure is permissible, it may reach out to 
the OCC. With respect to the commenter's concern regarding disclosure 
of fee arrangements, as discussed below, final Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(iv) 
requires disclosure of all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming 
payment stablecoins. Accordingly, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10(a)(5) 
as proposed, which allows permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
assess fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment 
stablecoins.
Acting as Principal or Agent With Respect to Payment Stablecoins
    The proposed rule, in Sec.  15.10(a)(6), also would have included 
the permitted activities outlined in section 16(b) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5915(b)), namely acting as principal or agent with respect 
to any payment stablecoin and paying fees to facilitate customer 
transactions.\45\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\45\ Section 16(b) of the Act provides in part that ``Entities 
regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are 
authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and 
investments contemplated by this Act, including acting as a 
principal or agent with respect to any payment stablecoin and 
payment of fees to facilitate customer transactions.'' 12 U.S.C. 
5915(b). The activities authorized under section 16(b) include, for 
example, acting as an agent for a customer with respect to the 
redemption of a payment stablecoin issued by a third party.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Addressing proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(6), one commenter suggested 
distinguishing between principal and agent roles and then tying each to 
capital, liquidity, and operational risk controls. Several commenters 
also recommended that the OCC recognize activities in which permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers act as principal or agent with respect to 
payment stablecoins, either as separately enumerated activities under 
Sec.  15.10(a), which sets out generally which activities a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer may engage in, or as examples of activities 
that directly support certain activities under proposed Sec.  
15.10(a)(8). Commenters cited activities such as limited, risk-
controlled principal activities supporting custody, settlement, 
payment, and liquidity functions; digital wallets and money 
transmission using payment stablecoins; facilitating customer 
purchases, sales, or redemptions of payment stablecoins; and holding 
payment stablecoins as principal to facilitate customer transactions. 
One commenter suggested addressing these examples in the preamble as 
published guidance. One commenter cautioned against adding prescriptive 
limits or conditions on principal or agency activities, arguing that 
the statute provides the relevant framework and that additional 
restrictions could narrow the flexibility that Congress intended. 
Another commenter noted that the OCC correctly does not view section 
16(b) as an open-ended grant of authority.
    With respect to the commenter who suggested distinguishing between 
principal and agent activities and tying each to capital, liquidity, 
and operational risk controls, the OCC notes that proposed Sec.  
15.10(a) serves a different function than the rule's risk

[[Page 67022]]

management requirements (final Sec.  15.13). Section 15.10(a) 
identifies the activities that are permissible for a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer. By contrast, final Sec.  15.13 establishes risk 
management requirements designed to ensure that such issuers conduct 
permissible activities in a safe and sound manner. The commenter's 
suggestion therefore conflates two related but distinct inquiries: 
whether an activity is permissible for permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers; and whether and how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
may conduct the activity safely in accordance with the relevant risk 
management-related requirements.
    With respect to the commenter's suggestion for the provision of 
digital wallets and money transmission using payment stablecoins, 
without additional detail, the OCC cannot definitively say that such 
activities are permissible. Money transmission is a broad term even if 
limited to payment stablecoins. To the extent the specific activity 
qualifies as an activity under Sec.  15.10 (for example, the issuance 
or redemption of payment stablecoins), it is permissible. With respect 
to the provision of digital wallets, such an activity may be 
permissible but might also make the entity a custodian in certain 
circumstances depending on the scope of related services provided. 
Refer to the custody discussion below for more detail.
    The commenter's proposed activities relating to facilitating 
purchases or sales of payment stablecoins on customers' behalf and 
acting as a customer agent for redemption of a payment stablecoin 
issued by a third party seem to fit within the enumerated activity in 
Sec.  15.10(a)(6). Additionally, holding payment stablecoins as 
principal to facilitate customer transactions likely would also fall 
under Sec.  15.10(a)(6).
    With respect to the commenter that cautioned against adding 
prescriptive limits to Sec.  15.10(a)(6), the OCC is not including any 
express limits or conditions around the manner in which a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer may act as principal or agent in the final 
rule. However, payment stablecoins are not a permitted reserve asset.
    One commenter recommended that the final rule confirm permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers may repurchase their stablecoins in 
secondary markets. The commenter explained that issuers may need to do 
so for several reasons, including stopping runs and managing the 
balance between circulating supply and holding additional reserve 
assets.
    Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may repurchase their 
stablecoins on secondary markets under proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(6). 
However, such transactions must not impair the ability of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to satisfy its statutory redemption 
obligations or its ability to comply with the capital and liquidity 
requirements in the final rule. Additionally, any such transactions 
must otherwise comply with the Act, 12 CFR part 15, and other 
applicable law. The OCC is finalizing proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(6) 
without change.
Paying Fees To Facilitate Customer Transactions
    Consistent with section 16(b) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5915(b)), proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(7) would have allowed permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to pay fees to facilitate customer 
transactions (e.g., network or ``gas'' fees). If an issuer's payment 
stablecoin operates on a blockchain that assesses transaction fees, 
then the issuer may choose to pay transaction fees on behalf of the 
customer. The OCC recognized in the proposal that if an issuer is 
paying transaction fees on certain distributed ledgers, the issuer may 
have to hold non-payment stablecoin digital assets to facilitate the 
payment of these transaction fees.\46\ Similarly, the OCC recognized 
that the holding of non-payment stablecoin digital assets as principal 
necessary for testing a distributed ledger is a permissible activity.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \46\ See OCC Interpretive Letter 1186 (November 18, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Relatedly, the OCC solicited comment in the proposal about whether 
the final rule should explicitly include specific provisions addressing 
the permissibility of an issuer's holding of non-payment stablecoin 
digital assets to facilitate the payment of transaction fees.
    Several commenters responded that the OCC should explicitly 
recognize that it may be necessary for permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to hold non-payment stablecoin digital assets where they are 
incidental to, and necessary for, the provision of payment stablecoin 
services and do not constitute a proprietary trading strategy. Other 
commenters similarly stated the OCC should allow permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to hold limited amounts of non-payment stablecoin 
digital assets to pay network protocol fees or to conduct testing. On 
the other hand, one commenter stated that holding non-payment 
stablecoin digital assets for testing is potentially risky and 
speculative, and that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have 
to seek prior written approval from the OCC.
    In response to the comments, the OCC is adding new Sec.  
15.10(a)(8), which provides that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
may hold as principal non-payment stablecoin digital assets as 
necessary to pay fees, including customer fees and network fees, or to 
conduct necessary testing on distributed ledger-based platforms, 
subject to the conditions noted below. The OCC agrees with commenters 
that these activities should be expressly recognized because paying 
network fees may be necessary for permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
to operate and transact on certain blockchains and testing is 
appropriate to ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
systems are functioning as intended. As discussed in more detail below, 
the conditions the OCC is putting on holding such non-payment 
stablecoin digital assets obviates the need for a pre-approval process.
    The OCC also asked in the proposal whether the final rule should 
include limitations on the amount of non-payment stablecoin digital 
assets that an issuer may hold at any time.
    In response, several commenters stated that the final rule should 
not impose rigid limits on non-payment stablecoin digital asset 
holdings, with some citing potential future changes in technology and 
industry practices that may render rigid limits obsolete. Some 
commenters recommended instead that the OCC adopt a qualitative, 
principles-based supervisory approach based around clear internal 
controls, documentation, and risk management which ensures that non-
payment stablecoin digital asset holdings are not commingled with or 
treated as reserve assets. In contrast, one commenter responded that 
the OCC should provide more prescriptive and stringent limitations on 
the holding of non-payment stablecoin digital assets. The commenter 
recommended that those limits be expressed as both an absolute dollar 
cap and a percentage and should be subject to regular reporting and 
examination. One commenter also stated that the amount of non-payment 
stablecoin digital assets should be capped as necessary for reasonably 
foreseeable transactions, such as one week of transactions, based on 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's needs from the last 30 days.
    In final Sec.  15.10(a)(8), the OCC is requiring that principal 
holdings of non-payment stablecoin digital assets to pay fees shall not 
exceed quantities necessary for the reasonably foreseeable

[[Page 67023]]

conduct of such activities.\47\ The OCC declines to set a quantitative 
limit because the activities of permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
may vary, and a quantitative limit could be unnecessarily limiting. The 
OCC would expect that permitted payment stablecoin issuers would 
consider, among other things, historical data and expected network fees 
to determine how much non-payment stablecoin digital assets to hold in 
such a scenario. The OCC intends to evaluate over time whether this 
limit is appropriate. Final Sec.  15.13 provides the principles-based 
risk management principles that apply to permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers, and consistent with those principles and the reserve asset 
requirements in final Sec.  15.11, permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
will not be able to commingle or identify non-payment stablecoin 
digital assets or payment stablecoins as reserve assets.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \47\ The OCC has stated that, as an activity incidental to the 
business of banking, national banks may pay network fees on 
blockchain networks to facilitate otherwise permissible activities 
and hold, as principal, amounts of crypto-assets on balance sheet 
necessary to pay network fees for which the bank anticipates a 
reasonably foreseeable need. OCC Interpretive Letter 1186.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC also solicited comment about whether the final rule should 
limit the payment methods a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may use 
to assess fees, including whether the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may assess fees in digital assets other than payment 
stablecoins.
    Several commenters responded that the final rule should not limit 
the methods of payment a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may accept 
when assessing fees. One such commenter responded that, if the OCC 
addresses non-fiat fee payments at all, it should be through a 
principles-based framework focused on transparency, risk management, 
and control discipline. Another commenter concurred and advocated a 
flexible, technology-neutral framework under which issuers are required 
to maintain transparent policies on fee assessment methods and disclose 
those methods to the OCC. Another commenter stated that the OCC should 
confirm in either the final rule or in subsequent guidance that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer must have appropriate procedures in 
place to ensure it can operate in a safe and sound manner if it accepts 
the payment of fees in the form of non-payment stablecoin digital 
assets.
    The OCC declines to limit the methods of payment a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer may receive at this time, provided that any 
such payment complies with applicable laws. As the market evolves, the 
OCC may reconsider whether certain methods of payment should be 
impermissible.\48\ All permitted payment stablecoin issuers, including 
those that accept the payment of fees in the form of non-payment 
stablecoin digital assets, are subject to the risk management 
requirements set forth in Sec.  15.13. Additionally, the OCC would 
expect that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers operate in a safe 
and sound manner regardless of whether they accept payment of fees in 
the form of non-payment stablecoin digital assets.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\48\ Any non-payment stablecoin digital asset received would not 
be a permissible reserve asset.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC notes that, after a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
assesses fees in the form of non-payment stablecoin digital assets, the 
issuer may only hold the collected fees for the purposes outlined in 
final Sec.  15.10(a)(8), namely, to pay fees or to conduct necessary 
testing on distributed ledger-based platforms. To the extent a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer holds non-payment stablecoin 
digital assets in excess of the amount necessary for the activities set 
forth in final Sec.  15.10(a)(8), the OCC would expect that the issuer 
divest of such assets as soon as practicable.\49\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \49\ The OCC would expect that most permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should be able to divest of any such excess non-payment 
stablecoin digital assets within one business day. In recent 
conditional approvals for national banks, applicants have converted 
digital assets received to fiat currency within one business day or 
held such assets for another permissible purpose. See Conditional 
Approval 1366, Conditional Approval 1362, Conditional Approval 1353.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Managing Foreign Exchange Risk
    Several commenters recommended that the OCC recognize that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers that issue non-U.S. dollar-
denominated stablecoins may engage in foreign exchange risk management 
as a permitted activity. Some of those commenters characterized the 
permissible foreign exchange risk management activities as conditional 
upon or related to the issuance of non-U.S. dollar-denominated 
stablecoins, while one commenter recommended the OCC allow broader 
powers related to foreign exchange risk management if the final rule 
permits non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins and narrower powers if 
the final rule does not permit non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins. 
Several commenters distinguished these foreign exchange management 
activities from purely speculative trading activities, while two such 
commenters recommended explicit prohibitions on speculative activities 
and regulatory controls to discourage speculation.
    One commenter recommended against rigid supervisory rules or 
capital add-ons for foreign exchange risk in favor of expectations of 
safe and sound controls including board-approved risk appetites and 
independent risk oversight. One commenter recommended that foreign 
exchange risk management be understood as a tool to meet permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer reserve and redemption requirements, rather 
than insulating payment stablecoin holders from fundamental currency 
risk and recommended that any requirements imposed by the OCC focus on 
such reserve and redemption requirements rather than rigid limits or 
capital add-ons that constrain legitimate hedging activities.
    The OCC agrees with commenters that engaging in foreign exchange 
risk management should be a permissible activity. Specifically, the 
definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901(22)) specifies that a payment stablecoin is a digital asset that 
the issuer ``is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed 
amount of monetary value.'' Additionally, under section 2(17) of the 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(17)), ``monetary value'' means ``a national 
currency or deposit . . . denominated in a national currency.'' These 
provisions may reasonably be read to indicate that payment stablecoins 
are not necessarily limited to U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins 
because it suggests that issuers may issue payment stablecoins backed 
by other types of national currencies. However, the list of permissible 
reserve assets that issuers may hold are generally U.S. dollar- or U.S. 
government-based reserve assets. Accordingly, to the extent that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer seeks to issue a non-U.S. dollar-
denominated payment stablecoin, it could incur substantial foreign 
exchange risk or else be limited to using a very narrow subset of 
reserve assets.
    Such foreign exchange risk would make it difficult for the issuer 
to ensure that it is able to meet the requirements of Sec.  15.11 and 
Sec.  15.13. The OCC therefore believes that managing foreign exchange 
risk is a permissible activity under managing reserves related to the 
issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins under Sec.  15.10(a)(3) 
and is permissible under final Sec.  15.10(a)(11) as an activity that 
directly supports the activities in Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (a)(3).
    The OCC is providing in new Sec.  15.10(a)(10) of the final rule 
that permitted payment stablecoin issuers

[[Page 67024]]

may manage foreign exchange risk. However, permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers that manage foreign exchange risk are subject to the risk 
management requirements in Sec.  15.13(a)(10) of the final rule. Those 
requirements impose conditions on foreign exchange risk management such 
as requiring that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must not use 
foreign exchange risk management as a means to speculate, including 
with respect to the appreciation or depreciation of any national 
currency.
Other Suggested Activities or Requests for Interpretations
    Separate from the specific activities enumerated in proposed Sec.  
15.10(a)(1) through (7), several commenters suggested additional 
activities that should be considered permissible activities. For 
example, one commenter recommended that the enumerated list include 
treasury management functions, including short-term investment-
optimization among permissible reserve assets subject to 
diversification and concentration limits. Another commenter recommended 
that the OCC recognize treasury management activities for reserve asset 
management within a non-exhaustive list of examples of activities that 
qualify under proposed Sec.  15.10(a)(8) as directly supporting core 
activities.
    At this time, the agency is not adding treasury management to the 
list of permissible activities enumerated in Sec.  15.10(a). The OCC 
notes that aspects of treasury management, including short-term 
investment optimization, are already included under Sec.  15.10(a)(3), 
which allows permitted payment stablecoin issuers to manage reserves 
related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins. 
Additionally, with respect to treasury management functions that are 
not encompassed by that provision, such functions may qualify under 
final Sec.  15.10(a)(11) as activities that directly support the 
activities in Sec.  15.10(a)(1) through (a)(4).
    The OCC declines to specifically add ``treasury management'' to the 
enumerated list of activities because that term is not clearly defined 
and could be read broadly, and therefore, the OCC would need to 
evaluate the specific treasury management functions a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer proposes to engage in to determine whether they are 
permissible under the final rule. For example, treasury management 
activities conducted to ensure liquidity to meet payroll demands and to 
pay business expenses incurred as a result of conducting payment 
stablecoin activities directly support core permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer activities and are permissible. The OCC invites 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification from the OCC 
as to whether a particular activity is permissible.
    One commenter recommended that the OCC add to the enumerated 
permissible activities list customer onboarding, identity verification 
and compliance functions reasonably necessary to support permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer operations. Another commenter recommended 
that the OCC recognize onboarding processes as an item in a non-
exhaustive list of examples of activities that qualify under Sec.  
15.10 as directly supporting core activities.
    The agency declines to include customer onboarding, identity 
verification, and compliance functions in the list of permissible 
activities enumerated in Sec.  15.10(a) at this time. As explained 
below, Sec.  15.12 provides that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's obligation to redeem does not begin until, among other things, 
the customer has been successfully onboarded. Accordingly, because the 
OCC addresses onboarding in Sec.  15.12 of the final rule, the OCC does 
not believe it needs to specifically include onboarding as an 
enumerated activity. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may onboard 
customers, so long as the onboarding complies with the Act, 12 CFR part 
15, and other applicable laws, including AML/CFT laws and regulations 
and economic sanctions obligations.
    Several commenters recommended the OCC add various specific 
interpretations to the final rule. One commenter recommended that the 
OCC clarify whether non-hosted or external wallets are permissible for 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and to set clear boundaries to 
keep payment control within regulated entities. Another commenter 
recommended that the OCC prohibit regulated entities from hosting or 
transacting with self-custody wallets due to money laundering 
concerns.\50\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \50\ As discussed below, self-custody generally refers to 
holding one's own assets directly even though technically no custody 
service is provided in such an arrangement.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Act does not specifically prohibit self-custody or non-hosted 
wallets. The OCC declines to explicitly prohibit the use of such 
wallets by permitted payment stablecoin issuers but notes that the use 
of such wallets must comply with the requirements of the Act, 12 CFR 
part 15, and other applicable laws. For example, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers that use such wallets still must comply with section 
4(a)(6) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(6)), which provides that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only 
if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will 
comply, with the terms of any lawful order. Additionally, permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers must comply with all applicable AML/CFT laws 
and regulations and economic sanctions obligations.
    One commenter recommended that the OCC require permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to use a formally defined wallet credential state 
machine describing the status of the wallet, explicit permitted and 
prohibited transactions, cryptographic wallet binding, compliance-gated 
activation preconditions, automatic cascading orders to force wallet 
compliance and freezing, and regulated credential expiration.
    The OCC declines to mandate particular technical requirements for 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are not required under the 
Act, consistent with 12 CFR part 15's generally technology-neutral 
approach. The OCC will not mandate the specific technical requirements 
in light of the continued evolution of the stablecoin industry and the 
likelihood that any technical requirements may become obsolete and 
potentially stifle innovation. However, the final rule in Sec.  15.13 
contains risk management requirements, including those related to 
information technology and security, which could implicate some of the 
commenter's suggestions. The OCC will continue to assess permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers' compliance with such risk management 
requirements against the potential risks posed to issuers throughout 
the supervisory process.
Prohibited Activities
Deceptive Names and Marketing
    In proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(1), the OCC would have imported the 
prohibition on the use of deceptive names from section 4(a)(9) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(9)). This provision would have prohibited 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from using any combination of 
terms relating to the United States Government, including ``United 
States,'' ``United States Government,'' and ``USG,'' in the name of the 
payment stablecoin. This prohibition would not have applied to 
abbreviations relating directly to the currency to which the payment 
stablecoin is pegged, such as ``USD.''

[[Page 67025]]

    Consistent with section 4(a)(9) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(9)), proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(2) would have prohibited permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers from marketing a payment stablecoin in such 
a way that a reasonable person would perceive the payment stablecoin to 
be legal tender as described in 31 U.S.C. 5103, issued by the United 
States, or guaranteed or approved by the Government of the United 
States. The OCC recognized that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
may want to market themselves as permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
under the GENIUS Act. There is no prohibition against issuers marketing 
themselves in this manner, so long as they do not run afoul of the 
prohibitions outlined in the Act and Sec.  15.10(c)(1) and (2), 
including the prohibition against marketing a payment stablecoin in 
such a way that a reasonable person would perceive the payment 
stablecoin to be guaranteed, issued, or approved by the United States. 
The OCC noted that misrepresentations by a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer cannot be cured by a general disclaimer and that representations 
and disclosures should be clear to payment stablecoin holders and 
customers.
    The OCC did not receive any comments specifically requesting 
changes to Sec.  15.10(c)(1) and (c)(2) and is therefore adopting Sec.  
15.10(c)(1) and (c)(2) as proposed. Refer to the discussion of Sec.  
15.12 for additional disclosure requirements that are related to the 
prohibition in Sec.  15.10(c)(2).
Eligibility for Deposit Insurance
    Consistent with section 4(e) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(e)), 
proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(3) would have provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer may not directly or through implication represent 
that payment stablecoins are backed by the full faith and credit of the 
United States, guaranteed by the United States Government, or subject 
to Federal deposit insurance or Federal share insurance.
    Two commenters recommended that the OCC explicitly codify that 
payment stablecoin holders are not eligible for deposit insurance, 
including on a pass-through basis. One commenter noted that this 
clarification would prevent issuers from implying ``insured-like'' 
status that could foster false confidence and increase run risk.
    As discussed in more detail below, the OCC is adding disclosure 
requirements in Sec.  15.12(e) that provide that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must include in its redemption disclosures that 
payment stablecoins are not deposits, not backed by the full faith and 
credit of the United States, not subject to deposit insurance by the 
FDIC, and not subject to share insurance by the NCUA. The OCC declines 
to opine on pass-through insurance in this rulemaking as that topic is 
subject to the FDIC's notice of proposed rulemaking that has not yet 
been finalized.\51\ The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10(c)(3) as 
proposed.\52\

    \51\ GENIUS Act Requirements and Standards for FDIC-Supervised 
Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers and Insured Depository 
Institution, 91 FR 18534 (Apr. 10, 2026).
    \52\ In addition, the OCC notes that, if a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer markets any products other than payment 
stablecoins, it shall also be subject to the prohibition in section 
4(e)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(e)(3)), which provides

Yield
    Consistent with section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(11)), proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(4) provided that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must not pay the holder of any payment 
stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or 
other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or 
retention of such payment stablecoin. The OCC noted that issuers might 
attempt to make prohibited payments of interest or yield to payment 
stablecoin holders through arrangements with third parties. The OCC 
also noted that there would likely be a large and changing variety of 
arrangements with third parties in which issuers could achieve the 
payment of yield to payment stablecoin holders. The OCC stated that it 
would not be possible to identify in detail all, or even most, of the 
potential arrangements between permitted payment stablecoin issuers and 
third parties that the OCC may prohibit under section 4(a)(11) of the 
GENIUS Act and the OCC's rulemaking authority under section 4(h) of the 
GENIUS Act,\53\ particularly as such arrangements may evolve over time. 
On the other hand, the OCC noted that a rule with only a general 
prohibition on the payment of yield could create uncertainty within the 
payment stablecoin market.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \53\ See 12 U.S.C. 5903(h) (providing that the OCC and other 
payment stablecoin regulators may issue regulations to ``carry out 
the requirements of [section 4], including to establish conditions, 
and to prevent evasion thereof'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC therefore proposed to include a presumption in paragraph 
(c)(4)(i) that certain types of arrangements with certain types of 
persons would be prohibited payments of yield or interest by the 
issuer. Specifically, the OCC would have presumed that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer is paying the holder of any payment 
stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or 
other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or 
retention of such payment stablecoin if: (A) the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer has a contract, agreement, or other arrangement with 
an affiliate or a related third party to pay interest or yield to the 
affiliate or related third party; and (B) the affiliate \54\ or related 
third party (or affiliate of such related third party) has a contract, 
agreement, or other arrangement to pay interest or yield (whether in 
cash, tokens, or other consideration) to a holder of any payment 
stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer solely in 
connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment 
stablecoin. To the extent that the person, or an affiliate of the 
person with whom the permitted payment stablecoin issuer had a 
contract, agreement, or other arrangement to pay interest or yield was 
a related third party of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer issues payment 
stablecoins on the related third party's behalf or under the related 
third party's branding, the arrangement between the related third party 
and the holder of the payment stablecoin would have considered the 
holder of the payment stablecoin to be the holder of the payment 
stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on the 
related third party's behalf or under the related third party's 
branding. With respect to a white-label relationship, the rebuttable 
presumption would have been triggered only to the extent the payment 
stablecoin holder was a holder of the related third party's white-
labeled stablecoin (as opposed to other payment stablecoins issued by 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \54\ A person would not have been included within this second 
prong solely because the person is an affiliate of an affiliate of 
the issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Related third parties were defined to include any person offering 
to pay interest or yield to payment stablecoin holders as a service 
(i.e., on behalf of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer) and any 
person that the issuer issues payment stablecoins on behalf of or under 
the branding of (i.e., persons that have entered into a white-label 
relationship with the issuer).
    Under the proposed rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
would have been able to rebut the presumption by submitting written 
materials that, in the OCC's judgment, demonstrate that the

[[Page 67026]]

contract, agreement, or other arrangement is not prohibited under Sec.  
15.10(c)(4) and is not an attempt to evade the prohibition.
    The OCC received many comments concerning the prohibition against a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin 
issuer paying the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest 
or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in 
connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment 
stablecoin (``the yield prohibition''). As discussed in greater detail 
below, after reviewing the comments, the OCC has determined to 
eliminate the rebuttable presumption from the final rule.
    Commenters held diverging views on the proposal's implementation of 
the yield prohibition and associated rebuttable presumption. Many 
advocated eliminating the rebuttable presumption. A large number 
advocated interpreting the yield prohibition narrowly and not applying 
the prohibition or associated rebuttable presumption to certain 
indirect payments, to payments based on transactions, or to payments to 
intermediaries (rather than payment stablecoin holders) made not solely 
in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment 
stablecoin. On the other hand, a substantial number of commenters 
advocated for a broadly applicable yield prohibition that captured 
indirect payments, transaction-based payments, and payments where 
holding, using, or retaining a payment stablecoin was a necessary 
condition of receiving payment. Many of these commenters advocated 
expanding the scope of the rebuttable presumption. Additional detail on 
these comments and other comments received is below.
    Several commenters stated that the statutory yield prohibition is 
not yet settled, noting ongoing legislation that could interact with 
the GENIUS Act's prohibition. Unless and until such legislation passes, 
the OCC must implement the GENIUS Act's yield prohibition, as enacted. 
If the GENIUS Act is amended, or legislation that clearly relates to 
the GENIUS Act's yield prohibition passes, the OCC will evaluate 
whether any amendments to the final rule are necessary and appropriate 
to give effect to such legislation.
    A few commenters advocated eliminating the yield prohibition from 
the final rule altogether. One commenter advocated allowing issuers to 
peg payment stablecoins to a fixed amount of purchasing power, arguing 
that doing so would not amount to paying any form of interest or yield 
(whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration).
    Eliminating the prohibition would be inconsistent with the 
requirements of section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(11)), and the definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) 
of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(22)), which hinges on an issuer being 
obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin for a 
fixed amount of monetary value (rather than a fixed amount of 
purchasing power). The OCC therefore is not revising the rule in 
response to these comments.
    One commenter requested that the OCC confirm that the yield 
prohibition does not capture interest paid on deposits, including 
tokenized deposits. The OCC confirms that the GENIUS Act's yield 
prohibition does not apply to deposits. The definition of payment 
stablecoin in section 2(22) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(22)) explicitly 
excludes deposits, regardless of whether the deposit is recorded using 
distributed ledger technology. Because the yield prohibition in section 
4(a)(11) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)) applies to holders of 
payment stablecoins solely in connection with the holding, use, or 
retention of payment stablecoins, the prohibition does not extend to 
paying interest on deposits, including deposits in tokenized form.
    Several commenters stated that the proposed yield prohibition and 
associated rebuttable presumption were too broad and exceeded the OCC's 
authority. One stated that the rebuttable presumption could raise 
issues under the major questions doctrine. One commenter stated that 
disclosures revealing the economic substance of arrangements between 
issuers, affiliates, and third parties would be more effective than the 
rebuttable presumption. Commenters also stated that the rebuttable 
presumption would invert the burden of proof, chill competition, and 
discriminate against savers in favor of borrowers. Commenters stated 
that the statutory prohibition applies to permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers and does not speak to 
payments from other entities or payments made by other persons in the 
secondary market. Several of these commenters noted that, unlike the 
prohibition against pledging, rehypothecating, or reusing reserve 
assets in section 4(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)), the 
prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)) does 
not contain language explicitly prohibiting a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer from indirectly 
engaging in activities that are proscribed for the issuer.
    Many of these commenters stated that the yield prohibition was 
intensely debated by Congress and that the final text of the Act 
reflects a considered decision not to prohibit indirect payments. Some 
of these commenters argued that any indirect payments should be 
permitted while others took a narrower view, arguing that payments made 
at the direction of, or on behalf of, the issuer should be prohibited 
while payments made by third parties that are not controlled by, or 
made pursuant to an agreement with, the issuer should be permitted. 
Some commenters stated that independently funded rewards paid by 
affiliates or third parties should be permitted under certain 
circumstances.\55\ Many of the commenters that advocated for a narrow 
prohibition stated that the OCC could not use its anti-evasion 
authority under section 4(h)(1) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)) to 
adopt a rebuttable presumption. These commenters argued that, since the 
statutory prohibition does not apply to indirect payments, some or all 
indirect payments should not be considered evasion. These commenters 
stated that the anti-evasion provisions of the Act should capture bad-
faith arrangements, including arrangements where an issuer actually 
directs a third party to make a payment on the issuer's behalf.\56\ 
Some commenters also stated that the anti-evasion language appears in 
section 4(h)(1) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)) and should be read to 
prevent the evasion of section 4's (12 U.S.C. 5903) requirements rather 
than to expand section 4(a)(11)'s (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)) yield 
prohibition.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\55\ Different commenters suggested a variety of potential 
conditions. Several commenters proposed including conditions that 
would require (1) the issuer not to control the decision to pay 
interest or yield, (2) the non-issuer to independently fund payments 
to payment stablecoin holders, and (3) the non-issuer to not have an 
agreement with the issuer to pay interest or yield. Some commenters 
additionally focused on whether the economics of any arrangement 
suggest that the issuer passes interest or yield earned on reserve 
assets though a non-issuer to payment stablecoin holders. Some 
commenters believed that the non-issuer should not be an affiliate 
whereas others believed that payments to and from affiliates should 
not be prohibited by the yield prohibition. One commenter stated 
that the yield prohibition is the functional descendant of 
Regulation Q, which permitted independent distributors to offer 
incentives to attract or retain customers.
    \56\ One commenter stated that the rebuttable presumption should 
be used as a focused tool to address bad-faith evasions but that the 
OCC should explicitly carve certain other arrangements from the 
scope of the presumption.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to this last point, section 4(h)(1) of the Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)) states that ``the primary Federal

[[Page 67027]]

payment stablecoin regulators shall . . . issue such regulations 
relating to permitted payment stablecoin issuers as may be necessary to 
establish a payment stablecoin regulatory framework necessary to 
administer and carry out the requirements of this section [(section 
4)], including to establish conditions, and to prevent evasion 
thereof.'' The yield prohibition in section 4(a)(11) (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(11)) is a requirement of section 4 and thus subject to the 
anti-evasion provisions of the GENIUS Act by the Act's own terms. 
Although the OCC is eliminating the rebuttable presumption from the 
final rule, the OCC emphasizes that the OCC retains its authority to 
address evasion of section 4 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903), including the 
yield prohibition.
    Many commenters advocated a broad prohibition that would capture 
indirect payments as well as direct payments. Some of these commenters 
advocated capturing additional types of transactions through the 
rebuttable presumption, including transactions involving indirect 
payments through persons with whom the issuer has a financial interest, 
contractual relationship, or business arrangement. Others advocated for 
a flat prohibition on direct and indirect payments, rather than 
employing a rebuttable presumption. These commenters stated that 
preventative measures, such as a broad prohibition, would be preferable 
to reactive measures, like the rebuttable presumption. Several of these 
commenters characterized indirect payments as a loophole that must be 
closed, either by regulatory action or Congressional action.
    Many of the commenters favoring a broad prohibition stated that 
permitting indirect payments could lead to deposit flight that would 
disproportionately affect community banks and reduce lending. One 
commenter stated that clear and enforceable treatment of the yield 
prohibition could reduce uncertainty around asset-liability dynamics 
and help preserve the intended protection provided by 1 to 1 reserve 
backing and the timely redemption obligation.
    The statutory yield prohibition can capture certain payments that 
commenters characterized as indirect payments. A person may pay another 
person through someone else and thus be within the scope of the yield 
prohibition. For example, interest or yield payments to payment 
stablecoin holders made by an agent of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer on the issuer's behalf 
solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment 
stablecoin would be within the scope of the prohibition. In these 
instances, the agent acts for the issuer. The issuer pays interest or 
yield to a payment stablecoin holder. Even if the issuer were not 
considered to be the payor, it would clearly evade the statutory 
prohibition on yield for an issuer to merely pay another entity to make 
an interest or yield payment that the issuer could not make directly. 
As discussed below, other scenarios may present closer questions. For 
example, indirect payments that are not made solely in connection with 
the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin are outside the 
scope of the prohibition by the Act's own terms. Depending on the facts 
and circumstances, a payment to payment stablecoin holders through an 
intermediary might be made solely in connection with the holding, use, 
or retention of a payment stablecoin or might be made, at least in 
part, for other reasons.
    One commenter stated that issuers should be permitted to pass yield 
from reserves through to institutional payment stablecoin holders but 
not to retail payment stablecoin holders. The GENIUS Act does not 
distinguish between retail and institutional payment stablecoin 
holders. Accordingly, the final rule applies the yield prohibition 
equally to payments by an issuer to institutional and retail payment 
stablecoin holders. One commenter requested that the OCC provide a cure 
period for violations of the yield prohibition. The final rule does not 
include such a cure period but, as discussed below, does not include 
the rebuttable presumption. The OCC will exercise its enforcement 
discretion appropriately, based on the given facts and circumstances.
    Commenters requested clarification about the various prongs of the 
rebuttable presumption, the process for rebutting the presumption 
(including standardized rebuttal language), and the particular wording 
of the presumption (e.g., the definition of ``related third party''). 
Commenters also requested a list of illustrative examples of 
arrangements that would not violate the prohibition. Because the final 
rule does not include the rebuttable presumption, the OCC is not 
further clarifying the terms of the presumption or the process for 
rebuttal. In response to requests for examples of activities that would 
violate or be permitted under the yield prohibition or that would be 
captured by the presumption or constitute evasion, the OCC is not 
including a list of prohibited or permitted arrangements. Rather, the 
OCC will apply the language of the statute to the facts and 
circumstances of any particular arrangement so that any such 
arrangement can be evaluated based on all relevant facts and 
circumstances.
    Commenters addressed a number of potential safe harbors or 
exclusions for certain activities. Some commenters stated that there 
should be a de minimis exemption for small payments or incidental 
payments that do not scale with the amount of payment stablecoins held 
by the payee. These commenters stated that such small payments pose no 
credible risk of evasion of the GENIUS Act and that subjecting these 
small payments to the rebuttable presumption would impose 
disproportionate burdens. Other commenters disagreed, stating that such 
a safe harbor or exclusion would be unnecessary and unsupported by the 
statute. The OCC is not adopting a safe harbor for de minimis payments 
because the statutory yield prohibition, by its terms, does not 
contemplate an exemption for such payments.
    Some commenters argued that the GENIUS Act was not intended to 
prohibit existing rewards programs and that rewards programs that were 
in existence as of the enactment of the GENIUS Act should be excluded 
from the statutory yield prohibition. Many commenters argued for an 
explicit safe harbor for these indirect payments or for excluding them 
from the scope of the rebuttable presumption. The OCC declines to 
presume that rewards programs that predated the GENIUS Act comply with 
the GENIUS Act. The fact that Congress may have had notice of these 
rewards programs does not necessarily imply that Congress endorsed them 
as permissible. Indeed, Congress could have provided a safe harbor for 
such programs but did not do so. Accordingly, rewards programs that 
predate the enactment of the GENIUS Act will be evaluated the same as 
rewards programs that are established after the enactment or effective 
date of the GENIUS Act.
    Many commenters argued that the prohibition and associated 
rebuttable presumption should not capture payments that the issuer does 
not control and that are not funded directly by the issuer. Commenters 
requested specific exclusions or safe harbors for fiduciary income 
earned by trust entities, certain DeFi arrangements, payments in 
connection with the promotion or distribution of payment stablecoins, 
rewards from staking, and interest from lending. Several commenters 
advocated for specific exclusions or safe harbors for various types of 
white-label arrangements. Commenters also requested exclusions

[[Page 67028]]

or safe harbors for certain arrangements subject to Federal securities 
laws, customer loyalty or rewards programs structured in good faith, 
and payments for services (including compliance, technological, 
operational, marketing, or distributional services).
    In response to comments, the OCC has not provided a general safe 
harbor. With respect to DeFi arrangements, the facts of each DeFi 
arrangement may bear significantly on whether such an arrangement is 
entered into to evade the yield prohibition. The OCC is also not 
adopting an explicit safe harbor for payments made for services. Absent 
additional facts to the contrary, payments for bona fide services 
generally would not be prohibited because such payments generally are 
not interest or yield paid solely in connection with the holding, use, 
or retention of a payment stablecoin.
    The OCC also has not adopted a safe harbor for arrangements subject 
to the Federal securities laws. Although payment stablecoins are 
excluded from the definition of security, an arrangement where an 
issuer pays interest or yield solely in connection with the holding, 
use, or retention of payment stablecoins could be a security, depending 
on the facts and circumstances. The statute does not provide a clear 
safe harbor from the yield prohibition for securities. Accordingly, the 
OCC declines to adopt a safe harbor for arrangements that are 
securities.
    The OCC also is not adopting a safe harbor for white-label 
partners. Payments to and from white-label partners may be more likely 
to be made on behalf of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer than other types of payments. 
Accordingly, the OCC believes that a broadly applicable safe harbor 
would be inappropriate.
    Many commenters stated that the key terms used in the prohibition 
and associated rebuttable presumption must be defined or clarified. 
Some argued that failing to include definitions for these terms 
violated the OCC's notice-and-comment obligations under the 
Administrative Procedure Act. Others stated that the terms were 
sufficiently clear and did not require further definition. As discussed 
below, the OCC has decided not to include additional regulation text 
defining certain terms used in the yield prohibition, with the 
exception of the term ``payment stablecoin holder,'' discussed 
elsewhere. The OCC believes that it is not necessary to do so and that 
including definitions for certain terms could encourage the adoption of 
arrangements that are intended to evade the prohibition.
    A large number of commenters stated that ``interest'' and ``yield'' 
should be defined. Several commenters favoring a broad yield 
prohibition stated that these terms should be interpreted broadly. 
Commenters noted that the prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)) applies to the payment of ``any form of 
interest or yield, whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration'' 
and stated that this language suggests that the terms ``interest'' and 
``yield'' should be interpreted broadly. Several commenters stated that 
``interest'' should include all scenarios where an issuer provides 
economic value to a partner or affiliate who then delivers yield-like 
benefits to payment stablecoin holders. Many commenters stated that the 
definitions of ``interest'' and ``yield'' should hinge on economic 
substance and not on how the term is labeled (e.g., as rewards). Many 
commenters stated that interest should be defined to mean economic 
benefits that scale with the amount of payment stablecoins that a 
stablecoin holder holds or the duration that the stablecoin holder 
holds the payment stablecoins. Some commenters stated that the terms 
interest and yield should include payments by an issuer based on the 
passive holding of a payment stablecoin. Some commenters noted that 
interest has long been interpreted to refer to a wide range of types of 
compensation and that the Supreme Court has rejected the notion that 
interest must be time- or rate-based. Commenters stated that, since the 
GENIUS Act prohibits yield, in addition to interest, the OCC should 
interpret the prohibition broadly.
    Several commenters stated that a broad definition of interest and 
yield, as part of a broad prohibition, would help maintain the 
distinction between payment instruments, like payment stablecoins, and 
investment instruments. In contrast, many commenters that favored a 
narrow yield prohibition advocated excluding certain types of payments 
from the definitions of interest and yield. One stated that the OCC 
should not prohibit arrangements that are the economic equivalent of 
paying any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other 
consideration), arguing that, if the OCC commits to regulating economic 
equivalents, rather than statutory categories, there is no principled 
stopping point. The OCC disagrees. Interest and yield are broad terms 
under their generally understood meanings. Interest does not stop being 
interest merely because it is given a different name. An approach that 
looked to labels rather than economic substance would render the yield 
prohibition meaningless.
    Other commenters requested carveouts (either from the definition of 
interest or yield, the scope of the prohibition, or through the 
implementation of a safe harbor) for certain commercial transactions, 
fee waivers, promotional or loyalty payments, merchant discounts and 
rebates (subject to certain requirements), white-label profit sharing, 
and transaction-based payments. Many of these comments focused on the 
idea that transaction-based rewards should not be considered interest 
or yield. Commenters disagreed as to whether customer rewards should be 
included within the definition and thus be subject to the yield 
prohibition. Commenters advocating a broad yield prohibition stated 
that rewards programs could act as an evasion of the prohibition, 
rewards would blur the line between payment and investment instruments, 
and excluding rewards from the scope of the prohibition could 
negatively impact competition between highly regulated banks and less 
regulated entities. Others stated that certain types of rewards (e.g., 
transaction-based rewards or independently funded third-party rewards, 
discussed above) should not be considered interest or yield.
    After considering the comments received, the OCC has decided not to 
define the terms ``interest'' or ``yield.'' The OCC will apply 
principles of statutory interpretation to the terms in light of the 
facts and circumstances before it. The OCC therefore declines to adopt 
a definition of these terms.
    Several commenters stated that ``pay'' should be interpreted 
broadly and that the OCC should look to the economic substance of a 
transaction to determine whether a payment has occurred. In contrast, 
in the context of the rebuttable presumption, one commenter said that 
the OCC should not interpret the term to capture any transfer of 
economic value, arguing that doing so would expand the OCC's authority 
and would cover general commercial relationships. The OCC is not 
defining the term in the final rule. The OCC will apply principles of 
statutory interpretation to the term ``pay'' in light of the facts and 
circumstances before it. Commenters had diverging views on whether and 
how to define ``holding,'' ``use,'' and ``retention'' for the purpose 
of implementing the statutory yield prohibition. Many commenters 
advocated for excluding transactional activities from the scope of 
``use''

[[Page 67029]] altogether, stating that the prohibition should apply to passive holding of payment stablecoins rather than active use of payment stablecoins. These commenters argued that the use of the terms ``interest'' and ``yield'' suggest that the prohibition applies to passive holdings and that the word ``use'' is intended merely to ensure that an issuer cannot evade the prohibition by mislabeling payments for passive holdings. Several commenters requested that the OCC clarify that ``use'' refers to bona fide customer-facing activity rather than ministerial issuance, redemption, settlement, or internal asset- transfer functions. Other commenters stated that the terms should be read broadly, such that payments that are conditioned on holding, using, or retaining a stablecoin are captured. The statutory yield prohibition applies to payments of interest or yield solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Thus, the statute contemplates that certain payments made in connection with the use of a payment stablecoin may be prohibited. Specifically, a payment would need to (a) be interest or yield and (b) be made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin to be within the scope of the prohibition. Transaction-based payments that did not amount to interest or yield or that were not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin would not be prohibited. Whether a transaction-based payment meets those criteria is a fact- specific inquiry, and the OCC will address the facts presented by particular arrangements as they arise. Commenters had diverging views as to the meaning of the term ``solely'' in the yield prohibition. Several commenters stated that the term must remain in the prohibition, should be included in the rebuttable presumption, if retained, and should be given the effect of excluding payments made even in part based on factors other than the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins. Commenters stated, for example, that payments made for commercial purposes, including marketing payments, payments for liquidity provision, and the posting of collateral should be outside the scope of the prohibition because they are not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Commenters also stated that payments made in connection with serving as a node, validating transactions, and staking are not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins. Some commenters stated that giving effect to the term ``solely'' would help distinguish payment instruments and investment products. A large number of other commenters stated that the term ``solely'' should be read narrowly to prevent evasion of the yield prohibition. These commenters emphasized that the term should be read in the broader context of the prohibition, which prohibits a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer from paying any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. Some commenters stated that the yield prohibition should capture the transfer of economic benefit to a payment stablecoin holder unless the person providing the benefit can demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the purpose of the payment is for a substantial business purpose other than incentivizing, or otherwise making payments in connection with, the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Similarly, another commenter stated that an economic benefit provided to a holder or user of a payment stablecoin should be presumed to be provided solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of that stablecoin if holding, using, or retaining the stablecoin is a necessary condition to receiving the benefit or is the reason the benefit is provided. The word ``solely'' in the statutory yield prohibition is best read under its plain terms to exclude payments made in connection with reasons other than holding, using, or retaining a payment stablecoin. Thus, payments made for other purposes are not barred by the GENIUS Act. To the extent that there are concerns that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer pays interest or yield only nominally for another purpose in an attempt to evade the statute, the OCC will look to the substance of the transaction to determine whether the permitted payment stablecoin issuer was truly paying solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin or whether the transaction was structured for the purpose of evading the yield prohibition. Commenters had widely varying views on the economic impact of the yield prohibition. A large number of commenters stated that the economic impact of a prohibition that allowed for indirect payments would be significant. These commenters stated that the promise of interest- or yield-bearing payment stablecoins could divert funds away from bank deposits (particularly at community banks) and diminish lending and the provision of financial services and investments within communities. Several of these commenters noted that community banks are important sources of loans, particularly for smaller communities and for farmers. These commenters stated that the scale of deposit flight would depend on the strength of the yield prohibition and the growth of the payment stablecoin industry. Specific estimates varied, but many of these commenters cited to reports that deposits could be reduced by trillions of dollars and that lending could decrease by hundreds of billions of dollars, with certain States being more impacted than others.\57\ Several commenters favoring a narrow prohibition criticized these estimates, including by arguing that some of these estimates represented advocacy, rather than research, stating that some of the estimates were inconsistent with past statements of the organizations that produced the estimates, and by questioning the applicability of the assumptions or models used to create these estimates. Many of these commenters stated that deposits would likely be recycled back into community banks in the form of reserve assets. A number of commenters favoring a broad prohibition disagreed, stating that reserve assets would likely be concentrated in large financial institutions (as opposed to in community banks) and that deposits held as reserves would be wholesale deposits, rather than retail deposits. These commenters stated that wholesale deposits serving as reserve assets would be less able to support credit creation than retail deposits. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \57\ Estimates cited included Jessie Jiaxu Wang, ``Banks in the Age of Stablecoins: Some Possible Implications for Deposits, Credit, and Financial Intermediation,'' FEDS Notes (December 17, 2025), available at https://doi.org/10.17016/2380-7172.3970; Treasury Borrowing Advisory Comm., ``Charge for the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee: Second Quarter 2025,'' available at https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge2Q22025.pdf; Andrew Nigrinis, ``The Lending Impact of Stablecoin-Induced Deposit Outflows, Legal Econ.
