One commenter stated that the OCC has indicated that it will monitor for deposit flight but has not stated how it would address deposit flight. One commenter stated that the OCC should clearly articulate any concerns about the similarities between payment stablecoins and deposits, so that commenters could provide meaningful input. Congress created a new regulatory framework through the GENIUS Act, and the payment stablecoin and banking industries may change as a result of this new framework. The scale and character of these changes may depend substantially on market developments, customer demand, and implementation of the GENIUS Act. For example, any estimate as to the impact of payment stablecoins on bank deposits or on the broader economy will depend, in part, on how much the payment stablecoin industry grows, where issuers hold their deposits, and whether those deposits are stable. While the OCC can estimate the economic impacts of the rule, there is necessarily a degree of uncertainty with respect to key variables. The OCC intends to monitor the impacts of the final rule as well as developments in the market. The OCC may consider revising the final rule, to the extent necessary and to the extent consistent with the text and purpose of the GENIUS Act. After carefully considering the comments concerning the yield prohibition, the OCC has eliminated the rebuttable presumption from the final rule. Because payment stablecoins are a nascent market, the OCC does not believe that it is appropriate to impose a rebuttable presumption with respect to the yield prohibition at this time. The rebuttable presumption could have been both overinclusive and underinclusive, capturing permissible arrangements that would have been subject to the rebuttable presumption and allowing the inference that impermissible arrangements not triggering the presumption are consistent with the yield prohibition. Requiring such arrangements to go through the rebuttal process risks imposing burden without a commensurate benefit. Instead of finalizing the proposed rebuttable presumption or otherwise providing guidance on the types of potentially prohibited transactions, the OCC will initially monitor arrangements with permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers as part of its review of issuers' applications and ongoing supervision of such entities. Where it identifies transactions that violate or evade the yield prohibition, the OCC will take action and provide the public with additional guidance regarding such actions and interpretations, as appropriate. As the payment stablecoin market develops, the OCC anticipates that it will gain sufficient experience with identifying prohibited transactions to allow it to propose a rulemaking clarifying the yield prohibition that does not have the disadvantages noted above. Prohibition on Rehypothecation Proposed Sec. 15.10(c)(5) included the language from section 4(a)(2) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)) that prohibits permitted payment stablecoin issuers from pledging, rehypothecating, or reusing any reserve assets required under 12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1), except for the purposes listed in section 4(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)). Consistent with the statute, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot pledge, rehypothecate, or reuse any reserve assets, either directly or indirectly (e.g., through a third-party custodian of the reserve assets), except for the purpose of: (i) satisfying margin obligations in connection with investments in permitted reserves under proposed Sec. 15.11(b)(4) or (5); (ii) satisfying obligations associated with the use, receipt, or provision of standard custodial services; or (iii) creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins, such that reserves in the form of Treasury bills with a maturity of 93 days or less may be sold as purchased securities in repurchase agreements,\59\ provided that either: (A) the repurchase agreements are cleared by a clearing agency registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission; or (B) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer receives prior approval from the OCC. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

``directly or indirectly'' in the prohibition, it is clear that 
Congress intended that a custodian that holds the reserves on behalf of

involving United States Treasury securities. The commenter requested 
confirmation that the rule would not prohibit a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer from granting a Treasury clearing agency a limited 
lien on purchased securities received in connection with a permitted 
cleared tri-party reverse repurchase transaction, where the lien is 
granted in lieu of margin and is subject to conditions limiting the 
Treasury clearing agency's ability to use the securities other than to 
effect settlement. The commenter also requested that the OCC clarify 
that Sec.  15.10(c)(5) would not prohibit a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer from granting its clearing member a lien on the 
issuer's rights under repurchase transactions cleared through the 
clearing member and related cash and securities, provided the clearing 
member holds the related cash and securities in a custodial capacity 
and the obligations secured by the lien are limited to the issuer's 
obligations under the related repurchase transactions.
    With respect to liens in Treasury repurchase agreements, the 
exception at Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(i) of the final rule allows a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to satisfy margin obligations in connection 
with reserve assets held either as money received under certain 
repurchase agreements or as certain reverse repurchase agreements. The 
agency understands from commenters that, for tri-party reverse 
repurchase agreements, the party receiving securities may need to 
satisfy market-standard requirements of the central counterparty. In 
certain circumstances, these requirements require a party to post 
margin or, as an alternative, grant a limited lien in favor of the 
central counterparty. If such a lien is specifically for satisfying 
margin obligations and effecting settlement, such a lien would likely 
be consistent with the exception in Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(i).
    Given that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may hold repurchase 
or reverse repurchase agreements as permissible reserve assets, and 
given that standard custodial services by a clearing member include the 
clearing member holding a limited lien, the prohibition in Sec.  
15.10(c)(5) of the rule does not prohibit a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer from granting a lien to a clearing member provided 
that the clearing member holds related cash and securities in a 
custodial capacity and that the secured obligations are limited to the 
customer's obligations under the related repurchase agreements.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC expressly permit a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to grant a covered custodian a first-priority 
lien, security interest, and set-off rights against reserve assets. The 
commenter also stated that these rights are a routine feature of 
custody arrangements and help protect custodians when they advance 
funds or securities to facilitate settlement in custody accounts.
    In the proposed rule, the OCC originally interpreted the exception 
to the prohibition on rehypothecation related to satisfying obligations 
associated with the use, receipt, or provision of standard custodial 
services to be limited to the purposes specified in section 10(c)(2)(B) 
of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(2)(B)). However, after considering the 
comments, the OCC believes that such an interpretation of the exception 
was unnecessarily narrow, and commenters have raised the important 
point that custody agreements routinely include giving a custodian a 
security interest in the reserve assets. Accordingly, the OCC reads the 
exception in section 4(a)(2)(B) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(B)) to 
allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to grant a covered 
custodian a first-priority lien, security interest, and set-off rights 
against reserve assets to the extent it is for the purpose of 
satisfying obligations associated with the use, receipt, or provision 
of standard custodial services as provided in section 4(a)(2)(B) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(B)) and Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(ii). Such a 
permissible lien, security interest, or set-off rights would be limited 
to the bona fide provision of custodial services and limited in scope.
    The third and final exception to Sec.  15.10(c)(5) of the rule, 
Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii), is for the creation of liquidity to meet 
reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins. In 
the preamble to the proposed rule, the agency explained that, due to 
the fungibility of money, the OCC would not scrutinize the exact uses 
to which repurchase borrowing proceeds are put. The OCC explained that 
rehypothecation would not be permissible if repurchase borrowings are 
obtained solely for some purpose other than obtaining liquidity to meet 
redemption requests or compliance with the rule.
    Some commenters expressed support for the proposal as written, 
while one commenter stated that if the OCC does not scrutinize how 
borrowed funds are used, issuers could effectively monetize reserve 
assets through the repo market. Accordingly, the commenter stated that 
the OCC should impose clear restrictions on the purposes for which 
repurchase proceeds may be used and require issuers to maintain 
contemporaneous records demonstrating that any repurchase borrowing was 
used exclusively to meet the issuer's redemption obligations.
    The OCC continues to hold the view it expressed in the proposal. To 
the extent the OCC scrutinized the exact uses to which repurchase 
borrowing proceeds were used, it could impair an issuer's ability to 
effectively use repurchase agreements to manage liquidity. 
Additionally, Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii) of the final rule still includes 
the condition that repurchase agreements should be for the purpose of 
creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to 
redeem payment stablecoins. Accordingly, if the OCC were to become 
aware that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer was entering into 
repurchase agreements for another purpose, the issuer may be in 
violation of that provision. While all permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers are subject to the recordkeeping requirements in Sec.  
15.14(f), the OCC does not believe an individualized recordkeeping 
regime for repurchase agreements would be beneficial because it could 
create additional burden that would make repurchase agreements a less 
effective liquidity tool, especially in times of stress.
Pre-Approval of Certain Repurchase Agreements
    With respect to the exception in proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii), 
the OCC proposed to deem any repurchase agreement approved under this 
section and section 4(a)(2)(C) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(C)), 
provided that the Treasury bills sold as purchased securities have a 
maturity of 93 days or less, consistent with the requirement

[[Page 67032]]

that Treasury bills held as reserve assets must have a maturity of 93 
days or less, and the liquidity obtained through repurchase borrowings 
is not being obtained solely for purposes other than meeting redemption 
requests or compliance with the requirements of this proposed rule. The 
proposal explained that section 4(a)(1)(A) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(A)) makes clear that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
may maintain identifiable reserves comprising money received under 
certain repurchase agreements. The proposal further stated that it 
would frustrate section 4(a)(1)(A)(iv)'s clear permission to maintain 
such reserve assets if permitted payment stablecoin issuers could only 
engage in repurchase borrowing transactions upon the completion of 
cumbersome procedures and one-off supervisory approvals.
    Several commenters responded to the OCC's request for input on 
whether it should pre-approve repurchase agreements by rule as proposed 
in Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii)(B). Several commenters supported the OCC's 
proposal to pre-approve repurchase agreements by rule and characterized 
case-by-case approvals as risking unnecessary operational delays. Some 
commenters offered specific suggestions for which types of repurchase 
agreements the OCC should approve by rule. One commenter recommended 
that the OCC pre-approve repurchase agreements collateralized by short-
term Treasury securities and overnight reverse repurchase agreements 
with the Federal Reserve given the minimal liquidity and credit risk. 
The commenter recommended that repurchase agreements collateralized by 
other permitted reserve assets be given broad but bounded approval.
    Another commenter recommended that the OCC pre-approve by rule both 
overnight and term-repurchase agreements collateralized solely by 
eligible reserve assets and cleared through a regulated central 
counterparty. That commenter recommended that pre-approval be 
accompanied by established guardrails. Another commenter responded that 
the rule should expressly permit pre-approved, rule-based use of 
``properly structured [repurchase agreements]'' as beyond prohibited 
``reuse'' provided the repurchase agreement is highly liquid and the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer can meet redemptions. The commenter 
described a list of parameters and noted that the OCC's treatment of 
such contracts should match established supervisory practice. Another 
commenter recommended that the OCC adopt a broad and flexible pre-
approval framework rather than limiting approvals to specific 
transaction types given continued evolution in the repurchase agreement 
market.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii)(B) as proposed, with 
certain clarifying edits described in more detail below. The OCC 
declines to extend the pre-approval of repurchase agreements beyond 
those where the Treasury bills that are sold as purchased securities 
have a maturity of 93 days or less. The OCC is pre-approving repurchase 
agreements wherein the Treasury bills that are sold as purchased 
securities have a maturity of 93 days or less because the money 
received under such agreements is a permissible reserve asset under 
section 4(a)(1)(A)(iv) (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(iv)). In addition, 
section 4(a)(2)(C) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(C)), which 
prohibits rehypothecation, provides an exception only for this same 
type of repurchase agreement. Congress's inclusion of only this limited 
exception suggests that Congress did not intend to automatically permit 
other types of repurchase agreements under the Act or permit other 
types of repurchase agreements without OCC approval.\61\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

(citation modified) (``This conclusion follows directly from the

    By contrast, one commenter expressed concern about repurchase 
agreements and recommended that the OCC exercise its safety and 
soundness authority to exclude repurchase agreements from the list of 
permissible reserve assets in the final rule because permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers that rely on repurchase agreements for cash are 
dependent on short-term funding that may not be available in stress. 
That commenter recommended in the alternative that, should it choose to 
permit repurchase agreements to count towards reserve assets, the OCC 
limit recognition to centrally cleared repurchase agreements.
    The OCC declines to categorically exclude repurchase agreements as 
a permissible reserve asset. Congress clearly intended for money 
received under repurchase agreements to be a permissible reserve asset 
type. The OCC also notes that repurchase agreements have the benefit of 
enhancing liquidity, allowing permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
receive the money necessary to facilitate redemptions. The OCC also 
declines to require central clearing as a precondition to entering into 
repurchase agreements as central clearing is not required by the 
Act.\62\ However, the OCC notes that central clearing can have the 
benefit of reducing issuers' counterparty credit risk.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \62\ The prohibition on rehypothecation creates an exception for 
repurchase agreements cleared by a clearing agency registered with 
the SEC or those that are approved by the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's Federal payment stablecoin regulator. See 
section 4(a)(2)(C)(i) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(C)(i)).

    Some commenters recommended that the OCC clarify terms used in the 
proposal. One commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that the 
standard for ``reasonable expectations of requests to redeem'' be 
assessed by reference to each issuer's historical redemption patterns, 
customer base, and risk profile rather than a fixed quantitative 
threshold.
    The OCC declines to set a specific quantitative threshold related 
to the language in section 4(a)(2)(C) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(2)(C)), which provides that repurchase agreements falling under 
the exception to the prohibition on rehypothecation must be for 
``creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to 
redeem payment stablecoins.'' The OCC believes that each individual 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer is generally in the best position 
to assess when such repurchase agreements are necessary to create 
liquidity to meet redemption demands, subject to OCC supervision for 
compliance with this requirement. A fixed quantitative limit could 
impair liquidity management, especially in times of stress. The OCC 
agrees that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's historical 
redemption patterns, customer base, and risk profile may be helpful to 
issuers when considering whether to enter into a repurchase agreement.
    Another commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that the 
standard includes the prudent and routine use of repurchase agreements 
as a core liquidity management tool, consistent with the commenter's 
position that the OCC pre-approve a defined category of low-risk 
repurchase agreements by rule.
    The OCC agrees that repurchase agreements can be a core liquidity 
tool for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, provided they are used 
in a manner consistent with the Act and part 15. As discussed above, 
the OCC is not expanding the category of repurchase agreements pre-
approved by rule beyond the category described in Sec.  
15.10(c)(5)(iii)(B).
    Some commenters made technical recommendations relating to a rule-
based pre-approval process. One commenter recommended that the OCC

[[Page 67033]]

clarify that creating liquidity to meet reasonable redemption 
expectations means maintaining a portfolio of reserve assets that can 
be monetized within T+1 under normal market conditions and T+0 under 
stressed conditions, calibrated to the issuer's historical redemption 
velocity and stress-tested against a variety of scenarios.
    The OCC declines to limit the phrase ``creating liquidity to meet 
reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins'' to 
require maintaining a portfolio of reserve assets that can be monetized 
within T+1 under normal market conditions and T+0 under stressed 
conditions. However, final Sec.  15.12(c)(1) provides that timely 
redemption may not exceed two business days following the date of the 
requested redemption. Accordingly, a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's use of repurchase agreements must not interfere with its 
ability to satisfy the timely redemption requirement.
    Another commenter recommended that the OCC confirm that the pre-
approval framework does not prohibit repurchase agreements where the 
repurchase agreement counterparty is also the custodian of the relevant 
reserve assets. That commenter described the relevant supervisory 
question as whether the issuer retains full legal ownership of and 
unimpeded access to reserve assets at all times.
    The OCC clarifies that the pre-approval framework does not prohibit 
repurchase agreements where the repurchase agreement counterparty is 
also the custodian of the relevant reserve assets.\63\

    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is adopting 
Sec.  15.10(c)(5) as proposed, with certain clarifying edits. 
Specifically, the OCC is making clarifying edits to Sec.  15.10(c)(5) 
to remove paragraph (c)(5)(iii)(C) and add new Sec.  15.10(d), which 
provides that pursuant to section 4(a)(2)(C)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(C)(ii)) and Sec.  15.10(c)(5)(iii)(B), the OCC 
approves, for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, repurchase 
agreements wherein the Treasury bills that are sold have a maturity of 
93 days or less. The OCC is also modifying paragraph (c)(5)(iii)(B) to 
provide that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may receive approval 
of a repurchase agreement by order or pursuant to final Sec.  15.10(d).
Prohibition on Evasion
    Section 4(h)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)) provides 
that the OCC may issue regulations to ``carry out the requirements of 
this section . . . and to prevent evasion thereof.'' Consistent with 
this authority, proposed Sec.  15.10(c)(6) provided that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must not engage in any activity that the OCC 
determines is an evasion of the requirements of section 4 of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903) or part 15.
    One commenter asked the agency to confirm that a stablecoin issuer 
that relies on published agency guidance in good faith (absent material 
misstatements or omissions) would not violate the evasion prohibition 
in Sec.  15.10(c)(6).
    The OCC declines to provide an explicit safe harbor because whether 
particular conduct constitutes evasion necessarily depends on the 
particular facts and circumstances, and because the OCC will gain 
experience in administering this standard after the final rule becomes 
effective. Nevertheless, when determining whether a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer acted to evade section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903) or part 15, the OCC would consider, among other relevant factors, 
the issuer's good faith reliance on OCC publications and whether the 
issuer made misstatements or omitted material facts.
Approval Process for Certain Activities
    Several commenters supported an application or approval process for 
determining the scope of permissible permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer activities. By providing clarity in advance, commenters believed 
an activity approval process could promote innovation, consistency, and 
appropriate agency-established boundaries. One commenter suggested the 
OCC, following notice and comment, either list permissible activities 
for stablecoin issuers or publish a framework for assessing 
permissibility. The commenter stated that this public notice and 
comment process could inform what activities the agency enumerates as 
permissible. Another commenter stated that the OCC should adopt an 
evolving framework to enumerate additional permissible activities and 
commit to issuing guidance on permissibility determinations.
    The OCC declines at this time to commit to publishing a list or 
framework for activity permissibility. As the OCC stated in the notice 
of proposed rulemaking, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
unclear about whether a particular activity is permissible, the OCC 
encourages issuers to ask the OCC directly. Because payment stablecoin 
activities will continue to evolve, a list would quickly become 
outdated, especially if the OCC was required to publish the list after 
soliciting notice-and-comment. The OCC anticipates that these 
implementing regulations will be updated, as necessary, in the years 
following the effective date of the Act as the business practices of 
issuers continue to evolve and develop.
    The OCC may also issue interpretive letters or guidance to help 
clarify which activities are permissible for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. One commenter asked that the agency commit to 
responding to requests for guidance within a defined timeframe. Because 
the agency does not yet know the frequency of requests, the complexity 
of requests, or how requests will change with the industry's evolution, 
the OCC is unable to determine or commit to how long a response may 
take. As a result, the agency is not defining a timeframe for responses 
at this time, but the OCC may revisit this matter in the future as it 
reviews requests and the industry develops.
Incidental and Digital Asset Service Provider Activities
    The rule of construction in section 4(a)(7)(B) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(B)) provides:
    Nothing in subparagraph (A) shall limit a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer from engaging in payment stablecoin activities or 
digital asset service provider activities specified by this Act, and 
activities incidental thereto, that are authorized by the primary 
Federal payment stablecoin regulator or the State payment stablecoin 
regulator, as applicable, consistent with all other Federal and State 
laws[.]
    In the proposal, the OCC explained that this rule of construction 
clarifies the scope of section 4(a)(7)(A) (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)) 
rather than providing an independent grant of authority.
    With respect to the relationship between sections 4(a)(7)(A) and 
(B) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A) and (B)), one commenter asked 
the agency to clarify that section 4(a)(7)(B) (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(B)) 
is not an independent grant of authority that allows permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to engage in payment stablecoin activities, digital 
asset service provider activities, and activities incidental thereto. 
Instead, the commenter argued section 4(a)(7)(B) (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(7)(B)) only clarifies section 4(a)(7)(A) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(7)(A)). The same commenter further suggested that, in 
clarifying

[[Page 67034]]

section 4(a)(7)(A), the incidental activities in section 4(a)(7)(B) are 
broader than strictly necessary activities and merit an evolving 
framework similar to how the OCC uses interpretive letters to describe 
the bounds of permissible bank activities.
    Similarly, another commenter suggested the agency not draw a sharp 
distinction between activities that directly support enumerated 
activities under section 4(a)(7)(A) and incidental activities under 
section 4(a)(7)(B). In contrast, a different commenter encouraged a 
distinction between 4(a)(7)(A) directly supporting activities and 
4(a)(7)(B) incidental activities, and another comment suggested the OCC 
only publish a list of permissible activities consistent with sections 
4(a)(7)(A) and (B) after public notice and comment.
    As explained above, section 4(a)(7)(B) clarifies the scope of 
section 4(a)(7)(A). With respect to the commenters that requested 
clarification on the distinction between 4(a)(7)(A) directly supporting 
activities and 4(a)(7)(B) incidental activities, based on the phrase 
``consistent with all other Federal and State laws,'' incidental 
activities in 4(a)(7)(B) must be separately authorized under Federal or 
State law. By contrast, section 4(a)(7)(A) provides permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers with an independent grant of authority to engage in 
activities that directly support certain payment stablecoin activities 
under 4(a)(7)(A). As stated above, permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
may ask the OCC to clarify whether an activity is permissible under the 
appropriate grant of authority. The OCC plans to evaluate whether 
specific activities are permissible for a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer under section 4(a)(7) on a case-by-case basis. The agency will 
decide how it will publish such determinations as it gains better 
insight into the volume, breadth, and analytical complexity of these 
evaluations, which will become more apparent once permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers begin operating and interacting with the financial 
system.
    Two commenters recommended that the OCC clarify in Sec.  15.10 that 
the effect of the GENIUS Act's rule of construction in section 
4(a)(7)(B) is that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may conduct 
digital asset service provider activities, and activities incidental 
thereto, when authorized by the OCC and otherwise conducted 
consistently with applicable law. One commenter stated that this 
clarification is necessary to prevent inconsistent interpretations 
among regulated entities, State supervisors, and market participants. 
Another commenter agreed with the need for clarity on this question and 
cautioned against a burdensome and slow prior-approval process for 
digital asset service provider activities, advocating instead for a 
notice-and-nonobjection framework and OCC publication of a non-
exhaustive list of permissible or impermissible digital asset service 
provider activities.
    One commenter suggested that Federally supervised digital asset 
service providers should not need further approval to carry out 
activities contemplated by the Act. In contrast, another commenter 
recommended that the agency define the scope of permissible digital 
asset service provider activities and establish a transparent approval 
process for digital asset service provider activities. One commenter 
suggested the agency clarify any differences in the limitations on 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer permissible activities and the 
limitations on digital asset service provider permissible activities. 
Another commenter suggested that the OCC only authorize permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to engage in digital asset service provider 
activities if they specifically enumerate such activities in their 
application, and that the OCC should require in its application a 
detailed description of the specific digital asset service provider 
activities an issuer proposes to conduct. The commenter recommended 
that applicants be required to publicly release that list and other 
portions of their applications as required for national banks and 
national trust charters, and that any subsequent expansions of digital 
asset service provider activities should require a new approval.
    With respect to comments regarding the scope of digital asset 
service provider activities, as stated above, such activities must be 
independently authorized by a Federal or State law, to the extent that 
any such State law is not inconsistent with Federal law.\64\ The OCC is 
adding new Sec.  15.10(b)(2) which codifies activities that are 
consistent with the rule of construction in section 4(a)(7)(B) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(B)). The OCC is adding this new 
provision to ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may, 
under part 15, engage in digital asset service provider activities 
specified by the Act, and activities incidental thereto, that are 
independently authorized by applicable Federal or State law, to the 
extent that any such State law is not inconsistent with Federal 
law.\65\ Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may contact the OCC with 
questions as they arise, and the OCC will provide additional 
clarification if appropriate.

    After considering the comments, the OCC is not instituting a new or 
separate approval process for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
engage in digital asset service provider activities. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may ask the OCC directly whether specific activities 
are permissible. The OCC will address activities as the market evolves 
and as the OCC is presented with specific facts and information to 
evaluate such requests. The OCC does not have adequate information to 
address such requests at this time nor does it want to constrain itself 
or permitted payment stablecoin issuers to a rigid process. As 
discussed below, the OCC will consider the appropriate means to publish 
any interpretations issued related to digital asset service provider 
activities. The OCC may reconsider in the future whether to institute a 
new or separate approval process once it gains experience supervising 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers and evaluating activity requests.
National Trust Banks
    Proposed Sec.  15.10(b) incorporated language from section 16(a) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5915(a)) and emphasized that nothing in 
proposed Sec.  15.10(a) may be construed to limit the authority of a 
depository institution, national bank, or trust company to engage in 
activities permissible pursuant to applicable State and Federal law. 
Consistent with this provision, for example, an uninsured national bank 
that is a permitted payment stablecoin issuer could engage in 
fiduciary, trust, and other related activities consistent with 
applicable law. Similarly, a national bank or Federal savings 
association could provide crypto-asset custody services, either in a 
fiduciary or non-fiduciary capacity, or use distributed ledger 
technology and related stablecoins to carry out payment activities.\66\ 
Uninsured national banks

[[Page 67035]]

that limit their operations to those of a trust company or activities 
related thereto (national trust banks) \67\ are one type of institution 
within the scope of institutions covered by section 16(a) of the Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5915(a)) and Sec.  15.10(b). Proposed Sec.  15.10(b) would 
also apply to other types of institutions.\68\

the Comptroller of the Currency to be limited to those of a trust 
company and activities related thereto. Any national bank chartered 
under 12 U.S.C. 27(a) is permitted to engage in activities under 12 
U.S.C. 92a or 12 U.S.C. 24(Seventh). A national trust bank chartered in 
reliance on the provision of 12 U.S.C. 27(a) quoted above must limit 
its operations to those of a trust company and activities related 
thereto pursuant to 12 U.S.C. 27(a). For a national trust bank that 
becomes a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the national trust bank 
would have to meet the requirements of both a national bank and a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. In other words, a national trust 
bank's permitted activities would stem from its authority as a national 
bank under 12 U.S.C. 92a or 12 U.S.C. 24(Seventh), including activities 
it is permitted to engage in as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, 
as long as all such activities constitute trust company operations or 
activities related thereto. If the OCC were to read subsection 16(a) of 
the Act narrowly as applying only to institutions that are not 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the rule would contradict how 
section 16(a) operates alongside section 4(a)(7). Rather, the rule does 
not change the scope of permissible activities for national trust 
banks.
    Notwithstanding the potentially broader set of permissible 
activities of national trust banks that are also permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, such national trust banks must still comply with 
the other restrictions of the GENIUS Act and 12 CFR part 15. For 
example, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are prohibited by section 
4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)) from paying yield 
solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment 
stablecoins. A different or broader set of permissible activities does 
not permit national trust banks to evade requirements that are 
applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. More generally, 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers must adhere to applicable laws and 
regulations, including, but not limited to, those regarding activities 
restrictions.
    Like the Department of the Treasury, the OCC also interprets 
section 16(a) such that it is not an independent grant of 
authority.\71\ This final rule addresses the activities that are 
authorized for permitted payment stablecoin issuers regulated by the 
OCC. The OCC will continue to coordinate with the Department of the 
Treasury, as appropriate, consistent with section 13 of the Act.

    One comment suggested the OCC lacks the legal authority to allow 
national trust banks to issue payment stablecoins because statutes 
limit national trust banks to fiduciary capacities and ancillary 
activities. The commenter asked the agency to rescind approvals and 
orders consistent with that interpretation.
    The OCC declines to rescind any approvals because its actions were 
properly taken under 12 U.S.C. 27(a) and 92a. Recent OCC decisions, 
regulatory revisions, and other policies have described the agency's 
understanding of 12 U.S.C. 27(a) and 92a, and nothing in 12 CFR part 15 
changes that understanding.\72\ The Act permits permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to issue payment stablecoins subject to limitations 
in the Act, and the inclusion of uninsured national banks within the 
definition of Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer in section 
2(11) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(11)) is a clear indication that 
Congress intended for national trust banks to be able to apply to be 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers and to issue payment stablecoins.
