    The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.10(b) as proposed, renumbered as 
Sec.  15.10(b)(1).
Proposed Single Brand Restriction
    In the proposed rule, the OCC sought comment on whether it should 
restrict each permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issuing only one 
brand of payment stablecoin and streamline the process for approving 
applications to become a permitted payment stablecoin issuer if an 
affiliate has already been approved as a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.
    Some commenters supported a restriction that would limit a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issuance of a single brand of 
payment stablecoin. Commenters provided various reasons in support of 
the restriction, including

[[Page 67036]]

that it would help ensure legal separateness, adequacy of reserves, and 
maintain safety and soundness. One such commenter stated that white-
label arrangements create risks such as obscuring actual reserves and 
implicit step-in risk for the sponsoring institution to prop up a 
distressed permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Another commenter 
mentioned potential de-pegging, run, and contagion risks and noted that 
appropriate reserve allocation does not necessarily protect against 
issues related to cyberattacks and money laundering.
    Many commenters opposed a requirement that would only allow a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue one brand of payment 
stablecoin. Commenters stated several reasons for their opposition to 
this requirement, including that requiring a separate affiliate to 
issue a different brand of payment stablecoin would create additional 
regulatory burden, make white-labeling economically unviable for all 
but the largest partners, and add complexity without a corresponding 
benefit. One commenter stated that costs of a one-brand requirement 
were not considered in the proposal's economic analysis. One commenter 
stated that the OCC did not identify evidence that a single brand 
restriction would meaningfully reduce risk and that it was not 
adequately explained, arguing that it would be arbitrary and capricious 
for the OCC to include such a limitation. Another commenter stated that 
a single brand restriction would impose asymmetric costs on nonbank 
fintech issuers, for which the white-label distribution model is a 
primary mechanism of market adoption. One commenter stated that the 
final rule should clarify that the supervisory focus is on the issuer 
and not on the branding.
    Some commenters also suggested that a single brand requirement was 
not consistent with the GENIUS Act. Commenters stated that the term 
``outstanding issuance value'' and Congress's use of the term 
``consolidated total outstanding issuance'' suggests that Congress did 
not intend to require product or brand-level segregation of reserves. A 
few commenters stated that language in section 5(g) of the Act (12 
U.S.C. 5904(g)) provides that regulators ``may not impose requirements 
in addition to the requirements specified under section 4,'' which 
militates against a single brand restriction. One commenter suggested 
that any insolvency concerns are better addressed by the statutory 
provisions of the GENIUS Act. A different commenter stated that even if 
a one-brand model were adopted, it would not be clear that a bankruptcy 
court would respect the separate structure because the court could 
potentially consolidate the assets and liabilities of affiliates.
    A few commenters acknowledged that a run on payment stablecoin 
reserves could be a concern in the event a single permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins but 
suggested that a single brand restriction was a disproportionate 
response. Another commenter stated that in times of stress, payment 
stablecoin holders are unlikely to parse legal entity structures or 
differentiate between affiliated issuing entities.
    The OCC is not implementing a one-brand-per-issuer requirement. 
While the OCC agrees with certain commenters that such a requirement 
could help mitigate contagion risks and protect the rights of payment 
stablecoin holders in the event of insolvency, the OCC acknowledges 
that such a restriction would also impose burden and is not clearly 
mandated by the statute. By not implementing such a requirement, the 
OCC is being responsive to the vast majority of commenters that stated 
that such a requirement would increase regulatory burden on permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC understands commenters' concerns 
that a categorical one-brand restriction could lead to duplication of 
supervisory obligations and could potentially make it harder for 
smaller issuers to issue multiple brands of payment stablecoins.
    While the OCC is not mandating a one-brand-per-issuer requirement, 
a one-brand-per-issuer structure may better protect the rights of 
payment stablecoin holders than other models as discussed in more 
detail below. Accordingly, the final rule accommodates business models 
that employ multiple SPV issuers and reduces the burden of using such 
business models, including by making certain technical changes. For 
example, while each SPV would require a license to operate as a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the OCC anticipates that the 
burden of seeking out a new license for an SPV will be limited compared 
to seeking or receiving the initial license, as the applicant could 
leverage information contained in previous applications for other 
related SPVs. Similarly, an SPV could rely on a risk management 
framework developed by its parent entity, provided that the framework 
met the requirements of Sec.  15.13.
    Many commenters suggested potential alternatives to a single brand 
restriction, including that the OCC could require potential disclosures 
to ensure transparency with respect to branding. Specifically, one 
commenter stated that such disclosures should capture same-branded 
issuance across affiliates. One commenter suggested a monthly reserve 
composition disclosure, examined by a registered public accounting firm 
and that includes: (i) the par value of outstanding stablecoins of that 
brand; (ii) the composition of reserve assets attributable to that 
brand; (iii) the legal segregation mechanism applicable to that brand's 
reserves; (iv) operational controls preventing cross-brand encumbrance; 
and (v) the holder claim priority rules applicable in the event of 
issuer distress. Another commenter recommended that the OCC require 
disclosure of the legal identity of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer that is behind each brand. One commenter mentioned that the 
disclosures should be prominent to payment stablecoin purchasers and 
holders and explain which permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
responsible for reserves, redemption, and regulatory compliance. The 
same commenter also stated that issuers should disclose whether the co-
branded payment stablecoins are backed by the same reserve pool, the 
aggregate outstanding issuance across all brands backed by that pool, 
and the co-branding arrangements in the issuer's regulatory filings and 
reserve disclosures.
    The OCC is not adopting additional disclosure requirements with 
respect to branding. The final rule, in Sec.  15.11(e), requires that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers publish a monthly composition 
report that lists the different classes or brands of payment 
stablecoins separately if reserve assets are segregated by brand. 
Accordingly, the monthly report may already contain the number of total 
outstanding payment stablecoins by class or brand and the composition 
of reserves for each brand. The OCC does not believe that additional 
disclosures related to the legal segregation mechanism, operational 
controls, or holder priority are necessary to include in rule text. The 
OCC is not mandating a legal segregation mechanism in the final rule, 
and a description of operational controls could potentially be complex, 
which could confuse payment stablecoin holders. Additionally, because 
of the current inherent uncertainty associated with resolving white-
label issuers, there is a risk that disclosures about a payment 
stablecoin holder's claim in the event of insolvency could misstate the 
legal protection that will ultimately be afforded to payment stablecoin 
holders.
    Moreover, the redemption disclosures in Sec.  15.12(e) of the final 
rule will require

[[Page 67037]]

permitted payment stablecoin issuers to provide the name of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues the payment stablecoin, 
which will allow payment stablecoin holders to identify the issuer 
behind each branded payment stablecoin, including in a white-label 
arrangement or other third-party relationships where the branded coin 
may not otherwise identify the issuer. Such disclosures are required to 
be conspicuous and readily noticeable under Sec.  15.12(e)(1) of the 
final rule, so no further requirements related to prominence are 
necessary. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may include additional 
disclosures regarding their co-branding arrangements and whether co-
branded payment stablecoins are backed by the same reserve pool so long 
as the disclosures comply with the Act, 12 CFR part 15, and other 
applicable laws.
    One commenter stated that issuers should be required to disclose to 
the OCC the internal policies and controls by which they achieve legal 
segregation. Another commenter stated that the OCC should prohibit any 
co-branding arrangement in which the distribution partner represents to 
holders that it, rather than the licensed issuer, is responsible for 
reserves, redemption, or regulatory compliance. Another commenter 
stated that reserve reporting should align with the statute and be at 
the entity level with the option for issuers to report reserves at the 
individual brand level. One commenter stated that there should be 
express disclosures to each brand's holders concerning the multi-brand 
structure and the cross-brand non-encumbrance regime. One commenter 
stated that the OCC should permit and encourage layered, technology-
enabled disclosure approaches.
    The OCC may review a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's internal 
policies and controls during the supervisory process, and therefore, no 
specific disclosure requirement to the OCC is expressly required. 
Additionally, if a distribution partner that is not a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer falsely represents that it is the issuer, the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer responsible for redemption may not 
be in conformance with the disclosure requirements in Sec.  15.12(e). 
For the entities under its jurisdiction, the OCC would ensure that any 
such misrepresentations, at a minimum, are handled through the 
supervisory process. Additionally, the monthly composition report in 
Sec.  15.11(e) of the final rule limits the need for additional 
disclosures around a multi-brand structure because issuers will already 
be required to publish the reserves on a per-brand basis if the brands 
are secured by distinct pools of reserve assets. The monthly 
composition report specifically requires that, to the extent that 
different classes or brands of payment stablecoins are secured by 
distinct pools of reserve assets, permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should publish a composition table for each class or brand of payment 
stablecoin and describe the legal and operational mechanisms, as 
applicable, for how the assets are separately secured. The final rule 
further specifies that if different classes or brands of payment 
stablecoins are issued by distinct issuers, including SPV issuers, a 
separate report must be provided for each issuer.
    Moreover, the final rule does not require that reserves of each 
branded stablecoin be legally separate, and therefore, the OCC is not 
requiring disclosures related to cross-brand encumbrance. Of course, 
reserve assets may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused as 
provided in the Act and in Sec.  15.10(c)(5), and every permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must maintain reserve assets that at all 
times have a reserve asset value that equals or exceeds the outstanding 
issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in accordance 
with Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(iii). As discussed in more detail below, the OCC 
is not prescribing a specific format for disclosures beyond the reports 
required in Sec.  15.14, but technology-enabled disclosures are 
acceptable as long as they conform with the requirements of the Act and 
this final rule.
    In addition to disclosures, many commenters suggested that as an 
alternative to a single brand restriction, permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should segregate reserves based on brand. Another commenter 
suggested specific regulatory text that would allow for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers to 
issue one or more distinctly branded payment stablecoins, provided that 
the issuer satisfies certain brand-level segregation and disclosure 
requirements, including that the issuers maintain reserves in 
segregated account structures, SPVs, or other legally recognized 
segregation mechanisms approved by the OCC. The commenter suggested 
that the OCC could consider on a facts-and-circumstances basis whether 
the issuer's segregation mechanism provides adequate protection for 
reserves. Another commenter stated that the OCC should recognize 
certain statutory cell structures established in other jurisdictions as 
satisfying the legal separateness objective and that not doing so would 
disadvantage issuers operating in jurisdictions whose corporate law 
specifically addresses the segregation issue. One commenter suggested 
that the OCC should address any concerns regarding branded stablecoins 
through its authority in section 4(h)(1) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(h)(1)) by imposing conditions, including maintenance of segregated 
reserves at the issuer level, brand-level attestations that reconcile 
to the issuer's reserves. The same commenter suggested that the OCC 
should condition certain arrangements where there is an evasion of the 
reserve requirements in the Act.
    In the proposed rule, the OCC also asked whether it should require 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to hold reserves in a SPV that is 
fully capitalized by the issuer and has no liabilities. While one 
commenter stated that the OCC has the authority to require the use of 
SPVs when warranted, a few commenters stated that the OCC should 
permit, but not mandate, the use of SPVs to hold different reserves. 
Commenters stated that SPVs should not be mandatory as they would 
impose substantial structural and operational costs, particularly for 
smaller issuers and would not provide meaningful additional protection 
to stablecoin holders. The commenter stated that while SPVs are not 
prohibited under the GENIUS Act, the regulators should work through 
resolution options for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and clarify 
how SPVs would fit into the bankruptcy protections of the GENIUS Act. A 
different commenter stated that if appropriate, issuers should provide 
a legal opinion or third-party attestation confirming that each brand's 
reserve pool is held in a bankruptcy-remote structure. Another 
commenter opposed requiring SPVs for each brand, stating that legal 
separateness would not prevent risk. One commenter stated that certain 
protections apply to the bankruptcy of an issuer, which would raise 
questions about the status of a SPV and how it would manage liquidity. 
One commenter stated that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should 
only be able to issue more than one brand of payment stablecoin if the 
reserves are in a SPV, each program's reserves are managed, valued, and 
reported on a stand-alone basis, and each brand has its own redemption 
arrangements under which redemptions are payable solely from the 
brand's reserves. One commenter stated that such SPVs must have 
documented controls preventing cross-brand reserve encumbrance.

[[Page 67038]]

    The final rule does not require a specific per-brand reserve 
segregation requirement, but reserve assets must comply with the 
requirements of Sec.  15.11, including that they are identifiable and 
segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC retains discretion to 
impose conditions through the licensing process and will consider any 
segregation mechanisms proposed by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer or foreign issuer as well as any alternative approaches and 
determine whether such a mechanism or approach provides adequate 
protection for payment stablecoin holders, which will include 
consideration of whether reserves are adequately protected. With 
respect to statutory cell structures, the OCC will evaluate any 
particular proposed legal segregation mechanism at the time of 
licensing or registration as well as during ongoing supervision. 
However, the OCC declines in this rulemaking to make a categorical 
determination that a particular legal segregation mechanism is 
sufficient or required. With respect to the commenter's concern 
regarding evasion, to the extent that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer evades the reserve requirements of the Act, the OCC would 
consider whether the issuer was violating the Act, Sec.  15.11, or any 
other requirements in part 15.
    As discussed previously, the one-brand-per-issuer structure may 
better protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders than other 
models. Specifically, such a structure could help to ensure that the 
reserves of each brand of payment stablecoin are legally separate, 
reducing the risk that a run on one brand of payment stablecoin causes 
a run on other brands of a related payment stablecoin. Accordingly, 
while the final rule does not require the use of SPVs, the OCC is 
making changes to the final rule to accommodate the use of multiple SPV 
issuers and reduce the burden of using such a business model, including 
by making certain technical changes.
    Commenters stated that the OCC should focus on establishing clear 
regulatory expectations for segregation, clear titling, recordkeeping, 
and labeling of reserve assets to ensure transparency and that the OCC 
should allow issuers to present specific mechanisms for separating and 
tracking reserves across differently branded stablecoins. One commenter 
suggested segregated account structures, including segregated custodial 
sub-accounts at eligible financial institutions, customer-property 
segregation regimes, or other segregation mechanisms approved by the 
OCC. The commenter further stated that the selected mechanism must have 
documented controls preventing the encumbrance, pledging, 
rehypothecation, or commingling of reserves. A few commenters suggested 
that permitted payment stablecoin issuers can set up separate trusts to 
otherwise manage reserve assets. Another commenter suggested token-
level ring-fencing and compliance controls as well as sub-ledgering of 
reserves to address concerns.
    While the OCC is not requiring a particular reserve segregation 
method, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are subject to the 
recordkeeping requirements in Sec.  15.14(f) of the final rule. 
Accordingly, the OCC believes that the final rule sets clear regulatory 
expectations for recordkeeping and labeling of reserves. The OCC agrees 
that issuers should be allowed to present specific mechanisms for 
separating and tracking reserves and will allow issuers to present a 
specific mechanism during the licensing or registration process and as 
part of ongoing supervision. The OCC will consider the use of custodial 
sub-accounts and other customer segregation mechanisms when making a 
facts-and-circumstances determination as to whether payment stablecoin 
holders are adequately protected, including in the event of insolvency. 
Any custodial sub-accounts must comply with the requirements in final 
Sec.  15.22(c). The OCC agrees that documented controls can help to 
strengthen a particular segregation mechanism, which will factor into 
the OCC's evaluation of whether the mechanism protects payment 
stablecoin holders. With respect to the use of separate trusts, the OCC 
again will consider such a mechanism as part of the application 
process, rather than making a categorical determination as part of this 
final rule that such a mechanism adequately protects payment stablecoin 
holders, to ensure a more detailed review of the trusts. Similarly, the 
OCC will need to evaluate in each instance how an issuer seeks to 
achieve token-level ring-fencing to better understand its utility. For 
issuers that use segregation mechanisms, the monthly composition report 
will already require the sub-ledgering of reserve assets.
    In addition to suggestions regarding disclosures and segregation of 
reserves, many commenters suggested other alternatives to a single 
brand restriction. For example, a few commenters suggested redemption 
rights, internal controls, and operational allocation as ways to 
mitigate concerns regarding uncertainty of reserve assets for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers with multiple brands of payment stablecoins.
    The OCC will consider an applicant's internal controls and 
operational allocation when evaluating the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer or foreign issuer during the licensing or registration process. 
An issuer's redemption policies must comply with the Act and, among 
other things, the requirements for redemption in Sec.  15.12. However, 
the OCC expects that there may be some situations where redemption 
rights alone will be insufficient to protect the rights of payment 
stablecoin holders in the event of insolvency.
    A different commenter suggested brand-level CPA examinations and 
explicit operational controls preventing cross-brand reserve 
encumbrance. One commenter suggested that the OCC use its supervisory 
tools to address any issues regarding reserve uncertainty in white-
label arrangements.
    With respect to the suggestion regarding brand-level CPA 
examinations, the monthly reserve composition report required under 
Sec.  15.11(e), which requires reporting of reserve assets by brand, if 
applicable, must be examined by a registered public accounting firm, 
and therefore, no further CPA examination is necessary as an across-
the-board requirement. Additionally, the OCC will use its supervisory 
tools to ensure that any concerns regarding white-label arrangements 
are being managed adequately.
    One commenter stated that the OCC should focus on ensuring that 
there is supervisory coordination and service provider/affiliate risk 
management to cover bank and nonbank consortium members, including 
distribution platforms. Another commenter stated that consistent 
treatment of comparable claimants and operational planning could help 
mitigate risks related to the issuance of multiple brands of payment 
stablecoins.
    The final rule includes risk management requirements related to 
affiliate transactions as well as service provider arrangements. 
Accordingly, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are already expected 
to ensure sufficient oversight of such arrangements. To the extent that 
members of a white-label arrangement are regulated by another entity, 
the OCC will strive to ensure there is supervisory coordination between 
agencies. With respect to treating comparable claimants consistently, a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer must comply with the

[[Page 67039]]

Act and the redemption requirements in 12 CFR part 15. Additionally, 
the OCC encourages operational planning and expects it would be prudent 
for most issuers to engage in such planning in the ordinary course of 
business.
    One commenter suggested that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
should be required to submit a brand-level stress-period redemption 
plan setting forth: (i) the threshold conditions that will trigger 
stress-period mechanisms for the branded payment stablecoins it issues 
or may issue in the future; (ii) the redemption queue, prioritization, 
and processing protocols applicable during stress; (iii) the 
communication and disclosure protocols for that brand's holders; and 
(iv) the operational steps to ensure that brand-level stress does not 
propagate to other brands.
    The OCC is adding monetization and stress-testing requirements for 
all permitted payment stablecoin issuers in Sec.  15.13(a)(9) of the 
final rule. In addition, final Sec.  15.11 requires that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers must demonstrate the operational capability 
to access and monetize identifiable reserve assets to meet redemptions, 
in both normal and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest 
rate conditions. Accordingly, the OCC is not instituting any white-
label specific stress testing because a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer that issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins must ensure 
that it can access and monetize reserve assets to meet redemption 
requests for all brands of payment stablecoins. As discussed above, the 
OCC is not instituting additional communication and disclosure 
protocols. The OCC will consider the operational steps an issuer takes 
to ensure that brand-level stress does not propagate to other brands as 
part of the licensing, registration, and ongoing supervisory process.
    A few commenters stated that the OCC should align with the FDIC's 
notice of proposed rulemaking implementing the GENIUS Act and manage 
brand-level obligations through mandating disclosures and ensuring that 
required reserves can be separately identified as backing a particular 
brand of payment stablecoin. A few commenters suggested that if the OCC 
were not to align with the FDIC, it would create regulatory divergence 
and favor FDIC-regulated issuers. Similarly, one commenter suggested 
coordination with the other Federal regulators to ensure consistent 
requirements for white-label arrangements.
    The OCC declines to take the same approach as the FDIC did in its 
notice of proposed rulemaking, which requires multi-brand issuers to 
have a segregated pool of reserves that are recorded separately, unless 
the FDIC approves in writing that the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may commingle reserves. Instead, the OCC is taking a case-by-
case approach during the licensing or registration process and will 
evaluate whether payment stablecoin holders are adequately protected 
when the issuer issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins. The OCC 
believes this approach allows issuers flexibility to explain to the OCC 
how it can adequately protect payment stablecoin holders when issuing 
multiple brands of payment stablecoins. The OCC will coordinate with 
other primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators and will 
continually evaluate its treatment of white-label arrangements to 
strive for consistent treatment.
    A few commenters stated some conditions they would favor if the OCC 
were to impose a single brand restriction. One commenter stated that if 
the OCC does require a separate issuer for each brand of payment 
stablecoin, the OCC would need to clarify how capital, liquidity, and 
other risk management requirements and governance arrangements would be 
applied across each separate issuer. Another commenter stated that if 
the OCC adopts such a restriction, it should clarify that the 
restriction applies to issuer and custodian functions and does not 
require highly duplicative per-brand separation of infrastructure.
    Although the OCC is not imposing a single brand restriction, the 
OCC is clarifying how capital, liquidity, and other risk management 
requirements and governance arrangements would be applied if a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer makes use of an SPV during the 
licensing or registration process. The OCC is committed to ensuring 
that the use of an SPV would not cause unnecessary duplication of 
supervisory obligations.
    A few commenters remarked on the language in the proposal that 
suggested that the OCC was considering streamlining the licensing 
process for affiliates if it were to impose a single brand restriction. 
A few commenters stated that if the OCC decides that separate legal 
entities are required for each brand, the OCC should adopt a 
streamlined approval process. One commenter suggested a notification-
based process, under which the OCC confirms approval within a defined 
timeframe. One commenter stated that the OCC should clarify that a 
license for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should extend to 
cover any consolidated affiliates of the issuer that issue the same 
token under the same brand and reserve framework, without requiring a 
separate license application for each affiliate entity. Another 
commenter stated that any requirements relating to multi-brand issuance 
should be applied consistently across all OCC-regulated entities. One 
commenter stated that State regulatory agencies would need to review 
applications for a new entity and a streamlined process for affiliates 
of already-approved issuers would be antithetical to how State 
regulatory agencies operate and would not enhance safety and soundness.
    The OCC is not revising the application process for affiliates 
because it is not imposing a one-brand restriction and the final 
application process is sufficiently streamlined to limit burden for SPV 
issuers. To the extent that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer makes 
use of an SPV, the OCC will ensure that the process is streamlined if 
the SPV is a separate issuer. If an affiliate is issuing the same token 
under the same brand and reserve framework but is a different issuer, 
the issuer would need to apply separately to the OCC through the 
licensing or registration process; a license to issue payment 
stablecoins is not a group-wide authorization that automatically 
extends to affiliates.
Multi-Jurisdictional Stablecoin Issuance
    In the proposal, the OCC asked whether it should address permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers that also issue or redeem the same or 
similar stablecoins in one or more foreign jurisdictions, sometimes 
referred to as multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance.
    Many commenters stated that the OCC should clarify that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers may engage in multi-jurisdictional issuance, 
emphasizing that fungibility, transferability, and global circulation 
are central features of payment stablecoins. Commenters stated that, 
absent OCC guidance, multi-jurisdictional issuance could be subject to 
uncertainty and barriers that impede cross-border adoption and prevent 
payment stablecoins from circulating on a global basis. One commenter 
specifically advocated for a safe harbor for such arrangements. One 
commenter stated that section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)) explicitly permits reserves at correspondents and 
foreign agents of insured depository institutions, reflecting that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers will conduct issuance and 
redemption activity outside of the

[[Page 67040]]

United States as a matter of ordinary operations.
    Commenters identified several issues that would result from the OCC 
not addressing multi-jurisdictional issuance, including duplicative or 
conflicting supervisory expectations, inefficient reserve allocation, 
inconsistent redemption architecture, and technical design mandates 
that fragment liquidity and undermine interoperability. One commenter 
stated that the OCC should ensure permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
licenses include like-branded stablecoins issued by consolidated 
affiliates to ensure OCC visibility and accountability for all like-
branded stablecoins. One commenter requested that the final rules 
enable a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its foreign affiliate 
to rebalance reserve assets to meet their redemption needs, provided 
that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its affiliate at all 
times hold reserves on a 1 to 1 basis against the total outstanding 
issuance of their aggregate payment stablecoins.
    Many commenters mentioned coordination with the United States 
Department of the Treasury or other regulators with respect to multi-
jurisdictional stablecoin issuance. Specifically, a few commenters 
urged coordination between the OCC and Treasury with respect to 
Treasury's obligations under section 18 of the Act regarding making 
determinations that foreign countries have comparable regulatory and 
supervisory regimes. A few commenters stated that multi-jurisdictional 
stablecoin issuance should be permissible when Treasury has made a 
comparability determination or entered into certain reciprocal 
arrangements.
    Another commenter stated that the OCC should not push stablecoin 
issuers to create multiple licensed entities in different jurisdictions 
to achieve multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance. One commenter 
stated that even if such a push would have short-term benefits, 
separate licensing for separate entities in separate jurisdictions 
would be inconsistent with the GENIUS Act, including with respect to 
reciprocal arrangements under section 18(d) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5916(d)). A different commenter stated that foreign jurisdictions 
seeking reciprocity should not be permitted to impose fundamentally 
different prudential requirements on permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. One commenter stated that the OCC should provide a safe harbor 
for foreign affiliates that operate under a comparable regime, 
including guidance that addresses reserve location, reserve 
rebalancing, disclosures, customer segregation, redemption routing, 
operational controls, and examination expectations for the relevant 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Another commenter stated that the 
OCC should clarify that the operations of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer are subject to compliance with applicable 
requirements under the laws of other jurisdictions in which it issues 
stablecoins. One commenter stated that the OCC should engage with 
relevant electronic money institution regulators in the European Union 
to further support global acceptance of multi-jurisdictional issuance. 
The commenter further stated that the OCC should prioritize functional 
coordination with foreign regulators whenever an OCC-supervised 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer operates through foreign regulated 
issuing affiliates, including through memoranda of understanding and 
information sharing protocols.
    As explained below, the OCC is not specifically addressing multi-
jurisdictional issuance in the regulatory text of the final rule. The 
OCC agrees with the numerous commenters that stated that the OCC should 
coordinate with the Department of the Treasury and foreign regulators. 
Under section 18 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5916), the Secretary of the 
Treasury may determine whether a foreign country has a comparable 
regulatory and supervisory regime upon a recommendation from the other 
members of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee. Additionally, 
the Secretary of the Treasury may also create and implement reciprocal 
arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States 
and jurisdictions with comparable payment stablecoin regulatory 
regimes. Accordingly, the OCC declines to provide any guidance on such 
determinations or reciprocal arrangements, as they are within the 
authority of the Department of the Treasury. Similarly, the OCC is not 
providing a safe harbor for foreign affiliates that operate under a 
comparable regime because these are determinations of the Department of 
the Treasury that have yet to be made, and as noted, the OCC plans to 
coordinate with the Department of the Treasury as appropriate on the 
continuing implementation of section 18 of the Act. Additionally, the 
OCC will not opine on the applicability of foreign laws because doing 
so is outside the scope of this rulemaking, which focuses on 
implementing the GENIUS Act.\73\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\73\ The OCC notes that section 3(e) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5902(e)) provides that section 3 is intended to have 
extraterritorial effect if conduct involves the offer or sale of a 
payment stablecoin to a person located in the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC also expects to be able to assess in more detail multi-
jurisdictional issuance arrangements on a case-by-case basis, including 
how such arrangements comply with the requirement in section 4(a)(1)(A) 
of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)) that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer ``maintain identifiable reserves backing the 
outstanding payment stablecoins of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer on at least [a] 1 to 1 basis.''
    Because multi-jurisdictional arrangements may involve the 
rebalancing of reserves among the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
and its affiliates, it is especially important that the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer comply with the requirement in Sec.  15.11(a) 
that it maintain reserves that at all times have a reserve asset value 
that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer.
    Commenters also suggested specific areas where OCC standards or 
guidance would be useful with respect to multi-jurisdictional issuance, 
including disclosures, reporting, supervisory expectations, risk 
management, the applicable governing regime, reserve treatment, 
customer-protection requirements, timely redemption, ring-fencing risk, 
redemption rights, customer segregation, and examination coordination. 
Several commenters focused on reserve and redemption issues. One 
commenter stated that the OCC should clarify whether cross-border 
redemption to foreign bank accounts may be subject to a reasonable 
timeline longer than two business days. Others stated that the OCC 
should address reserve rebalancing across jurisdictions, including by 
permitting reserve assets to move in both directions between a U.S.-
based permitted payment stablecoin issuer and cross-border affiliates. 
One commenter specifically stated that the issuer and its affiliates 
should maintain reserves on a 1 to 1 basis.
    As stated, the OCC is declining to provide specific guidance on 
multi-jurisdictional issuance beyond the fact that such arrangements 
must comply with the Act and part 15. The OCC intends to coordinate 
with Treasury and foreign regulators, as appropriate, prior to 
providing any guidance on these arrangements. The OCC declines to

[[Page 67041]]

provide an exception allowing cross-border redemptions to be completed 
on a longer redemption timeframe than domestic redemptions. All 
redemptions must comply with the requirements in Sec.  15.12 of the 
final rule, including that timely redemptions may not exceed two 
business days following the date of the requested redemption. As 
explained below in response to comments about Sec.  15.12, the final 
rule clarifies the beginning and end of the redemption timeline while 
retaining the baseline for timely redemption. Under Sec.  15.12(a)(1) 
of the final rule, the obligation to redeem begins with the receipt of 
a redemption order from a customer and the satisfaction of conditions 
necessary to permit redemption (such as customer onboarding). Under 
Sec.  15.12(a)(2) of the final rule, a redemption that involves an 
outgoing transfer of monetary value is deemed to occur when the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer has fully processed and initiated 
the outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer or customer's 
financial institution as directed by the customer. Given the changes to 
Sec.  15.12, a longer redemption timeframe for cross-border redemption 
is unnecessary as certain processes that could take longer in a cross-
border context (e.g., the time required for funds to be received or 
credited to an account) are outside the redemption timeframe. The OCC 
is not specifically addressing reserve rebalancing in the final rule, 
except to state that such arrangements must comply with the Act and 
this final rule, including the requirement that reserve assets must 
fully back outstanding payment stablecoins at all times.
    Commenters also urged clear reporting, disclosures, and brand-level 
transparency, including measures to distinguish United States issuance 
activity from foreign activity. With respect to technology, one 
commenter supported requiring or encouraging blockchain infrastructure 
to support jurisdiction-specific compliance rule sets, while another 
opposed OCC mandates for particular technical architectures, such as 
wrappers, separate token contracts, or separate token addresses. 
Another commenter stated that operational risks associated with multi-
jurisdictional stablecoin issuance should be addressed through existing 
contingency planning and robust risk management frameworks and that the 
OCC should require issuers to incorporate cross-border risks (e.g., 
redemption demand exceeding local liquidity) in contingency planning 
and liquidity management frameworks.
    The OCC agrees that clear reporting, disclosures, and transparency 
could be helpful in promoting clarity with respect to multi-
jurisdictional arrangements, but the OCC needs more information before 
it can specifically provide clarity on how these topics apply to such 
arrangements. Similarly, the OCC is not setting any technical mandates 
for such arrangements for the same reason. To the extent a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer engages in multi-jurisdictional issuance, any 
risk management requirements in the final rule will still apply.
    A few commenters urged the OCC to avoid prescriptive requirements, 
rigid segregation requirements, or a categorical ban that would 
disfavor multi-jurisdictional issuance. For example, one commenter 
stated that the OCC should evaluate issuers based on the adequacy of 
their risk management frameworks rather than impose mandates that could 
artificially segment tokens, reserves, infrastructure, or disclosures 
by jurisdiction. Commenters cautioned that such requirements could 
impair liquidity management, increase operational complexity, undermine 
fungibility, and worsen redemption risk. Commenters also stated that 
the OCC should permit shared infrastructure, compliance services, and 
personnel; allow holders to redeem through any participating permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer within a network, subject to BSA checks and 
OCC timely-redemption standards; and consider allowing a unified 
reserve pool for all outstanding tokens, provided United States holders 
retain clear redemption rights. One commenter stated that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer licenses should include like-branded 
stablecoins issued by consolidated affiliates. The commenter further 
stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuer licenses should 
encompass the issuer and any consolidated affiliates issuing the same 
token.
    The OCC is neither imposing prescriptive requirements nor a 
categorical ban on multi-jurisdictional issuance as it believes further 
coordination and experience would be useful to ensure any potential 
guidance on such arrangements is responsive and fully informed. For 
these reasons, the OCC declines to provide further guidance on shared 
infrastructure, redemption rights specific to such arrangements, and 
the idea of a unified reserve pool. As previously stated, any such 
arrangements must comply with the Act and the requirements in this 
final rule, including those related to redemption.
2. Reserve Assets (Sec.  15.11)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Sec.  15.11
    In both the proposed rule and the final rule, Sec.  15.11(a) 
contains reserve requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. 
The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.11(a)(1) largely as proposed except for a 
substitution of ``reserve asset value'' where the proposed rule had 
used ``total fair value'' in Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(iii). As in the 
proposal, final Sec.  15.11(a)(2) requires permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to demonstrate the operational capability to access and 
monetize the identifiable reserve assets, but the final rule further 
explains that such operational capability is to meet redemptions under 
various conditions after taking into account several relevant factors, 
which had been raised in the preamble of the proposed rule and are now 
being codified in the regulatory text itself. New Sec.  15.11(a)(3) 
requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to ensure that reserve 
asset value will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance value 
at all times and that the reserve asset portfolio will be capable of 
supporting timely redemption under both normal conditions and adverse 
economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, including, 
to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of reserve assets in 
excess of outstanding issuance value. The agency is adopting proposed 
Sec.  15.11(a)(3), renumbered as Sec.  15.11(a)(4) and revised, to 
address when a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may withdraw reserve 
assets in excess of outstanding issuance value. While the proposed 
version of this paragraph permitted withdrawals of surplus reserve 
assets only once per month and explained how a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must make such a withdrawal, the final version 
permits withdrawals of reserve assets at any time following appropriate 
due diligence and confirmation that the withdrawal would not cause 
reserve asset value to fall below outstanding issuance value. Final 
Sec.  15.11(a)(4) also deletes the phrase ``any surplus'' as 
superfluous because the phrase ``reserve assets in excess of 
outstanding issuance value'' sufficiently identifies what constitutes 
surplus reserve assets. Final Sec.  15.11(a)(4) does not subject income 
earned from reserve assets to due diligence and confirmation 
requirements for withdrawal, as long as a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer otherwise complies with the requirements of the final rule 
necessary to ensure that reserve asset value at all

[[Page 67042]]

times equals or exceeds outstanding issuance value.
    Final Sec.  15.11(b) describes the composition of reserve assets 
much as the proposed Sec.  15.11(b) did. The OCC is finalizing Sec.  
15.11(b)(1), (3), and (4) as proposed. In Sec.  15.11(b)(2), the OCC 
has modified the description of deposits and insured shares to more 
closely align with the Act. In adopting the phrasing used by the Act 
(``funds held as demand deposits''), the OCC is clarifying that reserve 
assets held as deposits must be deposits payable on demand (i.e., 
without features that would delay or condition withdrawals), 
notwithstanding interpretations of the phrase ``demand deposits'' from 
other contexts.\74\ In Sec.  15.11(b)(5), the OCC is making a minor 
technical change (adding the word ``or''). In Sec.  15.11(b)(6), the 
OCC is making a technical change to add paragraphs (b)(6)(i) and 
(b)(6)(ii) but is not changing substantively which securities are 
eligible as a reserve asset. In Sec.  15.11(b)(7), the OCC is 
finalizing the rule as proposed with the clarification that OCC 
approval of other liquid Federal Government-issued assets is subject to 
such conditions as the OCC may impose consistent with the purposes of 
the GENIUS Act. In Sec.  15.11(b)(8), the OCC is making minor technical 
changes.

    The final versions of Sec.  15.11(c) and (d) have substantial 
differences from their proposed versions. For Sec.  15.11(c), 
addressing reserve asset diversification and concentration, the 
proposal included two options, described in the proposal as Option A 
and Option B. The OCC is finalizing the version of Sec.  15.11(c)(1) 
from Option A but is splitting up proposed Sec.  15.11(c)(1) into 
paragraphs (c)(1)(i) and (c)(1)(ii) and adding a new paragraph 
(c)(1)(iii) clarifying that, in order to comply with paragraphs 
(c)(1)(i) and (c)(1)(ii), permitted payment stablecoin issuers may need 
to maintain a portfolio of reserve assets that exceeds the requirements 
of paragraph (c)(2) and the reserve asset value of which exceeds 
outstanding issuance value.
    For Sec.  15.11(c)(2), the OCC is finalizing an edited version of 
Option B. Whereas Sec.  15.11(c)(1) in Option B required a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to maintain at least 10 percent of its 
reserve assets as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand or 
money to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, final 
Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(i) requires at least 5 percent in demand deposits (or

does not include Sec.  15.11(c)(2) of Option B that would have required

modified Sec.  15.11(c)(3) of Option B, renumbered as Sec.  
15.11(c)(2)(ii), such that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must

version had required permitted payment stablecoin issuers to maintain 
no more than 40 percent of reserve assets at any one eligible financial 
institution across any of several listed exposures. The agency is 
finalizing Sec.  15.11(c) without Sec.  15.11(c)(4) and (5) from Option 
B, which addressed holdings at any one eligible financial institution 
and the weighted average maturity of reserve assets, respectively.
    The OCC replaced Sec.  15.11(d) of the proposed rule, which was 
about the minimum amount of reserve assets that must be insured, with 
final Sec.  15.11(d), which describes when reserve assets in the 
custody of one or more eligible financial institutions are not subject 
to the 40 percent limitation in final Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(ii).
    The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.11(e) as proposed with conforming 
and technical edits throughout, including to the template monthly 
composition report. Additionally, the agency is finalizing Sec.  
15.11(f) as proposed with certain clarifying edits. In Sec.  15.11(g), 
the agency is finalizing the rule as proposed with certain clarifying 
edits throughout, including using the phrase ``minimum reserve asset 
amount required by paragraph (a) of this section'' in Sec.  
15.11(g)(1), (g)(2), and (g)(3). Additionally, in Sec.  15.11(g)(2)(i), 
the OCC is clarifying that a noncompliant permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may issue new payment stablecoins if permitted by the OCC. The 
OCC is also making technical changes to Sec.  15.11(g)(4) and splitting 
that paragraph into three paragraphs (g)(4)(i) through (g)(4)(iii).
b. Reserve Requirements (Sec.  15.11(a))
    Section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)) 
requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain identifiable 
reserves backing the outstanding payment stablecoins of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer on at least a 1 to 1 basis with reserves 
comprising certain high-quality assets specified in the Act. Section 
4(a)(4)(A) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)) requires the OCC, among 
other regulators, to issue regulations to implement certain liquidity 
standards as well as reserve asset diversification and interest rate 
risk management standards that are tailored to the business model and 
risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and do not exceed 
the standards that are sufficient to ensure the ongoing operations of 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5909) also imposes requirements on the ``Custody of Payment 
Stablecoin Reserve and Collateral,'' including restrictions on 
commingling certain assets. Consistent with these various sources of 
authority, the proposed rule included requirements related to reserve 
assets in several sections, including proposed Sec.  15.11 (``Reserve 
Assets''), Sec.  15.13 (``Risk Management''), and subpart C 
(``Custody''). Proposed subpart C's custody requirements would have 
applied to OCC-regulated custodians while proposed Sec.  15.11's 
reserve asset requirements would have applied to OCC-regulated 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. These requirements mirror each 
other but apply to distinct sets of entities (the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers placing the reserve assets and the custodians 
holding them).
    Proposed Sec.  15.11 set forth (a) requirements relating to 
ensuring that there are sufficient reserves backing a payment 
stablecoin, (b) the assets eligible to serve as reserve assets, (c) 
diversification and concentration requirements, (d) minimum insured 
deposit requirements, (e) monthly reporting requirements, (f) monthly 
certification requirements, and (g) requirements relating to the 
failure to maintain the required minimum amount of reserve assets. With 
respect to diversification and concentration risk, the proposed rule 
presented two options: Option A (a principles-based general requirement 
coupled with a quantitative safe harbor) and Option B (mandatory 
quantitative minimums). The proposed rule also included risk management 
requirements related to reserve assets, including liquidity and 
interest rate risk management.
    Many commenters offered general comments on the proposed liquidity, 
diversification, and concentration requirements. Several of these 
commenters recommended that reserve and redemption requirements should 
be clear or strict to protect consumers and reduce run risk, and these 
commenters generally recommended that liquidity requirements should be 
in line with

[[Page 67043]]

those that apply to banks. One commenter stated that the proposed 
rule's emphasis on high-quality reserves, segregation of assets, 
defined redemption timelines, and operational backstops is 
directionally supportive of credit stability.
    A few commenters stated that the proposed liquidity and 
diversification requirements were overly strict or inflexible. One of 
these commenters also argued that the GENIUS Act grants the OCC 
authority to require reserve asset diversification but not 
diversification across reserve asset custodians. One commenter stated 
that liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements are not 
adequate to prevent the risk of stablecoins ``breaking the buck'' and 
that only capital protections are adequate to address those losses.
    One commenter stated that liquidity requirements should focus on 
the speed and reliability of monetizing assets since the relevant 
stress scenario for permitted payment stablecoin issuers is a surge in 
redemption rather than deterioration in asset quality. Another 
commenter recommended that liquidity requirements be tiered based on 
issuer size. One commenter stated that reserve composition requirements 
do not address the liquidity-during-receivership gap demonstrated by 
the failure of Silicon Valley Bank.
    A few commenters stated that concentration requirements should be 
calibrated to existing supervisory expectations to avoid duplicative 
burdens. One commenter argued that concentration risk should be 
assessed together with the quality and operational reliability of the 
counterparty, as it may be safer for large-scale issuers to rely on 
concentrated exposure to a stronger, better integrated institution that 
can provide operational liquidity at sufficient scale to satisfy timely 
redemption. One commenter favored a principles-based approach to 
concentration and diversification in lieu of fixed limits, and this 
commenter cautioned that concentration and diversification requirements 
could push reserve assets to institutions with less operational 
capability to manage and deploy reserve assets. One commenter 
recommended addressing concentration risk by requiring larger issuers 
to report sector-level concentrations. A few commenters recommended 
against adding additional categories of risk to be considered beyond 
credit, liquidity, interest rate, and price risk. One of these 
commenters stated that counterparty risks can be better addressed 
through the examination process than with quantitative limits.
    After carefully considering the comments received, the OCC is 
revising Sec.  15.11 to provide additional flexibility while still 
including certain core requirements intended to ensure that payment 
stablecoins remain appropriately reserved at all times and available to 
meet redemptions. A detailed description of the proposed rule and 
changes to it, including the OCC's reasoning for any changes, follows. 
At a high level, the OCC is adopting a principles-based approach with 
respect to reserve asset diversification and concentration requirements 
supplemented by two quantitative requirements designed to ensure a 
minimum amount of daily liquidity and avoid excessive concentration 
with respect to a single counterparty (e.g., to address the possibility 
of operational disruptions at certain counterparties and to mitigate 
potential credit risk posed by certain counterparties). The final rule 
also includes additional provisions designed to ensure that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers are able to monetize reserve assets in 
stressed conditions, including new stress-testing provisions in Sec.  
15.13, and provisions relating to the use of custodians.
i. Description of Proposed Rule
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1) would have required that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers maintain reserve assets that: (i) are 
identifiable; (ii) are segregated from and not commingled with other 
assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (iii) 
at all times have a total fair value that equals or exceeds the 
outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; 
and (iv) are either held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution. To 
maintain reserve assets that are ``identifiable'' and comply with 
proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(i), permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
would have needed to maintain appropriate records to ensure documented 
ownership and legal entitlement to individual reserve assets. 
Similarly, any ownership arrangements, including ownership of assets 
held via custodians, must comply with applicable laws and regulations, 
for example, requirements applicable to customer securities owned 
through the Fedwire Securities Service. An issuer would have been 
required to maintain the appropriate operational capabilities, internal 
controls, policies, and safeguards to ensure that stablecoins are 
always backed by reserves on an at least 1 to 1 basis. Among other 
things, safeguards could include mechanisms to prevent the issuance of 
abnormally large amounts of new payment stablecoins without additional 
approvals.
    To comply with the requirement in proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(ii), a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to ensure that 
reserve assets were appropriately segregated from and not commingled 
with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.
    To comply with the requirement in proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(iii), 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to ensure that 
the fair value of reserve assets equaled or exceeded the outstanding 
issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(iv) would have required that the reserve 
assets must either be held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution, 
which is defined in proposed Sec.  15.2.
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(2) would have required that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer demonstrate the operational capability to 
access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets, commensurate with 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business 
model. The issuer would have needed to be able to monetize the reserve 
assets, potentially quickly and at short notice, in order to meet 
redemption requests.
    To comply with proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(2), a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer would have needed to be able to demonstrate the 
ability to monetize all types of reserve assets it maintains.
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(3) included requirements for when permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers could withdraw reserve assets in excess of 
outstanding issuance value. In order to ensure that, at all times, 
sufficient reserve assets are maintained to back outstanding stablecoin 
issuance, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been 
permitted to withdraw excess reserve assets only after the monthly 
examination and certification required by section 4(a)(1) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)) and provided for in proposed Sec.  15.11(e) 
and (f). Specifically, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have 
been able to withdraw any surplus reserve assets in excess of 
outstanding issuance value, calculated and reported as of the last day 
of the previous month, only upon the publication of that month's public 
disclosure, due at the end of the subsequent month. Proposed

[[Page 67044]]

Sec.  15.11(a)(3) would have also required that, while withdrawals 
would be based on calculations as of the end of the previous month, a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer could only make withdrawals if the 
remaining reserve assets remained at least equal to the current 
outstanding issuance value, calculated as of the day of withdrawal.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
    Commenters expressed different views regarding proposed Sec.  
15.11(a)(1)(iii)'s requirement that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers maintain reserves that ``[a]t all times have a total fair value 
that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer,'' both regarding the ``at all times'' 
standard and the potential propriety of alternative valuation 
methodologies.
    Regarding the ``at all times'' standard, some commenters supported 
a real-time valuation standard, noting that proof of reserves 
technologies can provide near-real-time information regarding reserves. 
Some of the commenters further noted that the OCC should allow 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to rely on continuous, 
cryptographically verifiable on-chain attestations provided by eligible 
custodians to fulfill this requirement. However, other commenters 
believed that the language was ambiguous, that a strictly real-time 
valuation standard would introduce unnecessary complexity, be 
impractical and, in some cases, may be impossible, based on underlying 
technology, intra-day asset value fluctuations, and settlement or 
clearing timing differences, and would be out of step with how other 
assets are valued. These commenters instead supported an end-of-day 
standard as more practical and effective.
    Regarding the valuation of reserve assets, some commenters noted 
that fair value may not be applicable in all cases. These commenters 
noted examples such as money market mutual funds, which are measured at 
their net asset value, and reverse repo agreements, which may be 
carried at cost less impairment. Some commenters recommended allowing 
valuation using amortized cost.
    The OCC requested comment on whether ``the proposed rule [should] 
include additional measures to ensure that reserve assets are 
appropriately traceable and linked to their corresponding stablecoin so 
as to avoid any difficulties in resolving claims to reserve assets.'' 
One commenter responded that such traceability would be operationally 
impractical and would not have a commensurate risk management benefit. 
The OCC agrees and has not adopted any additional regulation text 
requiring that reserve assets be traceable and linked to their 
corresponding payment stablecoin for these reasons. The OCC notes, 
however, that permitted payment stablecoin issuers must maintain 
identifiable reserves backing the outstanding value of payment 
stablecoins.\75\ One commenter requested that the OCC clarify the 
permissibility of automated reserve asset management systems, including 
those executed via smart contracts.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \75\ See 12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing 
Sec.  15.11(a)(1) with one minor change. The final rule replaces a 
reference to ``total fair value'' with the new defined term ``reserve 
asset value.'' The final rule continues to require an issuer to 
maintain reserve assets, the value of which equals or exceeds the 
outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
at all times. This requirement follows directly from section 4(a)(1)(A) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)). The final rule also 
continues to require reserve assets to be valued at fair value (with 
the exception of United States coins and currency, which must be valued 
at par) as a result of the new defined term ``reserve asset value.'' 
Valuing reserve assets at fair value (i.e., market value) will help 
ensure that the reserve assets maintained by the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer reflect current prices and will be monetizable at a 
value sufficient to meet any redemption requests at par value. The OCC 
notes that ``outstanding issuance value'' is based on the total par 
value of all of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's payment 
stablecoins rather than on the fair value of the outstanding issued 
payment stablecoin. Thus, if the fair value of the payment stablecoin 
decreased (i.e., if the payment stablecoin de-pegged in the secondary 
market), the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would nevertheless be 
obligated to retain a stock of reserve assets, the fair value of which 
equals or exceeds the par value of outstanding payment stablecoins.
    Taking a contrary approach (e.g., basing the outstanding issuance 
value on the fair value of payment stablecoins) would be inconsistent 
with the plain text and goals of the GENIUS Act.\76\ Moreover, such an 
approach could allow permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
inappropriately remove assets from the required stock of reserve assets 
when stablecoins de-peg (as reserve asset requirements decline, along 
with the secondary market price of the stablecoin), rather than 
maintaining the reserve assets on behalf of stablecoin holders, which 
may in turn exacerbate run risk for a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. In response to certain comments, the OCC confirms that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers may use automated reserve asset 
management systems provided that the systems used conform to the 
requirements of Sec. Sec.  15.11, 15.13, and 15.14 as well as any other 
applicable requirements in part 15.

    The OCC notes that it anticipates that reserve assets generally 
will be recorded on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's balance 
sheet under GAAP and be included in the quarterly reports required 
under proposed Sec.  15.14(i) and on Call Report Schedule RC, Balance 
Sheet, for a parent insured national bank or Federal savings 
association.
    Several commenters addressed the requirement in proposed Sec.  
15.11(a)(3) that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may only 
``withdraw any surplus reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance 
value once per month, upon publication of the composition report 
required.'' Many commenters requested clarifications or amendments to 
this proposed requirement. Some commenters noted that the requirement 
may have unintended consequences--for example, it may disincentivize 
issuers holding excess reserves since the rule would impose a 
significant delay should the issuer decide to withdraw some amount of 
such excess. Other commenters suggested that the end-of-month timing 
may incentivize issuers to increase their reserves at month's end. One 
commenter argued that surplus reserve withdrawals should be calculated 
based on the present value of the reserves, rather than the value 
reported for the prior month. The commenter stated that this approach 
would decrease risk that withdrawals cause the reserve assets to fall 
below the 1 to 1 ratio. Still another commenter requested clarification 
as to whether withdrawals may only occur on the actual day of the 
specified report in Sec.  15.11(e) (discussed below).
    Some commenters requested clarity on when an asset becomes a 
reserve asset and recommended adding requirements concerning the 
handling of funds prior to the point at which they become reserve 
assets. Some commenters advocated for requiring reserve principal, 
earnings, and interest to remain identifiable and traceable until the 
issuer verifies the existence of excess and completes an authorized

[[Page 67045]]

withdrawal procedure. Others opposed treating interest generated from 
reserve assets as reserve assets, stating that such treatment is not 
mandated by statute. Some argued in favor of treating customer funds as 
reserve assets immediately on receipt of such funds.
    Relatedly, several commenters expressed views on the propriety of 
charging expenses related to management of the reserve assets against 
the reserve assets. Many commenters stated that, as a general matter, 
such expenses should not be chargeable against the reserve assets. 
However, several commenters offered exceptions, for example, one 
commenter noted that transaction-related expenses, such as interest on 
repurchase agreements or investment management fees, should be 
chargeable against the reserve assets. Another commenter stated that 
management should have discretion as to the use of excess reserves if 
the use of such excess reserve assets is subject to an appropriate 
policy or agreement.
    Several commenters noted the importance of liquidity planning 
regarding reserve assets in addition to an issuer's broader risk 
management obligations. Several commenters, for example, suggested that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to adopt 
written plans, policies, and procedures related to liquidity planning, 
noting the importance of formal documentation in forcing an issuer to 
identify risks in advance, assign responsibility, and assess 
contingency options prior to stress arising. Other commenters discussed 
specific contingency planning issues, such as Federal Reserve discount 
window or Federal Home Loan Bank lending access for certain issuers or 
mandated recovery and resolution plans. Still other commenters noted 
that liquidity and contingency plans should be tailored to an issuer's 
operational and risk profile or should take into account any related 
liquidity planning that an issuer may already be subject to under other 
regulations.
    Other commenters noted that it is also important for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to plan for interest rate and credit risk 
regarding reserve assets. For example, commenters suggested that the 
OCC require written interest rate and credit risk management plans, 
policies, and procedures. However, other commenters stated that the 
asset diversification and concentration expectations in the proposal 
are sufficient to address interest rate and liquidity risk.
    Commenters also suggested that the OCC provide guidance on 
liquidity, interest rate, and credit risk management, including, for 
example, expectations regarding liquidity depth, redemption flow, 
measurement methodologies, risk appetites, counterparty due diligence, 
the unique risks posed by custodians and other intermediaries, and 
other topics related to reserve asset risk management.
    In addition to the reserve asset risk management requirements 
included in the proposed regulation itself, the proposed rule requested 
comment on two specific potential requirements: stress testing and 
buffers. The OCC requested comment on whether permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should be required to conduct stress tests, 
including as to their management of liquidity and interest rate risk. 
Commenters largely supported the use of stress tests as a risk 
management tool, though commenters differed on their views as to how 
any stress-testing expectations should be implemented in the 
regulation. Numerous commenters stated that the OCC should expressly 
require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to undertake liquidity and 
interest rate risk stress tests, with some commenters providing 
proposed standards (e.g., documentation requirements, thresholds 
issuers would be expected to meet, consequences for failing to meet 
such thresholds) or scenarios. One commenter suggested that a stress 
testing requirement could substitute for the weighted average maturity 
requirement (or safe harbor) in proposed Sec.  15.11(c). Relatedly, 
several commenters suggested broader ``monetization testing'' to ensure 
that issuers' channels for converting reserve assets into liquid funds 
are operational and reliable under normal and stressed circumstances. 
Finally, one commenter suggested that the OCC design and conduct multi-
issuer stress tests prior to the effective date of the GENIUS Act and 
publish the results.
    Other commenters noted the utility of stress testing but stated 
that the OCC should not impose prescriptive requirements but rather 
adhere to a principles-based approach, under which stress testing may 
be an appropriate risk-based approach for an issuer depending on its 
characteristics. One commenter stated that any stress testing 
requirements would be better issued at a later date after the OCC gains 
experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers and an 
understanding of the potential utility of such stress tests.
    The proposed rule noted that it ``includes robust liquidity 
requirements but does not include capital-based overcollateralization 
or reserve asset buffer requirements. An alternative possibility would 
be to remove some of the proposed liquidity requirements, though this 
may warrant increased capital or buffer requirements.'' Additionally, 
the OCC posed several questions to commenters on how such an approach 
might be handled.\77\ Several commenters requested that the OCC require 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to hold a ``buffer'' of reserve 
assets--that is, to overcollateralize its reserves or apply haircuts 
against the values of certain reserve assets--such as a standardized 
across-the-board 1 percent buffer or a codification of the Fixed Income 
Clearing Corporation Government Securities Division Clearing Fund 
haircut schedule published by the Depository Trust & Clearing 
Corporation for United States Treasuries. Others rejected standardized 
approaches, arguing that they are inconsistent with the GENIUS Act's 
tailoring requirement. These commenters instead suggested that any 
buffers be specific to an issuer based on the facts and circumstances 
or else discussed the relative benefits of buffers in the GENIUS Act 
reserve asset context since such assets are generally low-risk assets.
