    Some commenters also recommended that the OCC explicitly address in 
guidance that both the monetization capability standard and the 
diversification framework are intended to be jointly satisfiable, and 
that supervisory assessments will take into account the operational 
constraints that diversification arrangements may place on monetization 
capability.
    After careful review of the comments, the OCC has made several 
changes to Sec.  15.11(a)(2) and (3) and added new paragraph (a)(4) to 
the final rule. As discussed below, the final rule reduces the number 
of quantitative requirements relating to reserve asset liquidity, 
diversification, and concentration from the number that were included 
in Option B of the proposed rule. To ensure that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers remain adequately reserved, the OCC is balancing 
these reduced quantitative requirements with new provisions emphasizing 
the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain the 
appropriate level of reserve assets and to monetize those assets. Some 
of those provisions, including those relating to stress testing, are 
also addressed in the final rule's risk management provisions. 
Paragraphs

[[Page 67046]]

(a)(2) through (4) also provide certain clarifications in response to 
comments.
    Paragraph (a)(2) of the final rule's Sec.  15.11 requires a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to demonstrate the operational 
capability to access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets to 
meet redemptions, in both normal and adverse economic, liquidity, 
market, and interest rate conditions, commensurate with the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business model, taking 
into account, among other relevant factors, market access, financing 
channels, haircut assumptions, and operational readiness. Depending on 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size, risk profile, business 
model, activities, and operations, a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may be able to demonstrate monetization in different ways. For 
example, it may be sufficient for some permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to demonstrate the ability to monetize Treasury bills they hold 
as reserve assets by establishing that they maintain appropriate 
repurchase arrangements through which they can quickly sell Treasury 
bills and receive liquid funds with which they can satisfy redemption 
requests.
    For other permitted payment stablecoin issuers, for example, larger 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers or permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers with more complicated operations, additional measures may be 
appropriate to demonstrate the operational capability to monetize. It 
may be appropriate for such permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
maintain multiple alternative methods of monetization (for example, 
multiple repurchase agreement lines or repurchase agreement lines plus 
arrangements allowing outright sales of Treasury securities) to 
satisfactorily demonstrate the ability to monetize their reserve 
assets. Such redundant arrangements may be necessary if a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer maintains a sufficiently large Treasury 
position that it could be difficult to monetize the entire position 
through transactions with a single repo counterparty or if a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer maintains concentrated positions in 
particular types of reserve assets. The availability of multiple 
monetization channels is intended to help ensure that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer is not required to monetize assets at reduced 
or ``fire sale'' prices. Having alternative monetization channels 
reduces the risk that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be 
obliged to accept unfavorable pricing when monetizing reserve assets 
under stress.
    For certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers, it may be 
appropriate to periodically conduct actual monetization transactions 
(that is, actual outright sales or repurchase transactions) in order to 
demonstrate the ability to monetize. Actual transactions can more fully 
confirm that monetization capabilities exist. In the absence of actual 
test transactions, potential barriers to monetization may still exist. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may be unfamiliar with or lack the 
procedures and systems to monetize assets at any time in accordance 
with standard settlement periods and processes. For example, internal 
staff may be unprepared to execute procedures, or borrowing agreements 
may name authorizing officials who are unavailable or inappropriate. 
Actual monetization transactions may be appropriate, for example, for 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers with unusually complicated 
operations or organizational structures, or for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers that are particularly dependent on certain 
monetization channels or the ability to monetize particular assets. 
Periodic actual monetization transactions can minimize the risk of 
negative signaling during financial stress and help prepare the issuer 
to move quickly if necessary to acquire additional liquidity.
    If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer begins using a 
monetization channel that it has not regularly used in the past, that 
may spark concerns about the financial health of the issuer. For 
example, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer has pre-established a 
repurchase agreement with a bilateral counterparty but never utilized 
it, sudden utilization of the repurchase agreement may generate 
concerns that the issuer is experiencing a run on its stablecoins. 
Periodic test transactions using multiple monetization channels can 
mitigate such concerns and may be particularly important for large, 
systemically important issuers where concerns about financial distress 
are more likely to contribute to contagion. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may be able to demonstrate the ability to execute 
actual monetization transactions in the ordinary course of their 
business (for example, redeeming stablecoins) and would not necessarily 
be required to engage in additional test transactions.
    Paragraph (a)(3) of the final rule's Sec.  15.11 requires a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to ensure that reserve asset value 
will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance value at all 
times and that the reserve asset portfolio will be capable of 
supporting timely redemption under both normal conditions and adverse 
economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, including, 
to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of reserve assets in 
excess of outstanding issuance value. This requirement will provide 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers flexibility in composing their 
reserve asset portfolio while ensuring that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers are able to maintain 1 to 1 backing at all times. 
The final rule does not mandate a particular buffer level but makes 
clear that such a buffer may be appropriate, depending on the makeup of 
the reserve asset portfolio of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers with certain reserve asset 
portfolios may not be required to maintain any buffer, or only a small 
buffer, in order to comply with paragraph (a)(3), for example, reserve 
asset portfolios consisting entirely of reserve assets that represent 
immediately available liquidity, such as deposits payable upon demand. 
In contrast, it may be necessary for permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers with longer-duration reserve asset portfolios to maintain a 
more substantial buffer.\78\

In response to comments, the revised paragraph provides additional flexibility, especially with respect to timing, to permitted payment stablecoin issuers with respect to removing reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value while facilitating the OCC's key goal of [[Page 67047]] ensuring that permitted payment stablecoin issuers meet, at all times, their obligations under section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)). Reserve Asset Composition (Sec. 15.11(b)) i. Description of Proposed Rule Under proposed Sec. 15.11(b), reserve assets would have comprised only: (1) United States coins and currency (including Federal Reserve notes) or money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank; (2) funds held as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand at an insured depository institution (including any foreign branches or agents, including correspondent banks, of an insured depository institution), subject to any limitation established by the FDIC and the National Credit Union Administration, as applicable, pursuant to section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)) to address safety and soundness risks of such insured depository institution; (3) Treasury bills, Treasury notes, or Treasury bonds with a remaining maturity of 93 days or less; \80\ (4) money received under repurchase agreements, with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer acting as a seller of securities and with a no longer than overnight maturity, that are backed by Treasury bills with a maturity of 93 days or less; \81\ (5) reverse repurchase agreements, with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer acting as a purchaser of securities and with a no longer than overnight maturity, that are collateralized by Treasury bills, Treasury notes, or Treasury bonds on a no longer than overnight basis, subject to overcollateralization in line with standard market terms, that are: (i) tri-party; (ii) centrally cleared through a clearing agency registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission; or (iii) bilateral with a counterparty that the issuer has determined to be adequately creditworthy even in the event of severe market stress; (6) securities issued by an investment company registered under section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-8(a)), or other registered Government money market fund, and that are invested solely in underlying assets described in proposed Sec. 15.11(b)(1) through (5); \82\ (7) any other similarly liquid Federal Government-issued asset approved by the OCC, in consultation with the State payment stablecoin regulator, if applicable, of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; or (8) any reserve described in proposed Sec. 15.11(b)(1) through (3), (6), or (7), in tokenized form, provided that such reserves comply with all applicable laws and regulations. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \80\ Section 4(a)(1)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(iii)) permits the inclusion of Treasury bills, notes, or bonds ``(I) with a remaining maturity of 93 days or less; or (II) issued with a maturity of 93 days or less.'' The proposed rule combined these categories since the former category includes the latter, at least for purposes of complying with the requirements of proposed Sec. 15.11. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may choose to categorize these assets separately for other reasons, for example accounting or risk management purposes. For clarity, the 93- day limitation begins as of the settlement date of the purchase of the Treasury securities. \81\ The proposed rule clarified that a repurchase agreement or reverse repurchase agreement with an intraday maturity could qualify as a permitted reserve asset. Sections 4(a)(1)(A)(iv) and (v) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(iv) and (v)) specifically refer to repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements with an overnight maturity. The OCC believes that these provisions are intended to permit repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements with a maturity no longer than overnight. Thus, the proposed rule would have explicitly permitted the use of intraday repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements. \82\ A money market fund that invests in any other assets, including in Treasury securities with a remaining maturity longer than 93 days, would not be eligible to be held as a reserve asset. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- In determining whether a potential reserve asset qualifies as ``any other similarly liquid Federal Government-issued asset,'' under proposed Sec. 15.11(b)(7) the OCC would have considered, among other relevant factors, whether: (i) the asset has liquidity characteristics, including during times of stress, comparable to the other reserve assets allowed under proposed Sec. 15.11(b); (ii) permitted payment stablecoin issuers will be operationally capable of monetizing the asset to meet redemption requests, including sudden and high-volume requests; (iii) the asset poses levels of risk comparable to the assets allowed under proposed Sec. 15.11(b), including interest rate risk and counterparty credit risk; and (iv) the asset introduces additional risks that may be difficult for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to manage. ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule A few commenters generally favored the reserve asset composition set forth in the OCC's proposed rule. One commenter recommended that issuer reserves should be permitted to be composed entirely of Treasuries, overnight Treasury repurchase agreements, and their equivalents, considering their low credit risk. Another commenter recommended that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to hold a majority of their reserves as deposits in insured depository institutions and Treasuries with a remaining maturity of no longer than 93 days. Physical Currency Overall, commenters supported limited recognition of physical currency, subject to basic safeguards rather than detailed prescriptive requirements. A few commenters addressed physical currency and generally suggested that the OCC adopt a simple, principles-based approach because physical currency is unlikely to serve as a significant reserve asset in [[Page 67048]] practice. One commenter stated that any physical currency held as a reserve asset should be valued at par. Another commenter noted that physical currency should be permitted only within defined limits, such as a small percentage of total reserves and potentially subject to geographic distribution requirements, while recognizing that some operating balance in physical currency may be practical for smaller issuers. The final rule does not impose direct limits on the use of physical currency in Sec. 15.11(b)(1) or elsewhere, but, as discussed above, physical currency must be valued at face value (rather than fair market value). In addition, risk management considerations, in particular operational risk, will likely discourage the extensive use of physical currency as reserve assets.\83\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \83\ See, e.g., OCC, Comptroller's Handbook, ``Cash Accounts'' 5-25 (1998) (discussing cash account risk management considerations in OCC exam procedures); OCC, Comptroller's Handbook, ``Custody Services'' 6-8 (2002) (discussing custody services risk management considerations). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Reserve Bank Balances Overall, commenters generally supported greater clarity on the treatment of reserve bank balances but differed on whether such balances should receive preferential treatment or be subject to concentration safeguards. Several commenters suggested that reserve bank balances be exempt from concentration limits and argued that balances at Federal Reserve Banks do not present credit risk and that treating reserve banks like insured depository institutions would impose unnecessary operational constraints without corresponding safety benefits. A few commenters stated that the OCC should work with the Federal Reserve to permit an operating subsidiary of an insured depository institution to open a master account directly or maintain a designated sub-account of its parent institution's Federal Reserve master account. In contrast, one commenter stated that exempting Federal Reserve master accounts from concentration limits could confer a competitive advantage on banks and urged the OCC to revisit the issue after the Federal Reserve further addresses payment account implementation or clarifies master account eligibility. Another commenter stated that, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer were to obtain master account access, the OCC should limit the share of reserve assets that may be held at a Reserve Bank. As discussed below, the final rule, like the proposed rule, imposes a 40 percent single counterparty limit with respect to money standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank. The OCC determined that, although Federal Reserve Banks do not present counterparty credit risk, providing preferential treatment for the placement of reserve assets at Federal Reserve Banks could implicate financial stability risks. In times of stress, permitted payment stablecoin issuers may generally have an incentive to move reserve assets out of commercial banks and into Federal Reserve Banks. Imposing a 40 percent single counterparty limit on commercial banks but not Federal Reserve Banks could exacerbate this dynamic. This flight could also lead to increased money market volatility and potentially impede the transmission of monetary policy. Thus, consistent with the OCC's authority and mandate under section 4(b) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(b)) to ensure financial stability, the final rule applies a 40 percent single counterparty limit with respect to money standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank. Although the OCC has coordinated and will continue to coordinate with the Federal Reserve in the agencies' implementation of the GENIUS Act, the OCC declines to provide guidance on Federal Reserve master account structures, consistent with its approach to national banks, as master account access is outside the OCC's statutory authorities. Deposits Some commenters suggested that permissible reserve assets should include a broader range of deposit arrangements, including ordinary deposit and settlement accounts. To emphasize that settlement accounts are a routine and important part of reserve operations, some commenters stated that reserves should not be limited to custody account arrangements. Other commenters stated that the term ``demand deposit'' should be interpreted to include money market deposit accounts and similar deposits that may not formally qualify as demand deposits, so long as the permitted payment stablecoin issuer can withdraw the funds at any time. One commenter stated that this interpretation is necessary to give effect to the concept of funds being ``payable on demand'' and would broaden the range of depository institutions permitted to hold reserve assets, including industrial loan companies that may not accept demand deposits. A few commenters opposed requiring or encouraging reserve assets to be held as insured deposits or shares, arguing that: (i) deposit insurance resources are not designed to support stablecoin volumes, (ii) increased coverage could raise unfair assessment burdens on banks, (iii) payment stablecoins are not deposits, and (iv) diversification into bank deposits could increase risks to the banking system. One commenter also cautioned that uninsured deposits are neither risk-free nor always highly liquid. A few commenters addressed insurance-related issues for reserve assets and generally urged greater clarity regarding the treatment and risks of insured and uninsured deposits. One commenter recommended that the OCC explore a supplemental excess deposit insurance or guarantee mechanism for stablecoin reserve deposits held in trust for payment stablecoin holders. Some commenters argued against permitting uninsured deposits because they would leave stablecoins highly vulnerable to runs. One commenter noted that disclosures should clearly explain the level of protection available for insured and uninsured deposits, including whether tokenized deposits qualify for deposit insurance or whether insurance does not pass through to token holders. One commenter also referenced the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants' (AICPA) stablecoin criteria as supporting explicit disclosure where deposit insurance does not pass through to the token holder. A few commenters urged the OCC not to categorically limit reserve deposits to United States insured depository institutions and instead to permit deposits held through foreign banking organizations, foreign branches, or correspondent banking arrangements under appropriate conditions. Some commenters stated that the statute permits deposits to be maintained at foreign banking organizations, including where those institutions maintain correspondent accounts with United States insured depository institutions. Some commenters stated that foreign banks operating in the United States should receive national treatment and thus should be allowed to conduct the same activities as United States financial institutions. Other commenters stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may have legitimate operational needs for reserves in non-U.S. locations, including to meet requirements established under reciprocal arrangements. Several commenters stated that restricting U.S. dollar-denominated payment stablecoins to demand deposits at United States-based depository institutions would be disproportionate, commercially harmful, and inconsistent with a competitive and accessible

[[Page 67049]]

stablecoin framework. Some commenters argued that the rule should avoid 
blanket haircuts or capital charges on reserve assets held at foreign 
branches or correspondent banks and instead require issuers to maintain 
documented risk management frameworks addressing the risks of such 
arrangements. One commenter urged the OCC to specify the conditions 
under which Eurodollar deposits would be appropriate in a manner that 
minimizes interference with free competition and to apply any 
restrictions on foreign branches, agents, or correspondent banks 
equally to U.S.- and foreign-headquartered firms.
    As discussed above, section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)) permits permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
to hold demand deposits at insured depository institutions. The 
definition of insured depository institution under section 2(15) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(15)) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Act 
excludes from the scope of permissible reserve assets deposits held at 
institutions that are not insured depository institutions under section 
3(c)(2) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. Accordingly, deposits 
that are not held at insured depository institutions (regardless of 
whether the deposits themselves are insured) are not eligible reserve 
assets.
    Some commenters also suggested that the OCC clarify that deposit 
placement networks may be used to hold reserve assets through eligible 
financial institutions. These commenters argued that such networks can 
improve diversification, operational efficiency, liquidity, and timely 
redemptions while also channeling deposits to community banks. One 
commenter stated that deposit placement networks are unlikely to 
increase run risk because deposits would be spread across institutions 
and stablecoins may be less likely to experience concentrated 
redemptions than some other liabilities. The OCC confirms that 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers may use deposit placement networks 
provided that the issuer does so in compliance with applicable 
requirements, including those in Sec. Sec.  15.11 and 15.13. For 
example, if a network's agreements included limitations on withdrawals 
that rendered the issuer unable to meet the liquidity demands of 
customers and to timely redeem tendered payment stablecoins, it would 
be inappropriate for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to place 
amounts of its reserve assets through that deposit placement network 
that rendered the permitted payment stablecoin issuer unable to comply 
with the final rule.
    The final rule does not substantively change the description of 
funds held as deposits or insured shares payable on demand at an 
insured depository institution in Sec.  15.11(b)(2). The final rule 
does, however, more closely match the language of section 
4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)) by 
replacing references to deposits payable on demand with demand deposits 
(or other deposits that may be withdrawn upon request at any time). The 
OCC notes that existing banking law and regulation use or define 
similar terms, such as 12 CFR part 204 and section 2 of the BHC Act; as 
other laws and regulations do not use the same phrasing as the GENIUS 
Act, may not be within the OCC's jurisdiction, and are based on 
different policy purposes, applying definitions, interpretations, or 
market practices based on other law for purposes of this provision of 
the Act is not appropriate. In addition, the OCC confirms that a 
deposit account that allows the bank to require prior notice of 
withdrawal or limits the number of withdrawals within a period of time 
would not be a demand deposit or other deposit that may be withdrawn 
upon request at any time under the GENIUS Act regardless of whether the 
deposit was treated as a demand deposit under other law. As discussed 
in greater detail below, the OCC is also eliminating the proposed 
requirement that certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers hold a 
set amount of reserves as insured deposits. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers continue to be expected to manage credit and 
concentration risks, including those regarding insured deposits and 
insured depository institutions. With respect to deposit insurance, the 
OCC notes that the FDIC has issued a notice of proposed rulemaking 
addressing insurance coverage rules in 12 CFR part 330 that apply to 
all FDIC-insured depository institutions by clarifying that deposits 
held as reserves backing a payment stablecoin would be insured as to 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the FDIC's coverage 
rules for corporate deposits, but would not be insured to payment 
stablecoin holders on a pass-through basis.\84\ The final rule also 
neither prohibits nor mandates the use of private deposit insurance. As 
discussed in the next section, Sec.  15.12 of the final rule also 
includes additional disclosures, including with respect to deposit 
insurance, which address several of the commenters' concerns.

    \84\ 91 FR 18534 (Apr. 10, 2026) (FDIC proposed rule for GENIUS 
Act requirements and standards for FDIC-supervised permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers and insured depository institutions).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Treasury Securities
    Several commenters recommended permitting reserve assets to consist 
predominantly or entirely of cash and short-term United States Treasury 
securities. One commenter stated that at least 80 to 90 percent of 
existing stablecoin reserves are already held in short-term Treasuries, 
while another urged that reserves be held 100 percent in Treasuries or 
cash. Some commenters stated that the effects of reserve requirements 
on the United States debt markets should be studied and monitored and 
that the final rule should recognize risks associated with 
concentration in Treasury securities (e.g., potential financial 
stability implications if stablecoin issuers become large Treasury 
investors). In contrast, some commenters suggested that it is not 
necessary at this stage to impose additional rule-based requirements 
specifically aimed at preventing disruptions in Treasury markets. 
Several commenters opposed limits or qualitative distinctions on 
Treasury holdings, including caps on older or off-the-run securities, 
arguing that such restrictions would be operationally harmful and 
unsupported by the risk profile of stablecoin reserve portfolios. One 
commenter also acknowledged liquidity concerns regarding off-the-run 
Treasuries but suggested addressing those concerns through existing 
mechanisms, such as the FICC haircut schedule, rather than through 
explicit portfolio limits.
    In Sec.  15.11(b)(3), the final rule does not impose any 
quantitative requirements with respect to how much of a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's reserve asset portfolio must comprise 
Treasury securities. The OCC believes that the changes to Sec.  
15.11(a) and the risk management provisions in Sec.  15.13 will be 
sufficient to ensure that the composition of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's portfolio is appropriate. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers will be expected to consider, among other things, 
the liquidity of a particular Treasury security (e.g., if the Treasury 
security is off-the-run) in relation to those requirements.
TIPS, FRNs, and STRIPS
    A few commenters urged the OCC not to adopt a prescriptive asset-
by-asset list and instead to use principles-based eligibility criteria. 
These commenters suggested that the criteria potentially be 
supplemented by illustrative examples

[[Page 67050]]

for Treasury Floating Rate Notes (FRNs), Treasury Inflation-Protected 
Securities (TIPS), and Separate Trading of Registered Interest and 
Principal of Securities (STRIPS). Some commenters stated that FRNs 
should be included as eligible reserve assets, particularly where they 
have relatively short remaining maturities or otherwise demonstrate 
sufficient liquidity, emphasizing their limited price volatility, 
strong secondary market liquidity, and risk characteristics comparable 
to Treasury bills. Other commenters supported including TIPS, with one 
commenter noting that TIPS could be used to hedge payment stablecoins 
pegged to a fixed amount of purchasing power. Another commenter 
suggested that FRNs and TIPS could be permitted subject to 
overcollateralization requirements. In contrast, one commenter stated 
that TIPS and STRIPS are too volatile to qualify as permissible reserve 
assets.
    Under Sec.  15.11(b)(3) of the final rule, consistent with the 
proposal, any Treasury bill, note, or bond with a remaining maturity of 
93 days or less may serve as a reserve asset. Thus, FRNs or TIPS with a 
remaining maturity of 93 days or less may serve as reserve assets. 
STRIPS are zero-coupon securities created from the individual interest 
or principal components of a Treasury note or bond. Because STRIPS are 
merely the individual component payments of Treasury notes, or bonds, 
and in light of the regulatory regime supporting the ability to 
reconstitute STRIPS,\85\ they may qualify as reserve assets, provided 
they have a remaining maturity of 93 days or less under section 
4(a)(1)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(iii)).\86\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \85\ See 31 CFR 356.31.
    \86\ For STRIPS, the maturity date is the payment date for each 
separate principal or interest component. For principal components, 
the maturity date is the same as the maturity date of the fully 
constituted (unstripped) Treasury security. For interest components, 
the interest payment date becomes the maturity date for the 
component. Treasury provides the CUSIP numbers and payment dates for 
the principal and interest components in auction announcements and 
on its website.

Repurchase Agreements and Reverse Repurchase Agreements
    Many commenters urged the OCC to clarify the permissible use of 
repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements as reserve 
assets, including the treatment of collateral, legal enforceability, 
operational controls, monetization timing, and whether intraday, 
centrally cleared, and on-chain repurchase agreement structures are 
permissible. Many commenters emphasized that repurchase agreements and 
reverse repurchase agreements present meaningful credit, liquidity, and 
market risks and recommended addressing those risks through 
counterparty standards, supervisory expectations, liquidity stress 
testing, and contingency funding planning. One commenter suggested 
limiting repurchase agreements to roughly 10 to 15 percent of reserves, 
and another commenter argued that repurchase agreements should not 
qualify as reserve assets at all because reserve assets should be owned 
outright. Some commenters stated that cash and deposits, including 
deposits held at tri-party custodians, should be expressly recognized 
as eligible collateral because those assets are permissible reserve 
assets and are commonly used in repo markets. In contrast, one 
commenter opposed allowing counterparties to pledge deposits and 
instead argued that reserve pools should receive cash directly into 
their own bank accounts. A few commenters opposed prescriptive minimum 
haircut requirements and instead recommended requiring 
overcollateralization consistent with standard market terms in the 
United States Treasury repo market, with documentation under industry-
standard agreements serving as evidence of compliance. Several 
commenters requested additional clarity regarding terms such as 
``severe market stress'' and ``centrally cleared,'' as well as guidance 
on how issuers should assess bilateral repo counterparty 
creditworthiness and whether net liquidity measures may account for 
expected inflows as well as outflows. One commenter opposed limits on 
repo funding altogether, arguing that repo funding can be more secure 
than unsecured bank deposits. Another commenter recommended enhanced 
disclosure and attestation requirements regarding repo counterparty 
tier, weighted average term, and rollover frequency.
    Consistent with the statute, Sec.  15.11(b)(4) and (5) of the final 
rule continue to permit the use of money received under certain 
repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements as reserve 
assets. The final rule does not impose any quantitative limit 
specifically with respect to these reserve asset types (though, as 
discussed below, counterparty limitations would continue to apply). The 
OCC recognizes that there are certain risks associated with relying 
excessively on repurchase agreements to facilitate redemptions (e.g., 
the risk that a regular repo counterparty will not roll over a repo). 
The OCC will receive detailed information concerning the makeup of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserve asset portfolio, 
including the extent to which a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
relies on repurchase agreements through the weekly reporting required 
in Sec.  15.14. This will provide the OCC with the ability to assess, 
among other things, whether a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
overly reliant on repo funding and unable to monetize its reserve 
assets in a timely fashion. In addition, the revisions to Sec.  
15.11(a) and Sec.  15.13 should address risks associated with relying 
excessively on repurchase agreements or reverse repurchase agreements, 
particularly in times of stress. The final rule also does not provide 
that money received from repurchase agreements or reverse repurchase 
agreements may be backed by cash, consistent with the requirements of 
section 4(a)(1)(A)(iv) and (v) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(A)(iv) and (v)). The final rule does not further define what 
constitutes ``standard market terms'' in recognition that standard 
market terms may evolve over time. Additionally, the final rule does 
not further define what constitutes central clearing, as that term is 
already sufficiently clear in the statute. The final rule includes one 
technical change to Sec.  15.11(b)(5), adding the word ``or'' between 
``Treasury notes'' and ``Treasury bonds.''
Securities Issued by an Investment Company
    Several commenters suggested that the OCC limit eligible securities 
issued by an investment company to registered government money market 
funds, particularly SEC Rule 2a-7 funds that maintain a stable $1.00 
net asset value, satisfy applicable liquidity requirements, and invest 
solely in assets otherwise permitted as reserve assets. Some commenters 
stated that prime and municipal money market funds, and more broadly 
non-government registered investment companies, should be excluded 
because they introduce credit, liquidity, and structural risks 
inconsistent with the statutory reserve framework. One commenter argued 
that money market funds are inherently vulnerable to runs. Several 
commenters also requested clarification that the phrase ``other 
registered government money market funds'' does not expand eligibility 
beyond funds registered under the Investment Company Act. Some 
commenters asked the OCC to publish a list of permissible funds and 
assets. Other commenters urged the OCC to interpret the category more 
broadly to

[[Page 67051]]

include other registered funds that hold qualifying assets, including 
Treasury-focused ETFs, ultra-short Treasury mutual funds, tokenized 
money market funds, and other funds they suggested were economically 
equivalent to direct holdings of permissible assets. Commenters noted 
that government money market funds are already comprehensively 
regulated under Rule 2a-7 and the Investment Company Act and stated 
that they therefore should not be subject to additional OCC 
diversification or concentration restrictions beyond the statutory 
framework. Other commenters recommended specific fund-level caps or 
exposure limits to address concentration risk. A few commenters sought 
operational clarifications, including that otherwise qualifying funds 
may hold small amounts of residual cash in other funds for cash 
management purposes or operate through fund-of-funds or master-feeder 
structures without losing eligibility.
    The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.11(b)(6) as proposed, with some 
minor technical edits, to ensure consistency with the language in 
section 4(a)(1)(A)(vi) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(vi)). 
Under the final rule, permissible reserve assets include securities 
issued by an investment company registered under section 8(a) of the 
Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-8(a)), or other 
registered Government money market fund, and that are invested solely 
in underlying assets described in Sec.  15.11(b)(1) through (5). To 
qualify under Sec.  15.11(b)(6), an investment company would need to be 
registered under section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act but need 
not be a mutual fund. Shares of an exchange traded fund registered 
under section 8(a) of the Investment Company Act that invested solely 
in the assets detailed in Sec.  15.11(b)(1) through (5) would 
constitute eligible reserve assets. As discussed in greater detail 
below, these funds would nevertheless be subject to reserve asset 
diversification and concentration requirements addressed in Sec.  
15.11(c). These reserve asset and diversification requirements will 
ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is not overly reliant 
on one entity and may, for example, look to other sources to fund 
redemptions in the event of an operational issue with such a fund. The 
OCC confirms that ``other registered government money market funds'' 
does not expand eligibility beyond funds registered under the 
Investment Company Act. In addition, the OCC confirms that a fund that 
invested in other funds would not meet the eligibility requirements 
under Sec.  15.11(b)(6) because such a fund would not invest solely in 
the reserve assets permitted under section 4(a)(1)(A)(i) through (v) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(i)-(v)).
    The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.11(b)(6) as proposed with some minor 
technical edits to add paragraphs (b)(6)(i) and (b)(6)(ii) to more 
clearly provide that the securities must be issued by an investment 
company and invested solely in the underlying assets described in Sec.  
15.11(b)(1) through (b)(5).
Other Similarly Liquid Federal Government-Issued Assets Not Listed in 
the GENIUS Act and Reserves in Tokenized Form
    Several commenters urged the OCC to preserve a process for 
approving additional ``similarly liquid'' Federal Government-issued 
assets beyond those expressly listed in the statute and to articulate 
transparent, principles-based eligibility criteria, rather than relying 
solely on a fixed prescriptive list. Some commenters stated that the 
permissible asset universe should be expanded to include longer-dated 
United States Treasury securities. These commenters argued that in some 
cases, agency securities remain deep and liquid, would improve 
portfolio flexibility and yield, and could reduce undue concentration 
at the short end of the Treasury curve. Several commenters noted that, 
if longer-dated assets are permitted, the OCC should address the 
associated interest rate and liquidity risks through tools such as 
haircuts, weighted-average-maturity limits, diversification 
requirements, overcollateralization, stress rebalancing, or redemption 
controls. A few commenters requested a formal, transparent, and time-
limited approval process for additional assets, including public 
disclosure of determinations, published eligibility criteria, and the 
ability for any interested party to petition for approval, with some 
also urging coordination with state and other relevant regulators. In 
contrast, some commenters opposed expanding the category to include 
Treasuries with remaining maturities beyond 93 days, arguing that 
longer-dated instruments introduce excessive interest rate risk and 
should not qualify, or should be subject to a portfolio-level weighted 
average maturity cap of no more than 93 days. A few commenters urged 
even broader expansion to include assets such as agency obligations, 
broader Rule 2a-7 government money market fund exposures, debt 
instruments economically equivalent to Treasuries but issued by third 
parties, commercial paper, or even other stablecoins. Other commenters 
argued that any such expansion should occur only after careful safety-
and-soundness review and interagency coordination.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC expand the list of permissible 
reserve assets to include AAA-rated corporate debt. This commenter 
suggested that highly rated corporate obligations should be eligible 
alongside other reserve assets.
    The final rule includes one technical change to Sec.  15.11(b)(7), 
to remove the redundant ``Whether'' from the proposed Sec.  
15.11(b)(7)(iv).
    One commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that for tokenized 
reserve assets, a covered custodian's demonstration of control should 
address both the on-chain custody of the token and the off-chain legal 
and operational arrangements ensuring the custodian can enforce the 
customer's rights against the underlying asset. The definition of 
``tokenized form'' in Sec.  15.2 sufficiently addresses the applicable 
legal requirements. As described above, a reserve asset in tokenized 
form must confer rights that are identical to those that would be 
conferred by a non-tokenized form of the asset under applicable law. In 
the case of a tokenized form of an asset under custody, a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer should consider the operational capabilities 
of the custodian as well as the legal rights that the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer has in the reserve asset. Some commenters argued 
against additional quantitative diversification limits on tokenized 
reserve assets. Other commenters cautioned that tokenization can 
introduce operational uncertainty and instability and should be 
addressed through collateral eligibility standards, disclosure, 
haircuts, or other risk controls. A few commenters also requested more 
specific guidance on operational and disclosure issues, including 
treatment of digitally native assets, explicit confirmation that short-
term on-chain Treasuries are permissible, disclosure of both on-chain 
custody locations and underlying real-world asset custody, and 
standards for addressing discrepancies between on-chain reserve 
attestations and off-chain custodian records. One commenter encouraged 
publishing reserve balances on-chain and eventually supporting 
programmatic controls that would prevent additional token minting when 
adequate reserves are not present. The OCC is not including a broad-
based haircut for reserve assets in tokenized form in light of the many 
different features, positive and negative, that a

[[Page 67052]]

reserve asset in tokenized form may have, depending on its design. 
Nevertheless, depending on the nature of the tokenized asset (in 
particular, any operational difficulties associated with monetizing the 
asset), it may be appropriate for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
to apply a haircut pursuant to its reserve asset and liquidity risk 
management requirements.
    The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.11(b) with minor changes in addition 
to the non-substantive change to paragraph (b)(2) described above. 
Specifically, Sec.  15.11(b)(7) now provides that, when the OCC 
approves the use of ``any other similarly liquid Federal Government-
issued asset'' as a reserve asset, the OCC may impose conditions 
consistent with the purposes of the GENIUS Act. This addition makes 
clear, for example, that the OCC may impose conditions (e.g., its 
maturity) on the use of a particular type of reserve asset to ensure 
that the asset is truly similarly liquid to the other types of reserve 
assets contemplated under the GENIUS Act. The OCC is not including 
corporate securities as permissible reserve assets. These assets are 
not Federal-Government issued, and thus section 4(a)(1)(A) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)) does not provide an avenue to 
permit such assets. The OCC is also making technical edits to Sec.  
15.11(b)(8) to delete ``or paragraph'' as redundant, such that it now 
reads ``Any reserve described in paragraphs (b)(1) through (3), (b)(6), 
or (b)(7) of this section in tokenized form, provided that such 
reserves comply with all applicable laws and regulations.''
d. Reserve Asset Diversification and Concentration (Sec.  15.11(c))
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)) 
requires the OCC to issue regulations implementing reserve asset 
diversification, including deposit concentration at banking 
institutions and interest rate risk management standards that (1) are 
tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers and (2) do not exceed standards that are sufficient 
to ensure the ongoing operations of permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. The proposed rule included two alternative options to 
implement these diversification and concentration limits in proposed 
Sec.  15.11(c). ``Option A'' included a principles-based general 
requirement with an optional safe harbor containing quantitative 
requirements. ``Option B'' would have made the quantitative 
requirements mandatory for all issuers. Option A's principles-based 
general requirement would have required a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to maintain reserve assets that are sufficiently diverse to 
manage potential credit, liquidity, interest rate, and price risks. In 
addition, the principles-based requirement in Option A in proposed 
Sec.  15.11(c) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to measure and manage the risk that concentrating reserve assets 
at one eligible financial institution or a small number of eligible 
financial institutions may impair the ability of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to satisfy redemption demands if individual eligible 
financial institutions are unable to return, or if there is a delay in 
returning, reserve assets placed by a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.\87\ The proposed rule's diversification and concentration 
requirements would have applied to custodial relationships, including 
sub-custodial arrangements. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers would 
have been expected to ``look through'' any sub-custodial relationships 
to ensure that reserve assets are custodied at a sufficiently diverse 
number of eligible financial institutions needed to comply with the 
proposed rule's requirements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \87\ Eligible financial institutions that hold reserve assets in 
custody or safekeeping must be subject to supervision and comply 
with the requirements set forth in section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5909). Institutions subject to OCC supervision would need to 
comply with the requirements set forth in proposed subpart C of part 
15.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Option A contained a safe harbor under which a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer would be deemed to satisfy proposed Sec.  15.11(c) if 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintains on each business day: 
(i) at least 10 percent of its required reserve assets as deposits or 
insured shares payable upon demand or money standing to the credit of 
an account with a Federal Reserve Bank; (ii) at least 30 percent of its 
reserve assets as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand, money 
standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, or 
amounts receivable and due unconditionally within five business days on 
pending sales of reserve assets, maturing reserve assets, or other 
maturing transactions (e.g., reverse repurchase agreements); (iii) no 
more than 40 percent of its reserve assets at any one eligible 
financial institution, whether as deposits or insured shares at any one 
insured depository institution, securities custodied at any one 
eligible financial institution, bilateral reverse repurchase agreements 
with any counterparty, or through other exposures; (iv) no more than 50 
percent of the amount provided in proposed Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(i) at any 
one eligible financial institution; and (v) reserve assets with a 
weighted average maturity of no more than 20 days.
    The safe harbor would also have required that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer maintain at least 30 percent of its reserve assets as 
deposits or insured shares payable upon demand, money standing to the 
credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, or amounts receivable 
and due unconditionally within five business days on pending sales of 
reserve assets, maturing reserve assets, or other maturing 
transactions.
    The safe harbor would have also required that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer maintain no more than 40 percent of its reserve 
assets at any one eligible financial institution, whether as deposits 
or insured shares at any one insured depository institution, securities 
custodied at any one eligible financial institution, bilateral reverse 
repurchase agreements with any counterparty, or through other 
exposures.
    The safe harbor would have also required that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer maintain no more than 50 percent of the required 
daily liquidity specified under proposed Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(i) at any 
one eligible financial institution. This requirement was intended to 
guard against the risk that problems at one eligible financial 
institution prevent a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from 
accessing its reserve assets. If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
is dependent on one eligible financial institution to maintain all or a 
large portion of its reserve assets, the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may be excessively exposed to, for example, operational concerns 
at that eligible financial institution or even the risk of the 
institution's failure.
    To qualify for the safe harbor, proposed Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(v) would 
have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserve 
assets have a weighted average maturity of no more than 20 days.
    Option B would have imposed the quantitative standards as mandatory 
requirements, rather than an optional safe harbor.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
    Generally, more commenters expressed support for the ``Option A'' 
approach to reserve asset diversification over ``Option B.'' Several 
commenters supporting Option A stated that it appropriately balances 
rigor, flexibility,

[[Page 67053]]

and clarity for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and enables 
appropriate tailoring. Some other commenters stated that Option A 
provides for appropriate tailoring to different business models and 
risk profiles. A few commenters stated that Option A would be 
consistent with established custody fundamentals or existing state-
level frameworks. A few commenters favored Option A because it offers 
predictability for new entrants and flexibility for mature issuers to 
demonstrate diversification through risk management practices tailored 
to actual operations. One commenter stated that Option B would depart 
from Congressional intent because the proposed reserve requirements 
would be excessive and not properly tailored.
    A few commenters supported Option A but suggested changes. One 
commenter stated that weighted average maturity provisions should be 
changed so as not to discourage holding longer-dated Treasuries 
(subject to the statutory 93-day cap). One commenter suggested the OCC 
make clear that Option A may require a buffer of extra reserve assets. 
One commenter suggested that small permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should be presumed to comply with Option A.
    Some commenters specifically addressed the proposed safe harbor 
provision. A few of these commenters stated generally that the safe 
harbor would provide flexibility for issuers. Several commenters stated 
that the safe harbor is improperly calibrated and suggested changes to 
the quantitative limits that they argued would reduce risk or better 
support liquidity needs. A few other commenters argued that 
quantitative thresholds were unnecessary, impractical, or inadequately 
supported by data. One of these commenters suggested that, if retained, 
issuers should be able to satisfy the safe harbor by meeting board-
approved diversification requirements. Several commenters stated that 
the safe harbor should not be treated as a minimum requirement or 
baseline expectation. One commenter suggested that compliance with the 
safe harbor should be measured as of the close of each business day, 
with opportunity for a cure period of one business day.
    Several commenters favored ``Option B'' instead. Some of these 
commenters stated that quantitative thresholds would create more 
certainty and consistency for both issuers and third parties compared 
to a principles-based approach without specific quantitative 
thresholds. A few of these commenters also recommended changes to the 
specific requirements under Option B. One commenter stated that 
mandatory limits including single-custodian caps could reduce risk but 
suggested the OCC should clarify that reserve composition requirements 
do not eliminate liquidity risk in the event of a third-party 
custodian's insolvency. One commenter supported Option B but suggested 
the OCC evaluate the impact of concentration limits and 20-day weighted 
average maturity to ensure they do not lead to unintended consequences.
    One commenter stated that neither Option A nor Option B fully 
addresses concerns related to deposit flight, impacts to credit 
creation, and potential systemic risk in light of increasing 
connections between stablecoin issuers and the banking system, citing 
the example of Silicon Valley Bank.
    A few commenters supported the establishment of minimum 
requirements for immediately available liquidity. One commenter noted 
that these requirements were preferable to issuers relying on sales or 
repurchase agreements to generate liquidity. A few commenters supported 
having a weekly minimum liquidity requirement. One commenter supported 
the 10 percent and 30 percent thresholds for daily and weekly liquidity 
requirements, respectively. One commenter recommended that the 10 
percent daily liquidity requirement should be adjustable based on each 
issuer's demonstrated redemption profile, with 5 percent being an 
appropriate baseline for experienced issuers. The commenter further 
recommended that an issuer should be permitted to propose a threshold 
below the 5 percent minimum if the issuer can provide support for lower 
daily liquidity needs. One commenter suggested that the daily 
requirement should be calibrated to reflect actual historical 
redemption patterns instead of worst-case scenarios. One commenter 
stated that the OCC may need to revisit the 30 percent threshold for 
weekly liquidity at a later date to determine whether that threshold is 
still appropriate. A few commenters recommended raising the daily 
minimum liquid asset requirement, to at least 20 percent or 25 percent. 
One commenter recommended raising the weekly minimum liquidity 
requirement to 50 percent.
    A commenter recommended that the timeframe used for the weekly 
liquidity framework should be calibrated to redemption expectations 
across the agencies. One commenter stated that the proposal would 
require issuers to honor redemption requests within two business days 
from the date of the redemption request. Accordingly, the commenter 
stated that liquidity and operational constraints would not prevent 
almost all permissible reserve assets from being monetized within the 
redemption window. Another commenter recommended that the rule clarify 
how issuers should comply with the daily and weekly liquidity 
requirements without maintaining a significantly high cash balance that 
does not promote the rule's liquidity objectives.
    One commenter opposed the weekly liquidity requirement, stating 
that the requirement would not have a meaningful effect. This commenter 
stated that any reserve asset can be monetized within five business 
days. Several commenters opposed the daily liquidity requirement. Some 
commenters stated that the daily liquidity requirement would create 
unnecessary credit risk. One commenter stated that the minimum daily 
requirement is unnecessary because the scope of eligible reserve assets 
is highly liquid, as demonstrated by the requirements of SEC Rule 2a-7 
(under which Treasury securities may count towards daily and weekly 
liquidity requirements). One commenter asserted that the 10 percent 
daily liquidity requirement lacks empirical or theoretical support and 
is inconsistent with international prudential standards, like the Basel 
III liquidity standards.
    A few commenters recommended that the final rule adopt a 
principles-based approach in which issuers would be required to 
demonstrate the capability to monetize at least 10 percent and 30 
percent of their reserves on an overnight and weekly basis, 
respectively. One of these commenters asserted that an issuer should be 
permitted to demonstrate its monetization capability through any 
combination of eligible reserve assets. Other commenters stated that a 
principles-based approach would permit issuers to hold reserves like 
tokenized money market funds, which have less credit risk than bank 
deposits and settle no later than the next day.
    Several commenters commented on which assets should be eligible to 
count towards the daily and weekly liquidity requirements. One 
commenter recommended that eligible government money market funds 
offering same-day redemption should count towards the daily liquidity 
reserves requirement. A few commenters recommended that assets eligible 
to count towards the daily liquidity requirement should include reverse 
repurchase agreements, conducted on either an open or overnight basis. 
One commenter recommended that same- and next-day high-quality 
instruments should be

[[Page 67054]]

considered eligible reserve assets for purposes of the daily liquidity 
requirement. Another commenter suggested that all GENIUS Act-compliant 
reserve assets should count towards the daily liquidity requirement.
    One commenter recommended that reserves for the weekly liquidity 
requirement should include any eligible reserve asset convertible to 
cash within five business days, including GENIUS Act-eligible money 
market funds. Such a liquidity framework, the commenter reasoned, would 
be focused on functional liquidity and, in turn, better reflect how 
liquidity is generated in funding markets. One commenter recommended 
that government money market funds should count towards the weekly 
liquidity requirement, as redemption and settlement typically occur 
within one business day. A few commenters recommended that qualifying 
registered funds, like exchange-traded funds, should count towards the 
weekly liquidity requirement, considering their short settlement period 
and their daily price and portfolio transparency.
    One commenter stated that deposits are more vulnerable than 
custodied securities. One commenter noted that tokenized funds under 
SEC Rule 2a-7 are being developed primarily as collateral instruments 
rather than as cash payment instruments. One commenter suggested that 
any offset for expected inflows should be permitted only on a 
conservative basis. One commenter recommended that the OCC remove or 
replace the requirement in proposed Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(ii) relating to 
Board review of the percentage of reserve assets required to be held 
that must be receivable within five days.
    One commenter argued that concentration limits should be limited to 
uninsured deposit holdings because further concentration restrictions 
would add little stability and could increase operational and run risk 
or reduce reserve yields. This commenter also stated that it is not 
possible to apply concentration limits to United States Treasury 
repurchase agreements because there is only one remaining tri-party 
repurchase agreement clearing bank for United States Treasury 
repurchase agreements and it handles virtually all of the cleared tri-
party repurchase agreement market.
    Several commenters specifically addressed the proposed 40 percent 
concentration limit under the proposed safe harbor. A few commenters 
stated that the 40 percent limit was well calibrated. One commenter 
suggested the limit should be raised to 60 percent to reflect the 
limited number of custodians currently willing to serve stablecoin 
issuers. Another commenter suggested reducing the limit to 15 percent 
and explicitly prohibiting the use of affiliated bank deposits as 
qualified reserves unless ring-fenced under separate capitalization and 
governance structures. One commenter stated that the 40 percent 
threshold was too limiting and that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should have flexibility to use one or more custodians. One 
commenter noted the limit could be breached due to changes in asset 
prices rather than redemptions or transfers. Another commenter stated 
that concentration restrictions should be based on gross exposures, 
aggregated across affiliates, custody, deposits, and bilateral 
transactions. This commenter further suggested that, if the OCC adopts 
deposit concentration caps, they should be tiered by bank credit 
quality, distinguish between insured and uninsured exposure, and also 
distinguish between deposit exposure and collateralized repo exposure. 
Some commenters categorically objected to the 40 percent threshold. One 
commenter explained that the concentration limit would still allow 
large exposures in the form of uninsured deposits, which highlights 
problems associated with a single numerical threshold without 
distinguishing between private credit risk and infrastructure or 
custodian concentration. A few commenters suggested that concentration 
caps should be tiered based on the issuer's size, and one of these 
commenters also recommended higher limits for assets collateralized by 
United States Treasuries or held at systemically important financial 
institutions.
    Several commenters argued that custodians or assets held in custody 
should be excluded from concentration limits. Some of these commenters 
stated that applying concentration and diversification limits to 
custodial arrangements would require permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to manage a larger number of transactions across custodians, 
which increases the risk of operational and process errors without 
meaningfully reducing risks. One commenter stated that few institutions 
currently provide custodial services to issuers. A few commenters 
stated that custodians are highly regulated and pose little credit risk 
with respect to non-cash assets held off-balance sheet that are 
segregated from the custodian's proprietary assets. A few of these 
commenters stated that custodian-level concentration limits may 
introduce risks for permitted payment stablecoin issuers by fragmenting 
reserve assets across numerous custodians and banking relationships. 
One commenter stated that custodian diversification requirements would 
be novel, as SEC-registered money market funds and similar instruments 
are not subject to similar requirements, and could drive issuers away 
from the institutions best able to provide secure custody services. A 
few commenters suggested that concentration caps would be ineffective 
at preventing failures and could contribute to instability by spreading 
and potentially commingling reserve assets among the same set of large 
asset managers.
    One commenter suggested that self-custodied assets should be 
explicitly excluded from the 40 percent limit. Another commenter 
suggested excluding deposits held at an OCC-regulated affiliate if the 
affiliate holds an equivalent amount of cash at its Federal Reserve 
master account and remains well-capitalized. A few commenters stated 
that the 40 percent cap should not apply to Federal Reserve Bank 
balances, and one of these commenters also suggested eliminating the 
cap for global systemically important banks (G-SIB).
    Several commenters raised other criticisms of concentration limits. 
One commenter suggested the OCC exclude ETFs from the 40 percent 
requirement, or at a minimum explain the benefit of imposing the limit 
on ETFs, since shares are generally held through a third-party 
custodian subject to a legal and regulatory framework that addresses 
asset segregation and protects the investor in the event of the 
custodian's insolvency. This commenter also stated the 40 percent limit 
should not apply to self-custodied money market funds or on a look-
through basis to a government money market fund's custodian or other 
service providers. One commenter stated that the 40 percent limit 
discourages the use of local banks for remote communities and proposed 
a higher limit for reserves held at insured depository institutions 
that are located in more remote areas and meet certain other criteria. 
One commenter stated that the 40 percent limit should apply 
specifically to uninsured deposits. One commenter suggested the OCC 
clarify the scope of ``other exposures'' and in particular should 
address whether and how intraday credit facilities, uncommitted 
liquidity lines, and custodial sub-arrangements extended by or through 
an eligible financial institution would count toward the cap.
    A few commenters criticized the proposed look-through requirement. 
One of these commenters stated that the

[[Page 67055]]

approach would increase compliance costs and likely impose substantial 
monitoring and reporting burdens, which could also reduce operational 
efficiency and increase the risk of settlement delays or frictions. 
Another commenter stated that the requirement could create significant 
operational challenges since reserve assets may be held through omnibus 
accounts, sub-custody chains, or collateral-agent structures that do 
not map cleanly onto a single-institution concentration calculation. 
One commenter recommended removing the phrase ``through other 
exposures'' so that issuers would not need to ``look through'' sub-
custodians to satisfy diversification requirements, as issuers would 
need to obtain and continuously monitor information about their 
custodians' internal sub-custodial arrangements and may be at risk of 
non-compliance due to subsequent events beyond their control. One 
commenter suggested the look-through requirement is unnecessary with 
respect to Treasury securities, repurchase agreements, and securities 
issued by a GENIUS Act-eligible investment fund, since these types of 
reserve assets ultimately reside with highly regulated central 
counterparties or central securities depositories.
    A few commenters recommended that the OCC remove the requirement 
limiting the amount of daily liquidity an issuer may hold at one 
financial institution. They reasoned that the requirement is 
impractical and the risks associated with cash reserves held at 
regulated institutions are already effectively addressed within the 
existing prudential framework. A few commenters noted that ordinary 
transaction flows could cause an issuer to routinely breach a 50 
percent limit on daily liquidity at a single institution, especially 
when an issuer places liquidity reserves in only two financial 
institutions. Commenters recommended the OCC address this issue by 
raising the limit to 60 percent or building flexibility into the limit 
on liquidity reserves held at a single institution.
    A few commenters objected to the limits on deposit concentration, 
in whole or in part. One commenter suggested that there should be no 
limit on deposits at a single institution, and if such a deposit limit 
is established, the limit should be in the 20 to 25 percent range. 
Another commenter recommended that limits on deposits should not apply 
to insured deposits, and that, for uninsured deposits, the OCC should 
adopt a tiered limit for uninsured deposits that reflects historical 
loss rates. A few commenters advocated for the establishment of a lower 
deposit concentration limit, including more granular limitations. One 
commenter suggested that an issuer should be permitted to deposit no 
more than 5 percent of eligible reserve assets at depository 
institutions and have no more than 2 percent exposure to a single 
institution, with additional deposit balances permissible for purposes 
of operational liquidity.
    Several commenters requested or suggested clarifications in the 
final rule regarding how to calculate the weighted average maturity. A 
few commenters requested confirmation that the weighted average 
maturity calculation would be performed on a portfolio basis, allowing 
issuers to hold a mix of maturities so long as the overall weighted 
average does not exceed the 20-day limit. Another commenter suggested 
the 20-day requirement be paired with amortized cost valuation. A 
commenter recommended that issuers whose stablecoins are predominantly 
used as settlement infrastructure for duration-bearing tokenized 
instruments be permitted to maintain a higher weighted average 
maturity, subject to supervisory approval. One commenter recommended 
that the weighted average maturity be extended in response to 
concentration in Treasury markets. Another commenter suggested the OCC 
have a two-year pilot program and modify the weighted average maturity 
requirements based on data collected during that timeframe. A few 
commenters opposed the use of SEC Rule 2a-7's methodology to calculate 
the weighted average maturity. One of these commenters explained that 
the key consideration for measuring liquidity is how quickly an issuer 
can convert a non-cash asset to cash. The commenter stated that use of 
the methodology in SEC Rule 2a-7 would effectively assign a 20- or 40-
day maturity to funds with shares that can be redeemed at par in much 
less time. Because of the speed with which reserves can be redeemed, 
the commenter recommended the OCC assign a weighted average maturity of 
zero for money market funds.
    Another commenter stated that payment stablecoins represent 
redemption-backed liabilities, whereas money market funds are 
investment products that seek to maintain stability of net asset value. 
Accordingly, the commenter stated that the calculation methodology 
under SEC Rule 2a-7, which includes ``maturity-shortening provisions'' 
for securities subject to a demand feature or interest rate reset, is 
not the appropriate measurement for stablecoin reserves. The commenter 
suggested that the final rule calculate maturity as the period 
remaining until the date on which, in accordance with the terms of the 
security, the principal amount must unconditionally be paid, or in the 
case of a security called for redemption, the date on which the 
redemption payment must be made. A few commenters supported the 20-day 
weighted average maturity requirement. Several other commenters opposed 
the 20-day weighted average maturity on various grounds. Several of 
these commenters were concerned that the weighted average maturity 
requirement would limit issuers' ownership of reserve assets with 
longer maturities, including Treasuries, which would otherwise be 
permissible under the GENIUS Act. Commenters also asserted that the 20-
day weighted average maturity requirement would constrain efficient 
reserve management, increase operational risk by requiring investment 
in short-term assets that mature or roll over rapidly, and would impose 
compliance burdens on issuers, who would need to ensure that reserve 
assets do not breach the 20-day weighted average maturity requirement. 
A few commenters stated that the proposed 20-day weighted average 
maturity requirement would provide little, if any, benefit to an 
issuer's liquidity and redemption capabilities.
    Several commenters recommended that the OCC increase the length of 
the weighted average maturity. A few commenters recommended increasing 
the length to 40 days, to allow smaller issuers more flexibility and to 
allow more issuers to use three-month Treasuries. A few commenters 
recommended increasing the length to 60 days to align with money market 
funds and SEC Rule 2a-7, and to afford issuers greater flexibility to 
use Treasuries. A few commenters recommended increasing the length to 
93 days, to align with permitted Treasury holdings.
    Several commenters proffered their views on how the reserve 
requirements of the proposed rule might affect community banks. One 
commenter, for example, noted that payment stablecoin reserves may not 
be as stable as demand deposits and thus may subject community banks to 
a greater run risk, while another noted that community banks for that 
reason may not be willing to provide services to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. Another commenter argued that reserve diffusion 
requirements could increase the financial stability risk of a run on 
one permitted payment stablecoin issuer throughout a large number of 
community banks. However, other

[[Page 67056]]

commenters worried that payment stablecoins will shift stable funding 
sources away from community banks, reducing their competitiveness, and 
believed that reserve asset diversification should be premised in part 
on the funding needs of community banks. A few commenters argued that 
diversification should be risk-based and should not increase the risks 
to permitted payment stablecoin issuers or payment stablecoin holders 
to achieve other aims.
    The final rule neither mandates that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers use community banks nor requires community banks to take on 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers as customers. The OCC believes 
that this approach appropriately allows community banks to exercise 
their business judgment with respect to payment stablecoin activities. 
The OCC acknowledges that deposits that serve as reserves backing a 
payment stablecoin could, at this time, be less stable sources of 
funding than other types of deposits. It is possible that these 
deposits may become more stable over time (i.e., as the GENIUS Act 
framework continues to be implemented). At this point, in light of the 
comments received, the OCC believes that diversification requirements 
that neither mandate nor discourage placement at community banks are 
appropriate.
    The final rule makes a number of changes to Sec.  15.11(c) in 
response to the comments received. Specifically, the OCC is adopting a 
hybrid approach using the principles-based approach from Option A and a 
modified and limited set of the quantitative requirements from Option 
B. The proposed rule included robust liquidity requirements but did not 
include stress testing or buffer requirements. The proposal noted that 
an alternative possibility would be to remove some of the proposed 
liquidity requirements, though this may warrant increased capital or 
buffer requirements. The final rule substantially lessens the 
quantitative liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements 
that apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and instead imposes 
stress testing and buffer requirements in Sec. Sec.  15.11 and 15.13. 
The OCC recognizes that, as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer sells 
more liquid assets to meet redemption requests in times of stress, it 
may temporarily fail to satisfy all of the terms in Sec.  15.11(c) of 
the final rule. For example, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
might draw first on its deposits to timely redeem payment stablecoins, 
and, as a result, may temporarily fall below the 5 percent minimum 
while it reconfigures its reserve asset portfolio. Depending on the 
facts and circumstances, negative supervisory consequences for a 
failure to maintain that 5 percent minimum may be inappropriate, and 
the OCC will consider any supervisory actions for such a temporary 
violation in light of the totality of the circumstances causing the 
violation. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer should nevertheless 
appropriately diversify its reserve assets as soon as practicable 
following such an event. However, at no point can a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's reserve asset value be less than the outstanding 
issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    Consistent with the proposed rule, Sec.  15.11(c)(1) provides that 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must maintain reserve assets that 
are sufficiently diverse to manage potential credit, liquidity, 
interest rate, and price risks. The final rule clarifies in Sec.  
15.11(c)(1)(iii) that, depending on relevant factors, including a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile, business model, and 
portfolio of reserve assets, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may 
need to maintain an amount of reserve assets that exceeds the 
requirements of Sec.  15.11(c)(2) and the reserve asset value of which 
exceeds outstanding issuance value. A permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer must measure and manage the risk that concentrating reserve 
assets at one eligible financial institution or a small number of 
eligible financial institutions may impair the ability of a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to satisfy redemption demands if individual 
eligible financial institutions are unable to return, or if there is a 
delay in returning, reserve assets placed by a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer.
    The final rule clarifies that, depending on relevant factors, 
including a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile, 
business model, and stock of reserve assets, a permitted payment
