stablecoin issuer may need to maintain reserve assets in excess of the 
daily liquidity amounts required under paragraph (c)(2) (discussed 
below). The OCC believes that this baseline principles-based approach, 
supplemented with the quantitative requirements described below, 
provides permitted payment stablecoin issuers sufficient flexibility 
while also providing a backstop against key risks that could result 
from undue concentration in assets that may be difficult to monetize 
within a day or exposures to a single counterparty. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers with less complex business models and lower risk 
profiles may be able to maintain a less diverse stock of reserve assets 
than permitted payment stablecoin issuers with more complex business 
models or higher risk profiles. However, section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)) mandates some reserve asset 
diversification for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, both in 
types of reserve assets maintained and in the number of eligible 
financial institutions holding a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
reserve assets. The OCC expects that all permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers will need to maintain multiple reserve asset types, if only to 
serve as a backup to what is otherwise a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's primary reserve asset. Some permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers may need to maintain more robustly diverse stocks of reserve 
assets to satisfy Sec.  15.11(c), depending on their business model, 
risk profile, and other relevant factors. For example, a large 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer with complex operations may need to 
maintain deposits with multiple eligible financial institutions, as 
well as a stock of Treasury bills, potentially custodied with more than 
one eligible financial institution in order to ensure they are capable 
of being monetized during periods of financial stress. Factors such as 
the number of parties that redeem directly with the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer, the volume of redemptions (and volatility with 
respect to such volume), and the number and nature of the blockchains 
on which a payment stablecoin is traded could all increase the 
complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations and 
weigh in favor of maintaining multiple different pools of reserve 
assets.
    Section 15.11(c)(2) of the final rule provides a modified version 
of the daily liquidity and counterparty concentration requirement from 
the proposed rule. Section 15.11(c)(2)(i) requires a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to maintain at least 5 percent of its reserve assets 
as demand deposits (or other deposits that may be withdrawn upon 
request at any time), funds in share accounts that are payable on 
demand, or money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal 
Reserve Bank.\88\ This minimum daily liquidity requirement is intended 
to ensure that a payment stablecoin issuer has readily

[[Page 67057]]

available funds necessary to meet redemption requests. While all of the 
proposed reserve assets should be liquid and easily monetizable, the 
requirement to have some minimum level of immediately liquid funds 
provides additional protection against the risk that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer would be unable to meet redemption requests 
in a timely manner, which is critical to maintain confidence in the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the stablecoin industry as a 
whole. Including a baseline requirement to maintain a minimum 
percentage of liquidity that is immediately available (without the need 
to sell any assets, even highly liquid assets like Treasury securities) 
will help ensure a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to 
meet redemption requests. In light of other changes to Sec. Sec.  
15.11(a) and 15.13 (e.g., stress testing requirements), the final rule 
lowers this daily liquidity requirement from 10 percent to 5 percent of 
reserve assets. The requirements of Sec. Sec.  15.11(a) and 15.13 are 
designed to ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are able 
to timely redeem payment stablecoins, including in times of stress. 
Since these requirements will necessarily entail measures the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must take to maintain capacity to meet short-
term redemption requests, it is appropriate to lower the quantitative 
requirement for daily liquidity. For example, when a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer has capabilities to monetize reserve assets quickly 
because a large portion of their reserve assets is in the form of 
Treasury securities, whether held directly or by a custodian, that may 
obviate the need to hold a higher amount of daily liquidity.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \88\ The final rule refers to ``funds in share accounts that are 
payable on demand,'' rather than ``insured shares,'' to clarify that 
such funds must be available on demand to meet the 5 percent minimum 
requirement in Sec.  15.11(c)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The final rule does not include the requirement from proposed Sec.  
15.11(c)(4) requiring no more than 50 percent of daily liquidity to be 
held at any one eligible financial institution in light of the fact 
that the total requirement has been reduced to 5 percent (the total 
amount of required daily liquidity that could be held at a single 
eligible financial institution under the proposed rule). The OCC notes 
that, under Sec.  15.12, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must 
notify the OCC when it receives redemption requests in excess of 10 
percent of its outstanding issuance value over a single 24-hour period. 
As discussed elsewhere, permitted payment stablecoin issuers that hold 
only 5 percent of their reserve assets as demand deposits or money 
standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank should take steps to 
ensure that they can timely redeem tendered payment stablecoins under 
stressed conditions.
    Section 15.11(c)(2)(ii)(A) of the final rule requires a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to limit its exposure to any one counterparty 
to no more than 40 percent of its reserve assets. Section 
15.11(c)(2)(ii)(B) lists various exposures that are not subject to this 
limitation. Under the final rule, the following exposures are excluded: 
(1) exposures to the United States Government, (2) exposures to an 
appropriate custodian (as described in Sec.  15.11(d)), resulting from 
reserve assets being held in the custody of the custodian, and (3) 
exposures resulting from centrally cleared repurchase agreements and 
centrally cleared reverse repurchase agreements. For clarity, reserve 
assets held directly by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer also are 
not subject to the 40 percent limit in Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(ii)(A) because 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot be its own counterparty. 
The requirement in Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(ii) is intended to prevent an 
issuer from being overly exposed to any one eligible financial 
institution or counterparty, including through a deposit relationship, 
bilateral repurchase agreement, bilateral reverse repurchase agreement, 
or investment company. While this requirement would not eliminate the 
chance of either temporarily or permanently losing reserve assets 
because of distress at an eligible financial institution holding 
reserve assets, it would ensure that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers have other reserve assets available to satisfy redemption 
requests. The final rule modifies the counterparty limit by explicitly 
excluding exposures to the United States Government. As discussed 
above, exposures to Federal Reserve Banks would remain subject to this 
limit. The final rule excludes exposures resulting from centrally 
cleared repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements due to 
the low credit risk associated with such transactions.
    The final rule also does not apply the 40 percent limit to 
custodians that meet certain requirements (as discussed in greater 
detail below). The OCC agrees with commenters that imposing a limit on 
custodians that comply with the requirements of the GENIUS Act may 
introduce unnecessary operational risks without a corresponding 
benefit. At the same time, it is important that there are mechanisms in 
the final rule to help ensure that custodians of reserve assets comply 
with the terms of the GENIUS Act if they are to be exempt from the 40 
percent limit. Accordingly, as discussed in the next section, the final 
rule imposes certain additional requirements on permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers with respect to custodians designed to ensure that 
the custodians comply with the requirements of the GENIUS Act.
    Paragraph (c) of the final rule's Sec.  15.11 does not include a 
weighted average maturity requirement. The OCC believes that changes to 
Sec. Sec.  15.11(a) and 15.13 will be sufficient to ensure that the 
reserve asset portfolio of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
sufficiently liquid without imposing a separate weighted average 
maturity requirement.
e. Custody of Reserve Assets (Sec.  15.11(d))
Self-Custody and Use of Affiliates
    Several commenters suggested that the OCC place significant limits 
on, or prohibit, an issuer holding its reserve assets itself (self-
custody). These commenters argued that self-custody and captive 
affiliate structures can undermine the independence of the custody 
function and create conflicts of interest inconsistent with safety and 
soundness. Some commenters stated that the proposed rule does not 
provide sufficient clarity on how self-custody would work in practice, 
including: (i) whether a permitted payment stablecoin issuer holding 
reserves directly would qualify as the covered customer or an eligible 
financial institution, (ii) how reserve assets would be segregated from 
proprietary assets, and (iii) whether the custody function would need 
to be separated from issuance and reserve management activities. A few 
commenters noted that, if self-custody is permitted, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should be required to maintain clear segregation, 
bankruptcy-remote protections, and operational separation. Some 
commenters argued that additional capital requirements should apply 
because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be assuming risks 
otherwise borne by an external custodian. Other commenters opposed 
intragroup reserve arrangements and urged the OCC to apply 
concentration limits across affiliated entities on a consolidated basis 
rather than institution by institution. In contrast, a couple of 
commenters stated that the OCC should not mandate fixed minimum 
allocations of reserve assets between affiliated and unaffiliated 
custodians and instead should focus on operational resilience, 
concentration risk, and effective segregation while allowing issuers 
flexibility in structuring custody arrangements.
    Many commenters addressed how reserve assets should be managed when

[[Page 67058]]

a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is affiliated with, or is a 
subsidiary of, an insured depository institution. Some commenters 
stated that affiliated custody arrangements should be subject to 
consistent risk management standards and that reserve assets, 
liquidity-management functions, and control frameworks should be 
clearly maintained at the subsidiary level, with dedicated personnel, 
independent governance, and clear entity-level accountability to reduce 
the risk of internal commingling, competing liquidity demands, or 
unclear authority during stress. In contrast, one commenter stated that 
the OCC should not impose permitted payment stablecoin issuer-specific 
governance or staffing mandates on bank-subsidiary issuers and should 
allow them to use centralized group treasury and risk functions so long 
as applicable statutory standards are met. Another commenter opposed 
any exception from concentration caps that would allow an insured 
depository institution subsidiary to place all reserves at its parent 
or an affiliate. These commenters argued that statutory flexibility for 
omnibus commingling increases, rather than reduces, the need to avoid 
single-bank dependency and ensure strong segregation, control, and 
auditability.
    Several commenters stated that the OCC should add additional 
requirements in instances in which a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer custodies reserve assets or deposits cash reserve assets at an 
affiliate. These commenters stated that affiliate custody of reserve 
assets may give rise to significant risks as there is no independent 
custodian to provide an added layer of protection to holders of the 
relevant payment stablecoin. Commenters suggested, for example, either 
limiting the amount of reserves that may be custodied or deposited at 
an affiliate, imposing enhanced capital buffers, or including affiliate 
concentration risk as a factor that the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's independent accountant must consider.
    The final rule, consistent with the proposal and the text of the 
GENIUS Act, does not prohibit self-custody of reserve assets or the use 
of an affiliate to hold reserve assets in custody. As discussed below, 
direct reserve asset holdings will not be subject to a counterparty 
limit but non-custodial exposures to affiliates will be. The OCC notes 
that, in the case of subsidiaries of national banks or Federal savings 
associations, the OCC will have clear visibility into the business of 
the parent and the subsidiary, through the supervisory process. The OCC 
agrees with commenters that reserve assets should be operationally 
separate from the other assets of a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. The OCC notes that Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(ii) requires a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to maintain reserve assets that are 
identifiable and that are segregated and not commingled with other 
assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. In 
addition, as discussed elsewhere, the final rule has been designed to 
permit the use of separate issuer SPVs, such that the reserve assets of 
each issuer would be segregated from one another. Finally, with respect 
to affiliate transactions, the OCC notes that insider and affiliate 
transactions must comply with the requirements of Sec.  15.13 
(described in greater detail below).
Fiduciary Responsibilities
    Commenters expressed differing opinions on whether fiduciary 
treatment should be avoided to reduce regulatory uncertainty or 
required to strengthen segregation and insolvency protections. A few 
commenters suggested that the OCC clarify whether directed custody of 
reserve assets constitutes a fiduciary activity under 12 CFR part 9. 
Some commenters stated that directed, non-discretionary custody should 
not be treated as fiduciary by default unless the custodian 
independently performs a fiduciary function identified in part 9. In 
contrast, one commenter stated that reserve assets should be required 
to be held in a fiduciary capacity and that all institutions with 
custody of stablecoin reserves should hold those assets in a legally 
segregated manner for the exclusive benefit of stablecoin holders. That 
commenter also noted that fiduciary custody at a national trust bank 
provides stronger insolvency protections because the assets are not 
part of the custodian's estate, unlike ordinary deposits at a 
depository bank, which become general liabilities of the bank. The OCC 
declines to make a blanket statement that directed custody of reserve 
assets is a fiduciary activity. Whether a custodian is subject to 12 
CFR part 9 or 12 CFR part 150 will depend, among other factors, on the 
charter type of the custodian and applicable law, including the 
agreement that the custodian has with its customer.
    Some commenters stated that responsibility for determining whether 
assets qualify as permissible reserve assets, whether reserves are 
sufficient on a portfolio-wide basis, and how reserves should be 
classified or reported should remain with the issuer rather than the 
custodian. Other commenters noted that custodians often lack visibility 
into an issuer's full reserve portfolio, particularly where multiple 
custodians or intermediaries are used, and therefore should not be 
required to independently verify reserve composition, adequacy, 
sufficiency, or compliance with diversification and concentration 
requirements. As discussed in greater detail below, the OCC confirms 
that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains responsible for 
ensuring compliance with all requirements in the GENIUS Act and 
implementing regulations related to reserve assets and other 
requirements pertaining to its issuance of payment stablecoins.\89\ 
Covered custodians under subpart C of the final rule are responsible 
for compliance with requirements contained within the GENIUS Act and 
subpart C related to appropriate custody of reserve assets and other 
covered assets.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\89\ As noted above, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may 
use an investment adviser or asset manager to manage reserve assets 
under Sec.  15.10 of the final rule, but the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer remains responsible for ensuring compliance with 
the GENIUS Act and its implementing regulations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Obligations of Third-Party Custodians To Ensure Compliance
    Commenters addressed oversight of custodians, service providers, 
and counterparties, with some stating that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should conduct thorough initial due diligence and ongoing 
monitoring of custodians' legal status, financial condition, 
operational resilience, cybersecurity, and compliance programs, 
consistent with third-party risk management principles. In contrast, 
one commenter suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should not be required to monitor the financial condition of all 
depository institutions holding reserve assets because those 
institutions are already subject to robust prudential regulation. 
Another commenter stated that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
should continuously monitor the condition of its counterparties and 
treat concentration risk as risk-sensitive.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC clarify that third-party 
custodians are not responsible for ensuring that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer directs reserve 
assets to the correct account, such as a reserve account rather than a 
proprietary account. The commenter stated that, consistent with the 
futures commission merchant framework, the issuer should bear 
responsibility for segregation and avoiding commingling, while the 
custodian's role should be limited to

[[Page 67059]]

recognizing and maintaining the designated account as separate. This 
commenter also noted that custodians should not be required to verify 
the sufficiency of reserve assets held by a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer at the custodian or be subject to additional 
requirements with respect to transaction services they provide. One 
commenter requested that the OCC expressly confirm that prior OCC 
guidance, including Interpretive Letter 1172, to the extent it required 
custodians to monitor 1 to 1 reserve sufficiency, has been superseded 
by the GENIUS Act framework. Another commenter requested additional 
clarity regarding reserve assets held through custodians or 
intermediaries, including governance, control, and access rights.
    As discussed in greater detail below, the final rule has been 
modified to provide additional clarity and notice to custodians. With 
respect to Interpretive Letter 1172, the OCC notes that the letter 
addressed deposit-taking activity and not custody. Nevertheless, the 
OCC confirms that a national bank or Federal savings association that 
holds deposits that serve as reserves or that holds other reserve 
assets in custody is not under an obligation to ensure that the reserve 
assets equal or exceed the outstanding issuance value of the payment 
stablecoin unless otherwise required by contract.
    Under Sec.  15.11(d) of the final rule, reserve assets in the 
custody of one or more eligible financial institutions will not be 
subject to the 40 percent limit in Sec.  15.11(c)(2)(ii) provided that 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer: (1) identifies itself to the 
custodian as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (2) ensures that 
the custodian commits to adhering to the requirements of section 10 of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909), including applicable implementing 
regulations; and (3) engages in appropriate due diligence and ongoing 
monitoring of its custodial arrangements to ensure compliance with 
applicable requirements of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.), 
including applicable implementing regulations. These changes are 
intended to benefit custodians by providing them notice of when their 
obligations under section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) attach. 
In addition, the requirements make clear that the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer has an ongoing responsibility to conduct appropriate 
monitoring of the custodians that it employs. The OCC believes that 
this ongoing monitoring requirement will be both more effective and 
less burdensome than imposing a hard limit on the amount of exposure 
that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer can have to a single 
custodian. The final rule's approach requires a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to take appropriate steps to ensure that its 
custodians comply with the GENIUS Act. This puts an emphasis on 
understanding and analyzing the activities of custodians, whereas the 
proposal could have allowed a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
meet its obligations merely by diversifying among different custodians 
without engaging with the substance of the custodians' activities.\90\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \90\ In response to certain comments, the OCC also confirms 
that, while a custodian may provide reserve asset valuation 
services, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is responsible for 
ensuring that its reserve asset value equals or exceeds its 
outstanding issuance value at all times.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

f. Minimum Insured Deposit Requirement for Large Issuers
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(d) would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer with an outstanding issuance value of $25 billion or 
more to, on each business day, maintain at least 0.5 percent of its 
reserve assets in the form of insured deposits or insured shares at an 
insured depository institution, up to a cap of $500 million.
    Several commenters opposed the proposed insured-deposit minimum. 
These commenters explained that the insured-deposit minimum would add 
significant operational complexity and liquidity risk without providing 
a commensurate prudential benefit, especially for large operational 
deposit balances that do not meaningfully benefit from deposit 
insurance. Regarding liquidity risk, a commenter asserted that many 
deposit insurance schemes have tighter settlement cutoff times than 
traditional demand deposit accounts, which would increase operational 
risk if reserves would not be immediately available. Furthermore, the 
FDIC's proposed restrictions on insured reserve balances would further 
complicate operationalizing the insured-deposit minimum requirement. A 
few commenters asserted that the OCC lacks the statutory authority to 
require issuers to place a percentage of reserve assets in numerous 
banks through the minimum insured deposit requirement. One commenter 
noted that the FDIC does not insure deposits above the $250,000 
corporate limit, a limit that could render the minimum insured deposit 
requirement operationally infeasible. A commenter stated that the 
minimum insured deposit requirement would confuse stablecoin holders 
regarding what percentage of reserve assets are insured. Another 
commenter asserted that the requirement would unduly restrict an 
issuer's ability to manage counterparty and credit risk. One commenter 
noted that it is expensive to open numerous deposit accounts, and the 
costs necessary to comply with the minimum insured deposit requirement 
could impede the adoption of stablecoins.
    One commenter requested clarification on how the minimum insured 
deposit requirement interacts with FDIC deposit insurance limits and 
capacity constraints at insured depository institutions. A few 
commenters suggested that if the minimum insured deposit requirement is 
finalized, it should not exceed the smaller of $100 million or 0.1 
percent of reserve assets. A commenter recommended the OCC calibrate 
the minimum insured deposit requirement to recognize the distinction 
between reserves held at smaller banks and other institutions.
    A few commenters were in favor of establishing a minimum insured 
deposit requirement and asserted that the proposed $25 billion 
threshold for issuers to be subject to the minimum insured deposit 
requirement is too high to prevent runs, de-pegging, and contagion. One 
of these commenters recommended lowering the threshold from $25 billion 
to $10 billion and raising the requisite percentage of reserve assets 
comprising insured deposits or shares from 0.5 percent to 5 percent, 
with total insured deposits or shares not to exceed $500 million 
regardless of the size of the issuer. A commenter opined that it is too 
early to determine whether all reserve deposits should be required to 
be insured in the event deposit insurance rules change, and that the 
final rule should not address such a requirement.
    One commenter supported permitting issuers to use deposit placement 
services to comply with the GENIUS Act's diversification requirements 
for stablecoin reserves, subject to appropriate due diligence, 
including independent audit reports and Federal Financial Institutions 
Examination Council examinations. A few commenters opposed the use of 
deposit placement services for compliance with the diversification 
requirements, as the addition of intermediaries would increase 
operational complexity and counterparty risk.
    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is not 
adopting a requirement to have a minimum insured deposit amount. The 
OCC agrees with commenters that this minimum requirement may introduce 
additional operational risk that does not merit the

[[Page 67060]]

reduction in credit risk associated with having a minimum insured 
amount.
g. Composition Report, Monthly Certification, and Failure To Maintain 
Minimum Reserve Assets (Sec. Sec.  15.11(e) Through (g))
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(e) would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to publish on its website by noon on the last day of 
each month the composition of the issuer's reserves held pursuant to 
the GENIUS Act as of noon of the last day of the prior month, using a 
format substantially similar to the template provided in table 1 to 
proposed Sec.  15.11(e). The report contained fields for the total 
number of outstanding payment stablecoins issued by the issuer and the 
amount (fair value) and composition of the reserves, including the 
average tenor and geographic location of custody of each category of 
reserve instruments. The information in the report, including the value 
of reserve assets, would have been reported as of the end of the 
previous month. Section 15.11(e) of the proposed rule would have 
implemented the requirement in section 4(a)(1)(C) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(C)).
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(f) implemented the applicable requirements of 
section 4(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(3)). This 
provision requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to, each month, 
have the information disclosed in the previous month-end report 
examined by a registered public accounting firm. Proposed Sec.  
15.11(f)(1) would have required the examination of the previous month-
end report to occur by noon on the last day of each month and would 
have required the report to be published on the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's website at the same time as the monthly report 
required under proposed Sec.  15.11(e). Consistent with the Act, 
proposed Sec.  15.11(f)(2) would have required the Chief Executive 
Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or the persons performing the 
equivalent functions) of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
submit to the OCC a certification that the monthly report is accurate. 
Under section 4(a)(3)(C) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(3)(C)), any 
person who submits this required certification knowing that such 
certification is false shall be subject to the same criminal penalties 
as those set forth under 18 U.S.C. 1350(c).
    Proposed Sec.  15.11(g) set forth the consequences and remedial 
measures that would have applied if a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer did not comply with the requirements of proposed Sec.  15.11. 
Proposed Sec.  15.11(g)(1) would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to notify the OCC through its appropriate supervisory 
office on any day in which its reserve asset amount has fallen below 
the required minimum in proposed Sec.  15.11(a). Proposed Sec.  
15.11(g)(2) would have barred a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
that falls below the required minimum from issuing new payment 
stablecoins until it had remediated the shortfall except as necessary 
to facilitate a transfer of payment stablecoins from one distributed 
ledger to another and provided that the net outstanding issuance value 
does not increase. Proposed Sec.  15.11(g)(3) provided that, if a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer fails to meet its reserve asset 
requirement for 15 consecutive business days, it must begin liquidation 
of reserve assets and redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins 
consistent with Sec.  15.12 and may not charge customers a fee to 
redeem their payment stablecoins at any time during the liquidation. 
The OCC would have been able to extend the time period under proposed 
Sec.  15.11(g)(3) in its sole discretion. Because of the importance of 
maintaining minimum reserve asset levels, the proposed rule included 
automatic consequences for any non-compliance intended to prevent any 
concerns from developing further. This provision was intended to 
prevent chronic non-compliance with minimum reserve asset requirements. 
Proposed Sec.  15.11(g)(4) stated that if at any point the OCC 
determined that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer had not 
demonstrated that it meets the reserve asset requirements in proposed 
Sec.  15.11(a), (b), (c), or (d), the OCC may require the issuer to 
submit a plan describing how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
will attain compliance and the timeline for the plan. If the OCC 
determined, either before or after the submission of a plan, that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer faces a significant risk of being 
unable to attain compliance with the reserve requirements in proposed 
Sec.  15.11(a), (b), (c), or (d) within a reasonable period, the OCC 
would have been able to order the issuer to initiate redemption of all 
outstanding payment stablecoins. Proposed Sec.  15.11(g)(4) also stated 
that the OCC's authority to require a compliance plan or order 
redemption did not limit the OCC's authority to pursue other measures, 
including enforcement actions, if appropriate.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
    Commenters generally supported proposed Sec.  15.11(e) through (g), 
although some had a few suggested changes. With respect to Sec.  
15.11(e) and (f), several commenters suggested that the once-a-month 
reporting standard be dropped in favor of enhanced reporting,\91\ such 
as through implementing random floating day attestations or surprise 
examinations. The OCC is not requiring an additional random floating 
day attestation at this time. The OCC has broad supervisory authority 
and may examine permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as appropriate, 
including on an immediate basis. In addition, the OCC will receive 
detailed information from permitted payment stablecoin issuers each 
week and will have the ability to flag any unusual activity using this 
information. In light of that, the OCC believes that imposing a random 
floating day attestation requirement across all issuers is unnecessary 
at this time. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may, nevertheless, 
decide to engage in random-day reporting and certification as a best 
practice.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\91\ Some of these commenters also addressed the requirement 
that excess reserves only be withdrawn once a month. The changes to 
Sec.  15.11(a)(4) in the final rule address these comments.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    One commenter suggested that the monthly certification section be 
made public. Under the final rule, the report required under Sec.  
15.11(f)(1) must be made public and the certification required under 
Sec.  15.11(f)(2) must be submitted to the OCC. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers or the OCC may choose to publish the certification. 
If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer failed to provide a 
certification, the OCC would take appropriate supervisory action. One 
commenter recommended using particular criteria for the monthly 
composition report. The OCC believes that the proposed criteria, 
supplemented by the reporting that the OCC will receive under Sec.  
15.14, is sufficient.
    One commenter recommended that the OCC consider the Stablecoin 
Presentation and Disclosure Criteria developed by the AICPA in its 
rulemaking, recognizing that these criteria are already in use today 
and will continue to serve as the basis for issuer reporting and CPA 
examinations. Another commenter suggested the final rule specify that 
Sec.  15.11(f) examinations are to be performed in accordance with the 
AICPA' Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements, which could 
suggest particular assurance and

[[Page 67061]]

independence standards for these examinations. The OCC recognizes that 
certain industry criteria have been adopted by accounting firms in 
evaluating disclosures by stablecoin issuers today, and the OCC 
recognizes the importance of suitable criteria for examination 
engagements that are relevant, objective, measurable, complete, and 
available for users of the report. However, the final rule does not 
mandate any particular criteria so long as the examination meets the 
statutory requirements under the GENIUS Act to preserve flexibility as 
industry standards continue to develop.
    The proposed rule requested comments on the treatment of white-
label arrangements or other arrangements where a single issuer issues 
multiple payment stablecoins. Several commenters stated that nothing in 
the GENIUS Act prohibits such arrangements. Other commenters noted that 
if such arrangements are allowed, the OCC should implement additional 
requirements. For example, several commenters requested clarification 
regarding whether proposed Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(ii)'s requirement that 
reserve assets be segregated from other assets owned or held by the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer applied as well to payment 
stablecoins issued on multiple blockchains (that is, whether the 
reserves backing issuances on each blockchain need to be segregated 
from each other or can be placed in an omnibus account). The OCC 
confirms that it is not necessary to separate reserve assets by 
blockchain for a payment stablecoin that is issued under a single 
brand. For example, a single brand of payment stablecoin could be 
available on both blockchain A and blockchain B. The payment stablecoin 
could be backed by a single pool of reserve assets. That pool of 
reserve assets would be subject to the identification and segregation 
requirements of Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(ii) of the final rule. Some 
commenters argued against allowing issuers to commingle the reserves of 
each payment stablecoin or to utilize a combined report under proposed 
section 15.11(e), as that could increase the risk that holders of one 
stablecoin are affected by deficient reserves of a separately marketed 
payment stablecoin. One commenter suggested that risks related to 
multi-brand issuers are best addressed through disclosure requirements 
akin to the treatment of white-labeled deposit or prepaid banking 
products.
    The final rule adopts Sec.  15.11(e) of the proposed rule with 
minor changes. Specifically, the OCC is adding new paragraph (e)(1) and 
renumbering paragraphs (e)(1) and (e)(2) to (e)(1)(i) and (e)(1)(ii), 
respectively. The OCC is also making certain clarifying edits 
throughout.
    The final rule also makes edits to Table 1 to paragraph (e). Table 
1 to paragraph (e) provides a template for the monthly composition 
report. Table 1 has been updated to reflect the definition of reserve 
asset value. Footnote 1 to the table provides guidance as to how to 
report if an issuer issues multiple classes of payment stablecoins. The 
final rule revises this footnote to make clear that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should separately list different classes or brands, 
if applicable. The OCC has generally used these terms interchangeably 
and is making this revision for clarity. The footnote also states that, 
if a class or brand is secured by distinct pools of reserve assets, the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer should describe both the 
operational and legal mechanisms for separately securing each brand or 
class (the proposal did not address operational mechanisms). Finally, 
consistent with other changes to the final rule, the OCC has revised 
footnote 1 to provide additional clarity for entities that use multiple 
separate issuer SPVs to issue payment stablecoins. The final rule makes 
clear that, if different payment stablecoins are issued by distinct 
issuers, such as SPV issuers, there should be a separate composition 
report for each class or brand. The final rule adopts Sec.  15.11(f) as 
proposed with certain clarifying edits.
    Regarding the consequences for failing to meet minimum reserve 
asset requirements in proposed Sec.  15.11(g), commenters were largely 
supportive but offered various amendments or requested clarifications. 
Regarding the required notification in Sec.  15.11(g)(1), one commenter 
requested that the OCC specify the exact format, submission mechanism, 
and timing window for the notification. The OCC is not revising the 
rule text in response to this comment. The final rule specifies that 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice through its 
supervisory office on any day in which the reserve asset amount falls 
below the required amount. The OCC believes that this is sufficient 
guidance and that adopting an overly formalistic submission mechanism 
may serve to delay prompt notification.
    Regarding the prohibitions that are triggered if a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer fails to satisfy the 1 to 1 reserve asset 
requirement at any time, several commenters asked that the OCC clarify 
that this does not apply to temporary and immaterial intraday 
shortfalls arising from normal settlement timing differences. These 
commenters are incorrect; the reserve asset requirement applies at all 
times and does not allow for shortfalls. It is important that payment 
stablecoin holders have confidence that their payment stablecoins are 
appropriately backed at all times, consistent with section 4(a)(1)(A) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)), which does not require 
that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer only maintain 1 to 1 backing 
on an end-of-day basis. The OCC has, however, made one change to Sec.  
15.11(g)(2)(i) in response to comments. The final rule provides that 
the OCC may permit a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is under-
reserved to issue new payment stablecoins. This additional language 
will provide additional flexibility to address situations where it may 
be appropriate to allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
continue issuing when under-reserved while ensuring that an under-
reserved permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains subject to 
appropriate scrutiny.
    Regarding the 15-consecutive-business-day trigger period for 
reserve asset liquidation in proposed Sec.  15.11(g)(3), commenters 
expressed views on both the length of the period and the consequences. 
First, one commenter stated that the 15-day threshold is too permissive 
and should be based on a failure for 12 days in any 15-day period. 
Another commenter believed the 15-day period was reasonable but stated 
that the OCC should retain discretion to accelerate the period for 
material shortfalls. Second, several commenters cautioned against 
automatic liquidation thresholds, arguing that this could be overly 
punitive and could be more likely to result in fire sales. Instead, 
these commenters suggested either that the issuers implement gradual 
remediation or wind-down plans or else that the OCC establish tailored 
remediation timelines based on the nature and severity of the 
shortfall. The OCC believes that the flexibility in paragraph (g)(4) 
eliminates the need for any revisions. If an issuer fails to be 
adequately reserved for a significant period, the OCC could require a 
remediation plan or order the redemption of all outstanding payment 
stablecoins of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer even if the issuer 
did not trigger the automatic redemption provisions in Sec.  
15.11(g)(3). The OCC also disagrees with the commenters who cautioned 
against automatic liquidation

[[Page 67062]]

thresholds. In the first instance, the OCC reiterates the importance of 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers meeting their required reserve 
levels at all times. Second, the OCC notes that the OCC has discretion 
to extend the 15 consecutive-business-day period. Thus, if 
circumstances warranted an extension, the OCC could provide one.
    In Sec.  15.11(g), the agency is finalizing the rule as proposed 
with certain clarifying edits throughout, including using the phrase 
``minimum reserve asset amount required by paragraph (a) of this 
section'' for consistency in Sec.  15.11(g)(1), (g)(2), and (g)(3). 
Additionally, in Sec.  15.11(g)(2)(i), the OCC is clarifying that a 
noncompliant permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue new payment 
stablecoins if permitted by the OCC. The OCC is also making technical 
changes to Sec.  15.11(g)(4) and splitting that paragraph into three 
paragraphs (g)(4)(i) through (g)(4)(iii).
Other Comments
Exceptions for Smaller Issuers That Are Subsidiaries of OCC-Regulated 
Depository Institutions
    Commenters had a variety of views concerning potential exceptions 
from the requirements of Sec.  15.11. A commenter opposed creating an 
exception for smaller issuers or issuers that are subsidiaries of 
insured depository institutions from the proposal's concentration and 
diversification requirements. One commenter supported the use of narrow 
exceptions from the proposal's concentration and diversification 
requirements, subject to enhanced disclosure requirements. A few 
commenters recommended that the exception for a subsidiary of an 
insured depository institution should be limited to parent institutions 
that are well capitalized. One of these commenters also supported 
permitting subsidiaries of insured depository institutions to hold all 
reserve assets as deposits at the parent institution only if the parent 
institution holds an equivalent amount of cash in its Federal Reserve 
master account. The commenter also suggested permitting reserve assets 
to be held in a designated sub-account of the parent institution's 
master account or in the master account of the subsidiary issuer.
    The OCC is not revising the rule in response to these comments. The 
OCC believes that applying the same general standards to permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of insured depository 
institutions and those that are not will enhance the safety and 
soundness of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, help to ensure 
financial stability, and facilitate competitive equity among different 
types of issuers. The OCC notes, however, that several of the 
requirements in the final rule are principles-based and tailored based 
on the size and complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. 
Thus, certain smaller and less complex permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers may be able to achieve compliance with these provisions using a 
simpler approach than that which would be necessary for a large and 
complex permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Reserve Asset Management, Mechanics, and Operations
    The OCC requested comments on whether to include additional 
measures to address de-pegging in the secondary market. Several 
commenters responded that the OCC should not consider secondary market 
transactions owing to the risk of market manipulation or a potential 
lack of depth or reliability. The final rule does not include 
additional text concerning secondary market transactions except in the 
context of final Sec.  15.16 (where such transactions are a factor the 
OCC may consider in determining whether unusual and exigent 
circumstances exist). While the OCC believes that secondary market 
transactions may provide important supervisory information (and the OCC 
intends to review such information for supervisory purposes), the 
requirements of the GENIUS Act do not impose requirements on permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers regarding reserve assets that directly bear 
on secondary market transactions.
3. Redemption (Sec.  15.12)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Sec.  15.12
    As described below, the OCC is adding new paragraph (a) (and 
renumbering subsequent paragraphs appropriately). This new paragraph 
addresses the timeline for redemption.
    The OCC is adopting paragraph (a) as proposed other than 
renumbering it to paragraph (b), changing a reference from ``customer'' 
to ``payment stablecoin holder,'' adding ``in the policy'' before the 
colon, and making other conforming edits to reflect the renumbering of 
paragraphs in final Sec.  15.12.
    The OCC is adopting paragraph (b) as proposed other than 
renumbering it to paragraph (c) in the final rule and making clarifying 
edits. The reserved numbering for proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(2) has been 
removed, which led to a renumbering and a minor clarifying edit in 
final Sec.  15.12(c).
    The OCC is renumbering proposed paragraph (c) to paragraph (d) and 
eliminating the automatic redemption provision that was contained in 
proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(1) and described in proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(2) 
and (c)(3). Section 15.12(d)(1) of the final rule provides that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice to the OCC 
through its supervisory office within 24 hours if it receives 
redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding issuance 
value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period. Under Sec.  
15.12(d)(2) of the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
that experiences redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the 
outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period may 
request that the OCC extend the timeframe for timely redemption. Under 
Sec.  15.12(d)(3) of the final rule, the OCC may, in its discretion, 
grant or deny an extension request or impose discretionary limitations 
upon timely redemption in accordance with section 4(a)(1)(B)(i) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(i)).
    The OCC is renumbering proposed paragraph (d) to paragraph (e), 
changing references from ``customer'' to ``payment stablecoin 
holders,'' and making other conforming edits to reflect the renumbering 
of paragraphs in final Sec.  15.12. Where proposed Sec.  
15.12(d)(1)(iii) required disclosure of a link to the monthly 
composition report, final Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(iii) requires disclosure of 
a web page that includes a link to the same report. The OCC is also 
adding new Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(v), which would require a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not 
legal tender, issued by the United States, or guaranteed or approved by 
the United States. The OCC is also adding new Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(vi) 
which requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that 
payment stablecoins are not deposits and are not backed by the full 
faith and credit of the United States, subject to deposit insurance by 
the FDIC, or subject to share insurance by the National Credit Union 
Administration. The OCC is removing the surplus phrase ``that it 
provides'' from Sec.  15.12(e)(4). Finally, the OCC is adding new Sec.  
15.12(f) to clarify that the OCC will not require a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to redeem a payment stablecoin

[[Page 67063]]

to the extent the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's actions to 
redeem the payment stablecoin would cause the issuer to violate other 
applicable law.
b. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Section 15.12 of the proposed rule addressed redemption 
requirements imposed by section 4(a)(1)(B) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(B)). Consistent with the statute, under proposed Sec.  
15.12(a), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must publicly disclose 
its redemption policy.\92\ The OCC proposed that, in disclosing its 
redemption policy, the issuer must include, at a minimum, certain 
information. Specifically, proposed Sec.  15.12(a)(1) provided that the 
issuer must include a timeframe in which the issuer will redeem payment 
stablecoins and the timeframe under which the issuer is required to 
redeem payment stablecoins (which, under proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(1)(i) 
may not exceed two business days following the date of the requested 
redemption). Proposed Sec.  15.12(a)(2) would have required the issuer 
to include a statement consistent with proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(1)(ii) 
that any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be 
imposed by the OCC or, in the case of a State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer, by the OCC, Federal Reserve, or the State payment 
stablecoin regulator, as applicable. Proposed Sec.  15.12(a)(3) 
required that issuers include in their redemption disclosures a 
statement explaining the scenarios when the redemption period may be 
extended as provided for in proposed Sec.  15.12(c). Proposed Sec.  
15.12(a)(4) provided that the issuer must provide a statement with 
clear instructions on how a payment stablecoin holder can redeem a 
payment stablecoin, including a link to the website(s) where a customer 
can redeem the payment stablecoin. Proposed Sec.  15.12(a)(5) would 
have required the issuer to specify the minimum number of payment 
stablecoins, if any, that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer will 
redeem, provided that the issuer must redeem any number greater than or 
equal to one payment stablecoin, subject to appropriate customer 
screening and onboarding.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \92\ Under section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(22)), 
the issuer of a payment stablecoin must be obligated to convert, 
redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of 
monetary value, not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed 
amount of monetary value.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(1) provided that an issuer's redemption 
policy must provide clear and conspicuous procedures for timely 
redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins. In proposed Sec.  
15.12(b)(1)(i), the OCC proposed to define ``timely'' to mean that the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have to redeem a payment 
stablecoin no later than two business days following the date of the 
requested redemption. The OCC proposed this two-business-day timeframe 
as an outer limit on when a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must 
redeem a payment stablecoin and understands that many issuers may 
choose a timeframe that is less than two business days. Proposed Sec.  
15.12(b)(1)(ii), consistent with the statute, provided that 
discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by 
the OCC or, in the case of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, 
by the OCC, the Federal Reserve, or the State payment stablecoin 
regulator, as applicable.
    Proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(1) provided that the period for timely 
redemption is extended to seven calendar days if a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer faces redemption demands in excess of 10 percent of 
its outstanding issuance value in a single 24-hour period. Under 
proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(2), the extended redemption period would have 
applied to all redemption requests that are outstanding at the time the 
10 percent threshold is met as well as any subsequent redemption 
requests following the time the threshold is met. Proposed Sec.  
15.12(c)(3) stated that the extension is non-discretionary and that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer may only redeem any of the 
outstanding or subsequent redemption requests prior to the seven-
calendar-day period if the OCC determines that the issuer has the 
ability to redeem sooner in an orderly fashion and through a fair and 
transparent process or the OCC otherwise provides notice to the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer that the extended redemption period 
no longer applies. Under proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(4), a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer that exceeds that 10 percent threshold would 
have been required to provide notice to the OCC through its supervisory 
office within 24 hours. Proposed Sec.  15.12(c)(5) provided that the 
OCC may, in its discretion, extend timely redemption described in 
proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(1) or (c)(1), as applicable, if the OCC 
determines that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer poses a threat 
to safety and soundness, financial stability, or such an extension is 
otherwise in the public interest.
    Proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(1) provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must also publicly, clearly, and conspicuously 
disclose in plain language and in a format that is readily noticeable 
to customers, readily understandable by customers, and segregated from 
other information: (i) the name of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer that issues the payment stablecoin; (ii) that the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer is the entity that is obligated to convert, 
redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of 
monetary value; (iii) the link to the monthly composition report of the 
relevant permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserves as required 
under proposed Sec.  15.11(e); and (iv) all fees associated with 
purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins. The OCC included a 
requirement that the disclosures under proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(1) be 
readily noticeable by customers, readily understandable by customers, 
and segregated from other information to provide more certainty on what 
it means to ``publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclose [the 
information] in plain language.'' \93\ The OCC proposed to include the 
requirement that the disclosures be segregated from other information 
to ensure that the information in the disclosures is not combined with 
other nonrelevant information that could obscure the importance of 
these disclosures.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \93\ 12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(ii).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(2) provided that an issuer must update the 
disclosures in proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(1)(iv) if there are any changes 
in the fees associated with purchasing or redeeming stablecoins and 
provide customers at least seven calendar days' prior notice of the 
change, including by securely delivering the notice to current 
customers. Proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(3) provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must publish the disclosures in proposed Sec.  
15.12(d)(1) and any updates made in accordance with proposed Sec.  
15.12(d)(2) on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's website. 
Proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(4) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer must include the disclosures in proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(1) and 
any updates made in accordance with proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(2) in any 
customer agreements that it provides.
c. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    Commenters generally supported the majority of the requirements in 
proposed Sec.  15.12(a). Some commenters disagreed on whether permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers should be permitted to set minimum 
redemption amounts. One commenter argued that the OCC should not 
require redemption

[[Page 67064]]

of amounts greater than or equal to one stablecoin because such a low 
threshold would create disproportionate know-your-customer and anti-
money-laundering burdens. Another commenter argued that the OCC should 
not impose a minimum redemption amount because redemption at par is a 
core feature of payment stablecoins. Commenters were also divided on 
whether permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to 
offer direct redemption to all payment stablecoin holders. Some 
commenters supported direct redemption for any holder, with no 
minimums, subject to compliance checks or the creation of a formal 
customer relationship through an onboarding process. In contrast, 
several commenters argued that issuers should be able to choose whether 
to have a fully retail redemption model or operate through 
institutional counterparties or authorized participants. One commenter 
went further by suggesting that redemptions should only be structured 
to take place with institutional counterparties and authorized 
participants, rather than through retail relationships. Similarly, 
another commenter indicated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should not be required to screen and onboard any stablecoin holder who 
requests redemption.
    In setting the requirement that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer must redeem any number greater than or equal to one payment 
stablecoin, the OCC looked to the structure of the Act and the relevant 
definitions. Notably, section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901(22)), defines ``payment stablecoin'' as a digital asset that an 
issuer ``is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed 
amount of monetary value.'' The statutory language indicates that, 
while an issuer could set a minimum redemption threshold at a fraction 
of a payment stablecoin, an issuer redeems any number greater than or 
equal to one payment stablecoin under the GENIUS Act. Otherwise, a 
payment stablecoin would not be redeemable for a fixed amount of 
monetary value.\94\ More generally, the OCC has identified nothing in 
the other provisions or structure of the Act, including the requirement 
to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin in section 2(22) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(22)) that distinguishes between 
retail or wholesale payment stablecoin holders.\95\ Accordingly, the 
OCC has determined that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must have 
the legal obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment 
stablecoin from any holder, subject to applicable law (e.g., Federal 
laws, including BSA and economic sanctions requirements, including 
requirements of the customer identification program rule, certain non-
U.S. laws, and State laws that are not preempted).\96\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \94\ As discussed in greater detail below, a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer could set a fee schedule that provided discounts 
for bulk redemptions or for new customers. Such a fee schedule would 
need to be publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclosed in 
accordance with the final rule.
    \95\ A permitted payment stablecoin issuer must also meet its 
Bank Secrecy Act and economic sanctions obligations under the GENIUS 
Act.
    \96\ As discussed in greater detail below, new Sec.  15.12(f) 
expressly confirms that the OCC will not require a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to redeem a payment stablecoin to the extent the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's actions to redeem the payment 
stablecoin would cause the issuer to violate other applicable law.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    To determine that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not 
have to redeem from any holder could result in the elimination of the 
obligation merely through a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
limiting its customer base. For example, if a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer were permitted to limit itself to only one 
institutional customer (e.g., a digital asset service provider that 
served as a cryptocurrency exchange), and that customer ceased 
operations or its legal existence, the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer would no longer have an obligation to convert, redeem, or 
repurchase from the remaining payment stablecoin holders. Such a result 
would not be consistent with the text of section 2(22) (12 U.S.C. 
5901(22)). However, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer need not have 
a business that focuses on retail customers. Whether or not the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer focuses on retail customers, it 
will have the legal obligation to be able to convert, redeem, or 
repurchase from such customers and should have appropriate procedures 
in place to onboard such customers, particularly in times of stress. In 
light of the foregoing, the OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.12(a) as 
proposed with certain renumbering changes to reflect other changes in 
Sec.  15.12, discussed in greater detail below. The provisions of 
proposed Sec.  15.12(a) are codified in the final rule at Sec.  
15.12(b), and references to other sections of Sec.  15.12 have been 
correspondingly updated. In addition, subsection (b) of the final rule 
includes ``in the policy'' before the colon and listed items, and 
paragraph (b)(4) of the final rule replaces a reference to a 
``customer'' that was in proposed Sec.  15.12(a)(4) with a reference to 
a ``payment stablecoin holder.'' The final rule also includes technical 
changes, including adding ``the'' in front of ``Federal Reserve'' in 
paragraph (b)(2) of the final rule.
    Several commenters supported retaining a two-business-day standard 
for onboarded holders, particularly for direct counterparties, while 
some recommended that the OCC encourage same-day or real-time 
capabilities or tie shorter issuer commitments in terms of service to 
compliance expectations. One commenter recommended a 24-hour standard. 
Other commenters urged a more flexible, risk-based standard that 
accounts for reserve structure, safety and soundness, cross-border and 
intermediary arrangements, compliance reviews, and real-world 
settlement constraints. Commenters stated that the OCC should provide a 
clear timeframe for when redemption begins and ends. Commenters urged 
the OCC to adopt a clear, technology-neutral definition of redemption 
that focuses on completion of the issuer's obligations. Commenters 
requested clarification on when redemption is complete for compliance 
purposes, including whether completion occurs on burn initiation, block 
confirmation, ledger finality, or fiat currency credit to the 
customer's bank account. Several commenters suggested that redemption 
should be considered complete when the issuer either initiates payment, 
credits the holder's account, or fully processes the outgoing transfer, 
or when the holder receives fiat currency funds in its account. One 
commenter recommended a final-settlement approach based on receipt of 
funds by the redeeming party. Another recommended measuring compliance 
from the issuer's initiation of payment rather than final settlement.
    Commenters also requested clarification on what is timely in 
various instances, including cross-border redemptions, court-ordered 
redemptions, and intermediated relationships. Several commenters 
supported preserving the two-business-day standard but allowing 
flexibility for delays caused by factors outside the issuer's control, 
such as payment-system disruptions, correspondent bank failures, or 
broader financial stress. Several commenters stated that the redemption 
timeline should begin only after the issuer is able to satisfactorily 
onboard the holder consistent with applicable laws and regulations. One 
commenter requested clarification that custodians should not be 
required to commit to specific settlement or release timeframes, and 
that the two-business-day standard should operate as an issuer 
liquidity and reserve requirement rather

[[Page 67065]]

than a direct custodian obligation. One commenter requested recognition 
of comparable home-jurisdiction redemption standards in section 18(b) 
comparability determinations. One commenter requested that the OCC 
specify the consequences for untimely redemption.
    The OCC agrees that it is important to provide a clear timeframe 
for when redemption begins and ends. Accordingly, the OCC is adding a 
new paragraph (a) (and renumbering subsequent paragraphs 
appropriately). This paragraph addresses the timeline for redemption 
and provides that, for purposes of Sec.  15.12: (1) a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's obligation to redeem begins once: (i) the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer has received a redemption order from a 
customer; \97\ and (ii) if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has 
onboarding procedures reasonably designed to not unduly delay the 
onboarding of retail or other customers, including in times of stress, 
the customer has been successfully onboarded and all other legal 
conditions necessary to permit redemption that complies with this part 
have been met. As discussed in greater detail below, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should have in place the capability to onboard new 
customers in times of stress. While many issuers may only interact 
directly with a small number of digital asset service providers in 
normal times, in times of stress or in the event of a failure of a 
digital asset service provider, payment stablecoin holders may seek to 
redeem directly with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The 
issuer should therefore have processes in place to address a sudden 
increase in customers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \97\ The OCC notes that the revised definition of customer 
includes a person who requests that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Accordingly, paragraph (a)(1)(ii) is designed to ensure that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot use deficiencies in its 
onboarding process as a pretext to artificially extend the timeline for 
redemption. Paragraph (a)(2) clarifies that redemption is deemed to 
occur when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has fully processed 
and initiated the outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer 
or the customer's financial institution as directed by the 
customer,\98\ or, if requested by the customer, credited monetary value 
to the customer's account with the payment stablecoin issuer. This 
approach to the redemption timeline appropriately (1) focuses on 
aspects that are within the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
control (i.e., the issuer sending monetary value rather than the 
customer receiving monetary value), (2) addresses potential 
complications that may arise in cross-border transactions or 
transactions with new customers, (3) ensures that an unduly short 
timeline will not conflict with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
BSA/AML obligations and economic sanctions compliance requirements, and 
(4) aligns with current market practices. With this clarification 
concerning the redemption timeline, the OCC is retaining the baseline 
two-business-day timeline for timely redemption. The OCC believes this 
timeframe provides sufficient responsiveness to stablecoin holders who 
seek to redeem their stablecoins while also ensuring that issuers can 
appropriately manage liquidity demands. The OCC is not amending the 
rule to address comparable requirements of other jurisdictions, as 
those are best addressed through the determination that the Secretary 
of the Treasury makes pursuant to section 18(b) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5916) and any associated reciprocal arrangements. In the event a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer fails to timely redeem a payment 
stablecoin, the OCC intends to evaluate the facts and may take an 
appropriate enforcement action. The two-business-day timeline for 
timely redemption is a ceiling, and the OCC acknowledges that in order 
for payment stablecoins to be considered ``cash equivalents'' under 
GAAP and qualify as margin collateral under other requirements, the 
payment stablecoins may need to have an on-demand contractual right. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may redeem earlier than two 
business days, but they may not redeem later than two business days, 
absent an extension of the period for timely redemption. Whether any 
particular payment stablecoin may qualify as margin collateral is 
outside the scope of this rulemaking.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \98\ Consistent with the revised definition, a payment 
stablecoin holder would become a customer of the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer upon requesting redemption.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    One commenter urged the OCC not to permit issuers to freeze 
redemptions, including in unusual and exigent circumstances. Other 
commenters recommended a narrow safe harbor or exception where 
suspensions or delays result from clearly defined circumstances outside 
the issuer's control, such as system-wide disruptions, fraud 
investigations, sanctions screening, or payment-system failures, 
conditioned on the issuer providing notice and disclosure when the law 
permits. Many commenters opposed the proposed automatic seven-day 
stress extension and argued that it is pro-cyclical, could reinforce 
panic, and may undermine confidence or contribute to de-pegging. 
Several commenters recommended a discretionary or multi-factored 
approach instead of an automatic trigger. Commenters proposed 
alternatives including tailoring automatic extensions around reserve 
liquidity, requiring OCC notification of stress events and approval for 
an extension, a reserve-to-circulating-token trigger, and treating 
seven days as an outer limit rather than a mandatory delay.
    Commenters also requested clarity on operational application of the 
trigger, including whether it would be triggered on a brand-by-brand 
basis for multi-brand or white-labeled coins, how to measure requests 
in pull-claim architectures where holders submit redemption requests 
but such requests are not immediately executed, whether the OCC may 
object or impose conditions, whether extensions apply to outstanding 
and subsequent requests, and queuing and communication practices during 
an extension. One commenter noted possible conflict where a United 
States issuer suspends redemption while a foreign affiliate remains 
redeeming.
    Commenters requested clearer operational expectations for 
redemption throughput, automation, contingency staffing, banking-rail 
dependence, and stress readiness. One commenter supported requiring 
clear rules for timely and orderly customer redemption.
    After considering the comments, the OCC is eliminating the 
automatic extension provided in proposed Sec.  15.12(c). The OCC agrees 
with commenters that the automatic extension could prove pro-cyclical 
and trigger or exacerbate runs. At the same time, the OCC believes that 
it is important that the OCC receive prompt notice of any sudden spike 
in redemption requests, which may indicate stress at a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer. Accordingly, Sec.  15.12(d)(1) of the final 
rule provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide 
notice to the OCC through its supervisory office within 24 hours if it 
receives redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding 
issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period. Under 
Sec.  15.12(d)(2) of the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer

[[Page 67066]]

that experiences redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the 
outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period may 
request that the OCC extend the timeframe for timely redemption. The 
OCC may, in its discretion, grant or deny the extension request or 
impose discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in accordance 
with section 4(a)(1)(B)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(B)(i)). The OCC expects to use this authority sparingly and 
that redemption extensions will be rare. The OCC notes that the OCC may 
also impose (and the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may request) 
discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in certain other 
circumstances, consistent with the statute.\99\ The OCC would impose 
any such limit so as not to trigger or exacerbate runs or other stress 
events. The notification requirement in the final rule will provide the 
OCC with an early opportunity to assess whether such limitations may be 
appropriate and justified under the statute. The OCC notes that, 
because permitted payment stablecoin issuers may face redemption 
requests from payment stablecoin holders (subject to appropriate 
onboarding and screening), permitted payment stablecoin issuers should 
have in place processes to appropriately and promptly screen and 
onboard new customers, including in times of stress. It would be 
prudent for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to provide 
disclosures concerning its onboarding process so that customers 
understand the process and how it may affect the timing of redemption 
(including when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is under 
stress).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \99\ See 12 U.S.C. 5904(a)(1)(B).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Commenters generally supported the proposed disclosures. Many 
supported including additional disclosures that payment stablecoins are 
not insured and, in one case, not legal tender. Several commenters 
requested clear disclosures regarding redemption rights, timeframes, 
fees, reserve composition, operational disruptions, and the identity of 
the legal issuer responsible for redemption.
    Several commenters supported disclosure of redemption fees and fee 
changes, limits on hidden or abusive fees, point-of-transaction 
disclosure flexibility, and clarification that fee disclosure 
obligations apply to issuers rather than all market participants. Other 
commenters requested clearer allocation of disclosure responsibilities 
among issuers, exchanges, custodians, and intermediaries.
    A few commenters supported disclosures requiring such an 
affirmative statement, with commenters stating that the OCC should 
either require such disclosure, provide sample disclosures, or require 
a standardized disclosure related to certain prohibitions against 
deceptive language in the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(9)). One 
commenter stated that such a requirement should be principles-based and 
should emphasize prominence, timing, and customer comprehension. A 
different commenter opposed a requirement for such disclosure, stating 
that such disclosures were not required by the Act, and the prohibition 
itself obviates the need for disclosures. The commenter further stated 
that to the extent the OCC believes such additional disclosures are 
required, the OCC should only consider requiring them if and when 
actual market practices or consumer confusion demonstrate a clear need. 
Additionally, a few commenters stated that the OCC should require 
disclosures that provide that the issuer's payment stablecoins are not 
insured by the FDIC and not eligible for pass-through insurance.
    The OCC is adopting proposed Sec.  15.12(b) and (d) but renumbered 
as Sec.  15.12(c) and (e) in the final rule, with certain additional 
modifications. First, the paragraph includes renumbering in light of 
new Sec.  15.12(a). Second, because the OCC is no longer reserving 
Sec.  15.12(b)(2), the OCC has consolidated proposed Sec.  15.12(b)(1) 
into final Sec.  15.12(c) with a clarification (adding ``that state'' 
before the colon) and appropriate renumbering.
    Third, final Sec.  15.12(e) includes certain disclosures beyond 
those proposed in Sec.  15.12(d). The OCC believes that the baseline 
disclosures in proposed Sec.  15.12(d) are appropriate and consistent 
with the statute but that certain additional disclosures would provide 
important additional clarity to customers and payment stablecoin 
holders. New Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(v) would require a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not legal 
tender, issued by the United States, or guaranteed or approved by the 
United States. This requirement would align with the prohibition 
against deceptive names in section 4(a)(9) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(9)) and Sec.  15.10(c) of the final rule. New Sec.  
15.12(e)(1)(vi) would require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
disclose that payment stablecoins are not deposits, not backed by the 
full faith and credit of the United States, not subject to deposit 
insurance by the FDIC, and not subject to share insurance by the 
National Credit Union Administration. This would align with the 
prohibition against misrepresentation of insured status in section 4(e) 
of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(e)) and the definition of payment stablecoin 
(which excludes deposits) in section 2(22) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5901(22)). The OCC has legal authority to require the disclosures under 
sections 4(a)(1)(B)(ii), 4(a)(9), and 4(e) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(1)(B)(ii), (a)(9), and (e)). Waiting for market practices to 
develop prior to requiring such disclosures does not appear prudent, 
given that the benefit of disclosing this information to payment 
stablecoin holders outweighs the minimal burden of including these 
statements in disclosures to payment stablecoin holders. This burden 
appears particularly minimal since such redemption disclosures are
