mandatory regardless of whether the OCC chose to add these additional 
requirements.
    The final rule also replaces certain references to ``customers'' 
with ``payment stablecoin holders'' to be clear that disclosures should 
be readily noticeable and understandable to payment stablecoin holders, 
including those who have not yet become customers (i.e., payment 
stablecoin holders who have not interacted directly with the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer, including by requesting redemption from the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer). Certain requirements would, 
however, apply only to customers with whom the issuer has a current 
relationship. These changes are appropriate in light of the change to 
the definition of ``customer'' described above. For a similar 
clarifying purpose, the OCC is replacing the phrase ``The link to the 
monthly composition report'' in proposed Sec.  15.12(d)(1)(iii) with 
``The website that contains a link to the monthly composition report'' 
in final Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(iii). Final Sec.  15.12(e)(4) does not 
include ``that it provides,'' which was included in proposed Sec.  
15.12(d)(4), because the phrase introduced a risk of ambiguity while 
adding no substantive description of the relevant disclosures.
    A few commenters provided suggestions for the format of 
disclosures, including that they should be on the issuer's website, 
provided at the point of issuance or sale, and in a standalone format 
before the transaction is completed. Commenters also stated that 
disclosures should be prominent and obvious on the issuer's website, 
application interface, and in any promotional materials. Another 
commenter stated that the OCC should adopt a specific standardized data

[[Page 67067]]

format for stablecoin-related disclosures and that on-chain disclosure 
has its advantages. One commenter stated that the OCC should not impose 
technically infeasible disclosure obligations at every downstream 
transaction touchpoint and that there should be issuer-level 
disclosures rather than at the point of sale. Moreover, one commenter 
stated that disclosures should not be made through terms of service 
while another commenter stated that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should provide a fuller set of disclosures on their primary 
user interfaces and web pages. One commenter stated that any such 
disclosures should be continuously available, prominent, and linked 
with the issuer's core redemption, reserve, and product-risk 
disclosures. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should establish 
safe harbors or standardized disclosure templates for payment 
stablecoin disclosures that emphasize clarity and brevity.
    The OCC declines to provide sample disclosures or a standardized 
format for such disclosures but notes that the disclosures must meet 
the requirements of Sec.  15.12(e)(1). That section requires that the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's disclosures must publicly, 
clearly, and conspicuously disclose the required information in plain 
language and in a format that is readily noticeable to payment 
stablecoin holders, readily understandable by payment stablecoin 
holders, and segregated from other information. Such sample disclosures 
are not necessary because the disclosure requirements are simple and 
clear. The OCC is not instituting a principles-based requirement 
because it believes that disclosing this limited additional information 
does not impose significant burden on permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers.
    The OCC does not believe it is prudent to pick a specific format 
for disclosures, given that a Federal disclosure regime specific to 
stablecoins did not exist prior to the passage of the Act. Therefore, 
the market needs to develop prior to the OCC considering whether there 
should be a specific format for disclosures. The OCC is not opposed to 
on-chain disclosures, so long as such disclosures meet the requirements 
in Sec.  15.12(e). Similarly, the OCC takes no view on whether 
disclosures should be at the issuer level or at the point-of-sale, so 
long as they meet the requirements of the Act and this final rule. To 
the extent the disclosures are made through the terms of service, but 
the disclosures are not conspicuous and readily noticeable to payment 
stablecoin holders, such disclosures would not comply with the 
requirement in Sec.  15.12(e)(1) of the final rule. The OCC is not 
establishing safe harbors or standardized disclosures because there may 
be different formats of disclosures that can satisfy the requirements 
in Sec.  15.12(e), and the OCC believes the disclosure requirements are 
straightforward and do not necessitate further clarification beyond 
what is in the final rule.
    While the OCC agrees with commenters that stated that permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers should have to disclose that payment 
stablecoins are not insured by the FDIC, the OCC did not include any 
requirements related to pass-through insurance as the FDIC's notice of 
proposed rulemaking addresses the applicability of pass-through 
insurance, and the FDIC's proposal has not yet been finalized. Once the 
FDIC finalizes its rulemaking, the OCC will consider whether any 
revisions to 12 CFR part 15 are necessary.
    Many commenters also made suggestions of other categories of 
disclosures the OCC should consider. One commenter stated that there 
should be clear disclosure requirements for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers and intermediaries regarding the timing, content, 
and roles of each party so consumers understand the relevant risks. 
Commenters also suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should disclose the redemption rights of payment stablecoin holders, 
the nature of the issuing entity, that the payment stablecoin is issued 
by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the identity of the primary 
Federal regulator, and a warning, if applicable, that all transactions 
using the payment stablecoin are not reversible. One commenter also 
suggested disclosures related to operational risk, including 
disclosures regarding blockchain network participation, all blockchain 
activities, risks from a network disruption, and third-party details. 
Another commenter stated that the OCC should work with the FDIC to 
require disclosures regarding how customer funds are protected by 
reserve requirements,\100\ how customers can convert their payment 
stablecoins back to dollars, and information about insured and 
uninsured balances. Commenters also suggested prohibitions on nonbank 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers using the word ``bank'' in their 
names, marketing materials, websites, application interfaces, and any 
other communications targeted at customers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \100\ Similarly, one commenter stated that there should be 
standards for the user interfaces that people will use to access 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers and that those standards should 
describe the payment stablecoin's relationship to reserves.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC is not adopting any additional disclosure requirements in 
the final rule beyond the changes already discussed to Sec.  15.12(e). 
With respect to disclosures surrounding intermediaries, the OCC 
believes that disclosing the name of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer that issued the payment stablecoin under Sec.  15.12(e)(1)(i) is 
sufficient to help customers understand the entity they can redeem 
from. Additionally, disclosing the primary Federal regulator might 
cause confusion because several Federal agencies have different 
responsibilities under the Act. The OCC also believes that disclosing 
that transactions using a payment stablecoin are not reversible, which 
may not always be the case, is unnecessary and could similarly cause 
confusion. The OCC also believes disclosure regarding blockchain 
activities need not be mandatory, but, to the extent issuers believe 
they would be helpful, they may provide this information to customers. 
While a nonbank permitted payment stablecoin issuer referring to itself 
as a ``bank'' is not explicitly prohibited by the Act, such 
representations might raise concerns under other applicable laws. 
Moreover, the OCC already requires public disclosure of reserve assets 
in the monthly composition report required under Sec.  15.11(e) of the 
final rule. The OCC is not adding a disclosure requirement for the 
token asset identifier, but issuers may disseminate this information if 
it would be helpful to customers.
    A few other commenters asked for additional clarity related to 
disclosures. One commenter stated that the OCC should articulate a more 
defined reasonableness standard based on the net impression of the 
communication and provide examples of likely violations and compliant 
communications. One commenter asked for clarity on the responsibility 
allocation and stated that issuers should remain responsible for their 
marketing materials while digital asset service providers should be 
responsible for their own customer-facing representations. The 
commenter further stated that both should be expected to maintain 
controls designed to prevent misrepresentation. Another commenter 
stated that it would be helpful to understand which factors the OCC 
would consider in evaluating such disclosures. Another commenter stated 
that the OCC should clarify how it will implement prohibitions on 
deceptive

[[Page 67068]]

marketing practices, provide clarity around marketing practices, and 
strengthen the customer protection objectives of the prohibition. The 
commenter further stated that the OCC should clarify the factors it 
would consider relevant to finding a disclaimer sufficiently clear and 
specific and provide examples of disclaimers that would be acceptable. 
Another commenter stated that the OCC should establish disclosure safe 
harbors for clarity and brevity.
    Section 15.12(e)(1) provides sufficient clarity regarding the 
requirements for the disclosures required by the final rule. The 
disclosure requirements under Sec.  15.12(e) apply to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, and therefore issuers are responsible for those 
particular disclosures. The OCC agrees that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should have controls designed to prevent 
misrepresentation, which would generally be part of an effective risk 
management program required under Sec.  15.13 of the final rule. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers are also responsible for 
overseeing service provider arrangements under Sec.  15.13(a)(7), which 
means that their service providers should have appropriate measures in 
place designed to meet the requirements of this final rule.
    Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may include additional 
disclosures as best practices. For example, depending on a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's business model, it may be important to 
provide disclosures relating to the timeframe for onboarding new 
customers (including in times of stress). As market practices develop 
and the OCC gains additional experience supervising permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, the OCC may consider proposing additional or 
revised disclosures, as appropriate.
    The final rule includes new Sec.  15.12(f), which confirms that the 
OCC will not require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to redeem a 
payment stablecoin to the extent the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's actions to redeem the payment stablecoin would cause the 
issuer to violate other applicable law.\101\ The OCC is adding this 
provision to make clear that the OCC would not consider it a violation 
of the Act or part 15 if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer failed 
to redeem a payment stablecoin due to, for example, its obligations 
under applicable BSA and economic sanctions requirements because the 
OCC would not require such a redemption. As another example, if a 
foreign jurisdiction required that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer be licensed or registered to redeem a payment stablecoin in a 
foreign country and the issuer did not have such a license or 
registration, the OCC would not require the issuer to redeem a payment 
stablecoin from a payment stablecoin holder who is in a foreign country 
in which the issuer was not licensed or registered. The OCC may 
consider revising Sec.  15.12(f) over time based on, among other 
things, the nature of the conflicting laws that arise.\102\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \101\ ``Applicable law'' does not include any State law that is 
preempted.
    \102\ The OCC will scrutinize attempts to inappropriately use 
Sec.  15.12(f) in a manner that attempts to evade the provisions of 
the GENIUS Act and 12 CFR part 15.

Relationship of Redemption Requirements to Liquidity and Reserve 
Requirements
    Several commenters stated that liquidity requirements should be 
calibrated to the issuer's actual redemption obligations or contractual 
redemption period. Some commenters requested clarification on how 
issuers are expected to satisfy redemption obligations under the 
proposed liquidity thresholds and settlement mechanics. Other 
commenters supported strict reserve, stress-testing, and prompt par 
redemption requirements to protect consumers and reduce run risk.
    One commenter argued that credit risk management should focus on 
actual counterparty and redemption risk rather than temporary fair-
value fluctuations, particularly for reserves held at supervised 
insured depository institutions. Commenters also requested flexibility 
for affiliate and cross-border reserve structures, including reserve 
rebalancing across regulated affiliates and recognition of on-chain 
reserves under reciprocity arrangements. Comments related to liquidity 
and risk management requirements are addressed in the sections of the 
preamble discussing Sec.  15.11 and Sec.  15.13, respectively.
Fees
    Commenters were divided on whether redemption fees should be 
permitted. Some commenters supported allowing fees if they are market-
driven, transparent, proportionate, and tied to genuine processing 
costs. One commenter also argued that minting and burning fees are 
ordinary in commercial transactions and may provide needed revenue in 
low-rate environments. Other commenters supported prohibiting 
redemption fees that reduce the value received below par, while 
distinguishing ancillary service charges such as foreign exchange 
conversion or expedited settlement. The GENIUS Act clearly contemplates 
that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may charge fees, subject to 
appropriate disclosures. See, e.g., section 4(a)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(ii)). Accordingly, the OCC is not limiting 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers from charging properly disclosed 
fees except in the event of liquidation for failure to meet liquidity, 
capital, or operational backstop requirements, or pursuant to an 
enforcement action, as appropriate.\103\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\103\ A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may, for example, use a properly disclosed fee structure to impose higher fees on redemption requests for small amounts of payment stablecoins or for redemption requests arising from foreign jurisdictions. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Foreign Jurisdictions One commenter requested that the OCC address issuers operating in foreign jurisdictions and the risk that economically similar instruments issued under different regimes could confuse holders about reserve backing and redemption rights. Disclosure requirements applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the requirements of section 18 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916), its implementing regulations, and any conditions imposed thereunder should help to address potential issues relating to confusion. Multiple Chains Commenters requested clarification on how reserve requirements, redemption timelines, reporting obligations, and the 10 percent threshold apply when issuance is distributed across multiple chains with different finality characteristics. Commenters also requested clarification that cross-chain and cross-network interoperability activities directly support issuance and redemption and that the OCC address the operational, settlement, interoperability, and control risks of cross-chain transfers used to meet redemption demands. The final rule applies in a technology-neutral manner and thus its application does not change based on the particular blockchain on which a payment stablecoin operates. The 10 percent threshold applies on a per-brand basis. With respect to interoperability, section 12 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5912) provides that the Federal payment stablecoin regulators, in consultation with the National Institute of Standards and Technology, other relevant standard-setting organizations, and State bank and credit union regulators, shall [[Page 67069]] assess and, if necessary, may prescribe standards to promote interoperability. The OCC is actively engaging in assessing issues relating to interoperability, in consultation with other regulators. The OCC is not, however, imposing interoperability standards in this rulemaking. Civil Recovery One commenter recommended tolling the ordinary two-business-day redemption timeframe upon receipt of a qualifying civil recovery order until the order is satisfied, requiring the issuer to satisfy order- related redemptions before ordinary requests and notify the OCC within 24 hours. The commenter stated that qualifying orders should include pre-judgment restraining orders under 18 U.S.C. 983(j), civil forfeiture orders under 18 U.S.C. 981 or 21 U.S.C. 881, restitution orders in Federal criminal proceedings, and writs of execution or judgment liens. This comment addresses an issue that is generally outside the scope of this rulemaking. Accordingly, the OCC is not revising the rule to address the issue at this time but may consider it as part of future rulemakings addressing part 15. The OCC may, in the interim, use its reservation of authority to toll the two-business-day redemption timeframe in connection with a civil order, as appropriate. Finally, the OCC notes that the requirements of Sec. 15.12 apply only to the redemption of a payment stablecoin by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (including any entity acting as agent on behalf of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer) and do not apply to secondary market trading. 4. Risk Management (Sec. 15.13) Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)) provides that the OCC must issue regulations implementing appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards that are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and are consistent with applicable law. This provision also requires that Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance standards be implemented. The Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance requirements are addressed in a different proposed rule.\104\ Proposed Sec. 15.13 addressed the remaining requirements and standards required under section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)). Proposed Sec. 15.13 also addressed interest rate risk management standards under section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \104\ See 91 FR 37840 (June 24, 2026). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Sec. 15.13 The OCC is adopting Sec. 15.13(a)(1) through (a)(5) as proposed except for changes to four provisions. In final Sec. 15.13(a)(1)(i) on internal controls and information systems, the description of the organizational structure no longer includes an internal control structure. The final version of this paragraph also has a new phrase at the end; the OCC moved the proposed segregation of duties to this phrase and added a reference to dual controls. In final Sec. 15.13(a)(2)(i), the phrase ``size, complexity, or scope of operations'' has been moved before ``permitted payment stablecoin issuer'' for clarity. In final Sec. 15.13(a)(3)(ii), the phrase ``adequate'' is changed to ``sufficient'' and moved after the term information, and ``to an extent commensurate with their duties'' now qualifies the information sufficient for management and the board of directors to assess the level of interest rate exposure risk. Both of these changes are meant to clarify the expectations related to the information provided in periodic reporting to management. Additionally, other technical edits were made to final Sec. 15.13(a)(4) to enhance readability of the provision. The agency is adopting Sec. 15.13(a)(6) on insider and affiliate transactions with several revisions. Paragraph (a)(6)(i) clarifies that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must ensure the listed conditions are satisfied alone and in the aggregate. Additionally, the OCC has replaced proposed Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A), which addressed transactions that would be excessive or pose significant risks of material financial loss, with Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A) and (B). The final Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A) addresses transactions that are quantitatively detrimental in light of the business model of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Transactions posing significant risks of material financial loss are covered in final Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(B). The OCC is adopting proposed Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(B) and (C), renumbered as Sec. 15.13(a)(6)(i)(C) and (D), as proposed with technical edits to add commas and replace ``or'' with ``and'' when referring to transactions with, or involving, non-insiders and non-affiliates. The OCC is adopting proposed Sec. 15.13(a)(7) and (a)(8) as proposed, except that final Sec. 15.13(a)(7)(ii) expands the list of applicable requirements to include GENIUS Act requirements and has technical edits to move the phrase ``by contract'' to enhance readability. There is also a technical change in Sec. 15.13(a)(7)(iii) to replace ``permitted payment stablecoin issuers'' with ``a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.'' The final rule includes new Sec. 15.13(a)(9) and (a)(10). Section 15.13(a)(9) concerns monetization and stress testing, with requirements addressing the capability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to support timely redemption, the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to reliably access and monetize reserve assets, and regular stress testing of the reserve asset portfolio. Section 15.13(a)(10) covers foreign exchange risk and the use of foreign exchange risk management instruments by permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC is adopting Sec. 15.13(b) as proposed with changes to five paragraphs. First, in Sec. 15.13(b)(2) addressing board oversight of an information technology and security program, the proposal's reference to a specific Information Technology and Security Officer title has become a reference to a qualified individual responsible for the program. Second, whereas proposed Sec. 15.13(b)(4)(i) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology program to ensure the security and confidentiality of records containing nonpublic personal information, final Sec. 15.13(b)(4)(i) also requires the program to ensure the security and confidentiality of sensitive customer information. Third, final Sec. 15.13(b)(6) is modified to clarify that it concerns the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to monitor and adjust the program. Related to this clarification, final Sec. 15.13(b)(6)(i) includes the proposed language for Sec. 15.13(b)(6) except for a phrase related to evaluation and adjustment of the program, and the OCC is adding Sec. 15.13(b)(6)(ii), which provides that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must evaluate and adjust the information technology and security program, as appropriate, based on the monitoring required by Sec. 15.13(b)(6)(i). Fourth, final Sec. 15.13(b)(7) is modified for non-substantive edits, to add clarifying language, and to separate the provision into Sec. 15.13(b)(7)(i)(A) through (C). In addition, final Sec. 15.13(b)(7)(ii) covering notification of unauthorized access to sensitive customer information for a group of customers includes clarifying edits, including that the proposal's reference to a group of files instead refers to the files of a group of customers. Fifth, final [[Page 67070]] Sec. 15.13(b)(8) on information technology resilience removes the specific reference to disruptions, and it corrects a preposition in the proposal. b. Description of Comments and General Overview of Final Rule Approach The GENIUS Act requires that the regulation's requirements and standards be ``principles-based.'' Accordingly, the OCC proposed flexible standards in Sec. 15.13 that scaled based on the nature, scope, and risk of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities. Most of the standards in proposed Sec. 15.13 were adapted from relevant provisions of 12 CFR part 30, appendices A and B, which in turn implement 12 U.S.C. 1831p-1.\105\ The OCC identified standards from appendices A and B of 12 CFR part 30 that fit the requirements of section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) or 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii) or (a)(4)(A)(iv)) and then, consistent with the statute, adapted and tailored those standards to the business models of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as appropriate. In addition, on July 14, 2025, the OCC issued a joint statement, together with the Federal Reserve and FDIC, on Risk Management Considerations for Crypto- Asset Safekeeping,\106\ and the standards in proposed Sec. 15.13 were consistent with the considerations described in the joint statement.\107\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \105\ While the standards listed in 12 U.S.C. 1831p-1 provide a useful reference point for standards that may be applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC is not invoking 12 U.S.C. 1831p-1 as a source of authority for issuing these risk management requirements. Accordingly, the specific requirements for violating 12 U.S.C. 1831p-1 would not necessarily apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers (e.g., a mandatory plan). \106\ See OCC News Release 2025-68, ``Agencies Issue Joint Statement on Risk-Management Considerations for Crypto-Asset Safekeeping'' (July 14, 2025), https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-ia-2025-68.html. \107\ Consistent with the recommendations in the Digital Financial Technology Report, the OCC intends to provide additional clarity with respect to digital asset activities undertaken by OCC- supervised entities. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

The OCC is adopting proposed Sec.  15.13 with targeted changes. The 
final rule retains the principles-based and technology-neutral approach 
of the proposed rule, but the final rule has been modified to provide 
additional clarity, include stress test requirements, and address 
foreign exchange risk management. A description of the general comments 
received pertaining to proposed Sec.  15.13 and the OCC's responses is 
below, followed by a description of specific comments relevant to 
proposed Sec.  15.13 and changes made in the final rule.
    Many commenters opined on whether Sec.  15.13 should be principles-
based as opposed to prescribing specific requirements. For example, a 
few commenters suggested that principles-based requirements and 
standards allow for needed flexibility while maintaining strong 
governance, operational resilience, and financial controls. Other 
commenters recommended principles-based requirements and standards 
accompanied by clear supervisory guidance. One commenter noted the 
importance of providing sufficient detail to enable consistent 
compliance and examination if maintaining a principles-based approach. 
A few commenters indicated that a principles-based approach allows for 
better scaling to an institution's size, complexity, and risk profile.
    Additionally, many commenters discussed whether the rule should 
remain technology-neutral. For example, several commenters suggested 
that in order to remain principles-based, Sec.  15.13 should not impose 
specific requirements around the use of particular technical elements 
of stablecoins due to rapid technological changes occurring in the 
industry. Other commenters, however, suggested that while requirements 
in general should be principles-based, the framework should focus on 
technology-specific risks given the technological nature of the 
industry. In particular, these commenters recommended addressing the 
risks or benefits associated with distributed ledger technology in 
greater detail.
    Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)) provides that risk management standards and 
requirements must be ``principles-based.'' In addition, the nature of 
many of the areas covered by the Sec.  15.13 risk management provisions 
is such that implementation will depend on the business model, 
activities, and circumstances of each institution. Because of this 
nature, principles-based requirements are appropriate as a matter of 
policy as well as required by law. Additionally, the OCC has 
historically taken a technology-neutral approach to rulemaking, which 
it intends to continue. Employing a technology-neutral approach will 
help ensure that the requirements of 12 CFR part 15 adequately address 
the core risks applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers even 
as technology changes. Thus, while the final rule includes certain 
references to concepts that generally apply to distributed ledger 
technology (e.g., private keys), the final rule does not favor one 
particular technological solution over another.
    Several commenters suggested requiring real-time monitoring of 
smart contract activity, distributed ledger activity, reserve 
management, and redemption activity. A few commenters suggested 
requiring real-time and API-based reporting for regulators. The above 
discussion of Sec.  15.11(a) considers these and similar comments with 
respect to how permitted payment stablecoin issuers satisfy their 
reserve requirements under the GENIUS Act, and the below discussion of 
Sec.  15.14 relates to audits, reports, and supervision. The final rule 
does not include a real-time monitoring requirement for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers (consistent with the technology-neutral and 
principles-based approach that the OCC has taken with respect to Sec.  
15.13). The OCC notes, however, that the final rule requires permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to back payment stablecoins with reserve 
assets on at least a 1 to 1 basis at all times. Refer to the 
discussions of Sec.  15.11 and Sec.  15.14 for more about how permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers satisfy this requirement.
    Several commenters suggested allowing a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer that is an insured depository institution subsidiary 
to satisfy risk management requirements through the insured depository 
institution's risk management framework. Commenters making this 
recommendation argued that doing so would reduce duplication of 
requirements. Some commenters made this recommendation specifically in 
situations where the parent insured depository institution's framework 
explicitly encompasses the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
specific activities and risk profile. Other commenters suggested that 
compliance may be based on a parent's risk management framework where 
the parent's framework already addresses the risks covered in Sec.  
15.13 in a manner that is at least equivalent in outcomes. A few 
commenters recommended that any compliance based on a parent's 
framework be subject to supervisory confirmation, rather than 
automatically and conclusively determining that the subsidiary is in 
compliance, and that the OCC retain discretion to require additional or 
standalone risk management for risks that are not adequately addressed 
by the parent's framework. Alternatively, one commenter argued that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured 
depository institution should not be allowed to satisfy risk management 
requirements

[[Page 67071]]

by reference to the parent institution's existing framework and that in 
all cases compliance should be demonstrated by the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer.
    A parent insured depository institution will separately be subject 
to the requirements of 12 CFR part 30, Appendices A and B, and other 
applicable requirements, and the OCC will separately supervise the 
insured depository institution parent's risk management. A permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository 
institution may rely on the parent's risk management framework to the 
extent that the parent's risk management framework addresses the 
requirements of the GENIUS Act and 12 CFR part 15 and to the extent the 
management of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer plays a 
meaningful role in the risk management framework related to the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities. Similarly, a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is an SPV may rely on the risk 
management framework of its parent entity, provided that the parent 
entity's risk management framework complies with and adequately 
addresses Sec.  15.13. The OCC will reduce duplicative regulatory 
requirements to the fullest extent possible.
    Many commenters discussed whether the rule should include 
additional tailoring of risk management requirements and standards 
across permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Several commenters called 
for consistent standards for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
regardless of size, which they asserted would establish a common safety 
and soundness baseline and promote regulatory clarity. Many other 
commenters supported a tailored framework to allow community banks 
better access to the stablecoin market. A few commenters advocated for 
a combination of standardized and tailored frameworks. For example, one 
commenter suggested that there be baseline risk management standards 
across permitted payment stablecoin issuers with tailoring that takes 
into account other regulatory requirements with which the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer is already required to comply. One commenter 
advocated for tailored requirements based on specific risk profile and 
complexity rather than simply by size.
    The Act requires ``risk management principles-based requirements 
and standards . . . that are tailored to the business model and risk 
profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.'' \108\ Consistent 
with the statutory requirement, it is appropriate to require risk 
management requirements and standards appropriate to the size and 
complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, 
scope, and risk of its activities. Accordingly, the final rule includes 
broad principles-based language that accounts for the size and 
complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \108\ 12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Some commenters suggested strategies to address challenges posed by 
interoperability in payment stablecoin transactions. The above 
discussion of Sec.  15.12 addresses commenters who referred to 
interoperability in the context of certain payment stablecoin 
transactions (issuance and redemption). Some commenters advocated for 
developing mandatory interoperability standards in coordination with 
the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Other 
commenters opposed including interoperability standards in the final 
rule. Some favored including high-level principles-based standards. The 
final rule does not mandate interoperability standards in recognition 
of the relative novelty of the payment stablecoin industry. The OCC 
notes, however, that under section 12 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5912), the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, in 
consultation with NIST, other relevant standard-setting organizations, 
and State bank and credit union regulators, shall assess and, if 
necessary, may prescribe standards for permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to promote compatibility and interoperability. As the industry 
develops, the OCC will continue to work with the other regulators to 
assess whether it is necessary to prescribe standards for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to promote compatibility and 
interoperability.
    A few commenters suggested that permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers should be required to acquire insurance against certain risks, 
for example, cyber, crime, or professional liability insurance. A few 
commenters suggested that there should be minimum coverage 
requirements, potentially tailored based on size and complexity of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. A few commenters suggested that 
disclosure of insurance coverage should be required to regulators but 
not the public. A few commenters argued that a potential problem posed 
by requiring insurance coverage may be the lack of availability of 
particular types of insurance.
    The OCC recognizes insurance as a piece of risk management but does 
not prescribe particular private insurance requirements. This approach 
is consistent with the OCC's treatment of other OCC-supervised 
entities.
c. Description of Proposed Rule, Comments, and Final Rule
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(1) would have required that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer have internal controls and information 
systems that are appropriate for the size and complexity of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of 
its activities and that provide for: (i) an organizational structure 
with appropriate segregation of duties and an internal control 
structure that establishes clear lines of authority and responsibility 
for monitoring adherence to established policies; (ii) effective risk 
assessment; (iii) timely and accurate financial, operational, and 
regulatory reporting, including with respect to reports required under 
proposed part 15; (iv) adequate procedures to safeguard, manage, 
control, and monetize assets, including reserve assets; and (v) 
compliance with applicable laws and regulations. Internal controls 
refer to the systems, policies, procedures, and processes effected by 
the board of directors and other personnel to safeguard permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer assets, limit or control risks, achieve 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer objectives, and ensure compliance 
with applicable laws and regulations. The internal controls standards 
in proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(1) were modeled on the internal controls 
standards in 12 CFR part 30, with some adjustments to accommodate the 
particular activities and risks of permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers.
    A few commenters discussed requirements relating to the risk 
assessments under Sec.  15.13(a)(1). One commenter suggested taking an 
open-methodology approach where OCC examiners could audit the risk 
assessment methodology rather than only its output and the OCC could 
establish principles for what constitutes an acceptable approach rather 
than needing to endorse any specific methodology. Several commenters 
discussed the benefits of real-time or continuous risk monitoring and 
reporting. One commenter opined that adequate risk assessment requires 
continuous monitoring of the full cycle of stablecoin activity, 
including both on- and off-chain activity. Another commenter suggested 
that risk assessment frameworks should be

[[Page 67072]]

assessed against a baseline standard for all permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. Some commenters supported strong internal controls, 
including segregation of duties, independent validation, dual or multi-
party approvals, and strong governance over issuance systems. Another 
commenter noted that, with respect to reserve asset management, while 
assets should be appropriately segregated and independently controlled, 
any personnel or governance requirements should be proportional to the 
size and complexity of the issuer and implemented through broader 
reserve asset and risk management standards rather than as a separate 
standalone requirement. In contrast, some commenters suggested more 
specific direction concerning the appropriate organizational structure 
and responsibilities, such as greater clarity on the oversight role of 
the board of directors and requiring boards of directors to approve and 
implement a risk appetite statement.
    The OCC is adopting paragraph (a)(1) as proposed with a change in 
Sec.  15.13(a)(1)(i). Section 15.13(a)(1)(i) has been modified to 
delete ``with appropriate segregation of duties and an internal control 
structure'' and add ``, including appropriate segregation of duties and 
dual controls.'' These modifications are not substantive but instead 
clarify that segregation of duties and dual controls may be elements of 
an organizational structure that facilitates internal controls. In 
response to commenters, the OCC is not mandating any particular method 
for risk assessment, and the OCC expects that different permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers may take different approaches based on the 
size and complexity of the issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of 
its activities. This approach is most consistent with the statutory 
requirement to provide tailored and principles-based risk management 
standards. Effective risk management depends on an effective risk 
assessment since a permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot 
effectively manage its risks without an understanding of its risk 
profile. Procedures to safeguard, manage, control, and monetize assets 
will be expected to include measures to monitor and ensure the deposit 
concentration and diversification requirements are met. Likewise, 
procedures will be expected to address potential risks related to fraud 
and the theft of payment stablecoins or other assets.
    The OCC proposed that Sec.  15.13(a)(2) require permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to have an internal audit system that is appropriate 
to the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities and that provides for 
(i) adequate monitoring of the system of internal controls through an 
internal audit function, or for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
whose size, complexity, or scope of operations does not warrant a full-
scale internal audit function, a system of independent reviews of key 
internal controls; (ii) independence and objectivity; (iii) qualified 
persons responsible for the audit function; (iv) adequate independent 
testing and review of internal controls and information systems, 
verification of published information available to customers, 
calculations for required reserves, and regulatory filings; (v) 
adequate documentation of tests and findings and any corrective 
actions; (vi) verification and review of management actions to address 
deficiencies; and (vii) review by the institution's audit committee or 
board of directors of the effectiveness of the internal audit systems.
    A few commenters discussed requirements related to internal audit 
systems in proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(2). A commenter suggested specific 
requirements to guide internal audit structure. Specific suggestions 
related to revising the rule to reference specific proprietary internal 
audit practice frameworks and clarifying who constitutes a qualified 
person by requiring that such persons possess appropriate education, 
relevant experience, and certain professional certifications that 
demonstrate competency in internal auditing or other relevant 
expertise. A few commenters suggested that the OCC clarify structural 
independence expectations. One commenter suggested that the OCC address 
governance as a distinct area of internal audit coverage; require that 
procedures be developed, implemented, and adhered to; ground internal 
audit monitoring in a risk-based approach; require clear ownership and 
timelines in management action plans; clarify internal audit's purview 
over all material risk areas in Sec.  15.13; require all permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to establish an internal audit function; and 
rely on internal audit work in carrying out its supervision activities. 
A few commenters recommended that the rule require third-party or 
independent audits, or at least that systems have the records or 
ability to be audited by an independent party.
    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is adopting 
paragraph (a)(2) as proposed except for a clarifying edit to Sec.  
15.13(a)(2)(i). Internal audit systems are intended to provide 
objective, independent reviews of permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
activities, internal controls, and information systems to help the 
board of directors and management monitor and evaluate internal control 
adequacy and effectiveness. An internal audit system, among other 
items, is expected to independently test and review systems, as 
appropriate, related to (1) a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's 
compliance with the GENIUS Act and requirements in any final rules 
implementing the GENIUS Act; (2) payment systems; \109\ and (3) third-
party risk management. Well-planned, properly structured audit programs 
are essential to effective risk management and internal control 
systems. Effective internal audit programs are a critical defense 
against fraud and provide vital information to the board of directors 
about the effectiveness of internal control systems. An internal audit 
program's coverage includes evaluating compliance systems, safeguards 
around use of payment systems, and risks posed by relationships with 
and dependence on third parties. While it is important that internal 
audit functions be conducted by qualified persons with an appropriate 
level of independence from other business lines, the final rule does 
not mandate a particular organizational structure (for example, three 
lines of defense). Section 15.13(a)(2) does not prescribe a one-size-
fits-all approach to risk management. Smaller permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers with a lower risk profile may be able to comply 
using a simpler, less delineated organizational structure, or may be 
able to outsource certain functions such as the internal audit 
function, while larger permitted payment stablecoin issuers, with 
higher risk profiles, may require organizational structures with more 
clearly delineated risk management functions, including internal audit 
personnel. The OCC's approach is grounded in the principles-based 
framework, and prescriptive requirements or references to proprietary 
frameworks or certifications are unnecessary for the rule text. 
Moreover, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of 
an insured depository institution or that is a SPV may rely on the 
audit framework of its parent, provided the parent's framework complies 
with Sec.  15.13. Final Sec.  15.13 does not mandate

[[Page 67073]]

the use of an external audit, but such an audit may be appropriate for 
some permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Moreover, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers must comply with the requirements of Sec.  15.14, 
including applicable audit requirements.
