people, markets, and agreements that make the exchange of payments 
possible. See OCC, Comptroller's Handbook, ``Payment Systems,'' 99 
(2021).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(3) addressed interest rate risk and would 
have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to (i) manage 
interest rate risk in a manner that is appropriate to the size and 
complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the 
complexity of its assets and liabilities and (ii) provide for periodic 
reporting to management and the board of directors regarding interest 
rate risk with adequate information for management and the board of 
directors to assess the level of risk.\110\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \110\ The GENIUS Act explicitly authorizes interest rate risk 
management standards under section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)) whereas section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)) authorizes the other requirements and standards 
proposed in Sec.  15.13. The OCC proposed that interest rate risk 
management standards be included under proposed Sec.  15.13 since it 
is a risk management standard like the other standards already 
included in proposed Sec.  15.13.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Several commenters discussed the interest rate risk provisions in 
proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(3). Some commenters suggested that the OCC 
replace specific requirements in other provisions of the rule (e.g., 
weighted average maturity in proposed Sec.  15.11) with more robust 
risk management capabilities for interest rate risk (e.g., stress 
testing, haircuts). Another commenter suggested that the OCC include 
interest rate risk, among other items, in capital requirements.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(a)(3) as proposed with clarifying 
edits. While permitted payment stablecoin issuers hold reserve assets 
that may, depending on their type, have limited or no duration (e.g., 
in the case of demand deposits), it is still important for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to be mindful of this risk, particularly in 
light of the role of interest rate risk in the previous failures of 
money market funds, whose investments, like those of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, were supposed to be limited to short-duration safe 
assets.\111\ Increases in interest rates, particularly in short time 
periods, can reduce the value of interest-sensitive reserve assets, 
potentially impacting their fair value, marketability, and the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to meet redemptions. 
Similarly, changes in interest rates can affect the earnings and long-
term viability of permitted payment stablecoin issuers since their 
earnings may rely in substantial part on interest earned on reserve 
assets. Likewise, increases in interest rates may reduce the demand for 
payment stablecoins, particularly since permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers are prohibited from paying interest to stablecoin holders 
solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment 
stablecoins under final Sec.  15.10(c)(4).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \111\ Mismanagement of interest rate risk was a leading cause of 
failure in two of the three money market funds in the United States 
in which the net asset value of the fund fell below $1 (also 
referred to as ``breaking the buck''), ultimately leading to 
liquidation. See In the Matter of John E. Backlund, et al., 
Investment Company Act Release No. 23639 (January 11, 1999) (SEC 
administrative order involving the Community Bankers U.S. Government 
Money Market Fund liquidated in 1994); In the Matter of First 
Multifund Advisory Corp. and Milton Mound, Initial Decision, File 
No. 3-5881 (December 29, 1982) (SEC initial decision involving the 
First Multifund for Daily Income liquidated in 1978).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(4) would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's asset growth to be prudent and commensurate with a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk management capabilities, 
operational capacity, and staffing. A couple of commenters addressed 
this provision. One stated that the interest rate exposure, asset 
growth, asset quality, and earnings standards from 12 CFR part 30 
should be adapted to focus on reserve composition, liquidity, 
redemption capacity, operational scalability, and run-risk management 
rather than traditional banking intermediation. Another suggested that 
the risk management standards should include an emphasis on growth 
management.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(a)(4) as proposed with clarifying 
edits. While there are no hard limits to how quickly permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers may grow, permitted payment stablecoin issuers must 
ensure that growth does not undercut the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's capabilities to comply with the requirements of this rule and 
other applicable law. For example, rapid issuance of new payment 
stablecoins would require a rapid increase in reserves, and permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers must ensure that they maintain the 
capabilities to maintain these reserves in compliance with Sec.  15.11 
and maintain the ability to access and monetize the reserves in order 
to meet redemption requests. The approach in the final rule is 
sufficiently tailored to the business models of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers and balances flexibility with the need to 
appropriately manage the risks associated with asset growth.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(5) would have required that a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer establish and maintain a risk management 
system that is commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's size and complexity and the nature and scope of its operations 
to evaluate and monitor earnings and ensure that earnings are 
sufficient to support operations and maintain the capital levels that 
would be required under subpart E of proposed part 15. Commenters 
generally supported requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
adopt risk management systems commensurate with their size and 
complexity and the nature and scope of their operations. Some 
commenters recommended including additional and more prescriptive 
requirements with respect to how a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
monitors its earnings and other risks. Some commenters stated that the 
rule should include more bank-like risk management requirements.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(a)(5) as proposed. To reflect the 
distinct characteristics of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the 
standards on earnings in Sec.  15.13(a)(5) do not include all the 
listed elements in paragraph II.H in appendix A to 12 CFR part 30, from 
which the earnings standard in proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(5) was adapted. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers must nevertheless comply with the 
overarching requirement to evaluate and monitor earnings. It may be 
particularly important for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
evaluate the volatility and sustainability of earnings, since changes 
in short-term interest rates could have sudden impacts on permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer earnings. Section 15.13(a)(5) provides risk 
management requirements that are appropriately tailored to the business 
model of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC declines to 
include additional prescriptive requirements in the rule text in 
keeping with the principles-based approach to risk management under 12 
CFR part 15 and section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)).
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(6) addressed insider and affiliate 
transactions and was intended to protect a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer from entering into detrimental transactions with insiders or 
affiliates. Under proposed paragraph (a)(6)(i), a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer would have been required to ensure that transactions 
between the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and insiders or 
affiliates: (1) are not excessive and do not pose significant risks of 
material financial loss; (2) are conducted on terms that are the same 
or at least as

[[Page 67074]]

favorable to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer as those 
prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with or involving 
non-insiders or non-affiliates (or in the absence of comparable 
transactions, are offered on terms and under circumstances that, in 
good faith, would be offered to, or would apply to non-affiliates or 
non-insiders); and (3) are appropriately documented and reviewed by the 
board of directors. Proposed paragraph (a)(6)(ii) would have required a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to appropriately monitor and 
validate compliance with these requirements.
    Some commenters requested additional clarity with respect to the 
scope of transactions that were prohibited under proposed Sec.  
15.13(a)(6). Some stated that the OCC should define what is 
``excessive.'' Others stated that the paragraph should incorporate 
additional provisions from Regulation W (12 CFR part 223) or Regulation 
O (12 CFR part 215). Others cautioned against using a more prescriptive 
or quantitative approach for insider and affiliate transactions. One 
commenter stated that the proposal needs further clarification, as the 
proposal used a principles-based standard that does not reflect 
differences among issuers. The commenter recommended separate rules for 
insured depository institution subsidiaries and nonbank permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers. Some commenters stated that Sec.  
15.13(a)(6) was appropriately scoped and tailored.
    The final rule modifies paragraph (a)(6) to provide more clarity 
while maintaining a principles-based approach. First, paragraph 
(a)(6)(i) has been modified to include the phrase ``alone or in the 
aggregate'' to clarify the scope of transactions between the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer and its affiliates or insiders to which 
paragraph (a)(6)(i) applies. In addition, the OCC has modified 
paragraph (a)(6)(i)(A) to remove the word ``excessive'' and provide 
greater specificity as to the types of transactions prohibited under 
the final rule. Paragraph (a)(6)(i)(A) of the final rule prohibits 
transactions that are quantitatively detrimental to the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer in light of the business model of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The degree of risk and potential 
loss associated with one or more transactions is dependent on the 
business model of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. As a result, 
the particular business model will be relevant to whether a particular 
transaction, a series of transactions, or transactions in the aggregate 
would be appropriate for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
consider in the context of fulfilling its Sec.  15.13 risk management 
obligations. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer that conducts 
insider and affiliate transactions consistent with sections 22(g), 
22(h), 23A, and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 375a, 375b, 
371c, 371c-1) and the implementing regulations of those sections 
(Regulations O and W) is likely to satisfy its Sec.  15.13(a)(6)(i)(A) 
risk management obligations. Paragraph (a)(6)(i)(B) of the final rule 
incorporates the requirement from proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(6)(i) that 
transactions between a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its 
affiliates or insiders do not pose significant risks of material 
financial loss. Within the language proposed at Sec.  
15.13(a)(6)(i)(B), the OCC is making non-substantive clarifying edits. 
The OCC is adopting the remainder of Sec.  15.13(a)(6) as proposed with 
renumbered paragraphs.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(7) addressed requirements for overseeing 
third-party service provider arrangements. Specifically, a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must (i) exercise appropriate due diligence 
in selecting its service providers; (ii) require its service providers 
by contract to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the 
requirements of part 15; and (iii) as appropriate, monitor its service 
providers to confirm they have satisfied their obligations under 
proposed part 15.
    Several commenters requested clarification on third-party risk 
management practices. For example, a few requests for clarification 
concerned whether banks may oversee stablecoin-related programs through 
established program-management structures. A few comments requested 
clarification that regulated entities are responsible for compliance 
outcomes even when relying on third-party providers. Other comments 
requested clarification that evaluating a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's service provider oversight program requires assessing 
performance in addition to contractual provisions. Some commenters 
requested robust third-party risk management expectations given 
community banks' reliance on third-party technology partners in the 
digital assets space. Other commenters requested specific reference to 
third-party service providers in the rule, for example, by referencing 
the establishment and monitoring of service level agreements as a 
component of the contractual and monitoring requirements in Sec.  
15.13(a)(7).
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(a)(7) as proposed with two minor 
changes. The final rule includes a reference to compliance with the 
GENIUS Act in addition to compliance with part 15. Paragraph (a)(7) 
provides an appropriately robust and principles-based approach with 
respect to third-party risk management. As part of this monitoring, a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer must review audits, summaries of 
test results, or other equivalent evaluations of its service providers. 
The final rule also moves the phrase ``by contract'' for clarity.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(a)(8) would have required a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to (i) appropriately monitor and validate compliance 
with the requirements of Sec.  15.11 and (ii) manage liquidity and 
concentration risk in a manner that is appropriate to the business 
model and risk profile of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    As discussed above, several commenters recommended that the OCC use 
a stress testing framework in place of the prescriptive and 
quantitative requirements in proposed Sec.  15.11. Consistent with this 
feedback, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(a)(8) as proposed but is also 
adopting new Sec.  15.13(a)(9), which provides monetization and stress 
testing requirements. Under the new Sec.  15.13(a)(9)(i), a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must ensure that the reserve asset portfolio, 
taken as a whole, is capable of supporting timely redemption under both 
normal and stressed conditions, including by conducting analyses 
considering a range of redemption scenarios.\112\ Under Sec.  
15.13(a)(9)(ii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must also 
maintain and demonstrate to the OCC the ability to reliably access and 
monetize reserve assets necessary to meet redemption requests in normal 
and stressed conditions, taking into account: (A) market access; (B) 
financing channels; (C) haircut assumptions; and (D) operational 
readiness. Additionally, under Sec.  15.13(a)(9)(iii), a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must engage in regular stress testing of the 
reserve asset portfolio in order to confirm that the portfolio of 
reserve assets will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance 
value in stressed conditions,

[[Page 67075]]

including in significant positive interest rate scenarios.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \112\ Permitted payment stablecoin issuers should consider the 
makeup of their reserve asset portfolio in light of their respective 
business models. For certain issuers it may be appropriate to hold 
reserves comprising money to standing to the credit of an account 
with a Federal Reserve Bank, funds held as demand deposits, or funds 
in share accounts that are payable on demand beyond the amount 
required under Sec.  15.11(c)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

The OCC is also adding new Sec.  15.13(a)(10) which addresses the 
risk management of foreign exchange risk. The proposal asked whether 
the OCC should explicitly provide that managing foreign exchange risk 
is a permissible activity for the issuers of stablecoins that are not 
denominated in the United States dollar and whether to include 
limitations relating to the management of foreign exchange risk. 
Commenters generally favored permitting foreign exchange risk 
management as a permitted activity. Commenters noted that permitting 
foreign exchange risk management would reduce risk. Some commenters 
emphasized that the final rule should not permit speculation.
    Consistent with this feedback, the final rule requires foreign 
exchange risk management for issuers that issue payment stablecoins 
that are denominated in monetary value other than the United States 
dollar, subject to certain conditions designed to ensure that the 
foreign exchange risk is appropriately hedged and that the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer does not use its foreign exchange risk 
management program as a means of engaging in impermissible speculation. 
Under the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues 
a payment stablecoin denominated in monetary value other than the 
United States dollar must hedge any residual foreign exchange risk 
identified pursuant to the monetization and stress testing requirements 
of Sec.  15.13(a)(9) in accordance with Sec.  15.13(a)(10). Section 
15.13(a)(10)(ii) states that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer: 
(A) may not take anticipatory positions or maintain residual positions 
in the instruments used to hedge the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's foreign exchange risk, except as necessary for the orderly 
establishment or unwinding of a hedging position; (B) must hedge to 
retain no more than minimal foreign exchange risk; (C) must not use 
foreign exchange risk management as a means to speculate, including 
with respect to the appreciation or depreciation of any national 
currency; and (D) must have in place policies and procedures that 
appropriately manage its foreign exchange risk and any attendant risks, 
including risks relating to the posting or collection of margin, 
foreign exchange counterparties, and basis risk. The policies and 
procedures must include adherence to the below-described Sec.  
15.13(a)(10)(iii) and (iv). Under Sec.  15.13(a)(10)(iii), before a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer engages in foreign exchange risk 
management, it must provide prior notice to the OCC through its 
supervisory office and receive the OCC's approval. Additionally, under 
Sec.  15.13(a)(10)(iv), the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must 
adhere to any limit or other condition to the OCC's approval under 
Sec.  15.13(a)(10)(iii). Such limits or conditions are likely to 
concern how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains both 
capable of meeting redemption requests in a timely manner and fully 
reserved.
    Notably, while a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues a 
non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoin must engage in foreign 
exchange risk management under the final rule, foreign exchange 
derivatives are not permitted reserve assets under section 4(a)(1)(A) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)). Accordingly, the fair 
value of foreign exchange derivatives used to hedge a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's foreign exchange risk is not included in the 
reserve asset value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, and a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer may need to hold a buffer to ensure 
that its non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoins remain properly 
reserved. Such derivatives may, however, be relevant to the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's liquidity risk management and ability to 
timely redeem payment stablecoins. A permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer that issues a non-dollar-denominated stablecoin should consider 
and address the effectiveness of its hedging instruments and how such 
instruments may behave in times of stress. For example, the need to 
rapidly unwind and reapply hedges in times of stress may limit the 
effectiveness of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's hedging 
strategy. Accordingly, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should 
carefully consider their ability to manage foreign exchange risk before 
issuing a non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoin. Likewise, the OCC 
expects it would closely review such activities, both as proposed and 
on an ongoing basis.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b) addressed risk management requirements 
relating to information technology and security. Several commenters 
suggested addressing risk management expectations for specific 
technologies, such as smart contracts or super intelligence. For 
example, a few commenters suggested requiring smart contract controls 
governing activities such as minting, burning, and freezing. Other 
commenters suggested establishing specific requirements governing the 
use of super intelligence, given that, as the commenters noted, its use 
may become commonplace among permitted payment stablecoin issuers in 
their compliance programs. The final rule includes a reference to smart 
contracts but does not impose detailed requirements with respect to 
particular technologies. This level of detail is consistent with the 
GENIUS Act and the principles-based and technology-neutral approach 
that 12 CFR part 15 is taking toward risk management.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(1) provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must implement a comprehensive written information 
security risk and control framework, including a program that assesses 
and manages information technology and information security risks. The 
OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.13(b)(1) as proposed.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(2), the board of directors of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or an appropriate board committee, 
would have been required to approve the information technology and 
security program described in paragraph (b)(1). The board would have 
been required to oversee the development, implementation, and 
maintenance of the program, including the appointment of a qualified 
Information Technology and Security Officer. The oversight required of 
the board or committee would have included assigning specific 
responsibility for program implementation and review of program-related 
reports.
    A few commenters supported requiring a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to have a Chief Risk Officer or Chief Audit Executive in 
addition to the Information Technology and Security Officer. Some 
commenters suggested that it is more important for the rule to require 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to have officers and employees 
with the responsibilities of certain roles, such as a Chief Risk 
Officer, rather than requiring a specific officer or role. A few 
commenters suggested requiring a Chief Risk Officer with explicit 
responsibilities distinct from the Information Technology and Security 
Officer, for example, requiring a Chief Risk Officer with explicit 
responsibility for protocol-level exposure above a materiality 
threshold. Another commenter suggested that a subsidiary permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer should be able to satisfy any requirement for 
a Chief Risk Officer if the subsidiary's parent has a Chief Risk 
Officer. Another commenter suggested that a tailored approach to 
requiring a Chief Risk Officer or Chief Audit Executive ought to be 
adopted,

[[Page 67076]]

where the requirements should be proportionate to the size and 
complexity of the issuer and consistent with standards applicable to 
comparable financial institutions.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(2) with a modification to refer 
to ``a qualified individual responsible for the program'' and deleting 
the reference to an ``Information Technology and Security Officer.'' 
The OCC agrees with some commenters that it is more important for a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to have qualified individuals with 
the relevant responsibilities for overseeing the information technology 
and security program rather than to prescribe certain required titles 
or role names. The OCC is not requiring permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to have additional named roles at this time. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should generally create organizational roles to 
appropriately manage their operations. As discussed above, a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository 
institution may rely on the parent's risk management framework, 
including certain shared employees, provided that the parent's risk 
management framework addresses the requirements of part 15 and the 
management of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer plays a 
meaningful role in the risk management framework related to the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(3), a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's information technology and security program would have needed 
to include (i) an inventory and classification of assets, processes, 
and sensitivity of data; (ii) controls supporting and safeguarding 
sensitive information and processes; (iii) evaluation, validation, and 
reporting processes to ensure that key information technology systems 
and controls, including smart contracts, are operating as intended; 
(iv) periodic independent testing; and (v) a comprehensive and 
effective incident identification and assessment process and incident 
response program.
    Several commenters suggested various specific information security 
requirements that, they argued, would be broadly appropriate for 
payment stablecoin issuers. These commenters' descriptions indicate 
that these reflect the current and latest standards given the existing 
operational models and technology related to payment stablecoins. The 
OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(3) as proposed. The OCC believes that 
the requirements of Sec.  15.13(b)(3) are appropriately principles-
based and technology-neutral. This approach will help ensure that the 
requirements remain relevant as relevant technology and best practices 
continue to develop.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(4), a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's information technology and security program would have had to 
include administrative, technical, and physical safeguards designed to 
(i) ensure the security and confidentiality of records containing 
nonpublic personal information about a customer; (ii) protect against 
any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of such 
records; (iii) protect against unauthorized access to or use of such 
records that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any 
customer; and (iv) ensure the proper disposal of such records.
    A few commenters suggested requiring permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to adopt privacy-preserving technologies to limit public 
disclosure of information. Some commenters suggested that demonstrating 
adoption of privacy-enhancing technologies should be sufficient to show 
compliance with risk management information security requirements. The 
OCC is not mandating the use of any particular privacy-enhancing 
technology in the final rule, consistent with the OCC's technology-
neutral and principles-based approach to Sec.  15.13. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers must ensure that their activities comply with Sec.  
15.13(b) and applicable BSA/AML-related requirements. Whether a 
particular privacy-enhancing architecture can comply with both 
provisions will depend on the facts of that particular architecture. 
Accordingly, the OCC is not commenting generally on whether a 
particular architecture is permitted or prohibited.
    Because Sec.  15.13 must be principles-based and technology-
neutral, as described above, the OCC believes that imposing 
requirements surrounding privacy-enhancing technology would be 
inappropriate. The OCC notes that Sec.  15.13(b) does include 
requirements concerning the security of customer information, including 
developing an information technology and security program, ensuring the 
security and confidentiality of records containing nonpublic personal 
information about a customer, protecting against any anticipated 
threats or hazards to the security or integrity of records that could 
result in harm or inconvenience to any customer, and ensuring the 
proper disposal of such records. The OCC is adopting paragraph (b)(4) 
with one clarifying change. The final rule includes a reference to 
sensitive customer information, in addition to nonpublic personal 
information. Sensitive customer information will generally be a subset 
of nonpublic personal information. The final rule clarifies that, to 
the extent there is sensitive customer information that is not 
nonpublic personal information, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
must nonetheless take appropriate steps to ensure the security and 
confidentiality of such information.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(5) provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must develop, implement, and maintain appropriate 
measures to ensure secure handling of digital assets, including private 
key management, backup, and recovery, incorporating: (i) relevant 
technical, operational, strategic, market, legal, and compliance 
considerations relating to each digital asset and its underlying 
ledger; and (ii) material developments specifically related to 
supported digital assets and their underlying ledgers.\113\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\113\ If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer holds digital 
assets on a customer's behalf, the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's risk management practices must reflect this activity. 
Consistent with the July 14, 2025 Joint Statement on Risk-Management 
Considerations for Crypto-Asset Safekeeping, a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer holding digital assets on a customer's behalf 
would be required to maintain risk management practices, and 
information security practices in particular, that reflect the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's capacity to understand a 
complex and evolving asset class, ability to ensure a strong control 
environment, and appropriate contingency plans to address 
unanticipated challenges in effectively providing services to 
customers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    A commenter described key backup and recovery procedures with 
continuity exercises as one facet of a broader risk management 
framework. Another commenter suggested that the rule emphasize robust 
practices for change management alongside other management tools like 
pre-implementation testing. A separate commenter asked for additional 
guidance on change management and information security in general. The 
OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(5) as proposed. The OCC believes that 
the requirements of the final rule are appropriately principles-based 
and technology-neutral. This approach will help ensure that the 
requirements remain relevant as relevant technology and best practices 
continue to develop. The OCC anticipates issuing additional guidance 
concerning various provisions of the GENIUS Act and will consider what 
additional guidance concerning change management and information 
security may be appropriate.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(6) would have required that a permitted 
payment

[[Page 67077]]

stablecoin issuer monitor, evaluate, and adjust, as appropriate, its 
information technology and security program in light of any relevant 
changes in technology, the sensitivity of its customer information, 
internal or external threats, and the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer's own changing business arrangements, such as mergers and 
acquisitions, alliances, joint ventures, third-party arrangements, and 
changes to applicable information systems. Some commenters recommended 
adopting a more prescriptive approach that would incorporate references 
to more specific types of technology and audits. Others stated that 
compliance with recognized industry security and risk management 
standards serves as evidence of compliance with Sec.  15.13(b)(6). The 
OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(6) as proposed with clarifying edits. 
Instead of the proposed language where Sec.  15.13(b)(6) was titled 
``Adjust the program'' and described the obligation to ``monitor, 
evaluate, and adjust,'' the final rule clarifies the requirement to 
both monitor and adjust through an edited title and a new structure: 
final Sec.  15.13(b)(6)(i) focuses the proposed language on monitoring, 
and the new Sec.  15.13(b)(6)(ii) addresses the need to evaluate and 
adjust the program in light of that monitoring. The OCC believes that 
the requirements of the final rule are appropriately principles-based 
and technology-neutral.
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(7)(i) would have required a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer to conduct a reasonable investigation when it 
became aware of an incident of unauthorized access to sensitive 
customer information, including a customer's private key, to determine 
the likelihood that the information had been or would be misused. If 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer determined that misuse of 
customer information had occurred or was reasonably possible, the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to notify the 
customer or customers affected or possibly affected as well as the OCC 
as soon as possible. Customer notice must be delayed if an appropriate 
law enforcement agency determined that notification would interfere 
with a criminal investigation and provided the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer with a written request for the delay. If delayed by 
investigation, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have 
needed to notify its customers of the misuse or possible misuse of 
customer information as soon as law enforcement notified the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer that notification would no longer interfere 
with the investigation. Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(7)(ii) recognized that 
there may be situations where the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
determines that a group of files has been accessed improperly but is 
unable to identify which specific customers' information has been 
accessed. If the circumstances of the unauthorized access led the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to determine that misuse of the 
information was reasonably possible, it would have needed to notify all 
customers in the group.
    Several commenters discussed the customer notification 
requirements. Some commenters suggested that due to the broad proposed 
definition of customer, the customer notification requirements were 
impractical. Some commenters also requested clarity as to the 
definition of ``sensitive customer information.'' Specifically, 
commenters requested clarification that GLBA data privacy protections 
apply by defining ``sensitive customer information'' or replacing that 
term with ``nonpublic personal information.'' The final rule, in Sec.  
15.2, narrows the definition of customer substantially. Accordingly, 
the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(7) with non-substantive adjustments. 
Specifically, the final rule replaces a reference to ``a group of 
files'' with ``the files of a group of customers'' for additional 
clarity. Additionally, the OCC is making clarifying edits, such as 
adding more precise wording to describe the actions of the relevant law 
enforcement agency. The OCC is also separating the proposed Sec.  
15.13(b)(7)(i) into final Sec.  15.13(b)(7)(i)(A) through (C).
    Proposed Sec.  15.13(b)(8) provided that a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program must 
include measures to ensure continuity of operations and recover 
critical functions in the face of disruptions, including by business 
impact analyses, testing of vulnerabilities, and testing with critical 
service providers.
    Some commenters stated that Sec.  15.13(b)(8) should be modified to 
include specific additional items such as ongoing monitoring of 
critical service provider performance. The language of Sec.  
15.13(b)(8) is broad enough to include such monitoring to the extent 
necessary to ensure continuity of operations.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.13(b)(8) with two modifications. 
First, the final rule omits the phrase ``in the face of disruptions'' 
because the phrase was not necessary to include. Recent corporate 
information technology system failures have demonstrated the importance 
of measures to maintain operational resilience. Permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should ensure that they have sufficient controls to 
reliably address operational issues that may arise with burning and 
minting new stablecoins and should conduct appropriate due diligence 
before supporting any new distributed ledger. Operational resilience 
will be particularly important for permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers, who will depend on customer confidence in the stable value and 
availability of their stablecoins. Second, the final rule changes 
``testing of vulnerabilities'' to ``testing for vulnerabilities'' to 
clarify the purpose of the testing.
5. Audits, Reports, and Supervision (Sec.  15.14)

15.14(d) as proposed.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.14(e) through (i) as proposed except 
for separating proposed Sec.  15.14(i) into Sec.  15.14(i)(1) through 
(3) with minor technical edits.
    The OCC is revising Sec.  15.14(j)(4) to limit the reporting 
requirement to ``Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuers'' 
by adding the following language to the beginning of the subparagraph, 
``In the case of a Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin

    The OCC is revising Sec.  15.14(k) by removing the reference to the

[[Page 67078]]

provided by the issuer's Bank Secrecy Act officer, board of directors,

15.30'' with ``set forth in Sec.  15.30.'' Furthermore, the OCC is

    The OCC is revising Sec.  15.14(l) by replacing ``$50 billion in

also adding the phrase ``rules and'' before ``auditing standards'' in 
Sec.  15.14(l)(1) and making a clarifying edit to Sec.  
15.14(l)(2)(ii). The OCC is renumbering paragraph (l)(2)(iii) as (l)(3) 
and renumbering the rest of paragraph (l)(3) appropriately. The OCC is 
adopting the remainder of Sec.  15.14(l) as proposed.
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.14(m) through Sec.  15.14(o) as
