b. Examinations
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Section 6(a)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)) authorizes 
primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, including the OCC, to 
supervise permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as defined in the 
statute, that are not State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with 
an outstanding issuance of less than $10 billion in payment 
stablecoins. Section 6(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(3)) 
authorizes the OCC to examine permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
assess the nature of their operations and the financial condition of 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; the financial, operational, 
technological, compliance, and other risks associated with the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer that may pose a threat to the 
safety and soundness of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or the 
stability of the financial system of the United States; and the systems 
of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring and 
controlling the risks. Pursuant to section 6(a)(4)(C) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(4)(C)), the OCC may only request examinations at a 
cadence and in a format that is similar to that required for similarly 
situated entities regulated by the OCC.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(a) provided that the OCC will conduct a full-
scope examination of every permitted payment stablecoin issuer subject 
to its supervision at least once during each 12-month period, unless 
otherwise specified in proposed Sec.  15.14(d).
    Consistent with the OCC's statutory authority to supervise 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers, proposed Sec.  15.14(d) would 
have provided the OCC with the option to examine some permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers on an 18- to 36-month cycle, as determined by the 
OCC, in its sole discretion, if the issuers satisfied the following 
conditions: (1) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer currently is 
not subject to a formal enforcement proceeding or order; (2) no person 
acquired control, as specified in Sec.  15.14(m), of the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer during the preceding 12-month period in which 
a full-scope examination would have been required but for proposed 
Sec.  15.14(d); (3) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has an 
outstanding issuance value of less than $1 billion or less than $25 
billion in total monthly trading volume; and (4) the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer is in compliance with all of the reserve requirements 
set forth in proposed Sec.  15.11 and the reporting requirements in 
proposed Sec.  15.14. The proposed criteria for certain permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to qualify for an 18- to 36-month 
examination cycle were similar to the factors the OCC considers for 
national banks and Federal savings associations under 12 CFR 4.6(b).
    Consistent with the OCC's statutory authority under the GENIUS Act 
and the OCC's supervisory authority over national banks and Federal 
savings associations, proposed Sec.  15.14(e) would have allowed the 
OCC to conduct examinations of permitted payment stablecoin issuers as 
frequently as the agency deemed necessary, including examinations of a 
limited scope.\114\ The OCC proposed this provision to ensure the 
agency had a clear mechanism, consistent with its statutory authority, 
to conduct ad hoc examinations when emergencies or risks to the safety 
and soundness of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or the financial 
stability of the United States required the agency to deviate from its 
routine 12- or 18- to 36-month examination cycle.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\114\ See 12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(3).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.14(b) would have required that, upon request, 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers grant OCC examiners prompt and 
complete access to all officers, directors, employees, agents, and 
relevant books, records, or documents of any type. The OCC, through its 
examination authority over national banks and Federal savings 
associations, has authority to access the officers, agents, and books 
and records of these institutions.\115\ The books and records of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer include, but are not limited to, 
information retained on distributed ledgers. Sections 6(a)(1), (3), and 
(4) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1), (3), and (4)) give the OCC 
similar authority to supervise and examine permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. Proposed Sec.  15.14(b) would have applied the OCC's 
examination authority to permitted payment stablecoin issuers in the 
same manner that it is applied to national banks and Federal savings 
associations. Additionally, proposed Sec.  15.14(c) would have 
clarified that the OCC may conduct examinations either on site or 
remotely. Proposed Sec.  15.14(f) would have provided that all 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers must maintain a complete set of 
books and records in English. Proposed Sec.  15.14(g) would have 
required all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to develop and 
implement a records retention policy that ensured the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer could demonstrate compliance with the GENIUS Act, 
this part, and all applicable laws and regulations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \115\ 12 U.S.C. 481 and 1464.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    Many commenters submitted general comments about the proposed 
examination framework and requested that the OCC modify or incorporate 
various concepts into the proposed examination framework. The OCC 
received several comments related to the imposition of uniform 
standards on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Specifically, 
several commenters stated that banks operate in a highly regulated 
environment, and if permitted payment stablecoin issuers offer bank-
like products, they should also be subject to the same supervisory 
expectations to which banks are subject. One commenter also stated that 
inconsistent standards or permitted payment stablecoin issuer-specific 
safe harbors risk creating perceived tiers of payment stablecoin 
quality. The commenter further added that keeping standards high and 
uniform protects the global ``singleness'' of U.S.-issued dollar 
stablecoins and urged the OCC to establish uniform examination, 
reporting, capital, and other prudential requirements. Another 
commenter claimed that nonbank stablecoin issuers present materially 
different supervisory considerations and argued that the OCC should 
apply more stringent, standalone audit, reporting, and transparency

[[Page 67079]]

requirements to nonbank issuers to account for the absence of 
consolidated supervision, ongoing examination, and access to the 
Federal banking safety net. The commenter further argued that applying 
uniform requirements across bank and nonbank issuers would fail to 
recognize these differences and could place community banks at a 
competitive disadvantage despite their significantly higher level of 
existing regulatory oversight.
    After considering these comments, the OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.14 
as proposed with certain minor changes and clarifications. The overall 
framework continues to recognize the key differences between the 
business models of banks and permitted payment stablecoin issuers while 
ensuring that the OCC receives sufficient information from permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers to carry out its supervisory duties under 
the GENIUS Act.
    One commenter stated that, where a technology provider has been 
examined by another Federal regulator in connection with stablecoin 
services, the OCC should consider that examination work as part of its 
own independent evaluation. The commenter stated that this approach 
would reduce duplicative burden on community banks and their technology 
partners without compromising OCC supervisory authority. The OCC takes 
seriously its obligation to reduce duplication in supervision and 
regulation and has substantial experience coordinating with other 
regulators. The OCC will take appropriate steps to minimize duplicative 
efforts while supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers, and 
therefore it is not necessary to change the final rule in response to 
this comment.
    Another commenter stated that the supervisory framework for 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers should align, to the greatest 
extent possible, with existing supervisory and regulatory structures 
applicable to banking organizations and financial institutions. Where 
entities are already subject to comprehensive oversight with respect to 
capital, liquidity, operational resilience, and risk management, 
additional requirements should be designed to complement, rather than 
duplicate, those obligations. As required by statute, the OCC will 
pursue examination and supervisory policies that maximize efficiency 
and minimize duplication, including, where appropriate, coordinating 
examination activities and leveraging existing supervisory 
frameworks.\116\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \116\ See 12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(4)(B).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Another commenter stated that the compliance window is very short, 
that the statutory penalties starting in January 2027 will mount 
quickly, and that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are likely to 
fail as a result. The effective date is set by section 20 of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5901 note (effective date)). The OCC will monitor 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers' compliance with the GENIUS Act 
and part 15 and take enforcement actions as appropriate in light of the 
facts and circumstances of any particular violation. While the OCC 
recognizes that the time period between the issuance of this final rule 
and the effective date of the GENIUS Act is short, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers should take seriously their obligations to comply 
with the provisions of the GENIUS Act as they become effective. 
Moreover, as discussed in more detail below, prospective permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers with pending applications with the OCC on 
the effective date of the Act may submit a request for a waiver not to 
exceed 12 months.
    One commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that it has 
exclusive authority to exercise visitorial powers with respect to 
subsidiaries of national banks in the final rule. Under section 6(a)(1) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)), a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer that is not a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer with an outstanding issuance value of less than $10 billion 
``shall be subject to supervision by the appropriate primary Federal 
payment stablecoin regulator.'' As described in the preamble section 
discussing Self-Executing Provisions, the OCC will not include 
provisions related to the visitorial powers in the final rule. 
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers are encouraged to discuss any 
issues or questions as they arise related to the OCC's visitorial 
authority.
    Another commenter recommended that the OCC not mandate the public 
disclosure of proprietary models, algorithms, thresholds, schemas, or 
decision logic. No provision in the proposal mandates the public 
disclosure of proprietary models, algorithms, thresholds, schemas, or 
decision logic, so the OCC is not making any changes to the final rule 
to address this comment.
    Two commenters stated that the OCC should provide supervisory 
guidance or examination manuals specific to payment stablecoin issuers 
over time to promote transparency, consistency, and predictability in 
examination practices as the regime matures. The OCC plans to issue 
supervisory guidance and examination manuals specific to permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers, as necessary.
    One commenter recommended that the OCC adopt an outcomes-based 
examination framework focused on customer protection, transaction 
integrity, and compliance rather than specific technologies. The 
commenter stated that this approach would avoid regulatory lock-in, 
preserve flexibility as technology evolves, and allow execution quality 
to be assessed through the Uniform Financial Institutions Rating System 
(i.e., CAMELS) component analysis supplemented by stablecoin-specific 
examination procedures. Another commenter urged the OCC to clarify that 
privacy-preserving distributed ledger architectures would be 
permissible under the proposal, so long as they remain verifiable and 
consistent with reserve, audit, reporting, and examination 
requirements. The commenter stated that such clarification would reduce 
uncertainty, remove a barrier to adopting more privacy-protective 
infrastructure, and support consumer privacy.
    First, no provision in the proposed rule expresses any preference 
for one technological approach or protocol over another. The OCC 
intentionally adopted a technology-neutral approach in the proposed 
rule, consistent with the agency's general approach towards technology, 
and this approach will continue in the final rule. Second, consistent 
with this approach, the OCC declines to include any language regarding 
the permissibility of privacy-preserving architectures. If a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's distributed ledger architecture would allow 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to comply with the requirements 
of the GENIUS Act and 12 CFR part 15, the OCC would generally regard 
such architecture as permissible. The OCC is not making any changes to 
the final rule to address this comment.
    After careful consideration of the comments received, the OCC is 
finalizing the examination provisions in Sec.  15.14 with certain 
modifications described below.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(a) provided that the OCC would conduct a full-
scope examination \117\ of each permitted

[[Page 67080]]

payment stablecoin issuer subject to OCC supervision at least once 
every 12-month period, unless the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
qualifies for an extended cycle under Sec.  15.14(d). One commenter 
stated that, if the OCC required each permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to issue only a single brand of payment stablecoin, maintaining 
multiple permitted payment stablecoin issuers would result in increased 
and duplicative examination and assessment costs. The commenter stated 
that under proposed Sec.  15.14(a), which provided that the OCC ``will 
conduct a full-scope examination of every permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer subject to its supervision at least once during each 12-month 
period, unless otherwise specified in proposed Sec.  15.14(d),'' given 
the common risk management and back-office functions of white-label 
issuers today, it is not clear what benefit multiple examinations 
across affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would 
accomplish. The commenter further stated that those costs were not 
considered in the proposal's economic analysis. This analysis was based 
on the proposed rule, which did not mandate that each permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer be limited to a single brand of payment stablecoin. 
As discussed above, and as required by statute, the OCC will pursue 
examination and supervisory policies that maximize efficiency and 
minimize duplication, including, where appropriate, coordinating 
examination activities and leveraging existing supervisory 
frameworks.\118\ The OCC is adopting this provision as proposed. With 
respect to the comments concerning limiting each permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer to a single brand of payment stablecoin, the OCC has 
elected not to impose such a requirement by regulation. The OCC has, 
however, made targeted edits throughout part 15, including in Sec.  
15.14, to accommodate business models that use multiple issuer SPVs. 
For such a business model, the OCC intends to examine the family of 
issuer SPVs at once as part of a single examination to reduce burden.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\117\ A full-scope examination refers to the comprehensive 
review of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's financial 
condition, risk management practices, compliance with laws and 
regulations, and overall safety and soundness. The OCC's proposed 
exercise of its examination authority over permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers mirrors the OCC's current examination authority 
over national banks and Federal savings associations. This mirroring 
ensures the OCC is requesting examinations and reports at a cadence 
and in a format that is similar to that required for similarly 
situated entities the OCC regulates, as required by section 
6(a)(4)(C) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(4)(C)).
    \118\ See 12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(4)(B).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.14(b) would have required permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, upon OCC request, to provide prompt and complete 
access to all officers, directors, employees, agents, and all relevant 
books, records, and documents of any type. One commenter stated that if 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer has a parent company, the OCC 
must ensure that the agency has appropriate visibility into and 
cooperation from the parent company, including access to relevant 
records and financial information. The OCC notes that its examination 
and supervisory authorities extend to information necessary to assess 
the condition, risks, and compliance of the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer. Where relevant information is maintained by a parent 
company, the OCC expects the issuer to ensure that such information is 
made available to the agency consistent with applicable law and 
supervisory requirements.\119\ The agency is adopting Sec.  15.14(b) as 
proposed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \119\ The OCC notes that it has examination authority with 
respect to certain affiliates of national banks and Federal savings 
associations. See 12 U.S.C. 481; 12 U.S.C. 1464, 12 U.S.C. 1820(d). 
In addition, the OCC notes that, under Sec.  15.14(m), the OCC would 
be made aware of certain changes in control with respect to a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.14(c) would have authorized the OCC to conduct 
examinations of each supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
either on-site or remotely. This subsection preserved supervisory 
flexibility as to examination modality while maintaining the 
examination requirement established in Sec.  15.14(a). The agency did 
not receive any comments related to this section and is adopting this 
provision as proposed.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(d) would have provided the OCC with the option 
to examine some permitted payment stablecoin issuers on an 18- to 36-
month cycle, as determined by the OCC, in its sole discretion, if the 
issuers satisfied the following conditions: (1) the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer currently is not subject to a formal enforcement 
proceeding or order; (2) no person acquired control, as specified in 
Sec.  15.14(m), of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer during the 
preceding 12-month period in which a full-scope examination would have 
been required but for proposed Sec.  15.14(d); (3) the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer has an outstanding issuance value of less 
than $1 billion or less than $25 billion in total monthly trading 
volume; and (4) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is in 
compliance with all of the reserve requirements set forth in proposed 
Sec.  15.11 and the reporting requirements in proposed Sec.  15.14. The 
proposed criteria for certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers to 
qualify for an 18- to 36-month examination cycle were similar to the 
factors the OCC considers for national banks and Federal savings 
associations under 12 CFR 4.6(b). In the proposal, the agency sought 
feedback on whether the criteria for eligibility for an extended 
examination cycle were appropriately calibrated and whether the 
timeframe for an extended examination cycle was appropriate.
    A number of commenters expressed support for the extended 
examination cycle available to smaller issuers. Two commenters stated 
that providing for an extended examination cycle would encourage new 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to enter the market by reducing 
the regulatory burden on smaller and less complex institutions that are 
in full compliance with reserve and reporting requirements. Two other 
commenters stated that the proposed timeframe for an extended 
examination cycle is appropriate, provided that the OCC applies these 
criteria flexibly and on a risk-sensitive basis rather than as a 
mechanical threshold test and retains supervisory discretion to shorten 
an issuer's examination cycle where emerging risks, market events, or 
supervisory concerns warrant more frequent review. The commenters 
recommended that the OCC adopt a broader risk-based assessment 
framework under which eligibility for an extended examination cycle may 
also take into account relevant qualitative and quantitative 
supervisory indicators, including: redemption volatility and 
concentration of redemption activity; reserve asset composition and 
liquidity profile; operational and governance maturity; prior 
examination findings and compliance history; and complexity of group 
structure and outsourcing arrangements.
    Two commenters stated that waiting multiple years between 
examinations of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is unreasonable. 
One of the commenters expressed support for supervising permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers in a manner similar to insured depository 
institutions but argued that due to the rapid speed at which the 
underlying technology can evolve, extending the examination cycle 
beyond 18 months is not prudent.
    After consideration of the comments regarding the extended 
examination cycle, the OCC is shortening the extended examination cycle 
in Sec.  15.14(d) to 18 to 24 months from 18 to 36 months. The 18- to 
24-month examination cycle is appropriate because, as discussed below, 
it will be supplemented by weekly and quarterly reporting from each 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. This reporting will allow the 
agency to conduct continuous

[[Page 67081]]

monitoring of the condition of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, 
which reduces the need for more invasive supervisory tools such as 
full- or limited-scope examinations. In the final rule, the OCC 
maintains its authority to deny a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
an extended examination cycle and to adjust the length of a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's examination cycle, including restoring the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to a 12-month examination cycle 
where appropriate.
    The OCC has also opted to remove ``trading volume'' as a factor for 
whether a permitted payment stablecoin issuer qualifies for an extended 
examination cycle. After considering the comments, the OCC believes 
that it will be sufficient to look to the outstanding issuance value of 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer without regard to the trading 
volume. As discussed in greater detail below, permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers will, nevertheless, be required to report certain 
information concerning trading volume.
    Finally, Sec.  15.14(d)(3) of the final rule provides that, to 
qualify for an extended examination cycle, the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must have an outstanding issuance value, together 
with any affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, of less than 
$1 billion. The OCC is making this change in recognition of business 
models that use multiple issuer SPVs. The OCC is adopting Sec.  
15.14(d) with the shortened extended examination cycle, removal of 
trading volume, and inclusion of affiliated permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers in the calculation of the $1 billion threshold 
discussed above.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(e) would have clarified that Sec.  15.14 does 
not limit the OCC's authority to examine a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer more frequently whenever the OCC deems it necessary. The 
provision expressly preserves the OCC's ability to conduct limited-
scope examinations, as well as more frequent examinations. One 
commenter stated that the OCC should clarify objective triggers for 
limited-scope or ad hoc examinations while preserving emergency 
authority. The OCC declines to adopt objective triggers or measures 
that could give rise to the initiation of a targeted or limited 
examination. The OCC has not adopted similar objective triggers or 
measures for national banks and Federal savings associations, and the 
OCC did not find any compelling reasons to deviate from that approach 
with respect to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. For example, 
miscalibration of objective triggers or measures for limited-scope or 
ad hoc examinations could result in a supervisory framework that is 
overly inclusive and imposes unnecessary burden on institutions through 
excessive examinations or a framework that is underinclusive and 
provides less opportunity to identify and address material financial 
risks to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC has significant 
experience in determining examination frequency and scope in the 
context of national banks and Federal savings associations. As the OCC 
develops experience in examining and supervising permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, it will consider whether it should revisit or 
revise the examination schedule and the triggers or measures for 
conducting limited-scope or ad hoc examinations. Therefore, the OCC is 
adopting Sec.  15.14(e) as proposed.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(f) would have required all permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to maintain a complete set of books and records in 
English. The agency did not receive any comments related to this 
section and is adopting this provision as proposed.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(g) would have required all permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers to develop and implement a records retention policy. 
The policy must ensure that the issuer can demonstrate compliance with 
the GENIUS Act, part 15, and all other applicable laws and regulations. 
One commenter recommended that the OCC revise the proposal to establish 
minimum standards for records retention. The OCC has elected not to 
codify minimum records retention standards in order to provide 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers with flexibility to manage and 
maintain their respective books and records while still being able to 
demonstrate compliance with applicable laws and regulations. Further, 
the agency has not established general retention standards for national 
banks and Federal savings associations, so establishing minimum records 
retention standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers would be 
inconsistent with the agency's supervisory approach for national banks 
and Federal savings associations. The OCC may revisit this approach in 
the future if permitted payment stablecoin issuers would benefit from 
minimum records retention standards. The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.14(g) 
as proposed.
c. Reports
i. Description of Proposed Rule
    Section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)) requires 
that each permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall, upon request, 
submit to the appropriate Federal payment stablecoin regulator a report 
on: the financial condition of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; 
the systems of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring 
and controlling financial and operating risks; compliance by the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer (and any subsidiary thereof) with 
the GENIUS Act; and the compliance of the Federal qualified nonbank 
payment stablecoin issuer with the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws 
authorizing the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the 
Secretary of the Treasury. Section 6(a)(4) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5905(a)(4)) requires the OCC to take certain actions to promote 
efficiency in the supervision and examination of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. The OCC, in supervising and examining permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers, to the fullest extent possible, must use 
existing supervisory reports and other supervisory information and 
avoid duplication of examination activities, reporting requirements, 
and requests for information.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(j) implemented section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS 
Act and would have required each permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
subject to the requirements of section 6(a)(1) of the Act to, upon 
request, submit to the OCC a report on: (1) the financial condition of 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (2) the systems of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring and controlling 
financial and operating risks; (3) compliance by the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer (and any subsidiary thereof) with the GENIUS Act and 
proposed part 15; and (4) compliance of the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer with the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws authorizing 
the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the Secretary of the 
Treasury. In an effort to clarify the GENIUS Act's requirements, the 
OCC proposed in Sec.  15.14(j)(4) to expand the requirement that 
Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuers produce reports of 
compliance with the requirements of the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws 
authorizing the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the 
Secretary of the Treasury to all permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers.\120\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\120\ The OCC notes that section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)) requires all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to provide the subsequent list of reports in section 6(a)(2)(A) through (D) to the OCC upon request, whereas section 6(a)(2)(D) refers to the compliance of ``the Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuer with the requirements of the Bank Secrecy Act.'' Based on the structure of section 6(a)(2), the OCC believes all permitted payment stablecoin issuers must, upon request, produce each of the listed reports and that the OCC could request the report required in section 6(a)(2)(D) from a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Additionally, section 6(a)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)) gives the OCC supervisory authority over all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, which provides the OCC with further authority to request the report in section 6(a)(2)(D). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- [[Page 67082]] In addition to the regulations codifying the reporting requirements in section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)), pursuant to its supervisory authority in section 6(a)(1) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)), the OCC proposed in Sec. 15.14(h) to require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to submit on a weekly basis, in the manner and form specified by the OCC, a confidential report containing the information requested in the form that will be available at www.occ.gov.\121\ Proposed Sec. 15.14(h) would have required all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to submit a confidential weekly report to the OCC in the manner and form specified by the agency. Under the proposal, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have been required to provide information regarding stablecoin issuance and redemption, trading volume, and reserve assets for each payment stablecoin it issued. The report would have included information relating to the blockchains on which the payment stablecoin was listed, outstanding issuance value, secondary market activity and price movements, redemption volume and timing, detailed information regarding reserve assets, and other relevant information. The agency published the weekly and quarterly reporting forms for notice and public comment on June 12, 2026.\122\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \121\ See 12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1) and (2). With regard to reporting by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer as to its assets under custody, section 10(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(d)) provides an additional statutory grant of authority. \122\ Proposed Information Collection; Reporting Forms and Instructions for Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 91 FR 35795 (June 12, 2026). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- At a high level, the OCC proposed requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to provide information regarding issuance and redemption, trading volume, and reserve assets for each payment stablecoin they issue. The OCC proposed that the weekly report would include information relating to the blockchains on which the payment stablecoin was listed, outstanding issuance value, secondary market activity and price movement, redemption volume and timing, detailed information regarding reserve assets, and other relevant information. In the proposal, the OCC stated that requiring a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to provide a confidential set of data on a weekly basis for each payment stablecoin it issued would allow the agency to understand the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations and the risks unique to its business model. This regular data reporting would have allowed the OCC to tailor its examinations to be risk-based, which would have reduced the burden of examinations by focusing the scope of examinations. In addition, the OCC stated that this regular reporting framework would have allowed the agency to identify and respond more quickly to emerging novel risks and financial stability risks. Further, in support of this reporting framework, the OCC stated its belief that the proposed set of information is currently tracked on a regular basis by stablecoin issuers. The OCC proposed in Sec. 15.14(i) a separate provision that would have required permitted payment stablecoin issuers to submit quarterly reports of financial condition to the OCC, including, but not limited to, an income statement, expenses, balance sheet, reserves, changes in equity, investments, capital, outstanding issuance value, and assets under custody, in a standardized format as prescribed by the OCC within 30 days of the end of the prior quarter. The OCC also proposed to require that each quarterly report of financial condition include a declaration from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's Chief Financial Officer, or the individual performing an equivalent function, that the report was true and correct to the best of their knowledge and belief. The correctness of the quarterly report of condition would have also been attested to by the signatures of the directors and senior management of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer other than the officer making such declaration, with the attestation stating that the report had been examined by them and to the best of their knowledge and belief was true and correct. The OCC proposed requiring these declarations and attestations to ensure that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's officers and directors were accountable for the accuracy of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reports of financial condition. Proposed Sec. 15.14(k) implemented section 5(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(i)). Consistent with the statute, under the proposed rule, not later than 180 days after the approval of an application, as defined in proposed Sec. 15.30, and on an annual basis thereafter, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have had to submit to the OCC a certification by its board of directors that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer had implemented anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs that were reasonably designed to prevent the permitted payment stablecoin issuer from facilitating money laundering, in particular, facilitating money laundering for cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations under section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1189) and the financing of terrorist activities, consistent with the requirements of the GENIUS Act. ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule Many commenters submitted general comments about the proposed reporting framework and requested that the OCC modify or incorporate various concepts into the proposed reporting framework. Several commenters expressed general support for the OCC's proposed reporting framework. The commenters stated that the cadence and data fields were sufficient to support the prudential regulation of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter expressed support for the reporting framework on the grounds that it may reduce the need for more intrusive or frequent on-site examinations. Another commenter expressed support for standardized reporting forms on the grounds that they are a proportionate mechanism to improve supervisory visibility into the operational, liquidity, and market risks of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Several commenters encouraged the OCC to coordinate stablecoin reporting requirements under the proposal with other Federal payment stablecoin regulators, stating that interagency coordination is essential to promote consistency, reduce duplication, and ensure an efficient supervisory framework for institutions subject to multiple Federal regulators. At this time, the OCC has determined that the issuance of OCC-specific reporting forms for OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers best ensures that the weekly and quarterly reporting forms are available when the agency's stablecoin regulations become effective. In the future, the OCC will consider potentially using an interagency framework for the submission of reports to promote consistency. Several commenters recommended additional reporting requirements to strengthen supervisory oversight of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. [[Page 67083]] One commenter urged the OCC to require monthly reporting of any instances in which a permitted payment stablecoin issuer extends the redemption period beyond two business days to complete compliance checks. Another commenter suggested that regulators consider collecting data on transaction rejections, delays, account closures, and geographic restrictions to improve visibility into access-related outcomes. A further commenter recommended that the OCC consider requiring an annual attestation report on management's assertions regarding the effectiveness of internal controls over stablecoin operations and reserves. Another commenter recommended that the final rule require every OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuer to file a current report with the OCC within one business day whenever the secondary market trading price of its payment stablecoin deviates downward from $1.00 by more than one quarter of one percent. One commenter stated that new reporting obligations should leverage information already maintained in the ordinary course of business wherever possible. The commenter noted that payment stablecoins may present supervisory visibility challenges that are not fully addressed by traditional banking or payments reporting, particularly once stablecoins circulate beyond initial issuance and redemption channels. The commenter stated that the OCC should consider whether targeted, standardized, machine-readable reporting fields are appropriate to capture material secondary-market activity, concentration, operational interventions, and other risk indicators that may be observable through issuers, service providers, or private or public blockchain data. The commenter claimed that such an approach would help avoid supervisory blind spots while remaining consistent with a risk-based and operationally practicable framework. One commenter stated that smaller institutions may lack the staffing and systems needed to support frequent or highly granular reporting, including weekly submissions, and urged the OCC to account for those operational constraints. The commenter recommended that the OCC rely on existing supervisory information and frameworks for bank- affiliated issuers wherever practicable and avoid requirements that would force new technology investments, additional staffing, or duplicative attestations without clear supervisory benefit. The commenter also urged the OCC to provide standardized reporting tools if more frequent reporting is required and supported an additional tier for small issuers to better align requirements with risk and operational capacity. The commenter further stated that nonbank permitted payment stablecoin issuers warrant more prescriptive reporting obligations, given the absence of an ongoing prudential supervisory relationship comparable to that applicable to insured depository institutions. Another commenter stated that traditional core systems are often limited to two decimal places, whereas other stablecoins require six. The commenter stated that the agency should consider the operational modernization required to support stablecoins. The OCC recognizes that some banks may currently lack the operational capacity to support certain payment stablecoin activities. Such institutions are not required to engage in payment stablecoin activities, but, to the extent that they do so, they must do so in a safe and sound manner, which may entail modernizing certain systems. Several commenters recommended that the agency adopt a risk-based reporting framework based on a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size, complexity, and risk profile. In general, the commenters recommended that the OCC implement reduced or streamlined reporting requirements for smaller and less complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The commenters claimed that these permitted payment stablecoin issuers do not present the same risk as larger, more complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers and therefore should not be subject to the same reporting requirements. Some commenters added that a reduced reporting burden would result in a reduction in operating expenses for smaller permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter recommended that the OCC impose reduced reporting requirements on those permitted payment stablecoin issuers that qualify for an extended examination cycle under Sec. 15.14(d). Upon consideration, the OCC has determined that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to submit weekly reporting and quarterly reports of condition because this information is essential to the oversight of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the stablecoin market. The OCC has proposed reporting forms for comment and will revise those forms, as appropriate, based on the comments received. In addition, the OCC intends to evaluate the information it receives from reports from permitted payment stablecoin issuers to consider whether to revise the reporting forms to reduce burden while still providing the information necessary to the OCC's supervision. Commenters urged the OCC to adopt a reporting framework that maintains regulatory differentiation between bank and nonbank stablecoin issuers. The commenters stated that bank-affiliated issuers should be permitted to satisfy stablecoin-specific reporting obligations through streamlined, integrated disclosures--such as supplemental schedules to Call Reports--while nonbank issuers should be subject to more robust, standalone reporting and audit requirements commensurate with their risk profile and lack of prudential supervision. Commenters stated that this approach would preserve safety and soundness, promote regulatory consistency, and support community bank participation in stablecoin activities without disadvantaging institutions that already operate under a rigorous supervisory framework. After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC has determined that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be subject to uniform reporting requirements. This approach ensures that the OCC receives a consistent set of data across all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. As discussed, the OCC considered the information to be collected to be an appropriate minimum amount of data for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The receipt of this data will also allow the OCC to calibrate its supervisory approach to each permitted payment stablecoin issuer and minimize supervisory disruptions associated with limited and full-scope examinations. Moreover, reporting consistency should help the OCC ensure comparability and better facilitate market oversight. A few commenters urged the OCC to focus reporting on primary market data, including primary market issuance, redemption activity, and reserve composition. One commenter emphasized that the proposed weekly reporting should focus on primary market data instead of secondary market data. The commenters added that, if the OCC does require secondary market reporting, the data collected should focus on material secondary market indicators relevant to prudential supervision and market integrity. Some of the commenters also noted the challenges with reporting secondary market data since market activity occurs across multiple venues and through intermediaries where the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may lack full visibility. The OCC will consider this comment in conjunction with comments

Another commenter stated that some data fields are not observable in

that a weekly reporting cadence is preferable to real-time reporting 
and suggested that the weekly reporting framework could be supplemented 
with event-driven reporting.
    Upon consideration, the OCC has declined to incorporate a real-time 
reporting component into the reporting framework for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. The OCC has determined that a weekly and quarterly 
reporting cadence will provide the agency with sufficient data and 
supervisory visibility into the stablecoin market. Further, the agency 
is sensitive to the increased operational expense and burden that the 
implementation of real-time reporting would impose on permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. For these reasons, the OCC has declined to impose a 
real-time reporting requirement on permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. The OCC may reconsider this position in the future if, for 
example, effective supervision of the stablecoin market demands the 
implementation of real-time reporting or future technological advances 
mean that implementing real-time reporting would not be overly 
burdensome for permitted payment stablecoin issuers.

Weekly Reports
    As discussed above, proposed Sec.  15.14(h) would have required all 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers to submit a confidential weekly 
report to the OCC in the manner and form specified by the agency. Under 
the proposal, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have been 
required to provide information regarding stablecoin issuance and 
redemption, trading volume, and reserve assets for each payment 
stablecoin it issues. The report would have included information 
relating to the blockchains on which the payment stablecoin operates, 
outstanding issuance value, secondary market activity and price 
movements, redemption volume and timing, detailed information regarding 
reserve assets, and other relevant information. As discussed above, the 
agency published the weekly and quarterly reporting forms for notice 
and public comment on June 12, 2026. The following discussion includes 
comments received in response to the proposal's issuance on March 2, 
2026, and the weekly reporting forms and instructions' issuance on June 
12, 2026.
    A few commenters expressed support for the weekly reporting cadence 
on the grounds that the reporting framework is generally well 
calibrated and directionally appropriate. However, the commenters also 
expressed a desire for the OCC to narrow the data fields to categories 
more closely tied to the statutory requirements and prudential 
oversight. For example, commenters recommended recalibrating the data 
fields to focus on liquidity, reserve management, and redemptions.
    Several commenters also expressed opposition to the weekly 
reporting requirement. Generally, the commenters opposed the weekly 
reporting requirement on the grounds that it is overly burdensome, 
particularly for smaller issuers. In some cases, the commenters 
questioned the supervisory value of weekly reporting. The commenters 
also expressed a preference for a variety of reporting alternatives, 
including monthly reporting, monthly reporting accompanied by event-
triggered reporting, and quarterly confidential reporting in addition 
to quarterly public reporting. One commenter added that if the OCC 
adopts weekly reporting, the data fields should be limited to the core 
data fields necessary to monitor a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
for safety and soundness.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.14(h), the weekly reporting submitted to 
the OCC would have been confidential. One commenter expressed the view 
that stablecoin holders would benefit from having access to weekly 
reporting and encouraged the OCC to make the weekly reporting available 
to the public. Two commenters opposed the disclosure of weekly data on 
the grounds that it could create market distortions, reveal 
commercially sensitive information, and risk encouraging short-term 
market reactions to normal operational fluctuations that do not reflect 
underlying prudential concerns. Further, the commenters stated that 
disclosures should be focused on statutorily required disclosures such 
as reserve composition. One of the commenters expressed an openness to 
the disclosure of aggregated statistics on payment stablecoin issuance 
and volumes, among other things, for payment stablecoins.
    One commenter stated that the weekly reporting under proposed Sec.  
15.14(h) is not designed to identify protocol-level exposure. 
Specifically, the commenter stated that the data fields enumerated in 
proposed Sec.  15.14(h) are appropriate for entity-level reserve and 
redemption oversight, but do not capture the protocol deployment of 
stablecoin-denominated assets where systemic risk is concentrated.
    Several commenters opposed the OCC's proposed weekly collection of 
``the 100 persons that hold or trade the stablecoin the most.'' 
Commenters generally opposed the collection of this information on 
several grounds. First, commenters stated that the OCC has not 
articulated a clear supervisory rationale for collecting this data and 
that this information is not essential to understanding a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's operations. Second, commenters claimed that 
issuers cannot reliably produce this data because payment stablecoins 
frequently trade through exchanges and intermediaries, which limits 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers' ability to reliably identify the 
top 100 holders on a recurring basis. Finally, the commenters claimed 
that the required disclosure of top-holder information raises 
significant privacy concerns. Several commenters presented solutions 
ranging from removing the collection of this data from the weekly 
reporting form to focusing the collection on the top 100 wallets, which 
would not include any beneficial ownership information.
    Upon review of the comments, the OCC intends to keep the weekly 
reporting confidential. The agency believes that the confidentiality of 
this reporting serves the interest of promoting the exchange of 
supervisory information between permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
and the OCC. In the future, the OCC may consider publishing a limited 
set of data if it would be useful to the public. For example, the OCC 
may consider publishing a limited set of aggregate statistics based on 
the weekly reporting. The OCC published a draft weekly reporting form 
for comment that requests information on the top 100 payment stablecoin 
wallet addresses, not information identifying the top 100 individual 
persons holding payment stablecoins of an issuer.\132\ The OCC believes 
the collection of this information will provide important supervisory 
data points related to concentration risk, payment stablecoin 
volatility, and other payment stablecoin characteristics that are 
important to the OCC's supervision of permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. The OCC plans to make adjustments to the reporting forms as 
appropriate to address comments received, as the market develops, and 
as the OCC gains experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers.

Under the proposal, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been required to submit quarterly reports of financial condition to the OCC, including, but not limited to, an income statement, expenses, balance sheet, reserves, changes in equity, investments, capital, outstanding [[Page 67086]] issuance value, and assets under custody, in a standardized format. The agency published the weekly and quarterly reporting forms for notice and public comment on June 12, 2026.\133\ The following discussion includes comments received in response to the proposal's issuance on March 2, 2026. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \133\ Id. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- A few commenters expressed support for requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to provide quarterly reports of financial condition. The commenters generally stated that quarterly reporting is an important tool to both compare permitted payment stablecoin issuers and prevent the deterioration of market confidence. Several commenters stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of national banks that already file Call Reports should not be required to submit a separate quarterly report in order to minimize duplicative reporting requirements, reduce reporting burden, and lower compliance costs. The commenters generally advocated that these permitted payment stablecoin issuers be allowed to submit a stablecoin-specific appendix or schedule. Some commenters stated that the OCC should allow other executives, besides the Chief Financial Officer or the individual performing the equivalent function, to provide the quarterly report attestation. The commenters also recommended that the OCC allow a subset of the board of directors and senior management, as opposed to all members of the board of directors and senior management, to attest to the correctness of quarterly reports. The OCC believes that the Chief Financial Officer, or the individual performing the equivalent function, is the correct member of senior management to be accountable for providing an attestation to the accuracy of quarterly reports. A single accountable member of senior management will help ensure that a member of senior management has ownership of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's financial reporting function. Similarly, the OCC believes that requiring all members of the board of directors and senior management to attest to the correctness of quarterly reports will help ensure that the board of directors and senior management are engaged in the oversight of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's financial reporting function. Upon consideration of the comments received, the OCC has elected to adopt the quarterly reporting provision as proposed with new subdivisions and other technical edits. Final Sec. 15.14(i)(1) requires a quarterly report on the financial condition, final Sec. 15.14(i)(2) requires a declaration that the report is true and correct, and final Sec. 15.14(i)(3) requires certain signatures of directors and senior management. The technical edits involve the addition of ``and'' to final Sec. 15.14(i)(1) for clarity and the addition of commas in final Sec. 15.14(i)(3) for clarity. In the interest of promoting transparency, the OCC has determined that each permitted payment stablecoin issuer must submit a quarterly report of condition. The agency has adopted this approach because it establishes a uniform requirement across all permitted payment stablecoin issuers and will minimize public confusion about where to find quarterly reports of condition for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. If some permitted payment stablecoin issuers were allowed to attach quarterly reports of condition to Call Reports, the public could find it challenging to locate stablecoin-specific quarterly reporting forms if it is not widely known or understood that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is a subsidiary of an institution that is a Call Report filer. Therefore, the OCC has elected to adopt a uniform quarterly reporting requirement for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter stated that large and complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers (e.g., those above $10 billion in payment stablecoin issuance or that meet the other criteria cited above) should be required to report at a much higher frequency than quarterly, similar to the prudential bank requirements for the largest banking organizations. Under Sec. 15.14(h) of the final rule, all permitted payment stablecoin issuers will be required to provide weekly confidential reporting to the OCC. One commenter stated that the quarterly reporting requirement in proposed Sec. 15.14(i) should be tailored to ensure proportionality across the rulemaking and consistency across prudential regulators, to avoid unnecessary duplication and be consistent with a risk-based supervisory approach. One commenter recommended making quarterly reporting data publicly available as the reports are likely to contain material facts that are pertinent to stablecoin holders and other data users. Similar to the publication of Call Reports, the OCC intends to publish the quarterly reporting forms for OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Other Supervisory Reports Proposed Sec. 15.14(j) addressed section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)) and would have required each permitted payment stablecoin issuer subject to the requirements of section 6(a)(1) of the Act to, upon request, submit to the OCC a report on: (1) the financial condition of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (2) the systems of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring and controlling financial and operating risks; (3) compliance by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (and any subsidiary thereof) with the GENIUS Act and proposed part 15; and (4) compliance of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws authorizing the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury.\134\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \134\ See 12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- In an effort to clarify the GENIUS Act's requirements, the OCC proposed in Sec. 15.14(j)(4) to expand the requirement in section 6(a)(2)(D) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)(D)) that Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuers produce reports of compliance with the requirements of the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws authorizing the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury to all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The proposal also requested feedback on this expanded approach and whether the OCC should apply this requirement to all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter stated that the requirement should apply to all OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The commenter stated that BSA and sanctions risks are not meaningfully reduced by charter type. The commenter also claimed that stablecoin- specific AML and CFT expectations are being applied internationally across issuer categories rather than solely to nonbanks. The commenter further recommended providing uniform substantive coverage with proportional, non-duplicative collection of information--i.e., if a bank subsidiary's parent already provides equivalent information through existing supervisory channels, the OCC can rely on that information to avoid duplicate reporting. Another commenter stated that the requirements to provide reports on compliance with the BSA should not be required for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are already subject to the BSA, including national [[Page 67087]] banks (whether insured or otherwise) and their subsidiaries. After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC has elected to revise Sec. 15.14(j) in the final rule to better reflect section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(2)). As a result, final Sec. 15.14(j)(4) will apply only to Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuers \135\ in the final rule, codifying the reporting requirements as provided for in the GENIUS Act and not expanding the requirement to all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC notes that it may nevertheless obtain information relating to the compliance of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer with the requirements of the Bank Secrecy Act and laws authorizing the imposition of sanctions as part of ongoing supervision. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \135\ Although not a defined term in the GENIUS Act, the OCC interprets the term ``Federal qualified nonbank payment stablecoin issuers'' to mean Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers that are nonbank entities. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- BSA Certification Proposed Sec. 15.14(k), implementing section 5(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(i)), would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, no later than 180 days after approval under Sec. 15.30 and annually thereafter, to submit a board certification regarding its AML/CFT and sanctions compliance programs. The certification would have needed to state that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer had implemented programs reasonably designed to prevent the permitted payment stablecoin issuer from facilitating money laundering, including money laundering for cartels and designated foreign terrorist organizations, and the financing of terrorist activities, consistent with the GENIUS Act. Commenters addressed the burden associated with the requirement. Specifically, one commenter stated that the proposed post-approval requirement to submit a certification of having implemented anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance programs is unnecessary, as such programs would have already been vetted by the OCC as part of the approval and organization process required for a national trust bank. As stated above, this regulation is implementing a statutory provision, so the annual post-approval certification is mandated by the GENIUS Act.\136\ Another commenter stated that if ongoing compliance certifications are required under Sec. 15.14(k), AML and sanctions- related certifications should be made by the AML officer rather than the board, given the officer's direct responsibility for and proximity to those programs. After careful consideration of the comments and burden associated with the requirement generally, the OCC has decided to amend Sec. 15.14(k) to provide permitted payment stablecoin issuers with increased flexibility to provide the annual certifications by allowing the board of directors to provide the initial certification and then all subsequent annual certifications may be provided by the board of directors, an appropriate committee of the board of directors, or the Bank Secrecy Act officer. While it is important that the board of directors demonstrates its oversight of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's compliance function through submission of the initial certification, this approach balances the goal of ensuring that the board of directors is actively involved in the oversight of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's compliance program at the initiation of operations and minimizing the board of directors' ongoing administrative burden. As required by statute, the OCC will pursue examination and supervisory policies that maximize efficiency and minimize duplication, including, where appropriate, limiting requests for supplemental or ad hoc reporting from OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers.\137\ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC is also revising Sec.  15.14(k) to replace the phrase 
``defined in Sec.  15.30'' with ``set forth in Sec.  15.30.'' This is a

d. Audits
    Section 4(a)(10) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(10)) requires 
that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer with more than $50 billion 
in consolidated total outstanding issuance value that is not subject to 
certain reporting requirements under Federal securities laws prepare an 
annual financial statement. Section 4(a)(10) further provides that a 
registered public accounting firm must perform an audit of the annual 
financial statement. Under this section, the audited annual financial 
statement must also be made publicly available on the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer's website and be submitted annually to the primary 
Federal payment stablecoin regulator.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(l) implemented the requirements of section 
4(a)(10) of the GENIUS Act. Under the proposed rule, each permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer with more than $50 billion in outstanding 
issuance value that is not subject to the reporting requirements under 
section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 
U.S.C. 78m(a) or 78o(d)) would be required to prepare, in accordance 
with GAAP, an annual financial statement that included the disclosure 
of any related party transactions, as defined by GAAP. Proposed Sec.  
15.14(l)(1) required that a registered public accounting firm conduct 
an audit of the financial statements in accordance with all applicable 
auditing standards established by the Public Company Accounting 
Oversight Board (PCAOB). This provision incorporates the requirement in 
section 4(a)(10)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(10)(A)(iii)) that an audit described in section 4(a)(10)(A)(ii) 
shall ``be conducted in accordance with all applicable auditing 
standards established by the PCAOB, including those relating to auditor 
independence, internal controls, and related party transactions.'' As a 
part of its oversight of accounting firms that audit public companies, 
the PCAOB has authority to establish the applicable audit standards

[[Page 67088]]

for those accounting firms. The GENIUS Act, however, did not amend the 
PCAOB's authority to establish audit standards for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers that are not required reporters under the Securities 
Exchange Act of 1934.\139\ Thus, none of the PCAOB's audit standards 
would be applicable to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer if the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer were not a required reporter under 
the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Nevertheless, the GENIUS Act 
states that audits conducted pursuant to section 4(a)(10)(A)(ii) must 
``be conducted in accordance with all applicable auditing standards 
established'' by the PCAOB. In light of the language of section 
4(a)(10)(A)(iii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(10)(A)(iii)), it is 
appropriate to clarify that the ``applicable auditing standards'' in 
this context means those auditing standards that would apply if the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer were subject to the reporting 
requirements under section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange 
Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78m or 78o(d)). The OCC determined that the most 
logical applicable audit standards are those that would apply if the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer were a filer under section 13(a) or 
15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 because section 
4(a)(10)(A)(i)-(iii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(10)(A)(i)-(iii)) 
appear intended to address those entities that would otherwise be 
subject to the requirements of sections 13(a) or 15(d) of the 
Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \139\ See section 4(a)(10)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(10)(A)(iv)) (providing that nothing in subparagraph A shall 
be construed to limit, alter, or expand the jurisdiction of the 
PCAOB over permitted payment stablecoin issuers or registered public 
accounting firms).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The standards would be enforced by the OCC for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers subject to the audit requirement under section 
4(a)(10)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(10)(A)(iii)). 
Consistent with this framework, the OCC may at any time request that a 
registered public accounting firm provide to the OCC certain additional 
information or documents relating to information provided by the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The registered public accounting 
firm must agree to provide copies of any working papers, policies, and 
procedures relating to services in connection with the audit required 
under section 4(a)(10)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(10)(A)(iii)). Proposed Sec.  15.14(l)(2) would have required 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to: (1) make the audited 
financial statement publicly available on its website, and (2) submit 
the audited financial statement annually to the OCC. Under proposed 
Sec.  15.14(l)(2)(ii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have 
been required to submit to the OCC annually, within 120 days of the end 
of its fiscal year, an audited financial statement. If a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer were unable to timely file all or any portion 
of its financial statements, proposed Sec.  15.14(l)(2)(iii) would have 
required the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to submit a written 
notice of late filing to the OCC that would: (A) disclose the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's inability to file all, or specified 
portions, of its annual financial statement and the reasons therefore 
in reasonable detail; (B) include the date by which the financial 
statement will be filed; and (C) be filed on or before the deadline for 
filing the financial statement.
    Many commenters submitted general comments about the proposed audit 
requirements in Sec.  15.14(l) and requested that the OCC modify or 
incorporate various concepts into the audit regulations. Several 
commenters recommended that the OCC clarify its interpretation of 
``applicable auditing standards'' in the rule text. One commenter 
recommended that the standards be equivalent to those that would apply 
under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 reporting, without importing 
the SEC's full registrant regime for non-registrants. The commenter 
added that in many cases, standalone issuer financial statements may 
more appropriately be prepared under the AICPA's standards, even where 
parent-level reporting follows a different framework. Two commenters 
stated that the final rule should state that the applicable auditing 
standards are those that would apply to an issuer subject to the 
reporting requirements of section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities 
Exchange Act of 1934. One of the commenters added that clear 
articulation of this standard is important given the differing 
regulatory auditing baselines applicable to bank and nonbank issuers.
    The OCC also received several comments recommending that the agency 
clarify that it would enforce audit standards and may request documents 
and information from a registered public accounting firm related to a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer. One commenter recommended that the 
OCC make clear that enforcement of audit standards for bank-affiliated 
issuers will be conducted within the OCC's existing supervisory 
authority and examination processes. The commenter further claimed that 
any authority to obtain information from registered public accounting 
firms should be narrowly tailored and exercised only where necessary. 
Another commenter stated that it would be appropriate for the OCC to 
clarify the statutory enforcement authority regarding audits performed 
under the statute. Another commenter stated that the OCC should also 
state that it may obtain additional documents and, where necessary, 
working papers from the registered public accounting firm, subject to 
confidentiality protections, because effective supervision depends on 
being able to evaluate the reliability and scope of the external audit. 
Another commenter stated that the OCC may retain authority to request 
additional auditor information, but that authority should be exercised 
on a targeted and risk-based basis rather than as an open-ended or 
routine working-paper production obligation. Any such request should be 
tied to a specific supervisory need, identified discrepancy, or 
materiality concern, and it should be subject to written scope and 
confidentiality protections. One commenter stated that it is not 
necessary to include in the rule text that the OCC would enforce the 
standards.
    One commenter noted that the audit under Sec.  15.14(l) must be 
performed in accordance with PCAOB auditing standards and performed by 
a public accounting firm that is registered with the PCAOB. The 
commenter encouraged the agency to consider the existing auditor 
oversight mechanisms in place when considering the enforcement of 
auditing standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers subject to 
the audit requirement. The commenter stated that in similar instances 
where laws or regulations require an audit to be performed in 
accordance with PCAOB auditing standards, but the audit does not fall 
within the scope of the PCAOB's oversight, such audits, insofar as they 
are performed by a United States public accounting firm, are subject to 
external oversight from the AICPA. The commenter further recognized 
that even if the OCC relies on these existing oversight mechanisms, 
there may be certain circumstances, such as in the event of a failure 
or major issue with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, when it is 
necessary for the OCC to ``request that a registered public accounting 
firm provide to the OCC certain additional information or documents 
relating to information provided by the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.'' The commenter

[[Page 67089]]

stated that such an approach would be consistent with frameworks 
adopted by other regulators, such as the FDIC, which acknowledge the 
importance of the Peer Review Program for ongoing oversight of audits, 
while still retaining the right to request access to auditors' working 
papers, policies, procedures, and other documentation as appropriate. 
Finally, the commenter stated that it would be important for the OCC to 
clarify that its ability to request access to documentation would not 
change the documentation retention requirements as established in the 
applicable auditing standards.
    One commenter stated that it would be helpful for the OCC to 
clarify the independence standards with which it expects public 
accounting firms to comply when performing audits for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers within the scope of Sec.  15.14(l). The commenter 
stated that clarification regarding whether the intent is to require 
all PCAOB and SEC independence requirements, including those that are 
only applicable to public companies, is needed. This comment had 
similarly suggested that the OCC clarify the standards for monthly 
examinations of reports by a registered public accounting firm under 
Sec.  15.11(f). A separate comment made a similar suggestion for 
clearer standards in the Sec.  15.11(f) context. Like how the OCC is 
not adopting more specific standards into Sec.  15.11(f), the OCC is 
not adopting the suggested change to Sec.  15.14(l) concerning the 
independence standard. The proposed regulatory text was sufficiently 
clear that auditors must comply with the independence standards 
established by the PCAOB. To avoid any confusion, the independence 
standards established through the PCAOB's rules are the applicable 
independence standards that auditors should adhere to when performing 
an audit pursuant to Sec.  15.14(l).\140\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \140\ See PCAOB Bylaws and Rules, Section 3--Auditing and 
Related Professional Standards, Part 5--Ethics and Independence 
(September 3, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    One commenter recommended that the OCC consider the competency, 
qualifications, and specialized expertise of CPAs in good standing in 
its interpretation of the GENIUS Act as it relates to monthly 
examinations and audits of nonpublic issuers. The commenter argued that 
restricting these services to PCAOB-registered firms could 
unintentionally limit CPA availability, reduce competition, and create 
bottlenecks--particularly for smaller or State qualified issuers--
without improving audit or examination quality. Additionally, the 
commenter stated that stablecoin-related engagements would not fall 
under the PCAOB inspection program, even if performed by a registered 
firm, and would instead be subject to the AICPA's robust peer review 
framework.
    One commenter stated that if a payment stablecoin issuer is a 
subsidiary of an entity that is subject to the reporting requirements 
under section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 
U.S.C. 78m, 78o(d)), the final rule could clarify whether the 
subsidiary's audited financial statements are still required, or if the 
parent's or holding company's consolidated audited financial statements 
are sufficient to comply with the rule's requirements. Consistent with 
the proposal, the OCC confirms that the audit requirement would not 
apply to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer whose parent company is 
subject to the reporting requirements under section 13(a) or 15(d) of 
the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to the extent that the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's operations would be reflected in its parent 
company's applicable reports.
    After carefully considering the comments, the OCC is adopting Sec.  
15.14(l) as proposed, with minor technical changes. First, the OCC is 
adding the word ``total consolidated'' in front of ``outstanding 
issuance value'' in light of changes to the definition of ``outstanding 
issuance value.'' These revisions do not change the substance of what 
was proposed in Sec.  15.14(l). Second, the OCC replaced ``an annual 
financial statement that must include'' in proposed Sec.  15.14(l) with 
``an annual financial statement and the statement must include'' for 
clarity. Third, the OCC is adding the phrase ``rules and'' before 
``auditing standards'' in Sec.  15.14(l)(1) for clarity. The PCAOB's 
independence guidance is established through rules and not auditing 
standards, so the OCC is clarifying that all ``applicable rules and 
auditing standards'' apply to audits performed pursuant to Sec.
