15.14(l). The OCC is also replacing references to the ``Securities and 
Exchange Act'' with ``Securities Exchange Act.''
    With respect to other comments, the OCC does not believe that 
additional changes to the regulation are necessary. Generally, the 
comments received related to proposed Sec.  15.14(l) expressed 
opposition to the statutory audit requirements in section 4(a)(10) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(10)) as opposed to the OCC's proposed 
implementation of the GENIUS Act's audit requirements. The comments 
were primarily focused on introducing clarifying language, implementing 
provisions that would relax the GENIUS Act's statutory requirements, 
and incorporating standards that were otherwise not provided for under 
the GENIUS Act. The OCC considered these recommendations and assessed 
whether there were compelling reasons to implement certain 
clarifications or modify the rule text to be more accommodating but 
ultimately concluded that the GENIUS Act clearly articulates the audit 
requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, and the final 
rule text should adhere closely to the GENIUS Act. As such, the final 
rule's audit provisions closely match those of the GENIUS Act and are 
sufficiently clear. Further, the auditing standards, rules, and 
interpretations established by the PCAOB provide accounting firms with 
sufficient guidance to conduct audits in compliance with the statutory 
requirements of the GENIUS Act. Fourth, the OCC is replacing ``the end 
of its fiscal year'' in proposed Sec.  15.14(l)(2)(ii) with ``the end 
of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's fiscal year'' for clarity. 
Fifth, the OCC is renumbering paragraph (l)(2)(iii) to (l)(3) and 
making corresponding renumbering changes to the rest of the paragraph.
e. Change in Control
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(m) would have applied the change-in-control 
framework in 12 CFR 5.50 to any person seeking to acquire control of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer as if the issuer were a national 
bank. Section 15.14(m) further provided that this requirement does not 
apply where the transaction is already subject to the notice or 
application provisions of 12 CFR part 5 or Sec.  15.30.
    The OCC received several comments on proposed Sec.  15.14(m). One 
commenter stated that the final rule should clarify that ``control'' 
for permitted payment stablecoin issuers must capture functional 
control, not only voting securities. The commenter explained that 
functional control can arise through contractual governance rights, 
administrative keys, privileged smart-contract controls, or other 
mechanisms that can materially affect issuance, reserve management, or 
redemption. The commenter also stated that the rule should state 
explicit consequences for noncompliance to improve enforceability and 
deter attempts to bypass review. One commenter, while a proponent of 
applying the 12 CFR 5.50 framework to change in control of permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers, advocated for any merger transaction 
involving a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to be considered a

[[Page 67090]]

change in control under Sec.  15.14(m) and to be subject to prior OCC 
approval. Another commenter requested that change-in-control 
requirements differentiate between permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
that are subsidiaries of banks and nonbank entities because the former 
group is already subject to comprehensive prudential supervision and, 
to promote parity and protect the safety and soundness of the financial 
system, any standalone obligations should solely apply to nonbank 
issuers.
    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to 
finalize Sec.  15.14(m) as proposed with a clarifying edit to the cited 
definitions in Sec.  15.14(m)(1). The framework in 12 CFR 5.50 has 
proven in practice to be operationally workable and to capture a wide 
range of transactions implicating control. Many transactions that 
involve the merger of permitted payment stablecoin issuers will have 
direct or indirect changes in ownership. Thus, such transactions would 
be subject to the provisions of Sec.  15.14(m). For other merger 
transactions that would not implicate Sec.  15.14(m), the OCC will 
continue to review and supervise the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers in the ordinary course and would take supervisory or other 
action if appropriate to address concerns related to a merger. 
Therefore, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are encouraged to 
discuss any planned merger activity with the OCC to ensure consistency 
with OCC requirements and supervisory expectations.
    With regard to noncompliance with the change-in-control 
regulations, section 6(b) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5905(b)) grants 
the OCC enforcement authority to pursue a variety of enforcement 
actions for violations of the GENIUS Act and its implementing 
regulations. Whether the OCC pursues an enforcement action and the type 
of enforcement action that the agency elects to pursue will be dictated 
by the facts and circumstances underlying any alleged violation of the 
GENIUS Act or the OCC's implementing regulations. Therefore, it is not 
necessary or appropriate to identify explicit consequences for 
noncompliance with the change-in-control regulations at this time.
f. Efficiency and Burden Reduction
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(n) provided that, in supervising and examining 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the OCC will use existing 
reports and other supervisory information to the fullest extent 
possible. The OCC stated that this subsection was intended to reduce 
unnecessary burden by allowing the OCC to leverage information already 
available through existing reporting or supervisory channels.
    Proposed Sec.  15.14(o) provided that the OCC will, to the fullest 
extent possible, avoid duplication of examination activities, reporting 
requirements, and requests for information. The OCC stated that this 
subsection reflects an express effort to minimize redundant supervisory 
demands while preserving the OCC's ability to obtain information needed 
for effective oversight.
    The OCC received a number of comments related to burden reduction 
and the avoidance of duplication. One commenter recommended that the 
agency explicitly recognize internal audit work product as a category 
of existing supervisory information that examiners may rely on where 
such work is relevant, current, and performed in accordance with 
recognized professional standards. The commenter claimed that this 
approach would reduce issuer compliance burden, improve supervisory 
efficiency, and create positive incentives for investment in high-
quality internal audit programs.
    Two commenters recommended that the OCC allow a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository 
institution to leverage its parent's enterprise-wide risk management 
infrastructure, including risk appetite statements and third-party risk 
management programs, where appropriate, to satisfy risk-management and 
supervisory requirements. One of the commenters further recommended 
that the OCC include guidance to this effect in its commentary to the 
final rule and the Comptroller's Handbook. The OCC confirms that a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer may leverage enterprise-wide 
infrastructure, provided that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
does so in compliance with the requirements of part 15.
    Another commenter encouraged the OCC to develop centralized and 
standardized reporting mechanisms--such as a secure reporting portal--
that are aligned with existing bank reporting systems and service 
provider capabilities. The commenter stated that new reporting 
requirements applicable to community banks should be limited, targeted, 
and designed to leverage data already maintained in the ordinary course 
of business. The commenter also claimed that stablecoin-related risks 
can be effectively evaluated by incorporating them into established 
examination modules. The commenter stated that stablecoin-related audit 
and reporting obligations for bank-affiliated issuers should be 
appropriately integrated into existing supervisory frameworks rather 
than imposed through separate or duplicative regimes. The OCC will 
continue to consider means of updating its reporting mechanisms, but no 
change in the text of the regulation is necessary at this time to 
address the comment.
    Another commenter stated that the reporting requirements across 
weekly, monthly, and quarterly intervals should build on one another 
rather than requiring duplicative reporting. Monthly reports should, to 
the extent possible, draw from weekly reports, and likewise quarterly 
reports should draw from monthly reports. The commenter claimed that 
such an approach can reduce operational burden while preserving the 
OCC's and the public's ability to assess risk over time. The commenter 
also stated that to best minimize the duplication of reports, the OCC's 
focus should be on mitigating risk while encouraging innovation. The 
commenter stated that requiring duplicative reports does not provide 
additional risk-mitigation benefits while diverting resources and 
creating unnecessary burden.
    Another commenter stated that the OCC can best minimize duplication 
by implementing a single annual audit package that satisfies 
overlapping requirements across Sec.  15.14(l), monthly reserve 
examination outputs, and related financial-condition reporting fields, 
rather than requiring multiple separate submissions of the same 
underlying data. The commenter stated that the goal should be to 
collect the necessary information once, in a standardized format, and 
reuse it across the prudential framework where possible. For issuers, 
or their parents, that are already subject to Exchange Act reporting or 
meet the Act's $50 billion public accounting threshold, the OCC should 
not require additional duplicative reporting beyond what is necessary 
to capture stablecoin-specific fields that existing filings do not 
address.
    Pursuant to its statutory obligations, the OCC will pursue 
supervisory policies that minimize duplication and maximize efficiency. 
The OCC notes, however, that the reports applicable to permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers serve distinct purposes. For example, the 
confidential weekly reporting is intended to provide detailed 
information that would be unnecessary to include in the quarterly or 
monthly reports. The monthly and quarterly reports are intended to 
provide information to the public and the OCC that may be stale or less 
valuable if received only on an annual basis.

[[Page 67091]]

    After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing 
Sec.  15.14(n) and Sec.  15.14(o) as proposed. As described above, the 
OCC is committed to pursuing supervisory policies that minimize 
duplication and maximize efficiency.
6. State Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers (Sec.  15.15)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Sec.  15.15
    The OCC proposed to issue Sec.  15.15 to implement the GENIUS Act's 
transition standards for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers 
with an outstanding issuance value of more than $10 billion. 
Specifically, proposed Sec.  15.15 would require an issuer to notify 
the OCC within five calendar days after the issuer triggers the 
transition threshold, request a waiver if the issuer seeks to remain 
supervised solely by the applicable State regulator, and, if 
applicable, provide the OCC with information necessary to evaluate an 
associated waiver request. Proposed Sec.  15.15 would have also 
established a timeframe for the OCC's review of an issuer's waiver 
request. Proposed Sec.  15.15(a) describes the scope of Sec.  15.15 and 
provides that the section addresses requirements related to a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity 
transitioning to the OCC's regulatory framework pursuant to section 4 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903).
    The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.15(a) as proposed with edits. The OCC 
is separating proposed Sec.  15.15(a) into Sec.  15.15(a)(1) and (2), 
with Sec.  15.15(a)(1) including the proposed language for Sec.  
15.15(a) and Sec.  15.15(a)(2) clarifying that, for purposes of Sec.  
15.15, the term State qualified payment stablecoin issuer refers only 
to those that are nonbank entities. Other edits were made in final 
Sec.  15.15 to conform to this clarification in final Sec.  
15.15(a)(2).
    Additionally, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.15(b) largely as 
proposed with certain technical and clarifying edits. Specifically, in 
Sec. Sec.  15.15(b)(1), (b)(1)(ii), (b)(2), (b)(2)(ii)(C), (b)(3), and 
(b)(4)(ii), the OCC is adding the phrase ``total consolidated'' before 
the defined term ``outstanding issuance value'' or replacing the phrase 
``an outstanding issuance value'' with ``a total consolidated 
outstanding issuance value.'' The OCC is also deleting surplus language 
in Sec.  15.15(b)(1) and adding clarifying language to Sec.  
15.15(b)(1)(ii) and (b)(4)(i). Additionally, in Sec.  15.15(b)(3)(iv), 
the OCC is capitalizing the word ``State.'' The OCC is adopting Sec.  
15.15(c) as proposed. In Sec.  15.15(d), the OCC is separating proposed 
Sec.  15.15(d)(1) into Sec.  15.15(d)(1)(i) and (ii). Within the 
language proposed as the last sentence in Sec.  15.15(d)(1), the OCC is 
replacing ``State payment stablecoin issuer'' with ``State payment 
stablecoin regulator'' as well as adding the words ``total 
consolidated'' prior to ``outstanding issuance value'' and adding the 
word ``threshold'' to the end of the final sentence. Similarly, in 
Sec.  15.15(d)(2)(iv), the OCC is replacing the term ``State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer'' with the term ``State payment stablecoin 
regulator.'' Otherwise, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.15(d) as proposed. 
The OCC is also adding new Sec.  15.15(e)(1) to provide that a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity that has 
transitioned to the OCC's Federal regulatory framework pursuant to 
Sec.  15.15 is not generally required to comply with part 15 and will 
cease to be supervised by the OCC upon the OCC's determination that the 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer no longer exceeds $10 billion 
in total consolidated outstanding issuance value. Moreover, the OCC is 
adding new Sec.  15.15(e)(2) to provide that the OCC may make the 
determination in Sec.  15.15(e)(1) upon the request of the payment 
stablecoin issuer supplemented by any information reasonably required 
by the OCC or without such a request.
b. Transition to Federal Oversight
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Section 4(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(d)) addresses the 
transition of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that are not 
State-chartered depository institutions to Federal oversight and 
provides the OCC with authority to supervise such issuers jointly with 
the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator.\141\ Proposed Sec.  
15.15(b)(1) would have implemented section 4(d)(2) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(2)) and would have required a State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity that crosses the $10 
billion outstanding issuance threshold to transition to the Federal 
regulatory framework under proposed part 15 and to comply with the 
provisions of part 15 applicable to Federal qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers within 360 days or cease issuing, on a net basis, 
new payment stablecoins until the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer's outstanding issuance value is under the $10 billion threshold.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \141\ Section 4(d)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(2)) 
refers to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers other than 
State-chartered depository institutions (addressed in section 
4(d)(1) of the Act). For simplicity, proposed Sec.  15.15 referred 
to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that are nonbank 
entities. Nonbank entity is defined by the Act to mean a person that 
is not a depository institution or a subsidiary of a depository 
institution. 12 U.S.C. 5901(20).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Section 4(h) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)) authorizes the 
OCC to issue regulations necessary to administer and carry out the 
GENIUS Act's requirements and prevent evasion thereof. To facilitate an 
orderly transition to Federal oversight, ensure compliance with the 
GENIUS Act's transition requirements, and manage agency resources, 
proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(2)(i) would have required a nonbank State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer of a payment stablecoin with an 
outstanding issuance value of more than $10 billion to provide written 
notification to the OCC within five calendar days after reaching such 
threshold.\142\ Proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(2)(ii) provided that the 
written notification would need to include the following information: 
the State or States that currently regulate the State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer; the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's 
outstanding issuance value as of the date of the notice; the date that 
the issuer reached the $10 billion outstanding issuance value 
threshold; and indication of whether and when the issuer has ceased 
issuing, on a net basis, new payment stablecoins and whether the issuer 
intends to seek a waiver from transitioning to the Federal regulatory 
framework.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \142\ The proposal would have required a nonbank State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer to provide written notification to the 
OCC, regardless of whether it intends to issue new payment 
stablecoins.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(4) provided clarity as to when a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer transitions to the Federal 
regulatory framework. Proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(4)(i) would have required 
a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to provide notification to 
the OCC that it is in compliance with the Federal regulatory framework 
implemented under proposed part 15. If the State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer were not in compliance with the Federal regulatory 
framework in proposed part 15, the written notice would have needed to 
identify the provisions that the issuer does not comply with, provide 
the issuer's plan for remediating its noncompliance, and explain why 
the issuer did not comply with the Federal regulatory framework within 
the 360-day transition period. Under proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(4)(ii), a 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that

[[Page 67092]]

does not cease issuing new payment stablecoins would have needed to 
transition to the Federal regulatory framework on the earlier of 360 
days after reaching the $10 billion outstanding issuance value 
threshold or the date on which the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer provides written notification under paragraph (b)(4)(i).
    To facilitate an orderly transition process, proposed Sec.  
15.15(b)(3)(i) would have required a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer that is a nonbank entity to submit an analysis of the issuer's 
current capital position and anticipated capital needs, sufficient to 
ensure ongoing operations, based on its business model and risk profile 
to the OCC within 270 days of reaching the $10 billion outstanding 
issuance value threshold. Proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(3)(ii) provided that 
the OCC would review the submitted analysis and establish a minimum 
capital requirement pursuant to proposed Sec.  15.41(a)(1). Proposed 
Sec.  15.15(b)(3)(iii) provided that, for purposes of complying with 
the transition requirements under proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(1)(i), the 
issuer would need to hold minimum capital as specified under Sec.  
15.41(a)(1)(ii) prior to the issuer's transition date. Proposed Sec.  
15.15(b)(3)(iv) provided that a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer would not have needed to submit an analysis of its capital if it 
received a waiver under proposed Sec.  15.15(d) or was not required to 
transition to the OCC's Federal regulatory framework under Sec.  
15.15(b)(1)(ii).
    Under Sec.  15.15(c), the OCC proposed to require that a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that transitions to the regulatory 
framework under proposed part 15 must undergo an initial examination at 
the OCC's request or no later than six months after the date on which 
the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer provides written 
notification under proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(4)(i).
ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    A few commenters suggested extending the 360-day transition 
timeline or providing case-by-case extensions (including for permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers that request but do not receive a waiver). 
The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.15(b)(1) as proposed with technical 
changes. The final rule includes the words ``total consolidated'' in 
front of ``outstanding issuance value.'' These revisions do not result 
in a substantive change but are necessary in light of the changes to 
the definition of outstanding issuance value. The OCC is also deleting 
surplus language from paragraph (b)(1) and clarifying in paragraph 
(b)(1)(ii) that the paragraph applies to a State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer.
    The 360-day transition deadline is a statutory requirement, and the 
OCC is not authorized to extend it. Consistent with the proposed rule, 
the final rule clarifies that the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer would cease issuing new payment stablecoins on a net basis. This 
is to permit a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to freeze, 
burn, mint, and issue new payment stablecoins to the extent necessary 
to transfer stablecoins from one blockchain to another without 
increasing the total outstanding issuance of the State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer.
    Related to the 360-day transition requirement, question 138 of the 
proposed rule asked whether the $10 billion threshold should be based 
on a point in time or a rolling average and whether the $10 billion 
threshold should take into account the outstanding issuance value of 
any payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates of the 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
    The OCC received several comments concerning how to calculate 
outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-day transition 
requirement. A few commenters generally suggested that the OCC should 
calculate outstanding issuance value as a point-in-time threshold. On 
the other hand, a few commenters generally suggested that the OCC 
should calculate outstanding issuance value as a rolling average.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC confirms that the 
transition threshold is determined through a point-in-time calculation 
and will not be based on a rolling average. Adopting a point-in-time 
calculation will safeguard against outstanding issuance value 
manipulation by a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that seeks 
to delay or avoid complying with the 360-day transition requirement. A 
rolling average calculated over a meaningfully long period of time 
could, in effect, extend the date of transition to the Federal 
regulatory framework beyond what Congress intended. Moreover, the OCC 
generally expects that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's 
outstanding issuance value is unlikely to meaningfully fluctuate back 
and forth across the $10 billion threshold. Thus, there would be 
relatively little utility gained from using a rolling average to 
calculate the threshold.
    Additionally, the OCC received a few comments concerning whether to 
include payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates in 
the calculation of outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-
day transition requirement. A few commenters generally suggested that 
outstanding issuance value should not automatically include non-
consolidated affiliates. Another commenter generally suggested that the 
OCC should include non-consolidated affiliates.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is clarifying that a 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer would not be required to 
include payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates in 
its calculation of outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-
day transition requirements. The OCC notes, however, that in certain 
situations, the OCC may consider a non-consolidated affiliate's 
issuance. For example, if a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
treats affiliate-issued payment stablecoins as fungible with its own or 
appears to use affiliates solely to stay under the $10 billion 
threshold for transition to the Federal framework, such behavior could 
indicate an attempt to evade the GENIUS Act or could, depending on the 
facts and circumstances, indicate unusual and exigent circumstances 
within the meaning of section 7 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906).
    The OCC received several comments concerning the five-day 
notification requirement in proposed Sec.  15.15(b)(2). One commenter 
suggested that five calendar days would be operationally feasible for 
issuers large enough to trigger the $10 billion outstanding issuance 
value threshold. The commenter further explained that five calendar 
days would provide the OCC with timely visibility into the State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
    A few commenters suggested that the OCC should extend the threshold 
notification deadline, for example, to 10 or 15 business days. One 
commenter suggested a five-day deadline would not provide enough time 
for the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to assess compliance 
implications, coordinate with State regulators, and complete 
substantive notification requirements. Another commenter generally 
suggested the OCC should extend the notification deadline to better 
reflect the operational and governance realities of State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuers.
    The OCC is finalizing the five-day threshold notification deadline 
and information submission requirements as proposed with one non-
substantive change. For the reasons discussed above, the final rule 
includes the words

[[Page 67093]]

``total consolidated'' in front of ``outstanding issuance value.'' 
Consistent with section 4(h) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)), a 
five-day notification requirement would facilitate an orderly 
transition to Federal oversight, compliance with the GENIUS Act's 
transition requirements, and agency resource management. Further, the 
transition notification requirement would apply only after a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer exceeds $10 billion in outstanding 
issuance value.\143\ State qualified payment stablecoin issuers of this 
size should have the capabilities to appropriately monitor issuance 
volume as a matter of basic risk management. Moreover, only limited 
information is required to be included in the initial notification.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \143\ As clarified in the proposed rule, a nonbank State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer is required to provide written 
notification to the OCC, regardless of whether it intends to issue 
new payment stablecoins.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC did not receive comments specific to the transition date 
and compliance notification requirements. The OCC is finalizing Sec.  
15.15(b)(4) as proposed with one non-substantive change. For the 
reasons discussed above, the final rule includes the words ``total 
consolidated'' in front of ``issuance value.'' As discussed in the 
proposed rule, regardless of whether the OCC receives notice under 
Sec.  15.15(b)(4), the OCC reserves the right to pursue appropriate 
action to ensure compliance with the GENIUS Act with respect to a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that transitions to the Federal 
regulatory framework administered by the OCC.
    The OCC received several comments related to the OCC adopting a 
mechanism for a previously transitioned State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer to transition back to sole State supervision. A few 
commenters suggested the OCC should not permit State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers to transition back to sole State supervision and 
expressed concerns such a mechanism could lead to regulatory arbitrage 
concerns. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should permit State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers to transition back to sole State 
supervision. One of these commenters suggested that the OCC does not 
have authority to prevent a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
with less than $10 billion in outstanding issuance value from 
transitioning back to sole State supervision.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is adding final Sec.  
15.15(e)(1) to specify that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
that is a nonbank entity that has transitioned to the OCC's Federal 
regulatory framework pursuant to Sec.  15.15 is not generally required 
to comply with part 15 and will cease to be supervised by the OCC upon 
the OCC's determination that the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer no longer exceeds $10 billion in total consolidated outstanding 
issuance value. Final Sec.  15.15(e)(2) clarifies that the OCC may make 
this determination based on an issuer's request or issue a 
determination without such a request. Sections 6(a) and (b) of the 
GENIUS Act provide the OCC with supervision and enforcement authority, 
respectively, over ``[e]ach permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is 
not a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer with a payment 
stablecoin with a consolidated total outstanding issuance of less than 
$10 [billion]. . . .'' The OCC has determined that Sec.  15.15(e) is 
consistent with the scope of the OCC's supervisory and enforcement 
authority over State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. 
Additionally, the OCC may review an issuer's request under section 
15.15(e) to prevent evasion of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903) and its implementing regulations, consistent with section 4(h) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(h)). The OCC would retain its backup 
enforcement authority over State qualified payment stablecoin issuers 
that transition back to being supervised solely by a State under 
section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)).
    The OCC received a few comments on the proposed capital analysis 
requirement. One commenter suggested that the 270-day timeline is 
reasonable. Another commenter suggested that the capital analysis 
should be tailored to the size and operations of the applicant. After 
consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.15(b)(3) 
as proposed with one non-substantive change. For the reasons discussed 
above, the final rule includes the words ``total consolidated'' in 
front of ``issuance value.'' As discussed in Sec.  15.41(a)(1), section 
4(a)(4)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(i)) requires 
the OCC to tailor capital requirements to the business model and risk 
profile of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and to not exceed 
requirements sufficient to ensure the ongoing operations of permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers. Consistent with this requirement, the OCC 
expects a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to provide a 
capital analysis with information sufficient for the OCC to evaluate 
the issuer's current capital position and anticipated capital needs 
based on its business model and risk profile. The OCC expects all 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers, including State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers, to maintain capital commensurate with the level and 
nature of all risks to which the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is 
exposed.
    As discussed above, a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
that seeks to transition to the Federal regulatory framework before the 
end of the 360-day period must certify its compliance with part 15, 
including applicable capital requirements. State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers that seek to transition early are therefore 
encouraged to submit their capital analysis to the OCC early, to ensure 
adequate time to address any deficiencies and raise additional capital 
if necessary.
    A few commenters addressed the timing of the initial examination 
requirement for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. One 
commenter suggested that the initial examination should take place 
prior to the issuer's transition date. Another commenter suggested that 
while the six-month time frame is reasonable, the OCC should consider 
more closely aligning the examination date with the transition waiver 
requirements. Another commenter expressed concerns that transitioned 
State issuers should be required to adhere to similar regulatory 
standards as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the 
examination requirement as proposed. A State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer that is required to transition to the Federal 
regulatory framework must do so within 360 days of exceeding the $10 
billion outstanding issuance value threshold. Under final Sec.  
15.15(d), a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer may request a 
waiver from the transition requirements within 240 days of exceeding 
the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold. The OCC has 
determined that requiring a transitioned State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer to undergo an initial examination no later than six 
months after its transition date would facilitate the issuer's pre-
transition requirements while retaining flexibility for the OCC to 
require an earlier examination on a case-by-case basis. Because a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that transitions to the Federal 
framework will already be in operation, the OCC intends to conduct this 
examination well before the six-month outer limit proposed to ensure 
that the issuer can effectively operate under the Federal framework.

[[Page 67094]]

Additionally, while the OCC does not generally plan to conduct a full-
scope examination prior to the issuer's transition date, the OCC 
retains discretion to request additional information about the 
operations and condition of the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer prior to the transition date.
c. Waiver From Federal Supervision
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Notwithstanding the transition requirements discussed above, under 
section 4(d)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)), the OCC may 
permit a nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that reaches 
the $10 billion threshold to remain solely supervised by a State 
payment stablecoin regulator. In determining whether to issue a waiver 
from Federal supervision, proposed Sec.  15.15(d)(2) would have 
implemented the requirement in the statute that provides that the OCC 
must consider four exclusive criteria: the capital maintained by the 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; the past operations and 
examination history of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; 
the experience of the State payment stablecoin regulator in supervising 
payment stablecoin and digital asset activities; and the supervisory 
framework, including regulations and guidance, of the State payment 
stablecoin regulator with respect to payment stablecoins and digital 
assets.
    Proposed Sec.  15.15(d)(1) would have required a State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer seeking a waiver to submit a written waiver 
request to the OCC within 240 days of reaching the $10 billion 
outstanding issuance value threshold.\144\ The request would have 
needed to include information necessary for the OCC to evaluate the 
waiver criteria enumerated in proposed Sec.  15.15(d)(2) and (3), 
discussed below. The preamble to the proposed rule specified that such 
information may have included the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer's reports of condition and examination, financial statements, 
investor statements, reports that detail significant examination 
findings, business activities, existence of past or current enforcement 
orders, and disclosure of any violations of law, as well as other 
information as requested by the OCC. Additionally, the waiver request 
would have described whether the State payment stablecoin regulator has 
experience regulating entities that have a similar risk profile. The 
waiver request would have also included information regarding the 
frequency and depth of the State payment stablecoin regulator's 
examinations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \144\ The OCC could also issue a waiver of its own accord, 
provided that it has information sufficient to evaluate the 
statutory criteria for issuing waivers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.15(d)(3) incorporated the waiver presumption 
standards for a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that submits 
a waiver request. Consistent with section 4(d)(3)(C) of the Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)(C)), the OCC would have presumptively approved a 
waiver request if the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator had 
(1) established a prudential regulatory regime for the supervision of 
digital assets or payment stablecoins as of April 19, 2025, that had 
been certified pursuant to section 4(c) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(c)) 
and (2) approved one or more issuers to issue payment stablecoins under 
the supervision of such State payment stablecoin regulator. The waiver 
presumption would have been lost if the OCC found, by clear and 
convincing evidence, that the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
did not substantially meet the waiver criteria in proposed Sec.  
15.15(d)(2) or that the issuer posed significant safety and soundness 
risks to the financial system of the United States. If an issuer 
believed it qualified for the waiver presumption, it would have needed 
to indicate so in the waiver request and provide information sufficient 
for the OCC to evaluate the waiver presumption standards.
ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    The OCC received several comments concerning the criteria the OCC 
should consider when evaluating a waiver request in proposed Sec.  
15.15(d). A few commenters suggested that the OCC should require waiver 
applicants to submit specific information, such as reports of 
examination, or demonstrate that the issuer would not present financial 
stability and safety and soundness risks. A few commenters suggested 
that the OCC should establish benchmarks, explicit standards, or other 
guidelines for when an issuer would satisfy the waiver approval 
criteria. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should not adopt 
bright-line rules or require issuers to provide additional information 
in connection with a waiver request. One commenter suggested that the 
OCC should subject waiver requests from large issuers to heightened 
scrutiny and require issuers to demonstrate that waiver approval would 
not introduce financial stability risks, have an anti-competitive 
effect, or create a heightened risk of illicit finance. Finally, one 
commenter noted that Sec.  15.15(d) included two references to State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers that should have referred to State 
payment stablecoin regulators.
    The OCC is finalizing the waiver approval criteria as proposed with 
a technical fix to change a reference to ``State qualified payment 
stablecoin regulator'' in Sec.  15.15(d)(2)(iv) to ``State payment 
stablecoin regulator.'' The GENIUS Act requires the OCC to consider 
four exclusive criteria when reviewing a waiver request. The OCC is not 
authorized to consider additional criteria and, accordingly, is 
finalizing the four criteria as proposed. Adopting bright-line 
requirements or presumptive standards would not facilitate the fact-
specific nature of waiver requests, as State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers may have varying business models, risk tolerances, 
scale of operations, and regulatory backgrounds. The OCC will review 
the issuer's waiver request and any associated information in relation 
to the waiver criteria.
    Under Sec.  15.15(d)(1) of the final rule, a waiver applicant must 
submit to the OCC a written waiver request containing information 
necessary to evaluate such request under paragraphs (d)(2) and (3) of 
that section. Such information may include the State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer's reports of condition and examination, financial 
statements, investor statements, reports that detail significant 
examination findings, business activities, existence of past or current 
enforcement orders, and disclosure of any violations of law, as well as 
other information as requested by the OCC. Additionally, the waiver 
request may describe whether the State payment stablecoin regulator has 
experience regulating entities that have a similar risk profile. The 
waiver request may also include information regarding the frequency and 
depth of the State payment stablecoin regulator's examinations. The OCC 
is adopting Sec.  15.15(d)(1) with a technical fix to change a 
reference to a ``State payment stablecoin issuer'' to ``State payment 
stablecoin regulator.'' In addition, for the reasons discussed above, 
the final rule includes the words ``total consolidated'' in front of 
``issuance value.'' The OCC is also making a technical change to add 
the word ``threshold'' at the end of paragraph (d)(1).
    Finally, a few commenters expressed concerns that the proposal did 
not specify standards for determining whether a State regulatory 
framework is ``substantially similar'' to the Federal regulatory 
framework for Federal

[[Page 67095]]

qualified payment stablecoin issuers. One of these commenters expressed 
concerns that the OCC's proposed rule did not provide standards 
governing the application and approval of State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers by State regulators. While the OCC will evaluate the 
experience and supervisory framework of a State payment stablecoin 
regulator when reviewing a waiver request, the Treasury Department is 
tasked with establishing broad-based principles for determining whether 
a State-level regulatory regime is substantially similar to the Federal 
regulatory framework under Sec.  4(c) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(c)).\145\ Similarly, the OCC does not have authority to establish 
standards governing the application and approval of State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuers by State regulators. Accordingly, the final 
rule does not adopt the commenters' proposed changes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \145\ See GENIUS Act Broad-Based Principles for Determining 
Whether a State-Level Regulatory Regime Is Substantially Similar to 
the Federal Regulatory Framework, 91 FR 16844 (April 3, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The proposed rule asked whether waivers approved under proposed 
Sec.  15.15(d) should be subject to renewal over some time period 
(e.g., one or five years) to ensure that the State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer continues to meet the waiver criteria. The proposed 
rule also asked whether the OCC should reserve the right to discontinue 
a waiver and, if so, whether 100 days would be a reasonable period to 
provide notice to the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
    The OCC received several comments that generally support the OCC 
retaining discretion to discontinue an approved waiver, impose 
conditions related to an approved waiver, or require periodic 
recertification of waiver approvals. One of these commenters suggested 
that a 100-day notice period would be appropriate. The OCC received one 
comment that suggests the OCC does not have authority to re-examine the 
status of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that receives a 
waiver. Another commenter suggested the OCC should limit waiver 
discontinuance to circumstances where the relevant State payment 
stablecoin regulator has been decertified under Sec.  4(c) of the 
GENIUS Act.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the rule 
as proposed with clarifying edits. The OCC is clarifying that a waiver 
request approved under Sec.  15.15 may include conditions related to 
the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's continued compliance 
with the waiver approval criteria under Sec.  15.15(d)(2) and (3). 
Subjecting waivers to conditional approval will facilitate the OCC's 
statutory mandate to ensure it provides transition waivers for State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers that satisfy the waiver criteria. 
Conditional waiver approvals will also provide the OCC with an explicit 
mechanism for addressing potential evasion of the GENIUS Act's 
requirements, such as where a waiver determination is made based on 
materially inaccurate or misleading information.
    The OCC received a few comments concerning the timing requirement 
for submitting a waiver request under proposed Sec.  15.15(d)(1). One 
commenter suggested that the OCC should extend the 240-day waiver 
request deadline to the maximum extent provided by law. Another 
commenter suggested the OCC should permit a State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer to submit a waiver request prior to exceeding the $10 
billion outstanding issuance value threshold.
    To facilitate an orderly waiver process, the OCC is finalizing the 
240-day waiver request deadline as proposed in final Sec.  
15.15(d)(1)(ii) with some additional clarifications. The GENIUS Act 
requires a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to transition to 
the Federal regulatory framework within 360 days after exceeding the 
$10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold unless it ceases 
issuing payment stablecoins immediately or receives a waiver from the 
OCC. Requiring State qualified payment stablecoin issuers to request a 
waiver within 240 days after exceeding the $10 billion outstanding 
issuance value threshold will provide 120 days for the OCC to review 
and respond to the waiver request.\146\ Nothing would prohibit a State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer that exceeds the $10 billion 
threshold from seeking a waiver earlier, and State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers are encouraged to submit waiver requests early to 
ensure adequate time and address any deficiencies.\147\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \146\ This would provide a similar timeframe to the OCC for 
evaluating waiver requests as the general 120-day timeline for 
evaluation of applications for national banks and Federal savings 
associations. See OCC, Comptroller's Licensing Manual, ``Charters'' 
36 (2021).
    \147\ The OCC could also issue a waiver of its own accord, 
provided that it has information sufficient to evaluate the 
statutory criteria for issuing waivers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC is also clarifying that a State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer may submit a waiver request prior to exceeding the 
$10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold. The OCC will 
generally accept waiver requests where the State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer makes a good faith determination to the OCC that it 
is likely to exceed the $10 billion outstanding issuance value 
threshold in the next 30 days. However, the OCC reserves the right to 
request that a waiver applicant revise, update, or provide further 
information related to any waiver request.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC should clarify that a waiver 
request that meets presumption criteria will be considered approved as 
of the filing of such request, unless and until the OCC finds grounds 
to affirmatively deny the request based on the criteria contained in 
section 4(d)(3)(C)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)(C)(ii)). 
The OCC is finalizing the waiver presumption standard as proposed. 
Under the final rule, a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that 
submits a waiver request must receive OCC approval, even if the State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer believes it qualifies for the 
presumption criteria. Requiring a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer to receive affirmative waiver approval from the OCC will promote 
consistent application of the waiver presumption standards and avoid 
potential confusion related to an issuer's transition obligations.
7. Unusual and Exigent Circumstances (Sec.  15.16)
a. Description of the Proposed Rule
    The OCC proposed to issue Sec.  15.16 to clarify the scope of the 
agency's enforcement authority over nonbank State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers during unusual and exigent circumstances, including 
the review of OCC enforcement actions imposed pursuant to this 
authority.\148\ Proposed Sec.  15.16(a) would have addressed the scope 
of Sec.  15.16 and the OCC's authority to impose restrictions on a 
State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity 
during unusual and exigent circumstances, pursuant to section 7 of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \148\ Proposed Sec.  15.16 would address ``unusual and exigent 
circumstances'' only for purposes of section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)); it would not interpret the meaning of 
that term under any other provision of law.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Section 7(e)(2)(B) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(B)) 
requires the OCC to issue rules to set forth the unusual and exigent 
circumstances in which the OCC would exercise its enforcement authority 
against nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. Section 
7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act provides that, during ``unusual and

[[Page 67096]]

exigent circumstances,'' the OCC must take an enforcement action 
against a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank 
entity for violations of the GENIUS Act, provided that the agency makes 
two determinations.\149\ First, under the Act, the OCC must determine 
that ``unusual and exigent circumstances'' exist. Second, under the 
Act, the OCC must determine that there is reasonable cause to believe 
that the continuation of any activity by an issuer constitutes a 
serious risk to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of the 
issuer. Under the Act, if the OCC determines that both conditions are 
met, the OCC must impose such restrictions as the OCC determines to be 
necessary to address the serious risks to the issuer during the unusual 
and exigent circumstances. For example, under the Act, the OCC can 
limit a nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's affiliate 
transactions. The OCC may also limit nonbank State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuer activities that might create a serious risk that the 
liabilities of the issuer's holding company and its affiliates will be 
imposed on the issuer. The restrictions must be issued in the form of a 
directive, with the effect of a cease-and-desist order that has become 
final, to the nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer and any 
of its affiliates.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \149\ The GENIUS Act does not impose these limitations on the 
enforcement authority of State payment stablecoin regulators. See 12 
U.S.C. 5906(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.16(b) would have incorporated the GENIUS Act's 
unusual and exigent circumstances requirement. Under proposed Sec.  
15.16(b), if the OCC determined that unusual and exigent circumstances 
existed, based on the information available to the OCC, and that there 
was reasonable cause to believe that the continuation of any activity, 
including failure to act,\150\ by a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer that is a nonbank entity would have constituted a serious risk 
to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of the nonbank entity, 
the OCC would have imposed such restrictions as the OCC determined to 
be necessary to address such risk in the form of a directive. The Act 
provides three examples of the limitations that the OCC may impose, 
which were incorporated into proposed Sec.  15.16(b). Such restrictions 
may include limitations on: (1) redemptions of payment stablecoins; (2) 
transactions between the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, a 
holding company, and the subsidiaries or affiliates of either the State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer or the holding company; and (3) any 
activities of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that might 
create a serious risk that the liabilities of a holding company and the 
affiliates of the holding company may be imposed on the State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \150\ Proposed Sec.  15.16(b) clarified that failure to act also 
constitutes the continuation of an activity, as contemplated by 
section 7(e)(2)(C) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(C)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Proposed Sec.  15.16(c) set forth the criteria the OCC would have 
considered when determining whether unusual and exigent circumstances 
exist. Specifically, under the proposed rule, the OCC would have 
considered: (1) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer 
is, or is expected to imminently be, engaging in an activity (including 
any act, practice, or omission) that poses an immediate risk to the 
financial safety, soundness, or stability of the issuer or the 
financial system of the United States; (2) the actions of the relevant 
State payment stablecoin regulator to promptly address the risk to the 
issuer or the financial system of the United States; (3) risks 
presented to payment stablecoin holders; and (4) any other factors the 
OCC deems appropriate in light of the particular circumstances, 
consistent with the purposes of the GENIUS Act.
    The OCC's proposed criteria were intended to capture circumstances 
that involve an immediate financial risk that cannot be sufficiently 
addressed through normal supervisory channels. Accordingly, the OCC's 
proposed criteria focused on the immediacy of the financial risks, 
whether to the issuer, the stablecoin holders, or the financial system, 
and the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator to 
respond to those risks. The OCC preliminarily determined that adopting 
flexible criteria focused on these considerations, as opposed to a 
limited set of specific circumstances, would establish an appropriate 
balance between providing stakeholders with clarity on when the OCC 
would act pursuant to this authority while implementing the GENIUS 
Act's clear intention to permit the OCC to respond to evolving and 
unforeseeable circumstances. The OCC asked whether to include 
additional factors including (1) whether a State payment stablecoin 
regulator or a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has made a 
request for the OCC to exercise its unusual and exigent circumstances 
authority; (2) significant price fluctuations in the secondary market 
for the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's payment stablecoin; 
(3) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has been, or 
will imminently be, unable to timely redeem its payment stablecoin; (4) 
whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has incurred 
significant unanticipated losses; and (5) whether the State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer has deployed nonstandard liquidity management 
tools.
    Finally, proposed Sec.  15.16(d) would have clarified that the 
administrative review procedures described in section 7(e)(2)(D) of the 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(D)) are applicable to a State qualified 
payment stablecoin issuer or any institution-affiliated party subject 
to an unusual and exigent circumstances directive.
b. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    The OCC did not receive comments specific to implementing the 
GENIUS Act's statutory criteria in proposed Sec.  15.16(b). 
Accordingly, the OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.16(b), with one minor 
clarification and a technical correction. The final rule clarifies that 
the list of limitations that the OCC may impose in Sec.  15.16(b)(1) 
through (3) is not exhaustive. This is consistent with the language in 
the proposed rule. The final rule, however, adds the phrase, ``but not 
limited to'' for the avoidance of doubt.
    Several commenters suggested the OCC should provide examples or 
additional guidance concerning when the OCC would invoke its unusual 
and exigent circumstances authority in proposed Sec.  15.16(c). One of 
these commenters suggested that the OCC should consider a broad and 
flexible set of criteria for assessing unusual and exigent 
circumstances, including secondary market price fluctuations. Two of 
these commenters suggested that secondary market price fluctuations 
should carry little to no weight independently, as market prices can 
reflect localized trading conditions, fragmented liquidity, or external 
sentiment. One of these commenters suggested that the OCC should 
consider whether a state regulator has requested Federal assistance.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the 
unusual and exigent circumstances factors with certain additions and 
clarifications. The final rule includes certain additional factors for 
which the OCC requested comment. Under the final rule, the OCC will 
consider: (1) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer is, 
or is expected to imminently be, engaging in an activity (including any 
act, practice, or omission) that poses an immediate risk to the 
financial safety,

[[Page 67097]]

soundness, or stability of the issuer or the financial system of the 
United States; (2) the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin 
regulator to promptly address the risk to the issuer or the financial 
system of the United States; (3) risks presented to payment stablecoin 
holders; (4) any request from the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer or State payment stablecoin regulator for the OCC to exercise 
its authority under section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5906(e)(2)); (5) significant fluctuations in the secondary market price 
of payment stablecoins issued by the State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer; (6) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has 
been, or will imminently be, unable to timely redeem payment 
stablecoins issued by the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; 
(7) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has incurred 
significant unanticipated losses; and (8) any other factor the OCC 
deems appropriate in light of the particular circumstances and 
consistent with the purposes of the GENIUS Act. The OCC has added these 
additional factors to provide additional clarity on the indicia that 
the OCC believes could warrant exercising the OCC's authority under 
section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)).
    The OCC's finalized unusual and exigent circumstances factors are 
intended to capture circumstances that involve or could indicate an 
immediate financial risk that cannot be sufficiently addressed through 
normal supervisory channels. Accordingly, the final factors focus on 
the immediacy of the financial risks and factors likely to correlate 
with such risks, whether to the issuer, the stablecoin holders, or the 
financial system, and the actions of the relevant State payment 
stablecoin regulator to respond to those risks. The OCC determined that 
adopting flexible criteria focused on these considerations, as opposed 
to a limited set of specific circumstances, would establish an 
appropriate balance between providing stakeholders with clarity on when 
the OCC would act pursuant to this authority while implementing the 
GENIUS Act's clear intention to permit the OCC to respond to evolving 
and unforeseeable circumstances.
    The proposed rule also asked whether the OCC should publicly 
disclose when it determines that unusual and exigent circumstances 
exist. Several commenters suggested that the OCC should not 
automatically disclose directives made pursuant to the OCC's unusual 
and exigent circumstances authority. Most of these commenters suggested 
that the OCC should avoid disclosure of confidential materials but 
retain discretion to make public disclosures as necessary to prevent 
future harm to the issuer or consumers. After consideration of the 
comments, the OCC is not adopting an automatic disclosure process for 
directives made pursuant to the OCC's unusual and exigent circumstances 
authority. Disclosures may be appropriate in certain circumstances, but 
an automatic process could pose significant risks to safety and 
soundness and financial stability. For example, a process that 
compelled immediate disclosures might cause or exacerbate a run while 
facts were still being developed and confirmed. The OCC may impose such 
restrictions as the OCC determines to be necessary to address serious 
risks to the issuer during the unusual and exigent circumstances.
    Additionally, a few commenters provided suggestions related to 
coordinating with State regulators. A few commenters suggested the OCC 
should explicitly codify the statutory 48-hour notice requirement. One 
commenter suggested the OCC should consult with the State regulator 
prior to invoking its unusual and exigent circumstances authority. 
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the rule as 
proposed. The GENIUS Act requires the OCC to comply with the 48-hour 
notice requirement and does not impose any requirements on State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers. Although the OCC may consult with 
a State regulator, adopting a mandatory consultation requirement in 
addition to the 48-hour notice requirement could hinder the OCC's 
ability to quickly respond when there is a serious risk to the 
financial safety, soundness, or stability of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer.
    The OCC did not receive comments specific to proposed Sec.  
15.16(d) and is finalizing the section as proposed.

C. Subpart C--Custody

1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart C
    The OCC is generally adopting subpart C as proposed with some 
modifications to enhance clarity described in more detail below.
    The OCC is modifying the definition of ``covered assets'' in Sec.  
15.20 to make two clarifications. First, the covered assets definition 
in final Sec.  15.20 is modified to clarify that the term ``covered 
assets'' only applies with respect to payment stablecoins that are 
offered, sold, or otherwise made available to persons in the United 
States. Second, the definition is modified to clarify that it includes 
only payment stablecoins used as collateral, where a covered custodian 
has actual knowledge that such payment stablecoins are being used as 
collateral. The OCC is also making non-substantive edits to the 
definition of sub-custodian.
    In addition to a technical correction, the OCC is modifying Sec.  
15.21(a) to clarify that a covered custodian must separately record and 
account for the covered assets of a covered customer. The OCC is 
modifying Sec.  15.21(b)(1) to clarify that taking appropriate steps to 
protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of 
creditors includes adopting, implementing, and maintaining written 
custody agreements. The OCC is making non-substantive edits to Sec.  
15.21(b)(2)(i). The OCC is modifying Sec.  15.21(b)(2)(ii) to clarify 
that it applies to a private key used to issue a payment stablecoin 
held in safekeeping under subpart C and to delete an unnecessary 
reference to using a distributed ledger. The OCC is making non-
substantive edits to Sec.  15.21(c). The OCC is modifying Sec.  
15.21(d) to use the term covered custodian.
    The OCC is modifying Sec.  15.22(a) to add a reference to Sec.  
15.22(c). The OCC is modifying Sec.  15.22(b) to clarify that steps to 
protect, possess, or control covered assets include appropriate 
recordkeeping.
    The OCC is adding new Sec.  15.22(c), which provides that 
notwithstanding any other provision of part 15 to the contrary, part 15 
does not prevent a covered custodian from custodying its own assets and 
the covered assets of a covered customer at a sub-custodian where the 
sub-custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered custodian's 
assets with the covered assets of its covered customers in one or more 
omnibus accounts of the sub-custodian; provided that the covered 
custodian maintains adequate safeguards and internal controls 
reasonably designed to ensure that the sub-custodian segregates all 
covered assets of the covered custodian's covered customers from, and 
does not commingle such covered assets with, the assets of the sub-
custodian.
    The OCC is modifying Sec.  15.23 to clarify its application to 
covered assets and that the provision applies only to national banks, 
Federal savings associations, Federal branches, or permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers when these entities neither control nor hold 
themselves out as controlling the relevant private keys associated with 
covered assets nor provide or hold themselves out as providing 
safekeeping and custodial services for such assets.

[[Page 67098]]

2. Overview of Proposed Rule
    Section 10 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909) imposes requirements 
on any person seeking to provide custodial or safekeeping services for 
payment stablecoin reserve, payment stablecoins used as collateral, or 
the private keys used to issue permitted payment stablecoins. Among 
other things, section 10 of the Act requires such persons to be subject 
to supervision or regulation by a primary Federal payment stablecoin 
regulator, primary financial regulatory agency, or State bank 
supervisor, to treat covered assets as customer property, to separately 
account for and not commingle covered assets unless permitted under a 
listed exception, and to provide their regulator or supervisor with 
certain information as determined by that regulator or supervisor. 
Section 10 also provides a priority regime elevating the claims of 
payment stablecoin holders over other claims on persons providing 
custody and exempting certain persons providing hardware or software 
services from the requirements of section 10.
    The OCC proposed to (1) establish relevant defined terms for 
purposes of subpart C to clarify the scope of custodial services to 
which subpart C would apply; (2) set minimum principles-based 
requirements for OCC-supervised institutions related to their provision 
of custodial or safekeeping services for the assets described in 
section 10 of the GENIUS Act that are appropriate to protect such 
custodied assets from the claims of creditors of the institution; and 
(3) implement other requirements and exclusions of the Act.
3. General Comments
    The OCC received 54 comments on this subpart. Many commenters 
generally supported the OCC's objective of establishing a clear and 
prudentially sound regulatory framework for GENIUS Act custodial 
activities and urged the OCC generally to adopt an approach recognizing 
the particular legal and operational characteristics of custody 
arrangements while preserving necessary flexibility for regulated 
institutions.
4. Definitions (Sec.  15.20)
    Broadly speaking, commenters were supportive of the proposed 
definitions in subpart C of the proposal. At a high level, several 
commenters stated that custody definitions should ensure technology 
neutrality and not codify practices, standards, or technologies that 
might quickly become outdated or impractical. The OCC agrees that its 
definitions are designed to be technology-neutral and functional, 
capable of being used without repeated amendment as technology changes.
    The OCC proposed to define ``applicable law'' as ``the law of a 
State or other jurisdiction governing a covered custodian's custody 
relationships, any applicable Federal law governing those 
relationships, the terms of the custody agreement, and any applicable 
court order.'' The OCC received no material comments on this definition 
and finalizes it as proposed.
    The OCC proposed to define ``covered assets'' as ``payment 
stablecoin reserves, payment stablecoins used as collateral, and 
private keys used to issue payment stablecoins, as well as cash and 
other property received in the course of the provision of custodial or 
safekeeping services for such assets.'' \151\ In proposing this 
definition, the OCC asked whether it should define ``covered assets'' 
in such a way that the requirements of sections 10(a) through (c) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(a) through (c)) would be read together 
to cover the same set of assets and provide a cogent and harmonized set 
of requirements, or whether the OCC should replicate the statutory 
language regarding the scope of assets covered separately in paragraphs 
(a), (b), and (c).\152\ Commenters primarily responded that the OCC's 
proposal to define ``covered assets'' in such a way that sections 10(a) 
through (c) of the Act would be read together to apply to all covered 
assets is a correct reading of the Act. Several commenters requested 
clarification that territorial application of subpart C be read to be 
coextensive with the territorial scope established in section 3 of the 
GENIUS Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \151\ One commenter sought clarification of the meaning of the 
phrase ``private keys used to issue payment stablecoins.'' The OCC 
confirms that the term refers to the private keys used in the 
issuance process to create and mint stablecoins and not the private 
keys associated with end-user wallets. The latter reading would 
vastly expand the scope of the GENIUS Act's custody requirements and 
is inconsistent with the plain meaning of the text (``private keys 
used to issue payment stablecoins'' (emphasis added)). As such, the 
OCC believes it is appropriate to retain the phrase as proposed, 
which mirrors the statutory text.
    \152\ Nothing in the definition of ``covered asset'' is meant to 
affect priority under section 10(c)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5909(c)(3)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

The OCC agrees that the Act is primarily focused on payment 
stablecoins and that there is a presumption against extraterritorial 
application of United States law absent specific language to the 
contrary. As such, the OCC has clarified in the final rule that 
``covered assets'' are only those assets associated with payment 
stablecoins that are offered, sold, or otherwise made available to 
persons in the United States.
    Several commenters also requested further clarification of certain 
terms used in the definition of ``covered assets.'' For example, the 
OCC sought comment on whether it is the correct approach to interpret 
``cash and other property'' as used in the definition of ``covered 
assets'' to refer only to the cash and other property that a covered 
custodian may receive in connection with the provision of custodial 
services for the Act's three core custody assets. Commenters generally 
agreed with the OCC's proposed approach but requested further 
clarification that cash held as a deposit liability at an insured 
depository institution is not and cannot be a custodial asset for 
purposes of the segregation requirements in subpart C. While the OCC 
acknowledges these commenters' concerns, it believes they are best 
addressed in the exception in Sec.  15.21(d) regarding deposit 
liabilities discussed below, rather than scoping out all cash from the 
requirements of subpart C, given the GENIUS Act's explicit references 
to ``cash'' in section 10. Certain protections in the GENIUS Act 
applicable to custodied assets are relevant to cash received from 
covered customers. For example, a covered custodian must properly 
account for cash that makes up the reserves of a payment stablecoin and 
treat such cash as part of the custody relationship governed by the 
terms of any applicable custody agreement.
    Other commenters requested that the phrase ``payment stablecoins 
used as collateral'' be further clarified, noting that a covered 
custodian may not necessarily know whether a custodied payment 
stablecoin is at any given time being held as collateral. Commenters 
suggested various amendments to the final rule including limiting the 
application of subpart C to either those situations in which the 
covered custodian is party to a collateral agreement with respect to 
the stablecoin used as collateral or to situations where the covered 
custodian knows or should have known that the custodied payment 
stablecoin is being used as collateral, or else requiring the covered 
custodian to undertake certain due diligence regarding the use of 
custodied payment stablecoins. The OCC acknowledges commenters' 
concerns and believes that an ``actual knowledge'' standard best 
balances the foregoing against the text and purpose of the Act. The OCC 
expects that in most cases, a covered custodian will have actual 
knowledge where it is a party to a collateral agreement, but the OCC 
believes that limiting the term only to such

[[Page 67099]]

circumstances would be inconsistent with the Act, which does not refer 
to such agreements. However, including a constructive knowledge 
requirement may offer insufficient clarity and may incentivize covered 
custodians to implement burdensome due diligence requirements, which 
may be inconsistent with the norms of custody practices and the Act's 
principles-based, rather than prescriptive, approach to custody. As 
such, the final rule specifies that the term ``covered assets'' refers 
to ``payment stablecoins used as collateral, where a covered custodian 
has actual knowledge that such payment stablecoins are being used as 
collateral.''
    The OCC proposed to define ``covered custodian'' to mean ``a 
national bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to the extent of such person's 
provision of custodial or safekeeping services for covered assets.'' 
\153\ The OCC proposed to define ``covered customer'' to mean ``a 
person for or on whose behalf a covered custodian receives, acquires, 
or holds covered assets.'' The OCC proposed to define ``sub-custodian'' 
to mean ``a person that provides custody and safekeeping services to a 
covered custodian, including through a digital wallet for which such 
person controls the associated private keys, with respect to covered 
assets of a covered customer, for which the covered custodian otherwise 
serves as a custodian under this subpart.'' One commenter recommended 
narrowing the definition of ``covered customer'' to apply only to 
custodial or safekeeping services provided with respect to the issuance 
of ``payment stablecoins.'' The OCC declines to narrow the definition 
of ``covered customer'' in this manner as to do so would be contrary to 
the statute's definition of ``customer'' in section 10(b)(1) of the Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5909(b)(1)), which is not limited to the issuance of payment 
stablecoins. Other commenters asked that the OCC clarify that the terms 
``covered custodian'' and ``sub-custodian'' do not include foreign 
entities. However, this reading appears contrary to the text of section 
10 of the GENIUS Act, as well as its purpose, which largely seeks to 
insulate permitted payment stablecoin issuers and United States holders 
of payment stablecoins from potential complications related to a 
custodian's or sub-custodian's insolvency, failure to properly maintain 
and record custodied assets, or other issues. As such, the OCC is 
adopting these definitions as proposed, except for certain technical 
edits to the definition of sub-custodian, described below. The OCC 
notes that the changes to the definition of ``covered assets,'' 
described above, should prevent undue extraterritorial application of 
subpart C.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \153\ The OCC notes that, consistent with its authority, subpart 
C applies to national banks, Federal savings associations, and 
Federal branches. Entities that are not supervised by the OCC are 
not ``covered custodians'' for purposes of subpart C (though they 
may be sub-custodians). As such, the OCC has not addressed comments 
concerning the application of subpart C to such entities, other than 
in the context of sub-custodians. However, even though entities not 
supervised by the OCC are not ``covered custodians'' for purposes of 
subpart C, they may nevertheless be entities subject to compliance 
with section 10 of the GENIUS Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC is making non-substantive changes to the definition of sub-
custodian. Specifically, the final rule replaces the word ``such'' with 
``the'' and eliminates an unnecessary comma.
    The OCC proposed to define ``custody agreement'' as ``a legally 
binding contractual agreement between a covered customer, as the 
principal, and the covered custodian, as the agent, that establishes 
the covered custodian's duties and responsibilities in providing 
safekeeping and ancillary services to the covered customer.'' The OCC 
proposed to define ``digital wallet'' as ``a software program or 
hardware device that stores and manages the private keys associated 
with a particular unit of a digital asset.'' The OCC received no 
comments on these definitions and finalizes them as proposed.
    The OCC requested comment on whether it would be helpful to define 
any other terms. One commenter recommended the OCC add a definition of 
the phrase ``custodial or safekeeping services'' as used in proposed 
subpart C. The OCC declines to define these terms as it believes the 
terms ``custody'' and ``safekeeping'' are well-established and well-
understood terms and that adding a new definition may introduce 
confusion or be underinclusive or overinclusive.
5. Covered Asset Custodial Property Requirements (Sec.  15.21)
    Proposed Sec.  15.21 included certain minimum principles-based 
requirements applicable to a covered custodian's provision of custodial 
and safekeeping services for covered assets to ensure that such covered 
assets are treated and dealt with as belonging to the covered customers 
and protected from claims of the covered custodian's creditors, as well 
as the creditors of any sub-custodian, as applicable. Under proposed 
Sec.  15.21(a), a covered custodian would have needed to separately 
account for the covered assets of each covered customer and would have 
had to treat and deal with those covered assets as belonging to such
