covered customer and not as the property of the covered custodian. 
Under proposed Sec.  15.21(b), a covered custodian would have to take 
appropriate steps to protect the covered assets of covered customers 
from the claims of creditors of the covered custodian and any sub-
custodian, as applicable, including through adopting, implementing, and 
maintaining written policies, procedures, and internal controls that 
are adequate to comply with applicable law and that are commensurate 
with the covered custodian's size, complexity, and risk profile and 
with the nature of the applicable covered assets for which it provides 
custodial or safekeeping services.
    The OCC noted its belief that setting certain minimum principles-
based requirements for the provision of these custody services, 
regardless of the use of omnibus accounts, is consistent with section 
10(b)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(b)(2)), which requires that 
applicable custodians ``take such steps as are appropriate to protect 
the [covered assets] of a customer from the claims of creditors of the 
[custodian]'' and section 13 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5913), which 
grants the OCC broad rulemaking authority to implement the GENIUS Act.
    The OCC sought comment on whether the proposed principles-based 
requirements accurately capture sound custodial management practices 
that are standard in the industry. Commenters largely supported the 
OCC's principles-based approach in proposed Sec.  15.21(a) and (b) as 
consistent with the GENIUS Act's own principles-based approach and as 
setting an appropriate baseline for sound custodial practice that is 
also sufficiently flexible to adapt to changing circumstances. Some 
commenters further noted that prescriptive requirements would not keep 
pace with technological changes and would impose disproportionate costs 
on smaller banks. Several commenters, however, recommended 
supplementing the principles-based approach with additional 
protections. Examples included mandated certifications (e.g., a public 
attestation as to compliance with subpart C); specific real-time 
recordkeeping standards; minimum policies, procedures, and controls, 
such as for key management and robust systems to authenticate customer 
instructions before effecting transfers; minimum technical standards, 
such as multi-signature architecture and requirements concerning the 
geographic distribution of key shards, quantum computing risk 
management standards, incident response and recovery, and

[[Page 67100]]

hardware specifications; special requirements related to smart contract 
administrative keys; mandatory contract provisions; real-time 
monitoring; regulatory reporting; independent audits; public 
disclosure; and a requirement that custody be conducted in a fiduciary 
capacity, among others.
    Other commenters stated that the OCC should add additional 
requirements in instances in which an OCC-supervised permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer maintains any reserve assets without the use of a 
custodian or when a covered custodian provides safekeeping and custody 
services to an affiliate permitted payment stablecoin issuer or to a 
payment stablecoin issuer that is not supervised by the OCC. These 
commenters noted that so-called ``self-custody'' and affiliate custody 
of reserve assets may give rise to significant risks as there is no 
independent custodian to provide an added layer of protection to 
holders of the relevant payment stablecoin. Additionally, these 
commenters noted that non-OCC-supervised payment stablecoin issuers, 
especially foreign payment stablecoin issuers, may raise additional 
complications, including jurisdiction and choice of law issues. 
Commenters offered several examples of heightened requirements in such 
situations, including increased levels of capital and assessments; 
mandatory governance standards designed to ensure independence; 
disclosure obligations to payment stablecoin holders; examination 
standards that address intragroup conflicts of interest; and blanket 
prohibitions on ``self-custody,'' among other conditions.
    A commenter suggested that as a condition to an OCC-supervised 
entity providing custody services to a foreign issuer, the OCC should 
require that the custodian's custody agreement authorize the custodian, 
and the custodian should be operationally prepared, to freeze, 
liquidate, or transfer reserve assets upon service of a final United 
States court order and stated that this requirement would be consistent 
with existing OCC requirements for custodians.
    One commenter stated that a covered custodian's custody and 
safekeeping functions should be organizationally and functionally 
separate from any trading, lending, asset management, and other market-
facing activities that the entity engages in, and that personnel with 
trading responsibilities should not participate in custody or 
safekeeping functions, in order to reduce conflicts of interest and 
protect customer assets from exposure to other business risks. Other 
commenters supported strong internal controls more broadly, including 
segregation of duties, independent validation, dual or multi-party 
approvals, and strong governance over issuance systems. Another 
commenter noted that while assets should be appropriately segregated 
and independently controlled, any personnel or governance requirements 
should be proportional to the size and complexity of the issuer and 
implemented through broader reserve asset and risk management standards 
rather than as a separate standalone requirement.
    Adding additional prescriptive requirements discussed in comments 
to the rule would be contrary to a principles-based and technologically 
neutral approach. Moreover, the technical and prescriptive standards 
discussed in the comments may be overly burdensome and at risk of 
becoming outdated quickly. Covered custodians are already OCC-
supervised entities subject to prudential supervision and regulation 
and the OCC has experience supervising crypto-asset custody. The GENIUS 
Act and part 15 already impose requirements on payment stablecoin 
issuers that would address stablecoin holder protection. A principles-
based approach maintains flexibility and technology neutrality and 
avoids imposing undue burden. Regarding comments on self-custody and 
affiliate custody of payment stablecoin reserve assets, the OCC 
believes these concerns are best addressed in the section of the final 
rule applicable to reserve assets (see Sec.  15.11). Therefore, the OCC 
declines to add further prescriptive requirements to Sec. Sec.  
15.21(a) or (b)(1).\154\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\154\ One commenter stated that the OCC should clarify that the 
custody, possession, and control concepts used in the final rule are 
not to be interpreted to alter or supersede the otherwise applicable 
rights and obligations of a custodian under OCC, SEC, or other 
applicable regulations. The commenter stated that the issue is 
particularly important for institutional custody models and for 
groups that include both bank and broker-dealer entities. The OCC 
believes that the principles-based framework articulated in Sec.  
15.21 is consistent with custodial standards otherwise applicable to 
OCC-supervised institutions. Therefore, the OCC does not believe any 
changes are necessary to Sec.  15.21 to clarify the rights and 
obligations applicable to a custodian under other applicable 
regulations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    However, the OCC is adopting Sec. Sec.  15.21(a) and (b)(1) with 
minor changes to address certain concerns of commenters. First, some 
commenters requested further clarity regarding the GENIUS Act's 
requirement, mirrored in Sec.  15.21(a), that a covered custodian 
``separately account'' for the covered assets for which it provides 
safekeeping and custody services. Sound custodial practices would 
entail that a covered custodian may not rely solely on a distributed 
ledger and must reconcile distributed ledger data, as applicable, with 
its internal records. As a point of clarity, the OCC is finalizing 
Sec.  15.21(a) with a reference to a covered custodian's obligation to 
``record,'' as well as to account for, the covered assets of a covered 
customer. Second, other commenters noted the importance of custody 
agreements in ensuring the protection of customers' covered assets in 
line with the GENIUS Act. The OCC is finalizing Sec.  15.21(b) to 
include the adoption, implementation, and maintenance of written 
custody agreements among the other enumerated examples in that section.
    The OCC also sought comment on whether the proposal provides enough 
detail regarding what steps are appropriate for a covered custodian to 
protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of 
creditors of the covered custodian. Several commenters recommended that 
the OCC provide guidance to facilitate compliance with the requirements 
of Sec.  15.21 or with regard to specific situations concerning covered 
asset custodial property requirements, including managing third-party 
risk and incident response and recovery planning. While the OCC may 
consider future requests for supervisory guidance as needed, the agency 
believes doing so concurrent with publication of this final rule is 
premature as it may interfere with the development of industry best 
practices, may quickly become dated due to changing technological 
norms, and may risk appearing to set minimum requirements that 
undermine a principles-based approach.
    Other commenters requested that the OCC create a safe harbor for 
good-faith attempts at compliance. One commenter offered that such a 
safe harbor could be conditioned on a covered custodian (1) not 
recording custodied covered assets, other than cash held as deposit 
liabilities, on its own balance sheet; and (2) providing prompt notice 
to covered customers, to the extent permitted by law, upon receipt of 
any adverse claims asserted against covered assets. The OCC believes a 
safe harbor for compliance with Sec.  15.21(b)(1) is unnecessary, as 
custody is a long-established business with clear norms of operation 
and legal frameworks. Inclusion of a safe harbor could be potentially 
counterproductive as the minimum conditions of a safe harbor could 
effectively serve as a regulatory baseline that disincentivizes more 
rigorous custodial standards. Therefore, the OCC declines to include a 
safe harbor provision in Sec.  15.21(b)(1).

[[Page 67101]]

    The OCC sought comment on whether, to the extent a covered 
custodian with fiduciary powers provides fiduciary services to a 
covered customer in connection with a customer's covered assets, the 
existing requirements of 12 CFR part 9 or part 150, as applicable, are 
appropriate to implement the GENIUS Act. Several commenters responded 
that the existing requirements in 12 CFR part 9 or part 150, as 
applicable, should generally be appropriate. However, several 
commenters noted that a directed custodian of covered assets should not 
be deemed to be providing services within a fiduciary capacity within 
the meaning of the OCC's fiduciary regulations solely for providing 
custody services, unless the service is expressly listed in 12 CFR 
9.2(e) or the custodian has agreed with the customer to conduct the 
service in a fiduciary capacity, even if such services are considered 
``fiduciary'' under State law. The OCC notes that whether an activity 
is conducted in a fiduciary capacity is based on the particular facts 
and circumstances and believes it would be neither appropriate nor 
consistent with law to opine in a general manner that any activity 
should be scoped out of its fiduciary regulations. Therefore, the OCC 
is adopting Sec.  15.21(b)(1) as proposed.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.21(b)(2), a covered custodian would have 
been required to maintain possession or control of the covered assets 
of a covered customer that are held directly, including in a digital 
wallet for which the covered custodian controls the associated private 
keys. A covered custodian would have been able to maintain the covered 
assets of a covered customer through the use of a sub-custodian if 
consistent with applicable law and the covered custodian would have 
needed to maintain adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably 
designed to provide the covered custodian with oversight of such sub-
custodian's compliance with the requirements of proposed subpart C. 
Under the proposal, with regard to any payment stablecoin or stablecoin 
reserve in the form of a tokenized asset held in safekeeping under 
proposed subpart C, a covered custodian, or sub-custodian, as 
applicable, would have maintained control for purposes of the proposed 
requirement in paragraph (b)(2)(i) if it could reasonably demonstrate, 
consistent with the standard of care established by applicable law, 
that no other party, including the covered customer, can transfer the 
payment stablecoin or tokenized asset using a distributed ledger 
without the consent of the custodian or sub-custodian, as 
applicable.\155\ The final rule adopts paragraph (b)(2)(i) with non-
substantive changes (adding the word ``that'' and replacing the word 
``such'' with ``the'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \155\ As noted in the proposal, this requirement is consistent 
with past OCC guidance on the control of crypto-assets for purposes 
of safekeeping. See OCC News Release 2025-68, ``Agencies Issue Joint 
Statement on Risk-Management Considerations For Crypto-Asset 
Safekeeping'' (July 14, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC sought comment in the proposal about whether the 
description in the proposed rule about how a custodian maintains 
control of a payment stablecoin or tokenized reserve assets is 
appropriately calibrated. Commenters generally supported the OCC's 
approach, noting the importance of a technology-neutral and functional 
definition of control, but requested that the OCC clarify that multi-
signature, distributed key-control architectures, multiparty 
computation, and shareable private keys are permissible. Multi-
signature approaches are consistent with the proposed regulatory text, 
which establishes that a custodian maintains control if ``it can 
reasonably demonstrate, consistent with the standard of care 
established by applicable law, that no other party, including the 
covered customer, can transfer the payment stablecoin or tokenized 
asset using a distributed ledger without the consent of the custodian 
or sub-custodian, as applicable.'' That is, it does not require that 
the custodian have the unilateral ability to transfer assets, but 
rather only that no other party can transfer assets without the 
custodian's consent, which would capture multi-party signatory systems. 
Therefore, changes to proposed Sec.  15.21(b)(2)(ii) are unnecessary to 
clarify that multi-signature, distributed key-control architectures, 
multiparty computation, and shareable private keys are permissible. The 
OCC is, however, making three technical changes to proposed Sec.  
15.21(b)(2)(ii). First, the OCC has added ``private key used to issue a 
payment stablecoin'' as one of the types of crypto-assets to which the 
term ``control'' applies, consistent with the GENIUS Act's use of this 
term. Second, Sec.  15.21(b)(2)(ii) includes a reference in the final 
rule to subpart C (whereas the proposal referred to Sec.  
15.21(b)(2)(i)). Finally, the final rule eliminates the phrase ``using 
a distributed ledger'' as surplusage.
    Commenters also raised specific amendments or additions to the 
proposal's discussion of control and the use of sub-custodians. For 
example, one commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that for 
tokenized reserve assets, a covered custodian's demonstration of 
control should address both the on-chain custody of the token and the 
off-chain legal and operational arrangements ensuring the custodian can 
enforce the customer's rights against the underlying asset. Requiring 
that a covered custodian have control not only of the contractually 
agreed custodied asset, but also effectively of the underlying 
reference asset would be inconsistent with industry norms of custody 
and may serve to significantly impede the use of tokenized assets. As 
such, it is inappropriate to impose those requirements on covered 
custodians. The OCC notes, however, that for an asset to qualify as a 
reserve asset in tokenized form, a tokenized asset would need to confer 
rights identical to those that are conferred, or would be conferred, by 
a non-tokenized form of the asset under applicable law.
    Other commenters recommended confirming in the final rule that 
cryptographic sub-ledgering (the mathematically verifiable tracking of 
beneficial ownership through on-chain proofs and real-time internal 
ledger reconciliation) inherently satisfies the adequate safeguards and 
internal controls standard for sub-custodian oversight under Sec.  
15.21(b). While cryptographic sub-ledgering may be an effective 
technological control, the OCC notes that the legal enforceability of a 
custodial relationship (i.e., bailor-bailee vs. debtor-creditor) will 
depend on the facts and circumstances and that the adequacy of a 
covered custodian's safeguards and internal controls will ultimately 
depend upon the nature of its custodial business and its sub-custodial 
relationships. As such, it would be inappropriate to implement a safe 
harbor regarding cryptographic sub-ledgering.
    Another commenter recommended that the OCC ensure that its 
principles-based framework includes clear expectations on due 
diligence, oversight, and contractual accountability for sub-custodian 
arrangements. Section 15.21 of the proposed rule provided sufficient 
protections regarding the use of sub-custodians, including the 
maintenance of ``adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably 
designed to provide the covered custodian with oversight of such sub-
custodian's compliance with the requirements of'' subpart C. The OCC 
also notes that covered custodians would typically consider sub-
custodians as third-party relationships and manage the risks from a 
third-party risk perspective as well, consistent with the covered 
custodian's size, complexity,

[[Page 67102]]

and risk profile and the nature of its sub-custodial relationships.
    The OCC also sought comment on whether certain specific issues 
should be incorporated into the required principles-based standards 
governing a covered custodian's treatment of covered customers' covered 
assets. First, the agency sought comment on whether it should require 
that any custody agreement a covered custodian enters into with a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer provide for prompt release of any 
custodied covered assets to the covered customer's control, including 
whether the OCC should require a covered custodian to release covered 
assets within a specific timeframe or to maintain custody agreements 
governing such release. Several commenters opposed a requirement that 
any custody agreement a covered custodian enters into with a payment 
stablecoin issuer provide for prompt release of custodied covered 
assets. The commenters stated that prompt release standards should be 
part of the service standards determined by the covered custodian and 
covered customer, and that custodians are constrained by the nature of 
the underlying reserve assets as well as by industry-standard deadlines 
for processing those assets.
    In contrast, a few commenters recommended the OCC require that 
custody agreements provide for the prompt release of custodied assets, 
although one such commenter also recommended that the OCC should not 
specify a universal timeframe and should make clear that the adequacy 
of a custodian's timeframes will be evaluated in the context of its 
overall risk management framework. The OCC believes that a regulatory 
requirement concerning prompt release standards would impose additional 
burdens on covered custodians to set up processes and procedures that 
are typically already addressed in contracts, contract law, and 
industry norms of conduct. Moreover, a prescriptive requirement could 
limit the development of better practices in this area. Therefore, the 
OCC declines to include a prescriptive requirement on prompt release 
and retains the proposal's principles-based approach.
    Second, the OCC sought comment on section 10(c)(3) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(3)), which provides a priority regime regarding 
the claims of covered customers against a covered custodian regarding 
any payment stablecoins used as collateral that also allows covered 
customers to expressly waive this priority. The OCC did not propose any 
regulations governing the waiver provision as it believes the statute 
is clear. However, a few commenters recommended that the OCC provide 
clear guidance or requirements on the circumstances in which priority 
waivers are appropriate, including the standard of disclosure required 
before a waiver can be validly obtained. One commenter, by contrast, 
noted that the waiver right may at times be necessary to preserve 
certain collateral arrangements that can provide flexibility and 
benefits to covered customers and covered custodians. The OCC continues 
to believe that the statute is clear and that additional regulatory 
requirements would impose burdens and not provide meaningful benefits 
to either covered custodians or covered customers. Furthermore, if 
consistent with applicable law, the OCC would not expect that section 
10(c)(3) of the GENIUS Act would prohibit covered custodians from 
including an express waiver as a standard term in their custody 
agreements.
    Under proposed Sec.  15.21(c), the OCC proposed codifying the 
exception in section 10(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)) to the 
customer property requirements described in section 10(b). This 
exception permits a covered custodian to withdraw and apply such share 
of the covered assets of a covered customer necessary to transfer, 
adjust, or settle a transaction or transfer assets applicable to that 
covered customer, including the payment of commissions, taxes, storage, 
and other charges lawfully accruing in connection with the provision of 
services to that covered customer by the covered custodian. The OCC 
proposed to specify that any such withdrawal must be consistent with 
any applicable law. For example, the OCC would expect any such 
withdrawal to be undertaken only in compliance with the terms of a 
covered customer's custody agreement and that any withdrawal of funds 
from an omnibus account would be properly recorded so as not to 
implicate the custodial assets of any other covered customer.
    The OCC sought comment on whether, in connection with Sec.  
15.21(c), the OCC should require any more prescriptive requirements 
related to the protection of payment stablecoin holders, such as those 
designed to ensure that such withdrawals do not cause any reserve to 
fall below any minimum coverage of a payment stablecoin. A few 
commenters responded that the OCC should require covered custodians to 
maintain controls to ensure that fee withdrawals do not reduce reserve 
coverage below applicable requirements, including, for example, 
specified controls or mandated custody account agreement terms that 
address pre-arranged fee schedules, authorized withdrawal instructions, 
and hard-stop controls where the custodian has sufficient visibility 
into the full reserve pool. The OCC notes that such additional 
requirements would likely be impractical for many covered custodians or 
inconsistent with the norms of custodial practices, since the covered 
custodian may lack visibility into a payment stablecoin issuer's 
reserve assets or may only custody a portion of the reserve assets. 
Rather, the payment stablecoin issuer is the party better positioned to 
ensure that it maintains required reserve assets, and it may be 
reasonable to expect that such an issuer should understand any 
applicable fee schedules and other situations in which a covered 
custodian may permissibly withdraw covered assets under custody as part 
of its ongoing monitoring of its reserve assets. Notably, final Sec.  
15.11(d) will require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to take 
certain steps with respect to custodians of reserve assets, including 
identifying itself as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and 
engaging in due diligence to ensure that the custodian complies with 
applicable requirements of the GENIUS Act's implementing regulations. 
The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.21(c) with non-substantive changes 
(replacing the word ``that'' with ``the'').
    Proposed Sec.  15.21(d) sought to clarify, consistent with section 
10(c)(2)(D) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(2)(D)), that an 
insured national bank or Federal savings association that provides 
custodial or safekeeping services for covered assets may hold covered 
assets that are in the form of cash on deposit, provided such treatment 
is consistent with Federal law. As noted above, several commenters 
observed that cash held in the form of a deposit liability is 
definitionally not a custodial asset and that such accounts cannot be 
held in a bankruptcy-remote manner because such accounts are 
fundamentally debtor-creditor relationships. As such, these commenters 
requested that such cash should be exempt from subpart C. However, the 
GENIUS Act refers specifically to ``cash'' as a potential covered 
asset. Generally, cash held in deposit accounts is not held in 
safekeeping as the property of the customer. Rather, the customer is a 
creditor of the bank unless the parties take steps to change the nature 
of the relationship.
    One commenter also recommended that the OCC clarify in proposed 
Sec.  15.21(d) that uninsured and insured Federal branches are 
permitted to hold ``covered assets'' that are in the form of

[[Page 67103]]

cash ``in the form of a deposit liability,'' to the same extent as 
insured national banks and Federal savings associations.\156\ The 
commenter believed that Congressional intent, principles of national 
treatment and equality of competitive opportunity, and public policy 
all support the broader reading that includes uninsured branches. 
Section 10(c)(2)(A) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(2)(A)) in part 
provides that certain cash held as a deposit liability at a depository 
institution shall not be subject to any requirement that custodied 
assets be segregated from the property of the applicable depository 
institution. However, section 10(c)(2)(D) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 
5909(c)(2)(D)) states that insured depository institutions ``shall be 
permitted to hold payment stablecoin reserves in the form of cash on 
deposit provided such treatment is consistent with Federal law.'' Both 
sections 10(c)(2)(A) and (D) of the GENIUS Act refer to ``payment 
stablecoin reserves.'' Since funds held as deposits at an uninsured 
depository institution would not qualify as a permissible reserve asset 
under section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)), 
an uninsured branch could not hold payment stablecoin reserves in the 
form of cash on deposit since such assets would not qualify as reserve 
assets.\157\ However, an uninsured Federal branch covered custodian may 
nonetheless hold other covered assets that are not payment stablecoin 
reserves in the form of cash on deposit. As such, the OCC has finalized 
Sec.  15.21(d) so that it refers to covered custodians generally and is 
not limited solely to insured depository institutions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \156\ The OCC notes that a Federal branch is scoped into the 
definition of covered custodian. Thus, for purposes of this 
question, the only relevant distinction is whether the Federal 
branch is insured or not.
    \157\ A permitted payment stablecoin issuer is likely better 
situated than a custodian to ensure that its cash reserve assets are 
held at insured depository institutions. As such, it is the 
obligation of the issuer to ensure its compliance with section 
4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act and Sec.  15.11(b) of this final 
rule. See Sec.  15.11(d).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

6. Use of Omnibus Accounts (Sec.  15.22)
    Proposed Sec.  15.22 covered the use of omnibus accounts by covered 
custodians. Proposed Sec.  15.22(a) addressed the segregation of 
covered assets, stating that, ``[a] covered custodian must segregate 
all covered assets of covered customers from, and not commingle them 
with, the assets of the covered custodian, except as permitted under 
Sec.  15.21(d).'' Proposed Sec.  15.22(b) stated that ``[a] covered 
custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered assets of 
multiple covered customers, in one or more omnibus accounts,'' provided 
the custodian has taken steps pursuant to Sec.  15.21(b) to maintain 
safe and sound practices and the use of omnibus accounts is consistent 
with applicable law. The OCC sought comment on whether the OCC should 
instead implement a more detailed regulatory framework regarding a 
covered custodian's use of omnibus accounts.
    Commenters generally supported the OCC's proposal in Sec.  15.22(b) 
to permit covered custodians to utilize omnibus accounts for covered 
assets consistent with the principles-based approach that the OCC 
proposed in Sec.  15.21. Several commenters, however, recommended that 
the OCC adopt more detailed expectations for omnibus account structures 
due to their potential to obscure entitlements and increase operational 
and legal risk or clarify that omnibus accounts should not refer to 
accounts held by a custodian on its own books.\158\ The OCC believes 
that the principles-based approach taken in subpart C should already 
largely address these operational and legal risks without imposing 
undue burdens. As noted above, sound custodial practices would entail 
that a covered custodian may not rely solely on a distributed ledger 
and must reconcile distributed ledger data, as applicable, with its 
internal records. Consistent with this practice, the OCC expects a 
covered custodian to maintain off-chain documentation and recordkeeping 
to the extent that it commingles the covered assets of multiple covered 
customers in an omnibus account to ensure that it is able to reconcile 
all omnibus accounts with individual customer custodial accounts--that 
is, that it has ``separately accounted for'' the covered assets of each 
covered customer.\159\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \158\ One commenter stated that allowing covered assets to be 
held in omnibus accounts would be inconsistent with appropriate 
custody practices. The GENIUS Act however is clear that covered 
assets, including the reserves of multiple permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, ``may, for convenience, be commingled and 
deposited in an omnibus account holding the [covered assets] and 
other property of more than 1 permitted payment stablecoin issuer or 
customer[.]'' 12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(2)(A).
    \159\ 12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    One commenter recommended that the OCC explicitly recognize that 
cryptographically segregated omnibus accounts satisfy the segregation 
and separate accounting requirements of Sec.  15.22. The commenter 
recommended explicitly allowing sub-ledgering within the same general 
omnibus wallet, meaning that the custodian would maintain multiple 
customers' assets at the same virtual address but maintain real-time 
internal records continuously reconciled against the blockchain showing 
exactly which customer owns which assets. As noted above, while 
cryptographic sub-ledgering may be an effective technological control, 
the OCC notes that the legal enforceability of a custodial relationship 
will depend on the facts and circumstances and that the adequacy of a 
covered custodian's safeguards and internal controls will ultimately 
depend upon the nature of its custodial business and its sub-custodial 
relationships. As such, the OCC believes it would be inappropriate to 
include a safe harbor in Sec.  15.22 regarding the use of cryptographic 
sub-ledgering alone, and the agency reiterates that a covered custodian 
must also maintain appropriate off-chain recordkeeping.
    Commenters also provided input on specific issues related to the 
use of omnibus accounts. First, the OCC asked whether a covered 
custodian may, for convenience, commingle in a single omnibus account 
both covered assets and other custodial assets that are not covered 
assets and asked whether the OCC should consider prescribing additional 
requirements in such situations. Several commenters supported 
confirming that covered custodians may hold covered assets and non-
covered digital assets within the same omnibus wallet structures, 
provided that the custodian maintains recordkeeping sufficient to 
identify, at any time, which assets within the omnibus account 
constitute covered assets and which customers are covered customers. 
One such commenter recommended that the OCC should make clear that such 
arrangements are appropriate only where traceability, accountability, 
and error-resolution processes are demonstrably robust. Another 
commenter stated that commingling covered and non-covered assets could 
raise complexity and would require enhanced safeguards. The OCC agrees 
that commingling in a single omnibus account both covered assets and 
other assets that are not covered assets may be permissible, provided 
the custodian maintains sufficient recordkeeping to identify, at any 
time, which assets within the omnibus account constitute covered assets 
and which customers are covered customers. However, to the extent any 
covered assets are reserve assets, a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer may not custody such assets in omnibus accounts since a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer is separately required to segregate 
and not commingle such reserve assets with other assets owned

[[Page 67104]]

or held by the issuer (see final Sec.  15.11(a)(1)(ii)). Additionally, 
while the OCC does not believe that the imposition of prescriptive 
technical requirements would provide meaningful additional customer 
benefits as measured against the costs, operational complexities, and 
potential for regulatory staleness, the agency believes that it is 
prudent that the final rule requires that the terms of any omnibus 
account are fully disclosed to customers, including whether covered 
assets and non-covered assets may be commingled.
    Second, commenters recommended that the OCC distinguish between 
internal omnibus accounts at a covered custodian and external omnibus 
accounts maintained by the custodian at sub-custodians (e.g., global 
custodians) or directly or indirectly at a market utility 
(collectively, ``downstream custodians'').\160\ These commenters stated 
that the OCC should confirm that the final regulation does not disturb 
established external omnibus accounts at downstream custodians, which 
may commingle in a single account the assets of many customers, 
including the covered custodian's proprietary assets and its covered 
customers' covered asset custody accounts. These downstream custodians 
may have limited or no insight into, or direct commercial relationship 
with, the covered custodian. Preventing commingling of assets at this 
level may be impractical and does not serve the purpose of the GENIUS 
Act in protecting covered customers from becoming general unsecured 
creditors of a covered custodian. The final rule does not override 
standard commercial practices when it comes to global custodians and 
market utilities. However, should a downstream custodian commingle its 
own assets in an omnibus account with the covered assets of a covered 
custodian, the customer protection purpose of section 10 of the GENIUS 
Act is nonetheless implicated. As such, the OCC is finalizing Sec.  
15.22 by adding a clarification that a covered custodian may custody 
its own assets and the covered assets of a covered customer at a sub-
custodian where the sub-custodian may, for convenience, commingle such 
assets in one or more omnibus accounts of the sub-custodian; provided 
that the covered custodian maintains adequate safeguards and internal 
controls reasonably designed to ensure that the sub-custodian 
segregates all covered assets of the covered custodian's covered 
customers from, and does not commingle such covered assets with, the 
assets of the sub-custodian.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \160\ One commenter requested that the OCC clarify that omnibus 
accounts should be limited to those accounts at downstream 
custodians and not to accounts maintained by the custodian on its 
own books for its customers. While some covered assets may likely be 
held at downstream custodians, the OCC neither believes that the 
GENIUS Act compels such a reading nor that all covered assets, which 
are not limited to securities, necessarily lend themselves to such 
arrangements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Third, one commenter recommended that the OCC consider how gas fees 
would be treated in custodial contexts.\161\ The commenter stated that 
a covered custodian may agree as a convenience to its customer to pay 
gas fees using the covered custodian's own relevant crypto-assets and 
that it may be operationally convenient to commingle such crypto-assets 
in a sub-ledger of the customer account such that the gas fees are paid 
from the same wallet as the customer's transaction. The commenter 
recommended that the final rule confirm that this limited operational 
commingling undertaken solely to pay gas fees is permissible. While the 
OCC acknowledges that limited commingling may provide certain 
operational efficiencies, the GENIUS Act does not provide such an 
operational exception. Rather, the statute clearly states that a 
covered customer's covered assets ``shall be segregated from and not be 
commingled with the assets of'' the covered custodian as required by 
section 10(c)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(c)(1)). 
Additionally, the OCC understands that many distributed ledger 
technologies allow gas fees to be paid from separate wallets and thus 
that a covered custodian could still use any permissible proprietary 
holdings of crypto-assets to pay a covered customer's gas fees without 
commingling. As such, the OCC has not included an exception to the 
segregation requirement related to gas fees.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\161\ For a description of gas fees and the permissibility of 
national banks to hold them as principal, see OCC Interpretive 
Letter 1186.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

7. Self-Custody Hardware and Software Exclusion (Sec.  15.23)
    Proposed Sec.  15.23 implemented section 10(e) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5909(e)), which provides that the requirements of section 10 
of the Act do not apply to any person solely on the basis that such 
person engages in the business of providing hardware or software to 
facilitate a customer's own custody or safekeeping of the customer's 
payment stablecoins or private keys. In proposed Sec.  15.23, the OCC 
sought to clarify that the requirements of this proposed subpart C do 
not apply to any national bank, Federal savings association, Federal 
branch, or permitted payment stablecoin issuer solely on the basis that 
such entity engages in the business of providing hardware or software 
to facilitate a person's or entity's self-custody of their payment 
stablecoins or private keys. The OCC sought comment on whether the OCC 
should consider implementing any other language to prevent the 
exception from being used to evade the custodial requirements of the 
Act, including, for example, whether the requirements of subpart C 
could nonetheless apply if, for example, an entity controls or holds 
itself out as controlling such payment stablecoins or private keys, or 
provides, or holds itself out as providing safekeeping or custodial 
services, including services that are ancillary or incidental to its 
custodial powers, for such payment stablecoins or private keys. In the 
alternative, the OCC sought comment on whether an OCC-supervised 
institution could provide ancillary custodial services to a user of 
such hardware or software while avoiding the minimum, principles-based 
requirements of the proposal.
    Several commenters recommended that the OCC clarify that the 
exclusion be applied on the basis of various factors that in essence 
mirror the control standard proposed in Sec.  15.21(b)(2). The OCC 
agrees and is clarifying Sec.  15.23 in accordance with these comments 
to prevent the section from being used to evade the custodial 
requirements of subpart C. Third-party services may in practice 
resemble the types of custody arrangements that the Act intended to be 
performed only by covered custodians. A simple non-control requirement 
and a requirement that the third party not hold itself out as a 
custodian is a low-burden means of preventing regulatory avoidance 
through this provision. Therefore, the OCC is adding a requirement to 
the final rule that the third party also not exercise or hold itself 
out as exercising control over the private keys associated with covered 
assets or provide or hold itself out as providing custody services for 
covered assets. In addition, the OCC is making non-substantive changes 
to the language of Sec.  15.23.
    Several commenters recommended that the final rule affirm that OCC-
supervised institutions may provide ancillary services to persons self-
custodying covered assets without triggering the requirements of 
subpart C. Examples of ancillary services cited by one commenter 
include permitted payment stablecoin issuers providing services such as 
trade execution, settlement routing, recordkeeping,

[[Page 67105]]

valuation, or tax reporting to users of self-custody tools. The 
commenter recommended that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer be 
permitted to offer such services without triggering full custody rules 
so long as the institution never takes possession or discretionary 
control of the user's payment stablecoins or keys. Another commenter 
similarly recommended extending the safe harbor for self-custodial 
wallets to all self-custodial interfaces, particularly to the 
engagement of distributed ledger protocol developers.
    The OCC believes that the ``control'' standard added to final Sec.  
15.23 satisfies these concerns and declines to further amend the 
regulation. However, if the permissibility of a national bank, Federal 
savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer providing such ancillary services is premised upon such an 
entity's custody powers, then such an entity could only provide those 
services in its capacity as a custodian. In such cases, the national 
bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer would not be covered by the self-custody hardware or 
software exception and would be subject to compliance with subpart 
C.\162\

    \162\ See, e.g., OCC Interpretive Letter 1170, 8, n. 39.

8. Reporting
    The OCC sought comment on the extent to which Schedule RC-T of the 
Call Report, in the case of national banks, Federal savings 
associations, or Federal branches, and the portions of the reports 
required under proposed Sec.  15.14 relevant to custodial activities, 
in the case of nonbank Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers and 
applicable State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, are appropriate 
to ensure that the OCC possesses the information necessary to supervise 
covered custodians. Several commenters responded that the OCC should 
not impose additional, distinct reporting obligations on custodians and 
should instead leverage existing custody reporting mechanisms. Some 
commenters recommended that the OCC clarify that reporting reserve 
compositions by permitted-investment category is strictly an issuer 
obligation, noting that requiring custodians to independently verify 
and classify covered assets exposes them to undue liability and costs. 
Other commenters acknowledged that existing Call Reports and Schedule 
RC-T may not be sufficient on their own for GENIUS Act assessment 
purposes, and recommended the OCC add a stablecoin-specific 
supplemental reporting requirement or alter Schedule RC-T of the Call 
Report. The OCC currently believes that existing reporting provides 
sufficient insight necessary for OCC supervision and assessment 
calculations, but will continue to monitor whether additional 
reporting, including amendments to Schedule RC-T, may be necessary.
9. Miscellaneous
Bridging Arrangements
    The OCC sought comment on whether there are particular 
circumstances for which the OCC should provide additional clarification 
as to the application of subpart C or the applicability of any 
exception. Several commenters recommended additional clarification on 
``bridging'' or ``wrapping'' arrangements, which facilitate use of 
crypto-assets between distributed ledgers that are not interoperable. 
One commenter described bridging as a practical necessity for multi-
chain stablecoin operations and recommended that the final rule make 
clear that payment stablecoins locked in a smart contract for bridging 
to an unsupported blockchain are not, by reason of that locking alone, 
subject to the custodial requirements of subpart C. Another commenter 
recommended the OCC clarify that a covered custodian that initiates a 
bridging transaction for a covered customer can still operate in 
compliance with subpart C, provided it maintains the ability to receive 
and custody the underlying asset upon unwrapping. That commenter 
further recommended that the OCC clarify that the covered custodian's 
obligations under subpart C continue with respect to the locked 
position, including the obligation to maintain accurate records of the 
customer's entitlement to the underlying asset. Other commenters stated 
that further clarification was unnecessary because of the exception for 
entities that solely provide hardware or software to facilitate a 
customer's own custody of payment stablecoins or private keys in 
section 10(e) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5909(e)). One commenter 
stated that the OCC should simply confirm that issuer obligations under 
subpart C do not extend to activities conducted outside the issuer's 
control, including third-party wrapping arrangements on unsupported 
blockchains.
    There are a number of unsettled legal questions surrounding the 
treatment of crypto-asset bridges. Furthermore, the mechanics of 
bridges can differ in important ways, and the bridge's technical 
design, the relevant legal contractual terms (or lack thereof), and the 
presence of parties exercising control over any locked assets, among 
other factors, may affect the analysis.\163\ Additionally, there are 
likely to be continued technical developments in this area, which may 
impact that analysis in the future. Therefore, the OCC is not able to 
provide definitive responses to the commenters' requests at this time.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \163\ The OCC notes that, in the case of a bridge for which the 
input is a payment stablecoin, the minted wrapped asset generally 
would not itself be a payment stablecoin as defined in the GENIUS 
Act. See GENIUS Act Sec.  2(22)(A)(ii)(I) (12 U.S.C. 
5901(22)(A)(ii)(I)) (providing that a payment stablecoin means a 
digital asset in which the issuer is obligated to convert, redeem, 
or repurchase a payment stablecoin ``for a fixed amount of monetary 
value, not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed amount 
of monetary value.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC expects covered custodians to understand the mechanics, 
legal roles, code, contract terms, redemption rights, and other 
relevant features of a bridge in which covered customers' covered 
assets are locked in order to understand the covered custodian's legal 
obligations.\164\ As case law and technology develop, or in response to 
requests involving particular bridging arrangements, the OCC may 
provide interpretations on the applicability of section 10 of the 
GENIUS Act to bridging arrangements. In the absence of definitive 
guidance from the OCC or clarity in relevant case law, covered 
custodians may rely on a well-founded legal analysis of compliance with 
section 10 with respect to bridging arrangements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \164\ The applicability of the exclusion from subpart C for 
covered custodians that provide hardware or software to facilitate a 
customer's self-custody of bridged assets, where the bridge provides 
for self-custody, will also depend on the facts and circumstances, 
including, as discussed above, whether the covered custodian 
controls or holds itself out as controlling any bridged-covered 
assets. Any analysis would also take into account the presence and 
features of any administrative key associated with the bridge.

Valuation of Private Keys Used To Issue Payment Stablecoins
    One commenter responded to the OCC's proposed approach to assign a 
nominal $1.00 value to private keys used to issue payment stablecoins, 
describing that approach as reasonable. However, that commenter noted 
that a nominal valuation may not fully capture the operational and 
control significance of private key custody, particularly where custody 
of the issuance keys and custody of reserve assets are held by 
different entities. The commenter recommended that the OCC address this 
potential gap without adding duplicative reporting by retaining the

[[Page 67106]]

nominal valuation framework and considering requiring limited, high-
level qualitative disclosures regarding private key custody 
arrangements. The commenter noted that such disclosures could include 
whether custody of the private keys is internal or third-party, whether 
it is segregated from reserve asset custody, and whether appropriate 
internal controls, access limitations, and incident response processes 
are in place. The OCC does not believe that any additional reporting 
requirements relating to the private keys used to issue payment 
stablecoins are necessary to implement through part 15, but it will 
consider whether any applicable reporting forms should be updated.

D. Subpart D--Applications and Registrations

    Section 5 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904) establishes a 
licensing regime for insured depository institutions that seek to issue 
payment stablecoins through a subsidiary and for nonbank entities, 
uninsured national banks, and uninsured Federal branches that seek to 
issue payment stablecoins as Federal qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers. Section 18(a) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)) provides 
an exception from the prohibitions in section 3 of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5902) for foreign payment stablecoin issuers registered with the 
OCC and sets forth the registration regime and other requirements for 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC proposed subpart D of part 
15 to implement these provisions of the GENIUS Act.

subpart D as proposed. The OCC is reordering and renumbering several 
provisions of subpart D. The OCC is making certain targeted changes to

2. General Applications Framework
    Several commenters either made general comments or requested that 
the OCC make certain revisions to the general proposed application 
framework. A few commenters suggested the final rule provide 
confirmation that applicants for a national trust bank charter that 
plan to custody stablecoin reserves for an affiliated issuer are 
required, as a condition of charter approval, to provide custody 
services to unaffiliated clients. This comment concerns the chartering 
of a national bank, rather than the licensing of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer, and is thus outside the scope of this rulemaking. 
One commenter recommended creating a public registry of authorized 
issuers so that downstream participants would know whether they are 
interacting with a legitimate issuer. The commenter suggested this 
registry be designed in a manner that incorporates fields for 
standardized data (e.g., entity's legal name, charter or license 
identifier, specific product and jurisdictional scope of authorization, 
and any specific conditions or limitations on the issuer's 
authorization), and includes near-real-time refresh of authorization 
status, a machine-readable interface so that downstream participants 
could consume registry data programmatically, and interoperability with 
State-level regulators to provide a comprehensive source of authorized 
issuers and prevent market fragmentation. The commenter suggested that 
reliance on the registry should act as a safe harbor for downstream 
participants. The statute does not mandate the creation of a registry 
like the one described by the commenter. The OCC does intend to publish 
the determination for when an applicant is licensed as a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer but is not including additional regulation 
text concerning the publication of a registry. In addition, the OCC, 
consistent with its approach to all matters, plans to operate 
transparently with regard to its application and registration 
decisions, including complying with its reporting obligations pursuant 
to section 15 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5914).
    Several commenters requested that the final rule expressly provide 
for a prefiling consultation or application checklist to promote 
certainty around the information an applicant should include in an 
application. One commenter suggested the OCC map the checklist to the 
statutory factors for completeness, while another commenter recommended 
against including a prescriptive checklist of safety and soundness 
criteria in the final rule. Two commenters recommended that the OCC 
publish an application guide, analogous to those available for 
organizers of de novo institutions, explaining how the OCC will assess 
the statutory and regulatory review factors under proposed Sec.  
15.30(c). One of the commenters also suggested that the guidance commit 
the OCC to transparently engaging with applicants on any filing 
concerns before deciding whether to approve or deny an application. The 
GENIUS Act does not require the OCC to offer a prefiling meeting or 
publish an application checklist. The OCC historically has not 
published checklists for applications, but it does provide significant 
guidance about the filing process in the Comptroller's Licensing 
Manual. The OCC anticipates issuing similar guidance with respect to 
filings for OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers. 
Accordingly, the final rule does not require a prefiling meeting or 
incorporate an application checklist. Nevertheless, applicants may 
request a prefiling meeting with OCC staff. The OCC plans to update the 
Comptroller's Licensing Manual in the near future to incorporate its 
chartering policy and procedural requirements for applicants seeking to 
become permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Applicants are encouraged 
to review these materials and any related publications prior to 
requesting a prefiling meeting. Further, pursuant to section 
5(d)(1)(B)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(1)(B)(ii)), which 
requires a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator to notify an 
applicant whether its application is considered substantially complete 
not later than 30 days after receipt, as incorporated under Sec.  
15.30(b)(3)(ii), the OCC will notify the applicant, within 30 days of 
receipt of the application, of the information required in order for 
the application to be considered substantially complete. The OCC 
believes this notification along with updates to the Comptroller's 
Licensing Manual will provide sufficient transparency regarding any 
filing concerns.
    Two commenters suggested that the OCC provide guidance confirming 
that registration as a money services business (MSB) with FinCEN would 
not disqualify a nonbank entity from making a filing under Sec.  15.30 
and that such registration would be treated as affirmative evidence of 
BSA/AML compliance. The GENIUS Act provides that permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers shall be treated as financial institutions for 
purposes of the Bank Secrecy Act. MSBs, like other nonbank entities 
seeking OCC approval to become Federal qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers, must make a filing with the OCC and comply with applicable

Proposed paragraph (b)(4) stated that the OCC may collect fingerprints of the individuals listed in proposed paragraph (b)(1)(ii) for submission to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for a national criminal history background check. Section 5(d)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(3)) provides that an application is deemed approved if the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator fails to render a decision within 120 days of receipt of a substantially complete application. Proposed Sec. 15.30(b)(5) provided that a substantially complete application under that section would be deemed approved as of the 120th day of receipt by the OCC of the substantially complete application, unless the OCC denies the application under proposed paragraph (d) of that section. Section 5(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)) prescribes factors for evaluating a substantially complete application: the ability of the applicant (or subsidiary in the case of an insured depository institution), based on financial condition and resources, to meet the requirements of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903); whether any of the applicant's officers or directors have been convicted of a felony offense involving insider trading, embezzlement, cybercrime, money laundering, financing of terrorism, or financial fraud; the competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders of the applicant, its subsidiaries, and parent company, including their record of compliance with laws and regulations and their ability to fulfill any commitments or conditions imposed by their primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator in connection with the application at issue or any prior application; whether the applicant's redemption policy meets the standards under section 4(a)(1)(B) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)); and any other factors established by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator that are necessary to ensure the safety and soundness of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Proposed Sec. 15.30(c) contained the four specific factors established by section 5(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)), cross- referencing proposed Sec. 15.12 for the redemption policy. Section 5(d)(2)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(2)(A)(i)) provides that a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator shall only deny a substantially complete application if the regulator determines that the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in section 5(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)). Section 5(d)(2)(B) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(2)(B)) requires that if a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator denies a substantially complete application, it must provide written notice to the applicant not later than 30 days from the date of denial, explaining the denial with specificity, including all findings with respect to identified material shortcomings and actionable recommendations on how the applicant could address such shortcomings. Proposed Sec. 15.30(d) set forth these provisions in regulation. Section 5(d)(2)(C) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(2)(C)) requires that an applicant whose application has been denied be given an opportunity for a written or oral hearing before the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator to appeal the denial. The primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator shall notify the applicant of a time, not later than 30 days after receipt of a timely request for a written or oral hearing, and place for the applicant to appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials or provide oral testimony and oral argument. The primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator must notify the applicant of a final determination, the basis for that determination, and specific findings, not later than 60 days after the hearing. If an applicant does not make a timely request for a hearing, the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator shall notify the applicant in writing not later than 10 days after the expiration of the hearing request period that the denial is a final determination. Proposed Sec. 15.30(e) set forth this appeals process, in accordance with the requirements of the GENIUS Act. Proposed paragraph (e)(1) provided that an applicant may request a written or oral hearing to appeal the OCC's denial of a substantially complete application within 30 days of receipt of the OCC's notice of denial. Proposed paragraph (e)(2) provided that, if the applicant does not make a timely appeal for a hearing, the OCC will notify the applicant, in writing and within 10 days of the date the applicant would have been able to request a hearing, that the denial of the substantially complete application is the final determination of the OCC. Proposed paragraph (e)(3) provided that, within 30 days of receiving a timely appeal request, the OCC would have notified the applicant of a time and place at which the applicant may appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials or provide oral testimony and oral argument. Proposed paragraph (e)(4) provided that the Comptroller or authorized delegate would conduct the appeals process, which would be a de novo review of the original substantially complete application, the material before the OCC official who made the initial denial decision, and any information submitted by the applicant at the time of the appeal. Proposed paragraph (e)(4) also provided that the Comptroller or authorized delegate could uphold or reverse the initial decision to deny the application. Proposed paragraph (e)(5) provided that the Comptroller or authorized delegate would have notified the applicant in writing of a final determination within 60 days of the hearing. The final determination would explain the findings on which the determination is based. If the initial decision were upheld, the decision to deny the substantially complete application would have been effective as of the date of the original denial. Finally, proposed paragraph (e)(6) expressly provided that denial of a substantially complete application would not have prohibited the applicant from filing a subsequent application, in accordance with section 5(d)(4) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(4)). Proposed Sec. 15.30(f) would have implemented the safe harbor contained in section 5(f) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(f)), which permits the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators to waive the requirements of the GENIUS Act for up to 12 months for (1) subsidiaries of insured depository institutions and (2) Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers with pending applications as of the Act's effective date. Description of Comments and Final Rule Application Process A few commenters suggested the OCC integrate the licensing of issuers into Federal bank oversight, particularly with respect to subsidiaries of national banks and Federal savings associations because national banks and Federal savings associations may engage in stablecoin activities including issuance and because these entities are already subject to consolidated supervision. Several commenters suggested that to promote administrative efficiency, the OCC expressly allow Sec. 15.30 to supersede all other OCC regulations addressing filing requirements. Other commenters argued against supersession where other licensing frameworks do not displace but rather operate in parallel with the framework of Sec. 15.30. For example, these commenters stated parallel applications for interdependent corporate transactions are necessary where a national bank seeks to establish a subsidiary through which it would issue payment stablecoins. The commenters suggested that a national bank must file both an operating subsidiary application under Sec. 5.34 and an application under Sec. 15.30 seeking approval to issue payment stablecoins through a subsidiary. The substantive licensing requirements for subsidiaries of insured depository institutions, uninsured national banks, Federal branches, and nonbank entities are the same under section 5 of the GENIUS Act. The only difference is that an insured depository institution applies to establish a subsidiary while prospective Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers apply to issue directly. Because the substantive requirements are the same, the OCC believes that it is appropriate to address licensing of all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, including subsidiaries of insured national banks and Federal savings associations, in part 15. In addition, the OCC notes that, pursuant to 12 CFR 5.36(d)(1)(iii), an insured national bank or Federal savings association would not need to submit a separate filing under 12 CFR part 5 to establish a subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC intends the process provided under Sec. 15.30 to be comprehensive for stablecoin issuance and other activities described in Sec. 15.10(a). This is consistent with the OCC's general approach of not requiring multiple filings for the same activity. For example, to the extent that stablecoin issuance would involve membership in a payment system and notice to join a payment system was provided during the filing process, no additional filing under 12 CFR 7.1026 would be required at that time. However, an applicant that wishes to establish an uninsured national trust bank that would be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer will need to apply to form a de novo national bank under 12 CFR 5.20 or convert to a national bank under 12 CFR 5.24 and apply to become a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under 12 CFR 15.30(a) because different statutory and regulatory requirements apply to the formation of national banks and the licensing of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.\170\ The OCC is adopting Sec. 15.30(a) with a non-substantive change to paragraph (a)(1) to clarify that the subsidiary of an insured depository institution, rather than the insured depository institution itself, may issue payment stablecoins under the GENIUS Act. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \170\ Compare 12 U.S.C. 21 et seq. with 12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Proposed paragraph (b)(1)(i) would have required that the applicant submit all the information required by the form for an application under this section that would be available at www.occ.gov. As discussed in greater detail below, the final rule adds as a review criterion, under Sec. 15.30(d)(5), the ability of the applicant to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins. The required application information will be consistent with the enumerated criteria, and information submitted by an applicant should be sufficient to allow the OCC to render a decision on whether the applicant satisfies the enumerated criteria. A commenter recommended that applications submitted pursuant to section 5 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904) be subject to notice and comment because the public may have material information regarding the competence, experience, or integrity of an applicant's officers, directors, or principal shareholders, and their history of compliance with applicable law. The commenter suggested that soliciting this information from the public would complete the record with respect to relatively new institutions that have not undergone supervisory evaluation over a meaningful period and would align with solicitation of public comments in other licensing contexts. Moreover, review of public comments can require material additional resources (especially considering the potential number of applicants) and might not provide the OCC with relevant information in the licensing context to which it may not already have access. Conditional Approvals
    A few commenters urged the OCC to establish a conditional approval 
process under Sec.  15.30 analogous to the process the OCC employs when 
chartering a de novo bank. Commenters suggested that conditional 
approvals be subject to continued compliance with applicable laws and 
regulations, including consumer protection obligations related to fraud 
and error resolution and data privacy and security. Commenters also 
recommended that conditional approvals incorporate a written commitment 
by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to operate in a safe and sound 
manner and by its parent company (where applicable) to serve as a 
source-of-strength. A separate commenter recommended the OCC consider 
certain precursor events such as an enforcement action by another 
regulatory agency or critical safety and soundness issues as triggering 
conditions for the rescission of a Sec.  15.30 conditional approval. 
The OCC agrees with commenters that it would be appropriate to 
explicitly provide for a conditional approval process in the final 
rule.
    Sections 4(h)(1), 5(c)(3)(B), and 6(b)(2) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5903(h)(1), 5904(c)(3)(B), and 5905(b)(2)) recognize the OCC's 
authority to impose conditions on a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. Including language in the final rule clearly articulating the 
OCC's authority to impose conditions through a conditional approval 
will provide transparency and clarity to prospective permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. Accordingly, the OCC is adding a new Sec.  15.30(c) 
stating that the OCC may approve, conditionally approve, or deny a 
substantially complete application under Sec.  15.30 based on a review 
of the factors specified in paragraph (d), which now contains the 
material included in Sec.  15.30(c) of the proposed rule.\173\ The OCC 
is also renumbering Sec.  15.30 in light of this new paragraph. Any 
conditions imposed will be designed to address the statutory review 
factors in section 5(c) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)) and the 
implementing regulation at Sec.  15.30(d), including the ability of the 
applicant to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound 
manner. Under new Sec.  15.30(c), the OCC may, for example, condition 
an approval on the applicant implementing policies and procedures 
necessary to comply with section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903) 
and as described in the applicant's application. The OCC may also 
include a condition requiring an applicant to provide notice before 
significantly deviating from its business plan or to hold reserve 
assets in a manner that adequately protects claims of payment 
stablecoin holders in the event of the applicant's insolvency. In 
general, the OCC expects that permitted payment stablecoin issuers will 
not incur material liabilities other than payment stablecoin 
liabilities or maintain significant assets other than those listed in 
final Sec.  15.11 without the OCC's express, written approval. While 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers could own other assets pursuant to 
final Sec.  15.10, the OCC generally expects these assets to be limited 
in quantity relative to assets permitted under final Sec.  15.11. Under 
proposed subpart D of part 15, the OCC would have reviewed the proposed 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's proposed activities, including 
its projected assets and liabilities, prior to deciding on an 
application. The GENIUS Act does not prescribe an obligation that an 
insured depository institution serve as a source of strength to a 
subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
