Application Standards and Additional Factors
    Proposed Sec.  15.30(c) included the statutory factors in section 
5(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)) that a primary Federal 
payment stablecoin regulator could have considered when evaluating a 
complete application. The OCC requested comment on whether the OCC 
should include additional factors necessary to ensure the safety and 
soundness of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    Several commenters supported inclusion of a principles-based safety 
and soundness factor based on objective benchmarks. Specifically, 
commenters recommended that the safety and soundness evaluation 
consider whether an applicant evidences operational and governance 
capacity to run a stablecoin business responsibly at scale, a mature 
compliance architecture that supports an effective control environment, 
and substantiated financial viability. Commenters recommended that 
operational capacity be assessed based on an applicant's technology 
infrastructure (including smart contract, private key, and 
cybersecurity management), exposure to third-party technology 
dependencies (e.g., blockchain validators, oracle providers, and cloud 
infrastructure), and capacity for business continuity and disaster 
recovery to preserve redemption reliability and avoid systemic 
contagion. Commenters recommended that governance capacity be assessed 
based on an applicant's ownership chain, board and senior management 
responsibility for stablecoin operations, oversight of interaffiliate 
service arrangements and transactions, and staffing adequacy.
    Commenters recommended that the maturity of an applicant's 
compliance architecture be evaluated based on the ability of its 
systems to monitor compliance with BSA/AML and OFAC requirements 
(including capabilities with respect to customer verification, the 
Travel Rule, and transaction monitoring and sanctions screening 
calibrated to the velocity and pseudonymity of on-chain activity), 
consumer compliance (including prohibitions on unfair or deceptive acts 
or practices, fraud prevention, and error resolution and dispute 
rights), and effective third-party oversight (including data privacy 
and security).
    Commenters recommended that financial viability be assessed based 
on reserve integrity observable in real time (including reserve 
composition, transaction flows, counterparty exposure, and funding 
strategy), liquidity management controls, the revenue model and 
projected operational expenses (including adequate funding of an 
applicant's operational backstop at inception), and sustainability of 
an applicant's redemption model under various stress scenarios. One 
commenter also encouraged the OCC to ensure that a nonbank applicant is 
assessed consistent with the principle of ``same risk, same 
regulation'' and also ensure that a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer transferring to OCC jurisdiction has obtained a unanimous vote 
of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee. While agreeing that a 
safety and soundness factor should be explicitly included in the 
regulatory text of the final rule, another commenter recommended 
against a checklist of safety and soundness criteria to avoid stifling 
innovation and discouraging non-traditional, low-risk business models. 
Other commenters opposed adding specific safety and soundness factors 
to the final rule as they would not be anchored in statutory 
requirements and would impose additional hurdles and unnecessary 
administrative gloss.
    The OCC agrees with some of the commenters that the final rule 
would benefit from an explicit reference to safety and soundness in the 
review factors given that it is included in the statutory factors for 
review and denial of an application. The OCC believes that this 
reference should be sufficiently detailed to provide applicants 
guidance. Accordingly, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.30(c) as proposed 
(renumbered as Sec.  15.30(d)) with the addition of a new review factor 
in subparagraph (5). Under the final rule, the OCC will also consider 
the ability of the applicant (or in the case of an applicant that is an 
insured national bank, Federal savings association, or insured Federal 
branch, of the subsidiary of the applicant) to conduct its proposed 
activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the 
applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and 
adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins.
    Some commenters expressed concern that they believe the standards 
under proposed Sec.  15.30 are weaker than those established for 
approvals of insured de novo banks. Specifically, commenters were 
concerned that the proposal did not address the convenience and needs 
of the community that an applicant intends to serve or require 
consistency of an applicant's corporate powers with the purposes of the 
Federal Deposit Insurance Act (i.e., ensuring the safety and soundness 
of FDIC-insured depository institutions and consumer protection). The 
GENIUS Act does not apply deposit insurance requirements to payment 
stablecoin issuers. Section 4(e) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(e)) 
explicitly states that payment stablecoins shall not be subject to 
deposit insurance by the FDIC. The OCC believes that the statutorily 
enumerated approval factors under Sec.  15.30, combined with the 
additional safety and soundness requirement under the final rule, are 
sufficient for the OCC to make an appropriate determination under Sec.  
15.30, particularly in light of the limited activities and authorities 
of permitted payment stablecoin issuers relative to insured depository 
institutions.
    One commenter recommended the OCC periodically revise application 
standards and processes to ensure that they remain appropriately 
tailored to observed risks and market developments. The OCC may engage 
in future rulemaking to revise this approach, as needed, as it gains 
additional experience and data concerning the application process.
Denial
    Section 5(d)(2)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5904(d)(2)(A)(i)) provides that a primary Federal payment stablecoin 
regulator shall only deny a substantially complete application if the 
Federal payment stablecoin regulator determines that the applicant's 
activities would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in 
section 5(c) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(c)). Section 5(d)(2)(B) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(2)(B)) requires that if a primary 
Federal payment stablecoin regulator denies a substantially complete 
application, it must provide written notice to the applicant not later 
than 30 days from the date of denial, explaining the denial with 
specificity, including all findings with respect to identified material 
shortcomings and actionable recommendations on how the applicant could 
address such shortcomings. Proposed Sec.  15.30(d) set forth the bases 
and process for denial of a substantially complete application. The OCC 
received no comments on proposed Sec.  15.30(d) other than the comments 
addressing timing concerns addressed above. The OCC is making five 
technical changes. First, the OCC is renumbering Sec.  15.30(d) to 
Sec.  15.30(e) and adjusting the references within Sec.  15.30(e) in 
light of new paragraph (c). Second, the OCC is breaking up Sec.  
15.30(e)(1) into two new paragraphs (e)(1) and (e)(2). Third, the final 
rule includes a new paragraph (e)(3) stating that the denial of a 
substantially

[[Page 67114]]

complete application does not prohibit the applicant from filing a 
subsequent application. This provision previously appeared in proposed 
paragraph (e)(6). Since the provision concerns the denial of 
substantially complete applications, the OCC is moving it to final 
paragraph (e). This provision would ensure that the OCC retains its 
authority under the remainder of proposed Sec.  15.30 and section 5 of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904) and would provide for appropriate 
review of applications. The OCC is also replacing the word 
``disapproval'' with ``denial'' to more closely align with the relevant 
statutory language. Finally, the OCC is breaking up certain paragraphs 
from the proposal into separate new paragraphs and renumbering 
appropriately. The OCC is otherwise adopting Sec.  15.30(d) as 
proposed.
Appeals
    Proposed Sec.  15.30(e) set forth the appeals process, in 
accordance with the requirements of section 5(d)(2)(C) of the GENIUS 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(2)(C)). The OCC received no comments on proposed 
Sec.  15.30(e) and is finalizing it as proposed with minor 
clarifications.
    First, the paragraph is renumbered as Sec.  15.30(f). Second, Sec.  
15.30(f)(1) has been rewritten slightly for clarity. The revised 
paragraph states that an applicant may request a hearing to appeal the 
OCC's denial of a substantially complete application within 30 days of 
receipt of the OCC's notice of denial. The request for a hearing must 
be in writing. The applicant may request that the hearing be on the 
written record, oral testimony and oral argument, or both. Third, the 
OCC is clarifying in final Sec.  15.30(f)(2) that the OCC will notify 
the applicant in writing within 10 days of the last date the applicant 
would have been able to request a hearing. The addition of the word 
``last'' removes ambiguity and ensures that applicants have sufficient 
time to request an appeal. The OCC is also revising final paragraph 
(f)(3) to provide additional clarity. The revised paragraph states that 
within 30 days of receiving a timely appeal request, the OCC will 
notify the applicant of a time and place at which the applicant may 
appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials, 
provide oral testimony and oral argument, or both. If filing a written 
appeal, the applicant must submit in writing all documents and 
arguments that the applicant wishes to be considered. The OCC is also 
revising final paragraph (f)(4) to replace the words ``de novo'' with 
``anew.'' The OCC is also breaking apart paragraphs (f)(4) and (f)(5) 
into multiple subparagraphs. The OCC is also adding new paragraph 
(f)(6) to clarify that the OCC will determine the procedures for a 
hearing under paragraph (f), including, but not limited to, the 
duration of the hearing; the order and timing of presentations, if 
applicable; and the deadlines and requirements for submission of 
written material. Finally, as discussed above, the OCC is moving 
proposed paragraph (e)(6) concerning submission of a subsequent 
application after denial so that it is in the paragraph concerning 
denials of applications. The OCC notes that the appeals process set 
forth in Sec.  15.30(f) is the exclusive means of appealing the OCC's 
determination under Sec.  15.30 within the OCC. Other processes, such 
as those set forth in 12 CFR part 4, are inapplicable.
Waiver Under Section 5(f) of GENIUS Act
    As discussed briefly above, proposed Sec.  15.30(f) provided that 
pursuant to section 5(f) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(f)), the OCC 
could waive the requirements of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903) for up to 12 months for subsidiaries of insured depository 
institutions and for Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers with 
pending applications as of the Act's effective date.
    A few commenters suggested the OCC adopt standards for review of 
waiver determinations that consider (1) the size, scope, and complexity 
of an applicant and its proposed activities; (2) the nature, scope, and 
duration of the requested waiver; (3) the applicant's existing 
supervisory framework and regulatory oversight; and (4) the applicant's 
risk management, compliance, and governance capabilities relative to 
the requirements being waived. Other commenters were generally 
concerned that waiver from the reserve, redemption, or capital 
requirements may pose systemic risks and that waivers should be 
construed narrowly and not used to confer a competitive advantage to 
any single applicant. Commenters also requested that the OCC clarify 
the factors it would consider in determining whether a waiver is in the 
public interest or justified by extraordinary circumstances and 
suggested waivers only be granted where an applicant demonstrates a 
compelling and well-substantiated need for the relief such as technical 
infeasibility based on existing infrastructure.
    One commenter suggested the OCC grant waivers subject to conditions 
necessary to ensure safe and sound operations and to mitigate potential 
risks to the broader financial system. Another commenter recommended 
that the OCC establish a transition mechanism or exemptive relief for 
noncompliance while applications remain pending rather than require an 
applicant to submit a waiver request. A third commenter recommended 
that the OCC distinguish between waivers at initial application and 
those meant to accommodate product evolution or market expansion. The 
same commenter also suggested that the OCC publish a public registry of 
waiver decisions to avoid differential treatment of similarly situated 
applicants and to produce consistent results. Conversely, one commenter 
stated that the waiver standards under proposed Sec.  15.30(f) are 
sufficient and any additional considerations would add unnecessary 
administrative gloss and complexity.
    After considering the comments, the OCC is adopting Sec.  15.30(f) 
with certain changes. Consistent with the language of section 5(f) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(f)), the final rule is not limited to 
waiving the requirements of section 4 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903) and 
instead refers to the GENIUS Act and part 15 more broadly.\174\ The 
final rule renumbers Sec.  15.30(f) as Sec.  15.30(g) and makes 
conforming renumbering changes throughout. The final rule also 
clarifies that the effective date of the GENIUS Act is January 18, 
2027, and moves certain language from paragraph (g)(3) to paragraph 
(g)(3)(i). An applicant seeking a waiver under final Sec.  15.30(g) 
should explain the basis for its request, the extent of the 
requirement(s) to be waived, the potential for disruptions to existing 
operations, and the applicant's plan to come into compliance with the 
relevant requirements. This information will enable the OCC to 
determine whether a waiver request is in the public interest or whether 
there are extraordinary circumstances justifying the waiver. Items that 
the OCC may consider in evaluating a waiver would include whether the 
waiver would pose prudential, compliance, or other concerns of a 
magnitude that would make a grant of waiver imprudent or impractical.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \174\ For example, the OCC could waive the limitation in section 
3(a) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(a)) that provides that it shall be 
unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC will make waiver determinations following receipt of the 
initial waiver request. While the OCC may grant a waiver for up to 12 
months, the OCC does not anticipate that a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer will need the full 12 months to come into compliance with the 
GENIUS Act. Additionally, while the waiver

[[Page 67115]]

provision allows the OCC to waive the requirements of the Act, the OCC 
retains discretion to choose which provisions of the Act to waive. The 
OCC generally expects that any such waivers will be limited to the 
relief necessary to ensure that it is not impossible or impracticable 
to comply with the Act. Further, in line with current OCC practice, the 
OCC plans to regularly publish, on its publicly facing website, 
conditional approvals and other decision letters.
    Two commenters also suggested that waiver requests under section 
5(f) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(f)) be subject to public notice 
and an opportunity to comment. One of the commenters was concerned that 
granting relief from the reserve, redemption, or capital requirements 
may affect the stability of the broader stablecoin market, the 
competitive position of compliant issuers, and the interests of 
consumers and counterparties. The commenter stated that public notice 
and comment would address this concern by permitting market 
participants and other affected parties to identify potential systemic 
or competitive risks and support consistent application of the GENIUS 
Act across the supervised population. Section 5(f) of the GENIUS Act 
(12 U.S.C. 5904(f)) does not require applicants seeking waiver to 
publish notice, and the OCC is not codifying a requirement to seek 
public comment on a waiver. Nevertheless, the OCC retains authority to 
request comment on waiver filings that would benefit from public 
comment concerning the factors set forth in Sec.  15.30(g) of the final 
rule.
    Two commenters supported interagency coordination to promote 
consistency and competitive neutrality across section 5(f) waiver 
regimes. The OCC has extensive experience in processing applications in 
coordination with other regulators to streamline application review and 
avoid regulatory deadlock. The OCC will continue to coordinate 
implementation of the GENIUS Act with the other primary Federal payment 
stablecoin regulators, as appropriate.
    Proposed Sec.  15.30(g) set forth the statutory bases and process 
for the OCC's ability to nullify the approval of a substantially 
complete application under proposed Sec.  15.30. The OCC received no 
comments on paragraph (g), renumbered as Sec.  15.30(h), and is 
adopting it with minor changes. Specifically, the final rule deletes 
the word ``thereunder'' as unnecessary. The OCC believes that the 
provisions in paragraph (h) will help preserve the integrity of the 
application process and are aligned with those in its licensing process 
under 12 CFR part 5.\175\ The OCC notes that it rarely, and only in 
extraordinary circumstances, nullifies decisions under Sec.  5.13(h).

4. General Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers Framework
    Section 18 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916) generally addresses 
foreign issuers and provides an exemption from the prohibitions of 
section 3 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902) for issuers that meet certain 
requirements. Under section 18, for an issuer to be exempt from those 
prohibitions, among other conditions, the Secretary of the Treasury 
must determine that the issuer is subject to regulation and supervision 
by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator that has a regulatory and 
supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act. In addition, the 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer must register with, and be subject to 
ongoing monitoring by, the OCC. Section 18 also contemplates that the 
Secretary of the Treasury may create and implement reciprocal 
arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States 
and jurisdictions with payment stablecoin regulatory regimes that are 
comparable to the requirements established under the GENIUS Act. The 
OCC proposed to implement the provisions of the GENIUS Act relating to 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC is responsible in 
Sec. Sec.  15.31 through 15.33. A discussion of comments received and 
the changes to those particular sections follows.
    Some commenters provided broad, overarching comments concerning the 
OCC's implementation of provisions relating to foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers. One commenter stated that the OCC should adhere to 
the principle of national treatment in its rulemaking and 
interpretation of the GENIUS Act, which the commenter said would 
support robust competition, market liquidity, and diversified sources 
of credit. One commenter suggested that the OCC's rulemaking authority 
with respect to foreign payment stablecoin issuers relates only to 
standards for approval of registration requests and the process for 
appealing denials of registration requests because the Department of 
the Treasury is charged more broadly with rulemaking authority to carry 
out section 18 of the GENIUS Act. Several comments focused on how a 
foreign regime is determined to be comparable to the GENIUS Act. Some 
commenters stated that the OCC's role does not extend to evaluating the 
quality of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's home-country 
regulations. One commenter suggested that the OCC clarify the criteria 
by which state and foreign supervisory regimes are evaluated for 
equivalence, including objective benchmarks for reserve localization, 
liquidity coverage, and supervisory intensity. Another commenter 
suggested that the OCC should adopt a stringent comparability standard 
that requires foreign regimes to demonstrate substantive equivalence--
not merely formal similarity--to United States reserve quality, audit 
standards, redemption protections, and AML/CFT requirements. The 
commenter asserted that U.S.-based issuers must not be placed at an 
economic disadvantage relative to foreign issuers operating under less 
rigorous regimes. The commenter also noted that the OCC should require 
ongoing monitoring and periodic recertification of foreign regime 
comparability and should establish clear triggers for the suspension or 
revocation of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer if that 
jurisdiction's standards deteriorate. The commenter also requested 
clarification of how the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee will 
evaluate foreign regimes and what specific role public input will have 
in that evaluation process. A commenter further stated that the OCC 
should not extend the regime applicable to permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers to foreign issuers not expressly provided for in the Act as 
Treasury is responsible for assessing the comparability of home-country 
requirements. One commenter suggested that the OCC publish guidance, 
interpretive materials, or supervisory statements setting out how each 
substantive requirement in the proposed rule applies to foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers, including where functional equivalence with home-
jurisdiction standards will be recognized and what the process is for 
demonstrating that equivalence.
    The final rule, like the proposed rule, does not require the OCC to 
evaluate the quality of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's home-
country regulations. That role is reserved for the Secretary of the 
Treasury. With respect to requirements of registration, the final rule, 
like the proposal, adheres closely to the statutory requirements with 
certain additional clarifications necessary to effectuate a 
registration process and give market participants clarity on how to 
register with the OCC.
    A few commenters argued that the OCC should not prescribe 
substantive requirements for foreign payment stablecoin issuers in the 
United States. A commenter stated that proposed subpart D should more 
closely reflect the statutorily specified role of the OCC

[[Page 67116]]

regarding the substantive regulation of foreign issuers while 
preserving the OCC's supervisory oversight. A commenter stated that it 
should not be necessary for the OCC to create any new requirements in 
the registration process beyond what is required by the Act. One 
commenter suggested that foreign payment stablecoin issuers should be 
subject to requirements that achieve equivalent outcomes as the 
requirements imposed on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Some 
commenters requested that there be no requirement limiting foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers to a single brand of payment stablecoin. 
Some commenters also stated that foreign payment stablecoin issuers 
should be required to redeem at par to provide parity with permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers, which must redeem at par. Commenters also 
asked whether foreign payment stablecoin issuers have an obligation to 
redeem with respect to any payment stablecoin holder. A few commenters 
discussed reserve requirements and the treatment of yield. One 
commenter suggested that the requirements addressing the interface 
between the issuer and United States customer and United States 
infrastructure, for example, reserve requirements, United States 
customer determination, and yield prohibition, should apply directly to 
foreign issuers. The commenter also suggested that the OCC should 
consider the Financial Action Task Force's March 2026 report on the 
regulation and supervision of offshore virtual asset providers in 
shaping its approach.
    Another commenter suggested that the OCC should provide explicit 
guidance on managing conflict-of-law risks and cross-jurisdictional 
regulatory obligations. The commenter also indicated that foreign 
issuers should be subject to requirements proportionate to and 
consistent with those applied to domestic issuers where comprehensive 
consolidated supervision is in place. The commenter noted that more 
extensive requirements on foreign issuers could discourage 
participation without materially improving safety or consumer 
protection.
    A few commenters suggested that the OCC not allow foreign-issued 
stablecoins to operate without reserve verification. The commenters 
argued that United States issuers should not be subject to rules that 
are more stringent than those for foreign issuers. Under the OCC's 
rule, foreign issuers are subject to the same reporting requirements as 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers, and monthly reporting requires 
providing information about reserve assets.
    The Act imposes substantive requirements on foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers, which the final rule, like the proposed rule, 
implements. These requirements include the yield prohibition in section 
4(a)(11) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)), the requirement to hold 
reserves sufficient to meet liquidity demands of United States 
customers in section 18(a)(3) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)), and 
the requirement to be subject to ongoing monitoring in section 18(c)(2) 
of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(2)). As described in greater detail 
below, the final rule imposes certain requirements directly related to 
the statute but does not impose all of the requirements applicable to 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC believes that imposing 
all such requirements on foreign payment stablecoin issuers would be 
inconsistent with the role of the Secretary of the Treasury in 
evaluating a foreign regime to determine if the regime is comparable to 
the GENIUS Act. The Secretary of the Treasury also retains the ability 
to enter into reciprocal arrangements that may include substantive 
requirements with respect to foreign payment stablecoin issuers' 
payment stablecoin activities. Moreover, the OCC may impose, as a 
condition of registration, certain requirements applicable to permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers on foreign payment stablecoin issuers, if 
the OCC determines necessary based on the facts relevant to a 
prospective foreign payment stablecoin issuer's registration. The OCC 
intends to use such conditions, as appropriate, based on the particular 
facts, including the degree to which the payment stablecoin circulates 
in the United States. With respect to a limitation on issuing more than 
one brand of payment stablecoin, as discussed more extensively in the 
portion of this supplementary information addressing subpart B of part 
15, the OCC is not adopting any such requirement in regulation text for 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers or foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers. The OCC may, however, impose conditions concerning the 
issuance of multiple brands, as appropriate, based on the facts of a 
particular applicant. The OCC also confirms that foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers, like permitted payment stablecoin issuers, must 
redeem payment stablecoins at par. This requirement follows from the 
definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5901(22)), which provides that the issuer is obligated to 
convert, redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin for a fixed 
amount of monetary value, not including a digital asset denominated in 
a fixed amount of monetary value. As with a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer, a foreign payment stablecoin issuer would likewise 
be required to redeem from any payment stablecoin holder, subject to 
appropriate onboarding. Although foreign payment stablecoin issuers 
might generally interact with a small number of customers (e.g., 
exchanges), they should ensure that they have the capacity to onboard 
and redeem from other payment stablecoin holders. This approach is 
consistent with the definition of payment stablecoin and helps ensure 
parity between permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers.
    Several commenters discussed issues relating to capital 
requirements for foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter 
supported having no formal capital requirements on registered foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter suggested that a capital 
requirement should be applied to the United States operations of 
foreign issuers. Another commenter stated that the OCC should apply 
subpart E to the United States operations of foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers, and it should do so with respect to United States operational 
continuity, United States compliance and control functions, United 
States customer servicing, United States legal and resolution risks, 
and United States wind-down capacity. Another commenter suggested that 
foreign issuers should be required to assess capital adequacy on a 
quarterly basis using the requirements in proposed subpart E. The 
commenter suggested that the foreign issuer determine capital based on 
total issuance activity that occurs in the United States over the 
quarterly assessment period. The commenter recommended that the burden 
fall on the foreign issuer to conduct conversions between relevant 
currencies. The commenter also recommended that the OCC require foreign 
issuers to submit a report demonstrating compliance with this 
assessment on the same quarterly frequency. One commenter suggested 
that the OCC should require foreign issuers that seek to operate in the 
United States to be subject to home-country capital requirements that 
are consistent with capital requirements to which domestic permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers are subject. The commenter further noted the 
importance of the OCC establishing a standardized framework to 
determine

[[Page 67117]]

the minimum capital requirements applicable to domestic permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers. A few commenters discussed adopting a 
functional equivalence approach. One commenter suggested that applying 
capital requirements to foreign issuers' United States operations would 
put foreign and domestic issuers in comparable positions. The commenter 
noted that if a foreign issuer is subject to comparable capital 
requirements under its home-jurisdiction regulatory framework, then the 
OCC should recognize those requirements of the relevant regulator. The 
commenter further noted that if no comparable home-jurisdiction capital 
framework exists for the foreign issuer, then the OCC should have 
discretion to apply proportionate capital requirements according to the 
scale and risk profile of the issuer's United States operations. 
Another commenter also supported applying capital requirements to 
United States operations of foreign issuers registered with the OCC. 
The commenter also suggested that the OCC should not require additional 
capital beyond what the home-country capital regime had already 
mandated where a foreign issuer's home-country regulatory framework 
imposed more stringent capital requirements than the United States 
requirements. Another commenter suggested that the OCC should apply 
capital or operational backstop expectations to the U.S.-facing 
operations of foreign payment stablecoin issuers in order to avoid 
asymmetries between domestic and foreign entities. The commenter noted 
that if a foreign issuer serves United States customers, then there 
should be a credible and accessible financial backstop supporting those 
United States obligations rather than an assumption that other 
protections will be available. The commenter suggested that the 
determination should be based on the foreign issuer's United States 
operations and United States customer exposure rather than on the 
foreign issuer's entire consolidated balance sheet. The commenter noted 
that this approach would be more consistent with the risks the OCC aims 
to address and would avoid transforming the United States registration 
framework into a duplicative capital regime for the issuer's global 
business. The commenter additionally suggested that home-jurisdiction 
resources, where those resources are enforceable and available for the 
protection of United States customers, should be recognized. The same 
commenter also suggested that the OCC should require that foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers maintain accessible United States-located 
operational backstop resources sufficient to support their United 
States-customer obligations. The commenter noted that this measure 
would be undertaken in order to create a credible United States 
safeguard rather than duplicative double-capitalization between the 
United States requirements and a comparable reciprocity regime.
    The final rule, like the proposal, imposes no direct requirement on 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers related to capital. As discussed in 
greater detail below, the OCC anticipates that comparability 
determinations and reciprocal arrangements will be generally sufficient 
to ensure that the United States operations of foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers are appropriately capitalized. In addition, the OCC 
may, to the extent not sufficiently addressed by the home-jurisdiction 
or reciprocal arrangement, impose capital requirements as a condition 
of registration.
    One commenter emphasized that it is appropriate to recognize the 
United States Federal framework already applicable to foreign banks' 
United States presence when operationalizing the permitted payment 
stablecoin framework. Although the International Banking Act applies to 
the United States operations of foreign banks, the GENIUS Act includes 
additional requirements related to foreign issuers of payment 
stablecoins in the United States.
    One commenter asserted that the proposed rule imposes asymmetric 
regulatory burdens that disadvantage permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers while leaving foreign competitors largely unaffected. The 
commenter suggested that the OCC should compare the effective 
regulatory burden against the benefits actually received for foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers. The final rule is consistent with the 
provisions relating to foreign payment stablecoin issuers in the 
statute. The OCC notes that, under section 18, a foreign issuer is only 
exempt from the prohibitions of section 3 if, among other conditions, 
the Secretary of the Treasury determines that the foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer is subject to a regulatory and supervisory regime 
that is comparable to the requirements established under the GENIUS 
Act. Thus, these issuers will be subject to certain requirements 
outside of this final rule. In addition, foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers may be subject to additional requirements pursuant to 
reciprocal arrangements or individualized conditions imposed under the 
registration process.
5. Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers (Sec.  15.31)
    Section 18(a) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)) exempts a 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer from the prohibitions of section 3 of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5902) if it meets all of the following 
requirements: (1) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is subject to 
regulation and supervision by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator 
that has a regulatory and supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS 
Act with respect to payment stablecoins, as determined by the Secretary 
of the Treasury under section 18(b) of the GENIUS Act; (2) the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the OCC pursuant to Sec.  
15.32; (3) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer holds reserves in a 
United States financial institution sufficient to meet liquidity 
demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a 
reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the 
Treasury under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(d)); and 
(4) the foreign country in which the foreign payment stablecoin issuer 
is domiciled and regulated is not subject to comprehensive economic 
sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary 
of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money 
laundering concern. The OCC proposed Sec.  15.31(a) to implement this 
exemption.
    Commenters requested additional clarity both as to what constitutes 
a United States customer and as to what would be sufficient to meet the 
liquidity demands of United States customers. In particular, commenters 
requested clarity on how to determine if liquidity was sufficient 
(e.g., what measures should be used, what thresholds a foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer must meet). One commenter suggested that the OCC 
adopt a flexible, principles-based approach to estimating United States 
customer liquidity demands for foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One 
commenter suggested that the OCC should confirm how residency for 
purposes of ``United States customer'' will be determined in practice. 
In particular, the commenter suggested that United States customers 
should be limited to persons with direct contractual or onboarding 
relationships with the issuer. The commenter also requested that the 
OCC confirm that the residence information from KYC checks of direct 
customers would be sufficient to determine whether a customer is a 
resident of the United States. One commenter stated that foreign 
issuers

[[Page 67118]]

will not always be able to precisely determine whether every holder is 
a United States customer, and that the rule should not require a single 
rigid methodology or rely on proxies for the estimated number of United 
States holders. This commenter further stated that foreign issuers may 
be able to identify United States nexus through a combination of 
indicators such as onboarding information for direct customers, IP 
data, wallet analytics, transaction patterns, and other reasonably 
available information.
    One commenter raised concerns regarding how a foreign issuer will 
be able to identify where its tokens circulate, where the payment 
stablecoin holders reside or are located, as well as the nationality of 
payment stablecoin holders. Some commenters advocated for a flexible, 
principles-based approach to requirements for foreign issuers. One 
commenter noted that employing a flexible approach would be 
particularly important until more data becomes available regarding the 
operations of foreign issuers. A number of commenters opposed requiring 
a fixed percentage of reserves to be held at United States financial 
institutions. Several commenters supported a principles-guided, 
outcomes-focused approach that imposes a risk-based standard that 
requires a defensible estimation methodology and periodic reassessment 
with no fixed percentage. These commenters argued that a fixed 
percentage could impose significant cost while bearing little 
relationship to the actual liquidity risk posed by a particular issuer. 
One commenter urged that the methodology adopted by the OCC to 
calculate default reserves should preserve flexibility for Treasury to 
negotiate reciprocal arrangements under section 18(d) of the Act (12 
U.S.C. 5916(d)). One commenter suggested that a methodology should be 
calibrated to the issuer's actual or reasonably estimated United States 
customer exposures with a modest liquidity buffer in the range of 10 to 
15 percent above estimated one-month United States customer 
redemptions. One commenter argued that a fixed percentage would impose 
a significant and potentially excessive burden on foreign issuers whose 
United States customer base represents a small or predictable fraction 
of their total issuance and would be disproportionate relative to the 
actual liquidity risk the requirement is designed to address. One 
commenter suggested that objective measures and thresholds should be 
included for when United States reserve assets are sufficient to meet 
demands of United States customers. The commenter noted the importance 
of ensuring standards are objective without prescribing a rigid 
formula. One commenter suggested that the OCC should not prescribe a 
single rigid methodology because foreign issuers will not always be 
able to determine whether a particular holder is a United States 
customer. One commenter suggested that the OCC should rely on home-
jurisdiction frameworks rather than prescribing detailed United States-
specific customer identification methodologies for foreign issuers, 
especially where those issuers are subject to ongoing supervision by a 
home regulator whose regime has been determined to be comparable under 
the Act. One commenter suggested that the OCC should confirm that 
foreign issuers distributing through regulated intermediaries may rely 
on those intermediaries' customer identification data for purposes of 
estimating their United States customer base, provided appropriate 
contractual arrangements are in place requiring the intermediary to 
share relevant customer data with the issuer for compliance purposes. 
One commenter discussed on-chain reserves, noting that they could 
better enable the issuer to meet redemption requirements and that 
flexible diversification that can be tailored and updated through 
guidance will provide the OCC maximum flexibility to respond to 
changing market conditions.
    A couple of commenters also requested clarification of which 
``United States financial institutions'' may hold reserves for foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers, urging the OCC to include United States 
branches and agencies of foreign banks and, more broadly, any 
institution located or organized in the United States that is 
authorized under Federal or State law to provide custodial or 
safekeeping services for payment stablecoin reserves. One commenter 
also noted that the proposed definitions appear to exclude foreign 
custodians from the custody provisions applicable to covered custodians 
and sub-custodians and asked the OCC to expressly confirm that 
understanding.
    The OCC agrees with commenters that additional guidance is 
necessary to determine what is sufficient to meet the liquidity demands 
of United States customers. As discussed above, the final rule defines 
United States customer as a customer that, at the time of onboarding 
(1) is an individual and resides in the United States, (2) is 
incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any 
State, or (3) has its principal place of business in the United States. 
This revised definition ensures that the customer has a clear nexus to 
the United States and is administrable.
    The final rule clarifies that a United States financial institution 
is an eligible financial institution that is incorporated or organized 
under the laws of the United States or of any State. The Act does not 
define financial institution, and it has been defined broadly in the 
context of other banking laws. The final rule uses ``eligible financial 
institution'' in this context. Eligible financial institutions 
generally are persons that are eligible to hold reserve assets in 
custody under section 10 of the GENIUS Act and otherwise comply with 
section 10 of the Act. As any entity holding reserve assets would be 
required to comply with section 10, the use of ``eligible financial 
institution'' broadly defines the scope of ``financial institutions'' 
under section 18(a)(3) of the Act, consistent with the Act's use of the 
term financial institution and with its structure.
    To effect the Act's requirement that the financial institution must 
be a ``United States'' financial institution, final Sec.  
15.31(a)(3)(i) confirms that the eligible financial institution must be 
incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any 
State. As the statute makes clear, the financial institution itself--as 
opposed to a branch, agency, or other office--must be a United States 
entity.
    The OCC also recognizes that there may be difficulties in 
determining what is sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United 
States customers. Accordingly, the final rule includes four different 
options that clarify how foreign payment stablecoin issuers can 
demonstrate compliance with the requirement in section 18(a)(3) of the 
Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)). Final Sec.  15.31(a)(3)(i) provides that a 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer must hold reserves in eligible 
financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the 
United States or any State that are sufficient to meet the liquidity 
demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a 
reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the 
Treasury under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(d)). 
This largely restates the statutory requirement in section 18(a)(3) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)). Paragraph (a)(3)(ii) sets forth 
the relevant options to achieve compliance with the requirement in 
section 18(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)). Under 
paragraph (a)(3)(ii), reserves are sufficient to meet the liquidity 
demands of United States customers only if the foreign payment

[[Page 67119]]

stablecoin issuer complies with one of four alternatives. Under one 
alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would (1) attest 
that fewer than 50 percent of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's 
outstanding issuance value is held by payment stablecoin holders 
located in the United States; and (2) hold reserves in eligible 
financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the 
United States or any State, the value of which equals or exceeds 50 
percent of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's outstanding issuance 
value. Under the second alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin 
issuer would (1) attest that it holds substantially all of its reserves 
in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the 
laws of the United States or any State and (2) hold substantially all 
of its reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or 
organized under the laws of the United States or any State. These first 
two alternatives are intended to provide simple and clear paths for 
compliance. Depending on the business model of a foreign issuer, these 
two alternatives may or may not be viable. Accordingly, the OCC is 
including two additional means of establishing compliance that, while 
somewhat more complicated, could accommodate a wider variety of 
business models than the first two alternatives. Under the third 
alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would ensure, on an 
ongoing basis, that the value and composition of reserves held in 
eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the 
laws of the United States will be capable of supporting timely 
redemption requests from United States customers under both normal 
conditions and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate 
conditions, including, to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of 
reserves.\176\ This alternative entails ongoing assessment of liquidity 
demands and recalibration of amounts held in United States financial 
institutions. Under the final alternative, the foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer would submit a detailed proposal to meet the 
requirements of paragraph (a)(3)(i) for the OCC's approval. The foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer would need to respond to all OCC requests for 
additional information regarding the proposal, receive the OCC's 
written approval of the proposal, and comply, on an ongoing basis, with 
the proposal approved by the OCC, including any conditions and 
limitations imposed on such approval by the OCC. This final option is 
intended to provide flexibility for foreign payment stablecoin issuers 
that can demonstrate alternative means of complying with paragraph 
(a)(3)(i) while ensuring that the OCC has the opportunity to opine on 
whether the method is reasonable.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \176\ This is similar to the requirement in Sec.  15.13(a)(9)(i) 
that requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to ensure that 
the reserve asset portfolio, taken as a whole, is capable of 
supporting timely redemption under both normal and stressed 
conditions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Paragraph (a)(3)(iii) of Sec.  15.31 imposes a limitation similar 
to that applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers under Sec.  
15.11 and provides that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must only 
withdraw reserves in excess of the amount required under paragraph 
(a)(3)(i) after appropriate due diligence and confirmation that the 
withdrawal would not cause the reserves held in eligible financial 
institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United 
States or any State to fall below the amount required under paragraph 
(a)(3)(i), calculated as of the time and date of withdrawal.
    Aside from the changes to paragraph (a)(3), the OCC is making one 
additional non-substantive change to paragraph (a). Section 15.31(a)(1) 
of the final rule has been reworded slightly to refer to the 
requirements of paragraph (a), rather than the broader language that 
was in the proposal. The OCC is otherwise finalizing Sec.  15.31(a) as 
proposed.
    One commenter suggested that the OCC should provide clarity on the 
criteria for determining whether a foreign issuer has met the 
requirements of the Act sufficient to exempt it from the prohibition, 
the timeline and process for OCC review of foreign registration 
applications, and the enforcement consequences for digital asset 
service providers that continue to offer noncompliant foreign 
stablecoins after the applicable deadline. The commenter noted that 
without additional clarity, the United States will compete on unequal 
terms with foreign issuers that face no equivalent obligations. The 
prohibitions in section 3 of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902) are outside of 
the scope of this rulemaking. The Department of the Treasury has issued 
a notice of proposed rulemaking to address the requirements in section 
3 of the Act.\177\

Another commenter stated that the OCC's requirements for foreign issuers should be no less stringent than those for United States issuers. A commenter suggested that the OCC should develop bilateral supervisory cooperation arrangements with comparable home regulators to facilitate information sharing and reduce duplicative reporting. One commenter suggested that weekly confidential reporting is not appropriate for foreign issuers because foreign issuers are subject to primary supervision from their home-state regulator and this would be duplicative without corresponding benefit. One commenter provided revised rule text for proposed Sec. 15.31(b)(2)(i) reflecting the commenter's suggestions. One commenter suggested that any reporting disparity between domestic permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers would create a two-tier market in which consumers, counterparties, and market participants may reasonably assume equivalent protections while in fact receiving less transparency from foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter suggested that if the OCC were to allow foreign payment stablecoin issuers to substitute home-jurisdiction reports under a reciprocity arrangement, that substitution should be available only where the foreign reporting is demonstrably equivalent in scope, timeliness, and assurance. One commenter suggested that the OCC should tailor its supervisory, examination, and reporting requirements regarding non-U.S. activity of foreign payment stablecoin issuers to what is reasonably necessary to monitor the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's United States payment stablecoin activity and its compliance with the Act, including United States reserve sufficiency, and any United States financial stability or illicit finance risks. One commenter discussed what foreign payment stablecoin issuers ought to be required to disclose. The commenter suggested that foreign payment stablecoin issuers should be required to disclose that their stablecoin issuance activity originates from, and is regulated by, a foreign jurisdiction as well as the specific bases on which it satisfies the Act's requirements. The commenter noted that these disclosures would help market participants distinguish between stablecoins issued under the GENIUS Act and those issued under foreign regimes. The commenter supported permitting foreign payment stablecoin issuers to use a single unified brand across jurisdictions only where the Secretary of the Treasury has entered into a reciprocal arrangement with the relevant foreign jurisdiction. The OCC may impose conditions relating to additional disclosures, as appropriate, based on the risks presented by and the scale of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's United States operations. After consideration of the comments, the OCC is adopting Sec. 15.31(b) as proposed with one technical change to paragraph (b)(1). Instead of stating that the foreign payment stablecoin issuer must fully accede to any request by the OCC regarding reporting, supervision, or examination of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer, the final rule states that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer registered with the OCC pursuant to Sec. 15.32 is subject to reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as determined by the OCC. the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(1)(C)) are not exhaustive.
    Given the unique and novel character of foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers, the OCC proposed certain conditions applicable to all foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has approved a 
registration. Section 18(c)(1)(C)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5916(c)(1)(C)(iii)) requires the OCC to consider whether a foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer will provide adequate information to the OCC 
as the OCC determines is necessary to determine compliance with the 
GENIUS Act. Proposed Sec.  15.32(d)(1) would have required that, upon 
request by the OCC, a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must grant the 
OCC prompt and complete access to all officers, directors, employees, 
and agents and to all relevant books, records, or documents of any 
type, in a form and location accessible to the OCC in the United 
States. This paralleled the provisions regarding access to books and 
records in proposed Sec.  15.14(b). Proposed paragraph (d)(2) would 
have further required that the information be provided in English.
    Proposed paragraph (d)(3) would have required information 
sufficient to determine that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer meets 
the reserve requirements of section 18(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)). Specifically, foreign payment stablecoin issuers 
would have been required to provide evidence that they hold sufficient 
reserves in the United States to meet liquidity demands of United 
States customers on an ongoing basis unless otherwise permitted under a 
reciprocal arrangement implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury 
under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(d)). Consistent 
with the statute, proposed paragraph (d)(3)(i) would have required the 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer to hold these reserves in United 
States financial institutions. Proposed paragraph (d)(3)(ii) would have 
required the foreign payment stablecoin issuer to provide to the OCC, 
on a monthly basis, a report describing the total number of outstanding 
payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer 
held by United States customers and the amount and composition of the 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer's reserves, including their 
geographic location and average tenor of reserve instruments. The 
proposed rule provided a template to facilitate reporting this 
information. Proposed paragraph (d)(3)(iii) would have required a 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer to promptly notify the OCC through 
its supervisory office on any day in which the issuer fails to meet the 
reserve asset requirements of paragraph (d)(3). Proposed paragraph 
(d)(3)(iv) would have required a foreign payment stablecoin issuer to 
promptly and fully address any deficiency in its compliance with 
proposed paragraph (d)(3) that is explained in writing to the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer by the OCC, including by depositing 
additional liquidity in United States financial institutions to the 
extent doing so would address the deficiency identified. These 
requirements were intended to help ensure that the registered foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer complies with the requirements of section 
18(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)).
    Section 18(c)(2)(B) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(2)(B)) 
requires a foreign payment stablecoin issuer to consent to United 
States jurisdiction relating to enforcement of the GENIUS Act. Proposed 
paragraph (d)(4) would have implemented this provision by requiring 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers to consent to the jurisdiction of 
the Federal courts of the United States and of all United States 
Government agencies, departments, and divisions for purposes of any and 
all claims made by, proceedings initiated by, or obligations to, the 
United States, the OCC, and any other United States Government agency, 
department, or division, in any matter arising under the GENIUS Act and 
other applicable Federal laws. The additional enumerated authorities to 
which consent must be given in proposed paragraph (d)(4) accorded with 
the OCC's standard conditions on approvals for establishment of Federal 
branches under the International Banking Act of 1978 and ensure that 
the OCC and other agencies have the ability to bring actions against 
foreign issuers. Lastly, under proposed paragraph (d)(5), foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers would have been required to comply with all 
understandings, commitments, or conditions contained in any 
determination by the Secretary of the Treasury or any arrangements 
entered into by the United States and the foreign jurisdiction under 
section 18 of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916).
    A couple of commenters suggested frameworks or approaches to how 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers make their records available to the 
OCC pursuant to Sec.  15.32(d)(1) as proposed. While Sec.  15.14, as 
described above, pertains to reports and supervision including OCC 
access to books and records, Sec.  15.14 applies to permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers, and foreign payment stablecoin issuers are not 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers (12 U.S.C. 5901(12)). However, the 
final rule's approach to accessing stablecoin issuer records is 
intended to be consistent between the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer context in Sec.  15.14 and the foreign payment stablecoin issuer 
context here in proposed Sec.  15.32(d)(1) (final Sec.  15.32(e)(1)). 
One commenter suggested that the level of access granted by proposed 
Sec.  15.32(d)(1) could extend the OCC's supervisory authority beyond 
what is necessary to satisfy the OCC's statutory mandate. This 
commenter further argued that the agency should replace the proposed 
standardized monthly report for foreign payment stablecoin issuers with 
a flexible approach to documenting liquidity demands. Another commenter 
suggested integrating the conditions proposed at Sec.  15.32(d) into a 
requirement that permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers write playbooks. These playbooks would 
include, among other things, records sufficient to document various 
requirements. Because of the agency's interest in parity between 
payment stablecoin issuers where practicable at this time, and because 
of the payment stablecoin industry's nascent nature, the agency is 
finalizing Sec.  15.32(e)(1) and (2) as proposed at Sec.  15.32(d)(1) 
and (2). The final rule also includes the monthly report as proposed in 
Sec.  15.32(e)(3) (proposed Sec.  15.32(d)(3)), with technical changes 
consistent with the changes to the report in Sec.  15.11. This rule, as 
finalized, will give the OCC the necessary flexibility to access the 
information it will need to meet its

[[Page 67124]]

obligations under the GENIUS Act and adapt to the expected changes in 
the industry.
    One commenter requested that the OCC require that foreign issuers 
submit to State jurisdiction for applicable State consumer protection 
laws. The commenter suggested that the OCC amend proposed Sec.  
15.32(d)(4), which requires a foreign issuer to consent to United 
States jurisdiction relating to the enforcement of the Act and its 
implementing regulations, but only requires consent to Federal 
jurisdiction. In particular, the commenter requested that the section 
be amended to include consent to the jurisdiction of State agencies for 
purposes of enforcing State consumer protection laws, where 
appropriate. The commenter noted that this requirement could improve 
efficiency by reducing the need for States to litigate jurisdictional 
questions when enforcing clearly applicable laws. The GENIUS Act does 
not reference foreign issuers consenting to State jurisdiction. The OCC 
will not require foreign payment stablecoin issuers to consent to State 
jurisdiction because including such a requirement would go beyond the 
scope of this rulemaking.
    A few commenters discussed civil recovery. One commenter suggested 
that the OCC should make it explicit that registration as a foreign 
issuer constitutes consent to United States judicial process for civil 
recovery orders directed at assets serving United States customers. 
This is outside the scope of this rulemaking, but the OCC will consider 
whether such consent may be appropriate to address in the future.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC is adopting proposed 
paragraph (d) (renumbered as paragraph (e)) with certain changes. Under 
Sec.  15.32(e)(3)(i) of the final rule, a foreign payment stablecoin 
issuer must provide evidence that it complies with Sec.  15.31(a), 
including by providing to the OCC, by noon on the last day of each 
month, a report describing the total number of outstanding payment 
stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer held by 
United States customers and the amount and composition of the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer's reserves, including their geographic 
location and average tenor of reserve instruments. The OCC believes 
that this simplified language reduces duplication. Section 
15.32(e)(3)(ii) specifies that the report required under Sec.  15.32 
must use a format substantially similar to the template in Table 1 to 
the paragraph. The final rule also includes minor technical corrections 
(adding ``issuer'' in final Sec.  15.32(e)(3)(iii)) and updates to the 
template for the monthly report for foreign issuers that align with 
changes to the template for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. These 
updates provide additional clarity for entities that employ multiple 
SPV issuers. Section 15.32(e)(3)(iv) incorporates non-substantive and 
conforming edits including edits to specify that, to meet the 
requirements under Sec.  15.32(e)(3), reserves must be held in eligible 
financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the 
United States or of any State.
    In accordance with section 18(c)(1)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5916(c)(1)(A)(i)), proposed paragraph (e) provided that the OCC 
may reject a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's application for 
registration by providing written notice of the rejection if the OCC 
makes a negative finding with respect to any of the factors described 
in proposed Sec.  15.32(c). Proposed paragraph (e) would have also 
permitted the OCC to reject an application if the OCC determines that 
the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would be unable to comply with 
the conditions in proposed paragraph (d), compliance with which would 
be required for all foreign payment stablecoin issuers registered under 
proposed Sec.  15.32.
    Section 18(c)(1)(D) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(1)(D)) 
provides the opportunity for a foreign payment stablecoin issuer whose 
application was rejected to seek review by appealing the OCC's decision 
within 30 days of receipt of the OCC's written decision. Proposed Sec.  
15.32(f) set forth this appeals process. Proposed paragraph (f) was 
substantially the same as that proposed for appeals of denials under 
proposed Sec.  15.30(e). Proposed paragraph (f) provided that a foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer may request a written or oral hearing to 
appeal the OCC's rejection of an application for registration within 30 
days of receipt of the OCC's notice of rejection. The request for a 
written or oral hearing would have needed to be in writing. If the 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer does not make a timely appeal for a 
hearing under proposed Sec.  15.32, the OCC would have notified the 
applicant, in writing and within 10 days of the date the applicant 
would have been able to request a hearing, that the denial of the 
application is the final determination of the OCC. Within 30 days of 
receiving a timely appeal request, the OCC would have notified the 
applicant of a time and place at which the applicant may appear, 
personally or through counsel, to submit written materials, provide 
oral testimony and oral argument, or both. If the applicant is filing a 
written appeal, it must submit in writing all documents and arguments 
that the applicant wishes to be considered. The Comptroller or 
authorized delegate would have considered all information submitted 
with the original application for registration, the material before the 
OCC official who made the initial decision, and any information 
submitted by the appellant at the time of appeal. The Comptroller or 
authorized delegate would have considered all submitted documentation 
de novo. The Comptroller or authorized delegate would have been able to 
uphold or reverse the initial decision to reject the registration. 
Within 60 days of the hearing, the Comptroller or authorized delegate 
would have notified the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in writing of 
a final determination. The final determination would have explained the 
findings on which the determination was based. If the initial decision 
were upheld, the decision to deny the application would have been 
effective as of the date of the original denial. The denial of an 
application would not have prohibited the applicant from filing a 
subsequent application. One commenter supported the appeals process in 
proposed Sec.  15.32(f).
    Finally, proposed paragraph (g) would have provided for 
nullification of an approval of a registration substantially the same 
as the procedure in proposed Sec.  15.30(g). Thus, under proposed Sec.  
15.32(g)(1), the OCC could nullify the approval of a registration under 
this section if: the OCC discovers a material misrepresentation or 
omission in any information provided to the OCC in the application or 
supporting materials; the decision is contrary to law or regulation 
thereunder; or the decision was granted due to clerical or 
administrative error, or a material mistake of law or fact. Proposed 
paragraph (g)(2) set forth the relevant procedures and provided that, 
when the OCC intends to nullify the approval of a registration, the 
OCC, in its sole discretion, would have: provided the applicant with 
notice of the intended nullification decision and granted the applicant 
an opportunity to present a written submission opposing the intended 
nullification; or taken any other action designed to provide the 
applicant with notice and an opportunity to present its views 
concerning the intended nullification.
    One comment explicitly supported proposed Sec.  15.32(e) and (f). 
The OCC did not receive any other comments on proposed paragraphs (e) 
through (g). The OCC is adopting proposed paragraphs (e) and (g) but 
renumbered as paragraphs (f) and (h). The final rule

[[Page 67125]]

also updates the internal cross-references within those paragraphs. In 
addition, the OCC is adopting proposed paragraph (f) renumbered as 
paragraph (g) with minor changes similar to those in Sec.  15.30(f)(1). 
Accordingly, final Sec.  15.32 makes clear that a foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer may request that an appeal hearing be on the written 
record, oral testimony and oral argument, or both. The final rule also 
clarifies that the OCC will notify the applicant within 10 days of the 
last date that the applicant would have been able to request a hearing. 
The final rule also clarifies that the OCC will determine the 
procedures for an appeal, including, but not limited to, the duration 
of the hearing; the order and timing of presentations, if applicable; 
and the deadlines and requirements for submission of written material. 
The final rule also separates and renumbers several paragraphs from 
proposed paragraphs (e) and (f). The final rule also replaces the word

the language of section 18(c) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)).
7. Revocation or Rescission of Approval (Sec.  15.33)
a. Description of the Proposed Rule
    Section 5(i)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(i)(3)(A)) 
permits the OCC to revoke the approval of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer that does not submit the certification regarding 
implementation of anti-money laundering and economic sanctions 
compliance programs required by section 5(i)(1) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5904(i)(1)). Proposed Sec.  15.14(k) set forth those 
requirements. Similarly, section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)) permits the OCC, in consultation with the 
Secretary of the Treasury, to rescind approval of a registration of a 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer if the OCC determines that the 
foreign payment stablecoin issuer is not in compliance with the 
requirements of the GENIUS Act, including for maintaining insufficient 
reserves or posing an illicit finance risk or financial stability risk.
    Proposed Sec.  15.33(a) would have implemented revocation of 
approval of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's application. 
Proposed paragraph (a)(1) stated that the OCC may revoke approval of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer's application under proposed Sec.  
15.30 if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not submit the 
certification required by proposed Sec.  15.14(k). Proposed paragraph 
(a)(2)(i) stated that the OCC may issue an order to revoke the 
application approval after providing notice to the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer and after providing an opportunity for a hearing. 
Proposed paragraph (a)(2)(ii) provided that the OCC would conduct a 
hearing pursuant to the OCC's Rules of Practice and Procedure in 12 CFR 
part 19. Proposed paragraph (a)(2)(iii) provided for expedited OCC 
action without an opportunity for a hearing if the OCC determines that 
expeditious action is necessary in order to protect the public 
interest. In this situation, the OCC could, in its sole discretion, 
provide the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with notice of the 
intended revocation, grant the permitted payment stablecoin issuer an 
opportunity to oppose the revocation in writing, or take any other 
action designed to provide the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with 
notice and an opportunity to present its views concerning the 
revocation of application approval. Proposed paragraph (a)(3) stated 
that a decision to revoke an application approval would be effective 
upon provision of notice to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, 
unless otherwise specified by the OCC.
    Proposed paragraph (b) provided procedures for rescission of 
approval of a registration of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer. 
Proposed paragraph (b) was substantially the same as proposed Sec.  
15.33(a), except that proposed paragraph (b)(1) referred to the OCC's 
consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, consistent with 
section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)). 
Proposed paragraph (b)(3) provided that a decision to rescind approval 
of a registration is effective upon publication in the Federal 
Register, as required by section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 
U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)), unless otherwise specified by the OCC. The OCC 
could, for example, specify a later effective date than the date of 
publication in the Federal Register. Under proposed Sec.  15.33(b), 
except as otherwise provided, the OCC could have issued an order to 
rescind the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's registration approval 
under proposed Sec.  15.32 after providing notice to the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer and providing an opportunity for a hearing. 
Proposed paragraph (b)(2)(ii) provided that the OCC would conduct a 
hearing under this section pursuant to the OCC's Rules of Practice and 
Procedure in 12 CFR part 19. Proposed paragraph (b)(2)(iii) provided 
that the OCC could act without providing an opportunity for a hearing 
if it determines that expeditious action is necessary in order to 
protect the public interest. Under the proposed rule, if the OCC found 
it necessary to act without providing an opportunity for a hearing, the 
OCC, in its sole discretion, could have: provided the foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer with notice of the intended rescission of approval 
registration; granted the foreign payment stablecoin issuer an 
opportunity to present a written submission opposing rescission of 
approval registration; or taken any other action designed to provide 
the foreign payment stablecoin issuer with notice and an opportunity to 
present its views concerning the rescission of approval registration.
    The revocation and rescission procedures in proposed Sec.  15.33 
largely parallel those for termination of a Federal branch or agency in 
12 CFR 28.24(b). Similar to termination of a Federal branch or agency, 
revocation of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's application 
approval or a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's registration removes 
the entity's authorization to conduct certain business activities in 
the United States.
b. Description of Comments and Final Rule
    The OCC received one comment on proposed Sec.  15.33 noting that 
the OCC should have broader authority to revoke or rescind approval of 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC is adopting Sec.  15.33 
with technical changes. The OCC is changing a reference to rescission 
in paragraph (a)(3) to revocation, consistent with the statute. The 
provisions of Sec.  15.33 directly implement sections 5(i)(3) and 18(c) 
of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5904(i)(3) and 5916(c)). In response to 
the commenter's concerns, the OCC notes that it has enforcement tools 
beyond the revocation contemplated in Sec.  15.33. Further, the effect 
of the OCC's action does not otherwise terminate an entity's corporate 
existence or affect any other rights. The OCC believes that the 
procedures in Sec.  15.33 strike the appropriate balance between 
ensuring that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer receives appropriate process before the 
revocation of its authorization to issue a payment stablecoin in the 
United States and the potential need for expeditious action by the OCC 
when necessary to protect the public interest. In addition, the OCC is 
replacing a reference to the ``OCC's rules of practice and procedures'' 
with ``the OCC's rules of practice and procedure'' in Sec.  
15.33(a)(2)(ii) and Sec.  15.33(b)(2)(ii).

E. Subpart E--Capital and Operational Backstop

    Section 4(a)(4)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C.

be tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment
