2. Capital (Sec.  15.40)
a. Description of Proposed Rule
    Under the proposed rule, regulatory capital for permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers would have consisted of two capital elements, common 
equity tier 1 capital and additional tier 1 capital. These two elements 
are generally consistent with the capital elements for national banks 
and Federal savings associations under 12 CFR part 3. These elements 
consist of common equity, retained earnings, and noncumulative 
perpetual preferred stock that meet certain terms designed to ensure 
significant loss-absorbing capabilities.
    Under the proposed rule, common equity tier 1 capital elements 
would have consisted of common stock instruments (par value, if any, 
and related surplus), retained earnings, and any accumulated other 
comprehensive income (AOCI), all as reported under GAAP. Common stock 
instruments would need to meet various proposed

[[Page 67127]] criteria, including being the most subordinated claim on the issuer's assets, being fully paid-in, having no maturity date, and not being redeemable except with prior OCC approval. Any dividends would have to be fully discretionary, paid out only after fulfillment of any other legal or contractual obligations. In addition, the holders of the instruments must bear losses equally, proportionally, and simultaneously with other holders of common stock instruments. As the most subordinated tier of regulatory capital, common equity tier 1 exhibits the greatest loss absorbency, as any dividends are discretionary and there is no expectation of redemption or repurchase of the instrument, ensuring any operating funds generated can be used for any other business need of the issuer. The proposed rule also included AOCI as a component of common equity tier 1 capital. While this treatment is consistent with the OCC's requirement in 12 CFR part 3, the OCC did not propose the option in 12 CFR part 3 that permits neutralization of AOCI. The OCC permits certain banks the option to neutralize some components of AOCI in part to reduce regulatory capital volatility associated with changes in value of available-for-sale fixed income securities due to changes in interest rates. These changes in value due to interest rate movements are generally more pronounced the longer the remaining maturity of the securities. As permitted payment stablecoin issuers can only hold securities with remaining maturities of 93 days or less as reserve assets, the change in value of these securities due to interest rate movements likely would generate immaterial amounts of AOCI. Additional tier 1 capital would have consisted of instruments that meet a different set of proposed criteria, generally consistent with noncumulative perpetual preferred stock issuances that are classified as equity under GAAP. Generally, these instruments would have been subordinated to all claims except those of common shareholders. Under the proposed rule, the instruments could not have a maturity date but may be callable after at least five years with prior approval of the OCC. To provide additional flexibility to the issuer when needed, the terms of the instrument would have needed to provide for the payment of dividends only if and when declared by the board of directors of the issuer. This feature provides the permitted payment stablecoin issuer the ability to retain earnings and capital if needed. These provisions were intended to help the instrument provide significant loss absorbency by limiting the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's obligations to holders. The OCC's capital framework in 12 CFR part 3 also permits tier 2 capital elements, which primarily consist of tier 2 capital instruments (subordinated debt instruments) and certain allowances for credit losses. However, proposed Sec. 15.40 did not include tier 2 capital elements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Like the proposed rule, the OCC's process for evaluating capital and liquidity requirements for new uninsured national trust banks also considers only common equity tier 1 capital and additional tier 1 capital but not tier 2 capital, so the proposed approach would promote parity among uninsured national trust banks and other permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The proposed rule would not have required any specific ratio between the regulatory capital elements or minimum amounts of any capital element. The OCC's current rule for national banks and Federal savings associations sets minimum ratios for common equity tier 1 capital, tier 1 capital, and total capital. The minimum ratio amount of each tier of capital is designed to promote more loss-absorbing capital by setting the minimum common equity tier 1 ratio at more than half of the minimum total capital ratio. The proposed rule would not have required any specific deductions from regulatory capital for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC's current rule for national banks in 12 CFR part 3 requires deductions from regulatory capital for goodwill, mortgage servicing assets, other intangible assets, and certain other assets such as deferred tax assets. b. Description of Comments and the Final Rule Several commenters addressed the capital elements. Most of these commenters objected to the bank-centric capital element framework and recommended the OCC adopt a measure that would be simpler for issuers to implement, such as tangible equity under GAAP. One commenter supported the proposed elements but requested that the OCC clarify that capital instruments issued under the bank regulatory framework also qualify as capital instruments in the same category in the permitted payment stablecoin issuer framework, in order to avoid the costs of having to reissue capital instruments. A few commenters supported the exclusion of subordinated debt from the capital elements and recommended extending that exclusion to preferred stock as less loss- absorbing than common stock or retained earnings due to required dividend or interest payments and maturities. Numerous commenters recommended that the OCC require deduction of intangible and certain other assets from capital, as these assets generally are not readily liquid, have volatile valuations, or have limited ability to absorb losses during times of stress. These assets include goodwill and deferred tax assets (which often have little or no value in a failure scenario). After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to adopt a capital element framework generally based on GAAP tangible equity. Specifically, any instrument that qualifies as equity under GAAP (including common stock, retained earnings, and certain preferred stock) would qualify as capital for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. This GAAP measure would also incorporate other accounts in the equity section (whether positive or negative), such as treasury stock and accumulated other comprehensive income. In addition, to calculate tangible equity, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would need to deduct any intangible assets (as defined by GAAP) from the capital amount, including goodwill, patents, trademarks, and certain crypto- assets. While not intangible assets under GAAP, the final rule also requires deduction of deferred tax assets (DTAs) for similar reasons. However, as discussed further under the operational backstop requirement, the final rule allows a limited amount of debt based on tier 2 capital instrument criteria \182\ to support a portion of the operational backstop requirement. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \182\ See 12 CFR 3.20(d). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Relying on a measure derived from GAAP, tangible equity would create a simple, transparent measure for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. In addition, most instruments that qualify as common equity tier 1 or additional tier 1 capital under the bank regulatory framework likely would qualify as equity under GAAP without the need for bank issuers to reissue those instruments. Another reason for this measure is that the adjustments to deduct intangible assets and DTAs reflect that those assets generally are not liquid, may have volatile or uncertain valuations, may present wrong-way risk (for example, an issuer that incurs regular losses that decrease retained earnings may need to report goodwill impairment, which further decreases retained earnings), and may have little or no value in case of a permitted [[Page 67128]] payment stablecoin issuer failure. Additionally, the deduction of intangible assets and DTAs, including crypto-assets classified as intangible assets under GAAP, is largely consistent with the OCC's current regulatory capital rules for banks as well as for capital calculations for recent preliminary approvals for national trust bank applicants. While the OCC's regulatory capital rules for banks permit certain timing difference DTAs to avoid deduction and instead receive a risk weight, the final rule at Sec. 15.40(b)(1)(iii) will require a full deduction of all DTAs. Importing the bank capital framework for DTAs would introduce a significant amount of complexity, particularly around categorization of DTAs and various netting and offset provisions, and the final rule for permitted payment stablecoin issuers has no equivalent to a risk-weighted assets framework. However, the final rule allows the DTA deduction to be net of valuation allowances, which are already deducted from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's net income, in order to avoid a double deduction for those amounts. The final rule also includes at Sec. 15.40(b)(2) a deduction from capital for any operational backstop assets funded by equity, i.e., those assets that are not funded by operational backstop debt. The qualifying criteria for operational backstop debt and justification for the deduction are discussed in the following Sec. 15.41 together with other comments on the operational backstop requirement. 3. Minimum Capital and Operational Backstop (Sec. 15.41) a. Description of Proposed Rule The OCC proposed establishing a minimum capital requirement framework based on the lifecycle of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Under this framework, the OCC would have established the minimum capital requirement for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer as part of the chartering or licensing process that will apply for a minimum timeframe, generally three years. For example, based on the recent approvals for national trust banks engaging in stablecoin issuance programs, the OCC would establish a monetary capital amount for each issuer that must be maintained and a portion of which must be maintained in certain liquid assets.\183\ Under this approach, the OCC would consider factors such as projected revenues and expenses, cash burn rates, and expenditures necessary to implement the proposed business plan and activities of the applicant. This analysis may include various scenarios based on projected stablecoin issuance volumes, planned composition of reserves, and projected returns on those reserves in different interest rate environments. During this time, and afterward, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer also would be required to assess its capital adequacy and maintain an amount of capital that is commensurate with its business model and risk profile, subject to review by the OCC. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \183\ OCC News Release 2025-125, ``OCC Announces Conditional Approvals for Five National Trust Bank Charter Applications'' (December 12, 2025), https://occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-occ-2025-125.html. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Under proposed Sec. 15.41, the initial minimum capital requirement would have applied during the ``de novo period,'' generally the three- year period following chartering or licensing by the OCC of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue stablecoins under this proposed rule, or, in the case of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, transitioning to the OCC's regulatory framework. This timeframe could be extended or shortened by the OCC. In proposed Sec. 15.41(a)(1)(i)(B), the OCC would have required a floor of $5 million on the minimum capital requirement during the de novo period. This floor was primarily intended to ensure that every proposed payment stablecoin issuer has sufficient resources to support initial operations, particularly to cover the losses that are expected to occur early in the startup phase of a new permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Based on the OCC's experience with chartering de novo national trust banks seeking to provide stablecoin programs, the OCC determined that minimum capital amounts ranging from $6 million to $25 million would be necessary to establish a viable business model.\184\ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\184\ See id. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- The proposed rule would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to calculate a minimum capital requirement based on an evaluation of the risks associated with its business model and risk profile. This amount would have been based on estimates submitted during the de novo chartering phase, and, after approval, this amount would have needed to incorporate the operating history of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and losses experienced from all sources, including operational risk. The OCC would have reviewed and monitored this requirement and the amount of capital held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer as part of the examination process. The amount of capital held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to appropriately incorporate the operating history and operational risk of the issuer, consistent with the standards described above that the OCC uses to determine the capital requirement for de novo stablecoin issuers. The OCC did not propose any floors on the minimum capital requirement or frameworks for determining a minimum capital requirement for those risks in the rule text. The OCC proposed that a payment stablecoin issuer must hold a designated pool of highly liquid assets to maintain the ongoing operations of the stablecoin issuer during a business disruption, referred to as the operational backstop. These proposed backstop assets would have been independent of the de novo or ongoing capital requirements and any assets held as reserve assets. The purpose of the operational backstop was to help ensure that during a business disruption that impacts operations of the stablecoin issuer, a liquid pool of identifiable assets exists to allow the stablecoin issuer to meet short-term liquidity needs, stabilize the issuer after the disruption, and continue or resume normal operations. The operational backstop would have been calculated based on the actual total expenses of the stablecoin issuer over the past 12 months. These expenses, including for utilities, data processing, and salaries, are highly correlated with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to maintain the operations of its payment stablecoin and stabilize from a business disruption. The operational backstop would have provided a runway for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to evaluate the source of the disruption and potential responses without needing to take urgent action due to lack of funds. The amount of the operational backstop requirement would be calculated each quarter, based on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's total expenses as reported in the four most recent quarterly reports filed under Sec. 15.14 of the proposed rule. For de novo permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the initial requirement would have been based on reasonable expense projections and adjusted each quarter based on actual amounts for that quarter. [[Page 67129]] b. Description of Comments and the Final Rule Calibration of Capital Requirement Many commenters responded to the above-described proposal of individualized minimum capital requirements during and after the ``de novo'' period. Approximately half of these commenters supported the proposed individualized assessment, while the other half recommended that the OCC adopt more objective standards for setting capital requirements. Commenters that supported the proposed approach cited various factors, including that individualized assessments allow for precise tailoring of capital requirements to the business model, risk, and size of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. One commenter noted that the OCC would lack sufficient empirical data on stablecoin operators to propose appropriate standardized capital requirements. Commenters that supported a more objective framework cited numerous factors, including that individualized capital calibration gives the OCC too much discretion to set capital requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Commenters argued this discretion includes the ability to set materially different capital requirements for similar issuers. Some commenters noted that the ``black box'' capital process harms potential new issuers, who will not know their capital requirements until after OCC approval, and stablecoin holders, who will not have objective metrics to compare the financial health of competing permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Numerous commenters noted that the OCC has long established standardized minimum capital requirements for banks, including capital requirements for credit risk, market risk, interest rate risk, and operational risk, which could be used to calibrate a framework for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and reserve assets that are subject to the same risks. A few commenters requested that, however the capital requirement is determined, the OCC should provide a capital discount to permitted payment stablecoin issuers that use the commenter's proprietary technology, blockchain protocol, risk modeling software, or other service. Another commenter requested that capital requirements for new issuers should phase-in over time to allow those issuers to build up capital during the de novo period. After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to retain the proposed approach of individualized capital requirements for each permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The varied business models of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and lack of empirical evidence make calibration of objective numeric capital requirements too challenging at this time to implement in a manner that is appropriate for the expected variety of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. However, to address the comments that the proposed rule's individualized approach lacked sufficient detail about the basis for the determination, the OCC is providing a more detailed list of what factors the OCC will consider in setting minimum capital requirements for issuers, consistent with the principles in OCC Bulletin 2007- 21.\185\ Although not all permitted payment stablecoin issuers will operate similarly to national trust banks, the factors in Bulletin 2007-21 have long provided an appropriate balance between providing notice to potential trust bank applicants of the factors the OCC will consider with the OCC's discretion to tailor capital requirements based on business model and risk. The OCC also has experience applying these factors to a number of recent trust bank applicants that have sought charters in part to issue payment stablecoins. The factors the OCC will consider, as adapted from the principles set out in Bulletin 2007-21, follow: --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \185\ OCC Bulletin 2007-21, ``Supervision of National Trust Banks: Revised Guidance: Capital and Liquidity,'' (June 26, 2007), https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2007/bulletin-2007-21.html. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- The composition, stability, and direction of revenue. Compare actual revenue against projected revenue. Evaluate revenue by business line. Consider growth expectations along with customer concentrations. Assess fee structure and pricing policies including negotiated concessions. Also, consider earnings sensitivity to market risk factors (e.g., exposure to changes in interest rates and foreign exchange rates). The level and composition of expenses in relation to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations. Consider fixed versus variable expenses, the level of cash expenditures for existing or planned contract agreements (employment, equipment, fixtures, premises, etc.), and the adequacy of the cash budgeting and planning process. The level of retained earnings. Evaluate the relationship between retained earnings and realized and anticipated growth. Consider shareholder/parent company expectations for dividends along with their commitment and ability to augment capital, if needed. Also, consider the volume of intangible assets and their effect on capital levels and capital requirements. The quantity and direction of strategic risk. Evaluate the volume, type, and growth in reserve assets as well as other assets that support the issuer's business. Consider the risks associated with the various product types, business lines, concentrations, investment strategies, and outsourcing arrangements. Evaluate the impact of customer complaints, pending lawsuits, and regulatory actions. Consider the likelihood and magnitude of a loss event along with the opportunity cost of lost business. The quality of risk management processes, including the adequacy of internal and external audit, internal controls, and the compliance management system. Consider the volume and significance of noncompliance with policies and procedures, laws, regulations, prescribed practices, and ethical standards. The quantity of transaction risk from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's issuance of stablecoins, as well as its delivery and administration of other products and services. Consider the condition, security, capacity, and recoverability of systems. Also consider plans for conversions, integrations, and system upgrades. The impact of external factors, including economic conditions, competition, evolving technology, legislative changes, and precedent-setting court decisions. In addition, the OCC will require as part of the quarterly reporting that every permitted payment stablecoin issuer disclose its current minimum capital and operational backstop requirements in order to promote transparency. This would also allow stablecoin holders to compare the minimum capital requirements and the amount of capital instruments and operational backstop assets held to satisfy those requirements. The OCC declines to adopt a capital adjustment for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that adopt a certain proprietary technology, as this would be beyond the scope of the rulemaking, may disincentivize changes in technology, and would be inconsistent with the role of the OCC. The OCC also declines to adopt a phase-in for new issuers to meet their minimum capital requirements. Those requirements are intended to reflect both the current state of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer as well as future growth projections and allowing a phase-in of capital requirements would increase the [[Page 67130]] risk as the issuer is ramping up growth in the early stages of its existence. De Novo Minimum Capital Requirement. The OCC proposed that de novo stablecoin issuers, generally those that have been licensed for three years or less, would have a $5 million floor on their capital requirements. A few commenters opposed the floor, noting that it would limit access for smaller applicants or may be higher than the individual capital requirement tailored to the risks of the individual permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Other commenters supported the floor as an appropriate prudential safeguard. One commenter recommended raising the floor to $15 million, suggesting that it is more in line with the capital requirements the OCC has imposed on de novo trust banks that plan to issue stablecoins. After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to adopt the $5 million floor as proposed, except for adding a more specific cross reference in Sec. 15.41(a)(1)(ii) (the proposal referred to waivers under Sec. 15.15, whereas the final rule specifies waivers under Sec. 15.15(d)). The OCC agrees that setting a capital floor is a valuable prudential safeguard and provides stability for smaller issuers. This safeguard is important to provide stability throughout the life of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and, therefore, the OCC is extending the $5 million floor beyond just the de novo period. Based on the OCC's experience to date with the minimum capital amounts necessary to operate a viable stablecoin business model, the OCC believes that a $5 million floor is appropriately calibrated. However, given the variety of possible business models of applicants, the OCC does not believe that a higher minimum floor is necessary, as the OCC can set a higher capital requirement for more complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers as necessary. Operational Backstop Requirement Calibration of the Backstop. As noted above, the operational backstop requirement would be calibrated based on the total expenses of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer over the prior 12 months, or on reasonable estimates of expenses for issuers with a shorter operating history. The OCC proposed the backstop to provide a source for immediate liquidity to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to assist the issuer with recovering from a business disruption in the near term. Many commenters recommended shortening the 12-month timeframe and limiting the purpose and expenses included in calculating the operational backstop. Specifically, many of those commenters recommended limiting the purpose of the operational backstop to those costs necessary to liquidate the stablecoin and that the amount not exceed 6 months or less of those more limited expenses. A few commenters supported limiting expenses if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer was a subsidiary of a bank, had a binding liquidity agreement with its parent entity, or used a specific software product that may accelerate the liquidation of the stablecoin. A few commenters supported the backstop as proposed, while a few other commenters recommended incorporating a forward-looking metric for expenses based on the projected growth of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Some commenters recommended that however expenses are determined, the OCC should ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers with affiliates do not attempt to artificially reduce expenses by running those expenses through affiliates. After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to calculate the operational backstop requirement based on the prior 12 months of total expenses. While past crypto-asset company failures have taken many years to resolve, the existence of prudential safeguards and requirements (including know-your-customer requirements) should help reduce the time required to identify claims and to facilitate the sale or liquidation of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (and the redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins). In addition, the operational backstop requirement has a broader purpose of addressing temporary business disruptions that would lead to failure absent the backstop, but that could resolve and lead to recovery of the stablecoin issuer within 12 months with the backstop. The OCC does not agree with commenters that the shorter 6-month expense backstop used for recent bank charter approvals is appropriate here, as the activities, business models, regulatory framework, and potential for resolution materially diverge. However, to address comments that using 12 months of total expenses may be overly broad, the OCC will allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to request permission to exclude one-time expenses that bear no relation to the ongoing operations of the stablecoin issuer when calculating the backstop. As the backstop is calculated each quarter based on the prior 12 months, one-time expenses will automatically be removed after 12 months, so the approval will only cover the timeframe until the one-time expense is no longer in that window. As a baseline to qualify for exclusion, expenses must bear no relation to the ongoing operations of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; common expenses such as for equipment, software, employee compensation (whether paid as salary, bonus, stock options, or in other forms) would not qualify for exclusion, as they support the operations of the stablecoin issuer. The OCC also is clarifying that in cases in which one permitted payment stablecoin issuer merges with another permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the acquiring issuer would be required to include the acquired issuer's expenses during the relevant timeframe when calculating the operational backstop requirement for the combined entity. This adjustment reflects that the acquiring issuer's expenses are likely to increase to support a larger payment stablecoin issuance post-merger. However, the acquiring permitted payment stablecoin issuer could request exclusion of one-time expenses associated with the merger incurred by either the acquired or acquiring permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the general exclusion in the final rule. In cases in which the combined entity may have additional operational risks post-merger, for example from stablecoin conversion or systems integration, the OCC may impose an additional operational backstop requirement under Sec. 15.42. The OCC is not adopting any adjustments based on whether a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is a subsidiary of a bank or has a liquidity agreement in place with a parent bank; while it is possible these arrangements may reduce the risk to the issuer, the arrangements may weaken the health of the parent bank if the issuer ever needs liquidity or other support from the parent bank. The OCC generally does not mandate use of a specific product or service provider in exchange for obtaining a capital benefit. For permitted payment stablecoin issuers with affiliates, the OCC agrees with commenters that those issuers must reflect the reasonable cost of any shared services provided by affiliates, whether reimbursed or not, when calculating the operational backstop requirement. The OCC is not incorporating a specific forward-looking assessment of operating expenses; historical increases in operating expenses will be included in the backstop each quarter, while the overall capital evaluation and stress testing performed by each issuer will already consider expected capital requirements based on future growth.

[[Page 67131]]

    Funding and Composition of the Backstop. Under the proposal, the 
operational backstop requirement would consist of a limited pool of 
highly liquid, low-risk assets. The proposed pool of eligible assets 
would have been narrower than those assets that qualified as reserve 
assets, and these assets would have been separately reported from the 
reserve assets. While the proposal did not specifically identify how 
the operational backstop would be funded, the minimum capital 
requirement and operational backstop requirement were defined as two 
separate pools to support the continued operation of a permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer.
    Some commenters recommended that the OCC expand the list of assets 
that qualify for the operational backstop to include one or more of the 
following: United States Treasury securities with maturities greater 
than 93 days; uninsured bank deposits; stablecoin reserve assets that 
are not currently backing any stablecoins; other unspecified assets 
that the OCC has approved as liquid assets in recent charter approvals. 
Many commenters recommended that the OCC require that the operational 
backstop be funded by equity accounts, not debt instruments, as the 
interest payments and maturities on debt instruments would weaken the 
availability of the backstop. Some of these commenters also requested 
clarification as to whether the backstop could be funded by equity 
instruments that also count toward the minimum capital requirement or 
if the minimum capital and operational backstop requirements had to be 
contributed separately.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to retain 
the list of permissible backstop assets with one technical change. 
While uninsured bank deposits are allowable as reserve assets, they are 
subject to credit and liquidity risks of the depository bank. 
Furthermore, uninsured deposits held at an affiliated bank would 
present wrong-way risk, as a failure of the bank would jeopardize funds 
available at the affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuer, while 
an operational failure at the issuer that required drawing on those 
deposits could increase the liquidity risk at the affiliated bank. The 
OCC is also declining to expand recognition to longer-dated United 
States Treasuries or other assets; while these assets may have low 
credit risk, they present heightened interest rate and price risk, as 
the backstop may require liquidation of these assets prior to maturity 
when the asset prices may be below par or acquisition value. The OCC is 
changing references to ``insured shares'' to funds in ``share accounts 
that are payable on demand'' to clarify that such funds, like deposits, 
must be payable on demand.
    The OCC agrees with the commenters that the operational backstop 
requirement should be funded significantly by equity accounts and be 
accounted for separately from the minimum capital requirement. 
Permitting the backstop to be funded only by debt increases the risk to 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, as funds that may be needed to 
assist the issuer may be obligated to be paid out as interest or 
principal on debt instruments, while it may be difficult for an issuer 
to replace or roll over those debt instruments if it faces a business 
disruption. However, the OCC also recognizes that debt funding is 
generally less expensive than equity funding, which could help improve 
the financial position of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. 
Therefore, the final rule allows a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
to rely on debt instruments to fund no more than 50 percent of the 
operational backstop requirement, provided those debt instruments 
include appropriate safeguards generally consistent with requirements 
for tier 2 capital instruments under the bank capital framework. These 
requirements, listed in Sec.  15.40, include that the instrument is 
paid in, has a maturity no shorter than five years from issuance, and 
may be called prior to maturity only after five years and with approval 
of the OCC. In addition, the amount of debt from an issuance that could 
qualify as operational backstop debt would be reduced by 20 percent of 
the otherwise qualifying amount of that instrument per year for each of 
the last five years until maturity of that issuance to reduce the cliff 
effect from maturity causing the full amount of operational backstop 
debt to disappear all at once. For example, when an instrument has 5 
years remaining until maturity, and the instrument would otherwise 
satisfy up to $100 of the operational backstop requirement (even if the 
amount of the instrument issued exceeded $100), only a maximum of $80 
could count as qualifying operational backstop debt. When that same 
instrument has 4 years remaining until maturity, only a maximum of $60 
could count as qualifying operational backstop debt, and so on. A 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer may have multiple debt issuances, 
and the phase-out would apply separately to each issuance based on its 
maturity date, subject to a total cap across all instruments of 50 
percent debt financing of the operational backstop requirement. This 
provides some flexibility to permitted payment stablecoin issuers while 
ensuring that debt funding of the operational backstop requirement will 
not disappear through early repayments or subject the issuer to a cliff 
effect upon final maturity of any operational backstop debt instrument. 
A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue debt instruments in 
excess of 50 percent of its operational backstop requirement, but only 
the portion of those debt instruments not in excess of 50 percent will 
qualify as operational backstop debt funding the operational backstop 
requirement.
    Allowing the same capital amount to count toward the minimum 
capital requirement and the operational backstop requirement would 
double the negative consequences from using the backstop, as any use of 
the backstop to pay expenses to support the stablecoin would reduce 
retained earnings, thus reducing available capital; conversely, as 
capital is depleted through operating losses it would also reduce 
capital available to support the operational backstop requirement. One 
way to achieve the result of independent minimum capital and backstop 
requirements, as suggested by one commenter, would be to require that 
the operational backstop requirement be deducted from tangible equity. 
The OCC is adopting this approach as it provides a simple, transparent 
mechanism to separately capitalize the minimum capital requirement and 
operational backstop requirement and avoid the risk of counting the 
same equity accounts for both purposes. Under the final rule, when 
calculating its capital, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must 
deduct the difference between its operational backstop requirement and 
its operational backstop debt (up to a cap of 50 percent of the 
operational backstop requirement).
    Capital Calculation Timeframes and Effects. Under the proposal, the 
capital requirements would be calculated as of the last day of each 
quarter and compliance would be evaluated at that time. An issuer that 
failed to meet its capital requirements at the end of a quarter would 
have been subject to certain restrictions on new stablecoin issuance 
during that quarter until it returns to a satisfactory capital level, 
and an issuer that failed its capital requirements in two consecutive 
quarters would have been required to liquidate the stablecoin.
    A few commenters recommended that the OCC replace the point-in-time 
capital calculation with a daily, weekly, or monthly average in order 
to avoid

[[Page 67132]]

issuers ``window dressing'' their end-of-quarter capital amounts. A few 
commenters supported the proposed effects of failing to meet the 
capital requirements but recommended that the OCC allow itself the 
ability to either accelerate or delay those impacts based on individual 
considerations of a specific permitted payment stablecoin issuer. One 
commenter opposed the stablecoin issuance and liquidation measures for 
failure to meet capital requirements if the stablecoin still had 
sufficient reserve assets.
    One commenter requested clarification on whether an applicant would 
be required to maintain an operational backstop equal to 12 months of 
total operating expenses in liquid assets as of the application date. 
As provided in the proposal, for de novo permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers, the initial operational backstop amount would be based on 
reasonable expense projections and adjusted each quarter based on 
actual amounts for that quarter. The requirement to hold the 
operational backstop would not attach until the applicant began 
operations as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    After consideration of the comments, the OCC has decided to require 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to track its compliance with the 
minimum capital requirement and operational backstop requirement 
throughout the quarter, and at quarter-end to report whether or not the 
issuer complied with those requirements every day of the quarter rather 
than just on the last day. This approach is more prudent and addresses 
commenter concerns about issuers artificially improving (i.e., ``window 
dressing'') quarter-end numbers, when capital may vary significantly 
throughout the quarter. Furthermore, to address commenter concerns 
about timeliness, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's capital 
falls below its minimum capital requirement at any time during the 
quarter, the issuer must notify the OCC within 24 hours. After 
notification, the OCC may decide to accelerate imposition of the 
penalties for failure to meet minimum capital requirements prior to the 
end of the quarter if it appears unlikely to the OCC that the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer will be able to raise sufficient capital to 
regain compliance or implement other actions to protect the interests 
of stablecoin holders. These measures will help reassure holders of 
stablecoins that issuers are addressing deficiencies in meeting capital 
requirements in a timely and appropriate manner. A permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer that fails to meet its capital or backstop 
requirements at any point during a quarter, but restores compliance by 
the end of that quarter, would not be subject to the new issuance 
restrictions or mandatory redemption requirements unless the OCC 
accelerates imposition of those requirements.
    The OCC also recognizes that one of the purposes of the operational 
backstop requirement is to provide a source of readily available liquid 
assets that can be used to support the continued operation of the 
stablecoin during a temporary disruption or other operational event. 
However, using those assets for the intended purpose of recovering from 
such an event could cause the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to 
temporarily fall below the minimum operational backstop requirement. 
Therefore, the final rule includes a limited waiver of compliance with 
the operational backstop requirement in this circumstance. 
Specifically, if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer suffers a 
temporary disruption or other operational event requiring use of the 
backstop assets; notifies the OCC of the event within 24 hours; submits 
a plan to the OCC within 7 days of the event to restore the backstop 
assets within 90 days, and the OCC deems the plan viable, then the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer will be considered to be in 
compliance with the operational backstop requirement during that time. 
The final rule also makes a technical change in Sec.  15.41(c)(3)(iii), 
changing a reference from ``stablecoin'' to ``payment stablecoin.''
    Final Sec.  15.41(d) describes requirements specific to uninsured 
national trust banks. There are several changes from the proposed Sec.  
15.41(d) that generally would require an uninsured national trust bank 
to apply to be subject to the capital requirements in part 15 in lieu 
of the requirements in 12 CFR part 3 and to provide notice if it 
rescinds the election to be subject to the capital requirements of part 
15. Because these requirements and the changes relate to the amendments 
to 12 CFR part 3, a description of the Sec.  15.41(d) requirements and 
changes is below alongside a description of the amendment to 12 CFR 
part 3.
4. Individual Additional Capital or Operational Backstop Requirement 
(Sec.  15.42)
a. Description of Proposed Rule
    The OCC proposed a process to impose an individual additional 
capital or backstop requirement on a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer. This process was permitted by section 4(a)(4)(B)(i) of the 
GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(B)(i)) and is generally consistent 
with the OCC's process to impose individual minimum capital ratios for 
national banks in 12 CFR part 3, subpart H. Uninsured national trust 
banks that are also permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have 
been subject to both the individual minimum capital ratio framework and 
the proposed individual additional capital or backstop requirement.
    The proposed rule included a list of illustrative examples of when 
the OCC may consider imposing an individual additional capital or 
backstop requirement, such as when a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer is facing a significant increase in operational risks, excessive 
volatility in stablecoin issuance or redemptions and the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer's management lacks a robust plan to address 
that volatility, or for additional risks that the stablecoin issuer is 
not appropriately managing or reflecting in the capital determination.
    Under the proposal, the OCC would notify the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer of the proposed individual additional capital or 
backstop requirement, including a justification for that requirement 
and a target achievement date. The board and management of the 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer generally would have 30 days to 
respond to that notice. The OCC could change this time period, as 
appropriate, based on the condition of the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.
b. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
    The OCC received no comments on the proposed framework for the 
individual additional capital or backstop requirement and, except for 
certain technical amendments described below, adopts it as proposed. 
The final rule eliminates a reference to an individual permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer in paragraph (a) as unnecessary. In addition, 
the final rule replaces the phrase ``in view of its circumstances'' 
with ``if appropriate under the particular facts and circumstances'' in 
the same paragraph. The final rule makes a grammatical correction in 
paragraph (c)(1) substituting ``is'' for ``are.'' In paragraph (c)(2), 
the OCC is making non-substantive clarifying edits, including replacing 
the word ``which'' with ``that'' and eliminating surplus language. The 
final rule also breaks apart and renumbers paragraph (c)(3) (so that 
the final rule includes paragraphs (c)(3)(i) through (iii)). Paragraph 
(c)(4) now

[[Page 67133]]

contains an express reference to paragraph (c)(3). Surplus language has 
been removed from language finalized at paragraph (c)(5). These changes 
are non-substantive. The provisions of Sec.  15.42 will allow the OCC 
to better tailor the capital requirements of a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer in a variety of circumstances, such as when that 
issuer fails to appropriately determine its minimum capital 
requirement, has material unaddressed risks, or faces excessive 
volatility in the operation of its stablecoin.
    Excessive Volatility. One of the proposed factors related to 
excessive volatility in the issuance or redemption of an issuer's 
stablecoin. The OCC asked a question in the proposed rule specifically 
around whether to further define what would qualify as excessive 
volatility for purposes of the individual additional capital or 
backstop requirement. A few commenters supported the OCC defining 
excessive volatility by listing objective factors but not linking those 
to any specific numerical outcome. The OCC is declining to define 
excessive volatility in the final rule, as the OCC currently lacks 
sufficient data to support a numerical threshold for this term as well 
as to preserve flexibility in how to apply that factor going forward.
    Capital Buffers. While the GENIUS Act permits the OCC to impose 
capital buffers, the OCC did not propose any buffers as part of the 
capital framework.
    A few commenters recommended that the OCC adopt capital buffers for 
various purposes or risks that issuers may face. One commenter 
recommended a buffer for permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
subsidiaries of banks that deposit stablecoin reserve assets at their 
parent banks to help address the risk that a failure of the parent bank 
will lead to insufficient reserves and a failure at the stablecoin 
issuer. One commenter recommended capital buffers to provide stablecoin 
holders with a larger cushion for fluctuations in reserve assets in 
order to reduce the risk of a run on the stablecoin. One commenter 
recommended adopting capital buffers to address operational failures, 
cybersecurity incidents, fraud, or a breakdown in internal controls at 
the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. One commenter recommended 
capital buffers for more complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
or those that hold money market mutual fund shares, uninsured bank 
deposits, or that are affiliated with a bank.
    The OCC is not adopting a capital buffer in the final rule. The 
risks that commenters raise are sufficiently addressed through the 
calibration of existing capital requirements or through other 
provisions within this rule without the need for imposing a capital 
buffer. Risks associated with the payment stablecoin reserve assets, 
including riskier reserve assets such as uninsured deposits, are 
addressed through the limits on reserve asset composition and 
monitoring requirements. Risks associated with operational failures, 
whether internal or external, are addressed through the individualized 
capital requirement and the operational backstop, which is intended to 
help ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer will have 
sufficient liquid assets available to address such a failure. As 
described elsewhere in the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer must conduct stress testing and must ensure that its reserve 
asset value will equal or exceed outstanding issuance value at all 
times. As a result, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may need to 
hold a buffer of reserve assets, which could mitigate the risks that 
might otherwise be addressed by a capital buffer requirement.
    Foreign Issuer Capital. The proposed rule requested comment on 
whether foreign issuers should follow the same capital requirements as 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC requested feedback on 
this proposal, as well as on any potential adjustments to the capital 
equivalency deposit for Federal branches or foreign banks that operate 
payment stablecoins. Generally, the capital equivalency deposit is 
calculated as 5 percent of liabilities of a Federal branch.\186\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \186\ Under 12 U.S.C. 3102(g), the capital equivalency deposit 
is calculated as the greater of the capital required of a national 
bank at the same location or 5 percent of total liabilities, with 
exceptions for certain accrued expenses and related party 
liabilities. In practice, the 5 percent of liabilities amount is 
generally the binding requirement.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Numerous commenters provided diverging views on how to address 
capital requirements for foreign issuers. These views ranged from 
allowing foreign issuers to follow home-country stablecoin capital 
requirements to reduce burden, requiring foreign issuers to follow 
United States requirements to maintain a level playing field with 
United States issuers, or requiring foreign issuers to follow the 
higher of home country or United States requirements to avoid 
regulatory arbitrage. A few commenters also supported exempting 
liabilities associated with stablecoin programs, such as stablecoin 
reserve deposits or stablecoin holder liabilities, from being in the 
calculation of the capital equivalency deposit for a foreign branch 
operating a payment stablecoin, or otherwise counting appropriately 
segregated reserve assets as satisfying the capital equivalency deposit 
requirement.
    After considering the comments, the OCC has determined that it is 
appropriate to consider whether a foreign issuer must follow the same 
United States minimum capital and operational backstop requirements as 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers through the registration process. 
Addressing capital requirements through the registration process 
recognizes that foreign payment stablecoin issuers eligible to register 
with the OCC must be subject to a regulatory and supervisory regime 
that is comparable to the GENIUS Act. As a result, in many 
circumstances, following home-country stablecoin capital requirements 
may be sufficient. However, if a foreign regime were generally 
comparable but required less capital to be held, it may be appropriate 
for the OCC to require additional capital to be held with respect to 
the United States operations of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer. 
Assessing capital requirements at the registration phase will allow the 
OCC to ensure that the United States operations of foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers are appropriately capitalized and are not unduly 
advantaged or disadvantaged relative to permitted payment stablecoin 
issuers. The OCC believes this will reduce the burden on these foreign 
issuers from having to comply with multiple equivalent capital 
frameworks, while ensuring that foreign issuers are not benefitting 
from lower home-country capital requirements to create an uneven 
competitive environment.
    The OCC also agrees with commenters that the current requirements 
for capital equivalency deposit calculations based on 5 percent of most 
liabilities could unnecessarily disincentivize Federal branches from 
offering stablecoin programs and disadvantage them relative to State 
branches. The OCC is considering addressing this concern in the near 
future through a separate rulemaking on 12 CFR part 28, the OCC's 
implementing regulation for Federal branches that includes provisions 
on calculation and maintenance of the capital equivalency deposit.

5. Proposed Adjustments to the Bank Capital Rule (12 CFR Part 3)
a. Description of Proposed Rule
    Section 4(a)(4)(C)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 
5903(a)(4)(C)(iii)) specifies that for stablecoin issuers owned by 
insured depository institutions or depository institution holding 
companies, the appropriate Federal banking agency (as defined in 12 
U.S.C. 1813(q)) cannot require an insured depository institution or 
depository institution holding company that is consolidated with a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer to hold any amount of regulatory 
capital with respect to such permitted payment stablecoin issuer and 
its assets and operations in excess of the capital that such permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer must maintain under the capital regulations 
promulgated under the GENIUS Act.
    Therefore, for regulatory capital purposes, the OCC proposed to 
amend 12 CFR part 3 to specify that an insured national bank or Federal 
savings association that owns a permitted payment stablecoin issuer 
consolidated under GAAP must deconsolidate the permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer for regulatory capital purposes. The insured national 
bank or Federal savings association would need to deduct any interest 
in retained earnings of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer from 
the insured national bank's or Federal savings association's common 
equity tier 1 capital. This amount would also be deducted from the 
asset reflecting the investment in the subsidiary for risk-based and 
leverage capital calculations. This interest reflects the insured 
national bank's or Federal savings association's share of retained 
earnings of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that have not been 
paid out as dividends, and the deduction ensures that the same amount 
would not count as capital at both the permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer and its parent insured national bank or Federal savings 
association. Once earnings from the subsidiary are paid as dividends to 
the parent national bank or Federal savings association, those funds 
would be available for general uses of the parent bank and no longer 
count as capital of the stablecoin issuer. Finally, any remaining 
assets associated with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (after 
deducting its share of retained earnings), such as investments in or 
intercompany receivables from a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, 
would have been excluded when calculating the insured national bank's 
or Federal savings association's standardized total risk-weighted 
assets, advanced approaches risk-weighted assets, average total 
consolidated assets, and total leverage exposure, as applicable. To the 
extent that a subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer incurs net 
losses, there would be no adjustment to increase its parent national 
bank or Federal savings association's assets or retained earnings to 
offset those losses, so as not to overstate the resources and financial 
condition of the parent bank.
    As proposed, this deconsolidation and deduction approach would have 
ensured that any assets and capital associated with the permitted 
payment stablecoin issuer are not double-counted when included in risk-
based or leverage capital ratio calculations at the parent insured 
national bank or Federal savings association, and that any retained 
earnings of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer are not double-
counted as capital that can be used by the parent insured national bank 
or Federal savings association.
    The proposed rule, like the statute, would have allowed uninsured 
national trust banks to issue payment stablecoins directly. Currently, 
uninsured national trust banks are subject to the full requirements of 
12 CFR part 3, including risk-based and leverage capital ratios. 
However, the capital required under those measures may significantly 
exceed the capital that would be required for other types of permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers under the proposal. In order to establish 
parity among all types of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC 
also proposed permitting uninsured national trust banks that issue 
stablecoins to elect to follow the proposed capital requirements in 
part 15 and not calculate or comply with the minimum capital 
requirements in part 3.
    Furthermore, to promote parity among uninsured national trust 
banks, whether or not they issue payment stablecoins, the OCC proposed 
to allow any uninsured national trust bank to similarly elect to follow 
the proposed minimum capital requirements calculated under part 15 
instead of those under part 3. As acknowledged in OCC Bulletin 2007-21, 
the leverage and risk-based capital ratios in 12 CFR part 3 generally 
are not optimal measures of capital adequacy for national trust banks. 
Under the proposed rule, a national trust bank seeking to follow the 
part 15 minimum capital requirements instead of the part 3 minimum 
capital requirements would submit a notice to the OCC indicating its 
election. The election would become effective 30 days after OCC 
receipt, unless the OCC objects in writing for good cause within that 
timeframe. After electing to be subject to the capital requirements of 
part 15, a national trust bank subsequently could revert to following 
the relevant capital measures in part 3 for good cause and with 
approval of the OCC.
    Under the proposal, an uninsured national trust bank would continue 
to follow the criteria and definitions for capital instruments in 12 
CFR part 3, subpart C, including any adjustments or deductions.
b. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
Bank Subsidiary Issuers
    The proposed rule included regulatory capital adjustments for banks 
that have subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuers, which 
generally would have required deconsolidating and deducting the issuers 
when computing the bank's regulatory capital under 12 CFR part 3. The 
proposed adjustments were intended to implement a requirement in the 
GENIUS Act that consolidated permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
should not also be subject to duplicative bank regulatory capital 
requirements when owned by a bank.
    Commenters responding to this aspect of the proposal generally 
supported the proposed treatment. A few commenters recommended also 
exempting the assets and activities of a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer subsidiary when considering the assets and activities of the 
bank in other contexts, such as under the high-quality liquid assets 
requirements, stable funding requirements, and for reserve asset 
deposits held at the parent bank. One commenter recommended that parent 
banks be required to enter into source of strength agreements with 
their subsidiary issuers to provide additional liquidity and capital as 
needed.
    After considering the comments, the OCC is adopting the capital 
adjustments to 12 CFR part 3 for bank parents of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers as proposed with one revision. Under the final rule, 
a bank that is consolidated with a subsidiary permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer must deconsolidate that issuer. The bank must then 
exclude any amount of its investment in the subsidiary reflecting 
undistributed earnings from both the bank's investment and equity 
accounts.
    Likewise, the final rule includes one revision to provide an 
adjustment to increase a parent bank's common equity tier 1 capital for 
any losses incurred by

[[Page 67135]]

its consolidated permitted payment stablecoin issuer. This adjustment 
will ensure that losses at the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, 
which reduce capital at the issuer, will not also reduce regulatory 
capital at the parent bank or require the parent bank to raise 
additional regulatory capital to cover those losses. The OCC will 
monitor any losses at the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and 
associated addback for potential manipulation, and the OCC may take 
action, such as through the use of the reservation of authority or 
imposing individual minimum capital requirements, as appropriate, to 
ensure the safety and soundness of the national bank or Federal savings 
association.
    Finally, the bank must exclude any remaining balance of its 
investment in the subsidiary when calculating any risk-weighted asset 
and leverage ratio requirements. For clarification, this provision also 
excludes the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations from the 
calculation of operational risk-weighted assets, which is a component 
of advanced approaches risk-weighted assets.
    The GENIUS Act only requires an adjustment for a bank that owns a 
consolidated permitted payment stablecoin issuer. To the extent a bank 
has any other exposure to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is 
not consolidated with the bank under GAAP, the bank would treat its 
interest under the existing 12 CFR part 3 framework. To the extent that 
the bank's consolidated permitted payment stablecoin issuer subsidiary 
has outside investors, which would be reflected as minority interest at 
the consolidated bank, this minority interest would be eliminated 
during deconsolidation and therefore would not also be includable as 
capital under the minority interest provisions in 12 CFR 3.21.
    The OCC does not agree that deposits of an issuer subsidiary should 
receive special treatment under regulatory capital or liquidity rules 
over other deposits of the bank; on the contrary, those deposits may 
exhibit increased liquidity risk compared to other deposits at the 
bank, depending on the form of the deposits. Many of the asset 
thresholds or non-part 3 regulatory requirements for banks that have 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer subsidiaries are contained within 
interagency rules and are better addressed on an interagency basis 
rather than through this standalone OCC rule. The OCC is declining to 
require parent banks to enter into capital maintenance agreements with 
their subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as this 
requirement would impose an extra burden on bank-affiliated issuers and 
increase risk to the bank to support its stablecoin subsidiary, 
potentially jeopardizing the parent bank's safety and soundness. The 
final rule does not include any requirement or supervisory expectation 
that a parent bank act as a source of strength for a subsidiary 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
    The final rule also adds a reference to the GENIUS Act in the 
authority citation for 12 CFR part 3.
National Trust Bank Capital Framework
    The OCC received numerous comments on the proposed capital 
treatment for national trust banks. Commenters generally offered four 
perspectives: not providing any special treatment to national trust 
bank permitted payment stablecoin issuers; allowing national trust 
banks with stablecoin programs to use the proposed GENIUS capital 
framework if those banks limited their activities solely to GENIUS-
authorized activities; allowing all national trust banks with 
stablecoin programs to use the proposed capital framework regardless of 
other activities; and allowing all national trust banks to use the 
proposed capital framework. One commenter suggested requiring 
additional capital for national trust banks that conduct more than half 
of their business in non-stablecoin activities. Some commenters agreed 
that the part 3 bank capital rules are not relevant for national trust 
banks, but that this issue should be proposed separately from 
implementation of GENIUS rules due to the potential magnitude of the 
shift for national trust banks. National trust bank commenters noted 
that attempting to bifurcate internal records between stablecoin and 
non-stablecoin activities to apply both capital frameworks would be the 
most burdensome and least favored option.
    After reviewing comments, the OCC has decided to allow all 
uninsured national trust banks to adopt the GENIUS Act regulatory 
capital and operational backstop requirements instead of following the 
capital requirements in 12 CFR part 3, regardless of whether the 
national trust bank issues a payment stablecoin. The OCC agrees with 
commenters that attempting to bifurcate the regulatory capital 
frameworks that apply to stablecoin activities and non-stablecoin 
activities would be overly burdensome for national trust bank issuers. 
Preventing national trust banks that do not issue stablecoins from 
opting in to the new framework could create an uneven competitive 
environment for trust banks engaged in similar activities, while 
restricting these banks to only GENIUS-authorized activities could 
present significant business disruptions, as numerous OCC national 
trust banks are or plan to engage in stablecoin programs prior to 
adoption of this final rule. The OCC has issued reservation-of-
authority letters to numerous trust banks addressing regulatory capital 
requirements under 12 CFR part 3 for stablecoin programs. These letters 
note that to the extent a final rule implementing the GENIUS Act 
presents a different capital treatment for stablecoin reserve assets 
than in 12 CFR part 3, those requirements would control notwithstanding 
the reservation in the letters. Therefore, existing national trust 
banks could face significant capital charges and business disruptions 
if they are not allowed to elect to use the GENIUS Act framework.
    The OCC is limiting the option only to uninsured national trust 
banks, as all insured depository institutions must comply with the 
prompt corrective action framework in 12 CFR part 6, which is tied into 
the capital requirements in 12 CFR part 3.
    A national trust bank that makes this election must follow all of 
the GENIUS capital requirements (including ongoing minimum capital 
assessments, operational backstop requirements, and intangible asset 
and deferred tax asset deductions), which may be more conservative for 
trust banks that do not issue stablecoins. In order to make this 
election, the national trust bank must submit a request for prior 
approval to the OCC with supporting documentation for its initial 
minimum capital and operational backstop requirements, and the OCC will 
provide an approval or denial within 60 days of receiving a request. 
This process will allow the OCC to review the appropriateness of the 
national trust bank's capital requirements upfront to ensure the bank 
retains a stable capital base under the GENIUS framework and has 
developed procedures for ongoing capital assessments as required for 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. After making an election, a 
national trust bank can choose to revert to 12 CFR part 3 without prior 
approval from the OCC by providing a notice to the applicable OCC 
supervisory office. While this rule helps address capital requirements 
for national trust banks in connection with the GENIUS Act, in the 
future the OCC may revisit the regulatory capital framework for all 
national trust banks in line with commenter feedback to provide a more 
robust and comprehensive proposed alternative to application of 12 CFR 
part 3.

[[Page 67136]]

    The OCC plans to propose revised regulatory reporting for national 
trust banks that elect the GENIUS capital framework to allow these 
trust banks to report their capital position and requirements in lieu 
of existing regulatory capital reporting in Schedule RC-R of the Call 
Report.
Stablecoin Capital
    One commenter requested that the OCC consider adopting a capital 
framework for stablecoins held by banks in order to provide more 
clarity to the industry. The proposed rule did not address the 
regulatory capital treatment of stablecoins that are held by national 
banks or Federal savings associations. Therefore, the request is 
outside the scope of this rulemaking. The OCC plans to address the 
capital framework for digital assets, including stablecoins, as part of 
a separate rulemaking project.
6. Amendment to Part 6
    When calculating total assets for prompt corrective action purposes 
under 12 CFR part 6, the definition of total assets in Sec.  6.2 of the 
rule specifies that certain assets deducted from capital are also 
deducted from total assets. Consistent with section 4(a)(4)(C)(iii) of 
the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(C)(iii)) and the deductions and 
adjustments proposed to 12 CFR part 3, the OCC proposed a conforming 
amendment to also incorporate the deductions related to an insured 
national bank's or Federal savings association's ownership of a 
permitted payment stablecoin issuer when calculating total assets under 
12 CFR part 6. As part 6 only applies to insured depository 
institutions, no adjustments are necessary for uninsured national trust 
banks.
    The OCC received no comments on this proposed amendment and is 
adopting it as proposed.

2. Background and Overview of the Proposed Amendments
    As described in the proposal, the OCC funds the activities it 
undertakes to carry out its supervisory responsibilities through 
assessments on institutions regulated by the OCC.\187\ The OCC is

[[Page 67137]]

authorized to collect assessments, fees, and other charges to meet the 
agency's expenses in carrying out authorized activities.\188\ In 
setting assessments, the Comptroller has broad authority to consider 
variations among institutions, including the nature and scope of the 
activities of an institution, the amount and type of assets that the 
institution holds, the financial and managerial condition of the 
institution, and any other factor the Comptroller determines 
appropriate.\189\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \187\ The National Bank Act authorizes the OCC to impose 
assessments on national banks and Federal branches and agencies. See 
12 U.S.C. 16, 481, and 482. The Home Owners' Loan Act, as amended, 
authorizes the OCC to impose assessments on Federal savings 
associations. See 12 U.S.C. 1467.
    \188\ See 12 U.S.C. 16, 481 and 482.
    \189\ 12 U.S.C. 16. See also 12 U.S.C. 1467(a) (providing that 
the Comptroller has the authority to recover costs of examination of 
Federal savings associations ``as the Comptroller deems necessary or 
appropriate'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC collects assessments from OCC-supervised institutions 
pursuant to 12 CFR part 8.\190\ Under current part 8, the base 
assessment for each national bank and Federal savings association is 
calculated using a table with eleven categories, or brackets, each of 
which comprises a range of asset-size values. The formula used to 
calculate an assessment for each national bank and Federal savings 
association is the sum of a base amount, which is the same for every 
institution in its asset-size bracket, plus a marginal amount, which is 
computed by applying a marginal assessment rate to the amount in excess 
of the lower boundary of the asset-size bracket.\191\ The marginal 
assessment rate declines as asset size increases, reflecting economies 
of scale in the OCC's supervision activities.\192\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \190\ Current part 8 covers assessments for national banks, 
Federal savings associations, and Federal branches and Federal 
agencies. For clarity, proposed subpart A as discussed below will 
cover the same institutions.
    \191\ 12 CFR 8.2(a).
    \192\ See 12 CFR 8.8(a) and notices published by the OCC 
thereunder.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC's annual Notice of Office of the Comptroller of the 
Currency Fees and Assessments (Notice of Fees) sets forth the marginal 
assessment rates applicable to each asset-size bracket for each 
year,\193\ as well as other assessment components and fees.\194\
