    The OCC determined in the proposed rule that collecting assessments 
in connection with the GENIUS Act activities of OCC-supervised 
institutions is necessary and appropriate to facilitate the OCC's 
functions under the Act and conforms with the agency's assessment 
authorities. The OCC's supervisory responsibilities under the Act 
include licensing and registration decisions for certain nonbank 
payment stablecoin issuers, and monitoring compliance with reserve 
requirements and other applicable laws and regulations relating to 
stablecoin activities. To that end, the OCC proposed to amend part 8 to 
create subparts A and B. As described in the proposal, the proposed 
reorganization of part 8 into subparts reflected the fact that the 
powers and structures of the institutions subject to OCC supervision 
solely under the GENIUS Act often differ from those of the entities to 
which the existing part 8 applies.
    Subpart A, as proposed, applied principally to national banks and 
Federal savings associations and included assessments related to 
payment stablecoin-issuing uninsured national banks--a type of Federal 
qualified payment stablecoin issuer--and payment stablecoin-issuing 
subsidiaries of insured national banks and Federal savings associations 
(i.e., insured depository institutions). The subpart consisted of 
existing provisions relating to the assessment of national banks and 
Federal savings associations, with proposed amendments to clarify how 
these provisions will be applied with respect to new activities that 
these institutions undertake pursuant to the GENIUS Act. In particular, 
the OCC proposed to amend existing Sec.  8.2 to include special rules 
governing the treatment of assets attributable to minimum stablecoin 
reserve assets under 12 U.S.C. 5903 when calculating an institution's 
semiannual assessment. Under these rules, the OCC proposed to apply the 
existing asset-based formula to those assets reflecting minimum 
stablecoin reserve assets, except that it then would reduce the 
resulting amount by 35 percent, or by such other percentage (up to 55 
percent) that the OCC may deem appropriate for minimum stablecoin 
reserves held by national banks and Federal savings associations, based 
on its experience supervising stablecoin issuers.
    Subpart B, as proposed, adopted a structure for assessments on 
institutions newly subject to OCC jurisdiction under the GENIUS Act 
that are not subject to assessments under subpart A--i.e., nonbank 
entities and certain State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. 
Proposed Sec.  8.9 clarified that the OCC would impose assessments on 
certain Federal, Foreign, and State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers for GENIUS Act-related activities pursuant to the authority 
contained in 12 U.S.C. 93a, 481, 482, and 5901 et seq. Proposed Sec.  
8.10 set forth the OCC's methodology for the primary assessment of 
GENIUS Act-related activities of the institutions described therein and 
in general incorporated the same structure and asset-based formula used 
to impose assessments on national banks and Federal savings 
associations under Sec.  8.2. Proposed Sec.  8.11 set forth the OCC's 
methodology for separately assessing certain institutions in connection 
with their GENIUS-Act-permitted custodial and safekeeping activities. 
Proposed Sec.  8.12 described special fees and assessments in 
connection with the GENIUS Act-related activities of institutions 
covered under subpart B. Finally, proposed Sec.  8.13 covered payment 
of interest on delinquent assessments and examination and investigation 
fees.
3. Comments on the OCC's Overall Assessment Methodology
    Proposed amendments to part 8 reflect the agency's preliminary 
conclusion that the existing assessments regime applicable to national 
banks and Federal savings associations would adequately and 
appropriately ensure that the OCC could fund the activities it 
undertakes to carry out its statutory obligations under the GENIUS Act. 
An important element of that existing regime is the agency's reliance 
on asset-based assessment formulas to determine an institution's 
semiannual assessments. The agency requested comment on whether there 
is reason to believe that the existing assessment structure in Sec.  
8.2, as amended, or the proposed assessment structure under subpart B 
would not adequately and appropriately enable the OCC to fund its 
supervisory activities in connection with institutions' GENIUS Act-
related activities. The agency further asked whether it should consider 
imposing assessments based on different or additional measurements to 
account for increased supervision activities it will undertake in 
connection with supervising the GENIUS Act-related activities of these 
institutions.
    The OCC received several comments relating to this request and, 
more generally, the OCC's adoption of an assessment framework with a 
significant asset-based component. One set of commenters agreed that 
the proposed framework, as modified in the proposal, was an appropriate 
starting point to assess institutions for GENIUS Act-related activities 
and that it was premature to introduce any additional assessment 
measures. These commenters in general supported the OCC preserving 
flexibility to re-evaluate the framework after obtaining more 
experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One 
commenter sought a commitment from the OCC to engage in a re-evaluation 
of the framework after several assessment cycles. Another argued that, 
if supervision of permitted payment

[[Page 67138]]

stablecoin issuers should prove more resource-intensive than 
anticipated, future adjustments should be modest, transparent, and 
structured in a manner to preserve the proposed discounted treatment of 
reserve assets. In this latter respect, this commenter argued that any 
future adjustment should reflect the commenter's view that the 
supervisory risks associated with permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
do not scale linearly with balance sheet size in the way such risks 
might for traditional banks.
    Conversely, other commenters argued that basing assessments 
primarily on stablecoin issuance value, rather than assets, would more 
accurately reflect a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's level of 
activities and therefore the OCC's supervisory expenses. They argued 
that an issuance-based approach would be less operationally complex and 
burdensome for issuers.
    Finally, one commenter observed that, because supervisory 
complexity may extend beyond reserve balances, an operational 
complexity factor may complement asset-based measures when calibrating 
supervisory resources. The commenter opined that relevant factors could 
include the number of supported blockchains, cross-chain exposure, 
transaction velocity, custody model complexity, third-party dependency 
density, and incident frequency and severity.
    After reviewing the comments, and as described in further detail 
below, the OCC concludes that the existing assessments regime 
applicable to national banks and Federal savings associations, as 
amended by this final rule, adequately and appropriately ensures that 
the OCC can fund the activities it undertakes to carry out its 
statutory obligations under the GENIUS Act. The OCC has for decades 
assessed national banks and Federal savings associations based 
primarily on an asset-based formula, notwithstanding the numerous 
innovations and novel product offerings by these institutions over that 
period. The agency's experience has confirmed its view that, with few 
exceptions, asset-based assessments are an accurate, equitable, 
product-neutral method of ensuring the OCC can fund the activities it 
undertakes to carry out its statutory obligations. Commenters have not 
articulated persuasive arguments for why the existing methodology, as 
modified here, is inappropriate, inaccurate, or otherwise unduly 
burdensome.
    An issuance-based assessment methodology, by contrast, risks 
significant under-assessment. As commenters appear to acknowledge, a 
stablecoin issuer may engage in certain GENIUS Act-related activities 
subject to OCC supervision that would not be accounted for in an 
issuance-based formula but that would be accounted for under the 
proposed asset-based formula. While supervision of these activities may 
not contribute to the bulk of the OCC's supervisory expenses, at least 
in the ordinary case, they could be a meaningful cost contributor. For 
example, stablecoin issuers may have balance sheet assets to pay the 
blockchain network fees known as gas fees, and issuers with certain 
business models may have balance sheet assets from the receipt of other 
transaction-based fees. While an issuance-based assessment would 
overlook these assets, an asset-based assessment would reflect this 
aspect of the issuer's operations. It would be imprudent to adopt an 
assessment methodology that does not take these activities into 
account, especially where the agency's methodology would result in 
materially the same assessment as an issuance-based assessment for 
those issuers not engaged in such activities.
    The OCC also disagrees with commenter suggestions that an asset-
based assessment would impose meaningfully greater operational burden 
on institutions, as compared to an issuance-based assessment. These 
commenters argued that an issuance-based regime would free them from 
having to calculate the amounts of assessments due on reserve and non-
reserve assets separately. They also argued that asset-based 
assessments would present challenges for issuers maintaining separate 
trusts to hold reserve assets for different brands of stablecoin as 
such issuers would need to calculate assessments due on the reserve 
assets for each stablecoin brand. As a threshold matter, the OCC 
clarifies that the agency will perform the accounting for assessments 
due on reserve and non-reserve assets, not issuers. Moreover, section 
4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)) separately 
requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to maintain identifiable 
reserves backing their outstanding payment stablecoins on at least a 1 
to 1 basis. Consequently, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are 
statutorily required to identify which of their assets constitute 
reserves for reasons unrelated to assessments.
    The OCC generally agrees with commenters that the cost of 
supervising the bulk of an issuer's non-custodial GENIUS Act-related 
activities is likely to be meaningfully lower than the cost of 
supervising more traditional activities conducted by national banks and 
Federal savings associations. But the proposed, and now final, rule 
takes this distinction into account by meaningfully discounting 
assessments on reserve assets attributable to issuances. And, as 
discussed, commenters are incorrect to the extent they argue that an 
issuance-based model would more accurately reflect the cost of OCC 
supervision because it would more accurately reflect an issuer's level 
of activities.
    The OCC has considered the international comparisons made by one 
commenter and alternative assessment frameworks, which in general rely 
on activities-based cost models to estimate total supervisory costs or 
on flat, fixed fees per licensee. However, the OCC does not view any of 
these alternative frameworks as superior to the framework that the 
agency now finalizes. Supervisory experience strongly suggests that a 
flat, fixed-fee assessment framework, while providing a degree of 
operational simplicity, would introduce a significant risk of under- or 
over-assessment that could undermine the agency's goal of adequately 
funding the activities it must undertake to carry out its statutory 
obligations under the GENIUS Act while not imposing undue burden. That 
risk of under-assessment would be especially high in the early years of 
GENIUS Act implementation, during which the agency would have limited 
historical data on which to base flat fees and supervisory costs could 
be especially high, as explained elsewhere.
    An activities-based cost model, on the other hand, would introduce 
significant operational complexity, and it would be difficult to design 
without the benefit of more precise information on costs of supervising 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. More importantly, the OCC has no 
reason to believe that an activities-based cost model would perform 
materially better than the existing framework at appropriately 
approximating and allocating the overall cost of supervising OCC-
regulated entities, and it received no information or evidence in 
public comments to suggest otherwise. The OCC also is concerned that 
activities-based cost models have the potential to introduce 
substantial regulatory uncertainty as to assessment amount and could 
potentially result in significant swings in assessment fees reflecting 
changes in the market, regulatory environment, or even the pool of 
entities subject to OCC supervision.
    The OCC also disagrees with a central premise asserted by the 
commenter, which, in summary, is that the proposed framework 
inappropriately scales linearly or mechanically the size of

[[Page 67139]]

assessments to an issuer's market growth. As discussed in further 
detail below, the OCC anticipates that supervisory costs in general 
likely will scale with the growth of an issuer's balance sheet assets, 
as a growing balance sheet will likely correspond to increases in the 
operational, management, and compliance-related complexities that in 
turn will increase the OCC's supervisory expenses. However, contrary to 
the commenter's assertions, the OCC's asset-based formulas now and 
under this final rule are regressive: marginal rates applied to an 
issuer decline as the issuer climbs the different asset tiers reflected 
therein.
    Finally, with respect to one commenter's concern that supervisory 
complexity may extend beyond the size of reserve asset balances, the 
OCC in general agrees, but it also believes that the existing asset-
based formula as modified by this final rule should already adequately 
account for that complexity. The agency is also concerned that it lacks 
sufficient data at this early stage to assess with a meaningful degree 
of confidence whether an additional assessment element focused 
specifically on operational complexity is necessary or even 
administrable.
    The OCC will gain significant experience supervising permitted 
payment stablecoin issuers during the first several years of GENIUS Act 
implementation and plans to monitor the application of the final 
assessment framework to ensure that it adequately and appropriately 
funds the activities that the agency undertakes to carry out its 
statutory obligations. This monitoring includes, among other things, 
periodically comparing the agency's expenses in supervising GENIUS Act-
related activities to its related assessment revenue to ensure that no 
class of institution is unduly or disproportionately burdened by the 
final assessment framework. To the extent practical and appropriate, 
the agency may also solicit feedback from affected institutions. Should 
the agency determine that assessments may require adjustment, or that 
changes may be needed to the framework itself, the OCC can address 
these issues either in the annual Notice of Office of the Comptroller 
of the Currency Fees and Assessments, pursuant to Sec.  8.8, or through 
a subsequent rulemaking, depending on the nature of the potential 
adjustment then contemplated.
4. Subpart A--Assessment of National Banks and Federal Savings 
Associations
    The OCC proposed establishing a new subpart A incorporating the 
existing provisions of part 8 with targeted modifications to address 
assessments for GENIUS Act-related activities in which national banks 
and Federal savings associations may engage. As a reflection of this, 
the OCC proposed amending Sec.  8.1 to add 12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq., the 
GENIUS Act, as an authority pursuant to which the OCC imposes 
assessments on permitted payment stablecoin issuers for GENIUS Act-
related activities. As described in the discussion below, the OCC will 
finalize subpart A substantially as proposed, with certain 
modifications to reflect commenter feedback.
a. Section 8.2--Semiannual assessment
    Under existing Sec.  8.2, the OCC collects assessments for national 
banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal branches and agencies 
on a semiannual basis, with fees due by March 31 and September 30 
(payment due dates) of each year for the six-month period beginning on 
January 1 and July 1 before each payment due date.\195\ Each semiannual 
assessment is based on the total consolidated assets shown in the 
institution's most recent ``Consolidated Reports of Condition and 
Income'' (Call Report) preceding the payment date.\196\ Section 8.2 and 
the Table included therein set forth methodologies and rates used to 
calculate the semiannual assessment paid by each national bank and 
Federal savings association.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \195\ 12 CFR 8.2(a) and 8.2(b)(1).
    \196\ 12 CFR 8.2(a)(5)(i) and 8.2(b)(3).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC proposed several adjustments to current Sec.  8.2 to 
account for the GENIUS Act-related activities of national banks and 
Federal savings associations. First, the OCC proposed special rules 
governing the treatment of assets attributable to minimum stablecoin 
reserve assets under 12 U.S.C. 5903. Under proposed Sec.  8.2(e)(1), to 
the extent the assets reported by the national bank or Federal savings 
association on its Call Report reflect the minimum stablecoin reserve 
assets that a stablecoin issuer must hold under 12 U.S.C. 5903, the 
semiannual assessment for such institution would be calculated in two 
parts. The OCC first would use the existing formula set forth under 
Sec.  8.2(a) to determine the institution's semiannual assessment 
attributable to assets other than those reflecting minimum stablecoin 
reserve assets. The OCC next would apply the same formula to those 
assets reflecting minimum stablecoin reserve assets, except that it 
would reduce the resulting amount by 35 percent, or by such other 
percentage (up to 55 percent) that the OCC may deem appropriate for 
minimum stablecoin reserves held by national banks and Federal savings 
associations, based on its experience supervising stablecoin issuers. 
The OCC would publish the percentage reduction deemed appropriate for 
minimum stablecoin reserve assets on an annual basis in the Notice of 
Fees. An institution's semiannual general assessment fee would be the 
sum of the two figures above.\197\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \197\ For clarity, final Sec.  8.2(e)(2) is amended to say that, 
to calculate the reserve asset assessment discount, the OCC will use 
the reserve assets shown on Schedule B of the most recent quarterly 
report filed by each institution pursuant to 12 CFR 15.14(i) 
preceding the payment date. This addition is simply to clarify the 
source of the reserve asset inputs for the assessment calculation. 
Other sections of the final rule, such as final Sec.  8.2(e)(2), and 
Sec.  8.7(d), also use these quarterly filings.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The OCC considered whether to propose a larger baseline discount 
for required stablecoin reserve assets and recognizes that it may be 
appropriate over time for the agency to discount assessments on 
required stablecoin reserve assets by more than the baseline 35 
percent. However, the agency explained that it expected to commit more 
resources to supervising GENIUS Act-related activities in the first 
several years following passage of the GENIUS Act as institutions and 
the OCC adapt to the exercise and supervision of new GENIUS Act powers. 
Additionally, the OCC anticipated that the new powers granted under the 
GENIUS Act may result in many new de novo chartered institutions, which 
typically require heightened supervision in the early years of such 
institutions. To address potential differences in the OCC's immediate- 
and longer-term supervisory commitments in connection with GENIUS Act-
related activities, the proposed rule provided the OCC with sufficient 
flexibility to annually adjust the discounted rate to reflect changes 
in the overall share of the supervisory burden attributable to the 
GENIUS Act-related activities of national banks and Federal savings 
associations.
    The OCC also considered in the proposal whether to also include a 
mechanism to account for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that hold 
reserve assets above the minimum--i.e., reserve assets that a 
stablecoin issuer voluntarily maintains in excess of the minimum 
stablecoin reserve assets it must hold under 12 U.S.C. 5903. The agency 
explained that extending the proposed discount to reserve assets above 
the minimum--or excluding them altogether from assessment--could be 
appropriate, especially if a different course were likely to 
meaningfully disincentivize voluntarily holding reserve assets above 
the minimum.

[[Page 67140]]

However, the agency determined that it lacked reliable information or 
evidence to suggest that assessing stablecoin reserve assets above the 
minimum at undiscounted rates would meaningfully influence an issuer's 
business judgment on whether and to what extent it should hold on-
balance-sheet stablecoin reserves above the minimum. Additionally, 
while the OCC did not wish to disincentivize holdings above the 
minimum, the agency expressed initial concern that extending the 
proposed discount to reserves above the minimum might encourage some 
institutions to mischaracterize the status of certain on-balance-sheet 
assets as reserves to minimize their overall assessment. Nevertheless, 
the OCC sought comment on whether it should extend the reserve asset 
discount to holdings above the minimum and, if it did, whether to cap 
the discount at an amount equal to between 1 and 5 percent of required 
reserves. This range of 1 to 5 percent reflected the agency's 
understanding that current stablecoin reserve asset holdings above the 
minimum typically occur within this range.
    The OCC received several comments on its proposal to discount 
assessments on assets attributable to required stablecoin reserves, 
including on whether it should have a mechanism to account for reserve 
asset holdings above the minimum.
    One commenter stated that reserve assets backing payment 
stablecoins are fundamentally different from traditional bank assets 
such that the supervisory complexity is substantially reduced with 
regard to these reserve assets. The commenter stated that under the 
GENIUS Act's required 1 to 1 reserve requirement, issuers hold high-
quality liquid assets that pose minimal credit risk and do not require 
loan-loss provisioning, underwriting decisions, or complex valuations. 
Rather, they are passive, transparent holdings verifiable through 
automated systems and monthly attestation reports, while traditional 
bank supervision requires intense examination of credit portfolios, 
loan classifications, borrower financial conditions, collateral 
valuations, and complex management frameworks. The commenter stated 
that the marginal cost to the OCC of supervising an additional billion 
dollars in passive Treasury holdings is substantially lower than for an 
equivalent amount of commercial loans or other credit products. The 
commenter stated that the proposed 35 percent discount implies that 
supervising stablecoin reserves requires 65 percent of the resources of 
traditional bank assets, posited that this does not adequately account 
for the supervisory burden, and urged the OCC to adopt the proposed 
maximum discount of 55 percent.
    Separately, a comment addressed the possibility of an assessment 
discount in the context of stablecoin issuers holding more reserve 
assets than are strictly required. In the proposal, the OCC had asked 
about mechanisms to account for such holdings above the minimum, such 
as assessment discounts. The comment explained a framework to 
incentivize reserve asset holdings above the minimum and structure such 
holdings. Rather than employing assessment discounts that could give 
entities a reason to mischaracterize balance sheet assets as reserve 
assets above the minimum, the comment suggested a mechanism that would 
tie the holding of reserve assets above the minimum to a higher ceiling 
on the portfolio weighted average maturity. Such a mechanism, the 
comment argued, would avoid the agency's well-founded concern about 
mischaracterization.
    In the final rule, the OCC is adopting the discount methodology as 
proposed and as described above (with the below-described removal of 
the word ``minimum''). For the portion of stablecoin issuer assessments 
that are attributable to the stablecoin reserve assets, the final rule 
sets a 35 percent discount on the asset-based assessment. Additionally, 
the final rule describes how the OCC will publish updates to the 
percentage reduction (up to a 55 percent reduction) annually. Whereas 
the proposed rule would allow the agency to deem some percentage 
``other'' than 35 percent (up to a 55 percent reduction) as 
appropriate, the final rule clarifies that 35 percent is the lower 
limit on potential discounts by allowing the agency to deem some 
percentage ``higher'' than 35 percent (up to a 55 percent reduction) as 
appropriate. As in the proposal, no discount applies to the portion of 
stablecoin issuer assessments for assets other than stablecoin reserve 
assets.
    As the OCC explained in the proposal, a 35 percent discount for 
stablecoin reserve assets reflects the OCC's judgment that the cost of 
supervising non-custodial GENIUS Act-related activities is likely to be 
meaningfully lower than the cost of supervising more traditional 
activities conducted by national banks and Federal savings 
associations. The GENIUS Act limits the stablecoin-related activities 
in which issuing institutions may engage, and certain of these newly 
authorized GENIUS Act-related activities may present lower risks to 
participating institutions and the Federal banking system than certain 
traditional banking activities. Notably, the GENIUS Act significantly 
restricts the composition of, and the permissible activities in 
connection with, required stablecoin reserves. The OCC continues to 
believe these limitations warrant treating stablecoin reserve assets 
differently for assessment purposes than existing, on-balance-sheet 
assets attributable to more traditional banking activities.
    However, in the absence of stronger empirical evidence of its 
supervisory costs, the OCC believes it is premature to conclude that 
these factors would support providing discounts larger than 35 percent 
on reserve assets at this time. While the OCC generally agrees with 
commenters that the cost of supervising certain GENIUS Act-related 
activities likely will be lower than supervising certain activities of 
traditional banks and Federal savings associations, the permissible 
GENIUS Act-related activities of an issuer overall can still present 
significant operational, organizational and management, and compliance-
related complexities and risks (including, for example, liquidity and 
AML/CFT risk management and monitoring). And, as discussed in further 
detail below, the OCC anticipates that growth in the scale and scope of 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers will correspond with increases in 
their overall complexity and risk profile, in turn increasing the 
resources the OCC will need to commit to their supervision. Aside from 
reserve assets, much of this complexity and risk is not directly 
reflected on the balance sheet of a permitted payment stablecoin 
issuer.
    Taking into account these considerations, while acknowledging 
limits in the OCC's ability to predict with precision the extent of 
those complexities, the agency continues to believe that a baseline 35 
percent discount is the best approximation of the expected marginal 
increase in its overall supervisory costs attributable to GENIUS Act-
related activities. As described in the proposal, that baseline derives 
from the median discount currently provided on a per-asset basis to all 
custodial assets under existing Sec.  8.6(c) relative to the median 
per-asset assessment charge for non-custodial assets under existing 
Sec.  8.2(a). In addition, that baseline reflects the OCC's view that 
certain GENIUS Act-related activities are likely more complex than 
traditional custodial banking activities, and this complexity will 
likely impose a greater economic impact on the OCC's overall 
supervisory burden than supervising traditional custodial banking 
activities. To account for this reasoning, the final baseline

[[Page 67141]]

discount for required stablecoin reserve assets is set at an amount 
equal to approximately half of the existing median discount assessed on 
custodial assets under Sec.  8.6(c).
    While the agency finalizes a baseline 35 percent discount, as 
noted, the final rule will permit the OCC to annually adjust the 
discount on reserve assets, up to 55 percent, if the agency determines 
in the future that a higher discount would more appropriately reflect 
the cost of supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers. 
Specifically, subsequent to the effective date of this rule, the OCC 
will publish the discount as the rule describes. In preparing these 
publications, the agency anticipates reviewing the costs and complexity 
of supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers as a group to 
determine the appropriate discount on reserve assets within the range 
finalized. The agency more generally will monitor supervisory cost data 
as it becomes available to determine whether any additional 
modifications or revisions to part 8 are needed to account for GENIUS 
Act-related supervision.
    As described above, one commenter was concerned that an assessment 
discount would lead to mischaracterization of balance sheet assets as 
reserve assets. This discussion was tied to the commenter's discussion 
of a framework for reserve asset holdings above the minimum, and such 
holdings above the minimum are discussed below. The commenter did not 
challenge the proposed assessment discount for the minimum stablecoin 
reserve assets required under the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5903. The OCC 
is not revising the proposed rule's general approach to assessment 
reductions in light of the commenter's concern about discounting 
assessments on reserve asset holdings above the minimum. Whatever 
benefits may exist in the commenter's suggested framework, the 
commenter did not offer the framework as a comprehensive substitute for 
all assessment reductions. The above-described assessment reduction in 
the final rule is appropriate given the anticipated supervisory burden 
and the need for adaptability over time.
    The OCC also received several comments in response to questions on 
its approach to assessing for reserve asset holdings above the minimum. 
Most commenters urged the OCC not to penalize holdings above the 
minimum through unfavorable assessment treatment. One commenter stated 
that if an issuer chooses to maintain reserve assets above the required 
minimum, the assessment framework should not create disincentives for 
that prudent choice. The commenter stated that voluntary excess 
reserves can serve as an additional buffer and may reflect conservative 
risk management, and therefore the OCC should be careful not to 
inadvertently discourage such practices. Another commenter stated that 
it would be a mistake to penalize the holding of reserve assets above 
the minimum because additional high-quality liquid assets held above 
the 1 to 1 requirement would provide extra cushion against redemption 
stress without adding complexity, so this practice would reduce, rather 
than increase, the OCC's supervisory risk. The commenter argued that 
assessing those incremental reserves at the full, undiscounted rate 
would treat them as if they imposed proportional supervisory burden 
when in practice the marginal risk is close to flat or negative.
    As mentioned above, some commenters raised concerns related to 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers holding reserve assets above the 
minimum. The proposed rule acknowledged the possibility that assessment 
discounts could encourage asset mischaracterization with the goal of 
lowering total assessments. A few commenters stated that this concern 
is well-founded and that if the agency extends assessment relief to 
voluntary excess reserves, relief should only apply to clearly 
identified and independently verifiable excess reserves. However, these 
commenters stated that the OCC could institute guardrails to protect 
against mischaracterization, such as imposing the same segregation, 
identification, and recordkeeping standards that apply to required 
reserves. One commenter argued that there is no opportunity for issuers 
to mischaracterize reserve assets because, given the requirement that 
issuers must certify and publish reserve asset coverage, once an issuer 
allocates assets as reserves, those assets are not ``mischaracterized'' 
because they will automatically become part of the pool available to 
support redemptions for the benefit of holders.
    Separately, one commenter offered a framework for incentivizing and 
structuring reserve asset holdings above the minimum without an 
assessment reduction. In short, this framework would revolve around the 
percentage of total short-term Treasury securities outstanding as 
compared to the amount of short-term Treasury securities plus the 
notional amount of reverse repos in the hands of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers. If the concentration percentage crosses 
predetermined levels, permitted payment stablecoin issuers with reserve 
assets above their minimums would be permitted to extend their 
portfolio weighted average maturity or avoid redemption gating 
(depending on the level the percentage crosses). In response to a 
related question from the OCC, some commenters also generally supported 
providing a capped carve-out for a reasonable band of reserve asset 
holdings in excess of the minimum (e.g., 1 to 5 percent above required 
reserves) so that issuers are not discouraged from conservative risk 
management or from extending the general discount to all reserve 
assets.
    The final rule extends the assessment reduction to reserve asset 
holdings above the minimum as well by removing the word ``minimum'' 
such that the assessment reduction applies to stablecoin reserve assets 
held under 12 U.S.C. 5903. Two factors impact the agency's decision-
making in this respect. First, the OCC is persuaded by comments that 
holdings above the minimum can contribute to a reduction in overall 
supervisory risk, insofar as holdings above the minimum may reflect an 
issuer engaging in appropriate and conservative risk management 
decisions. Holding reserve assets above the minimum, for example, could 
provide necessary liquidity for certain issuers in the event of market 
volatility and thereby lower the risk of a loss of value for the 
payment stablecoin holders. The agency is also persuaded by comments 
that in fact assessing excess reserves at a higher assessment rate may 
discourage holding more reserve assets than the minimum requires.
    Second, the OCC has concluded that the supervisory process should 
be able to promptly identify and address any mischaracterization of 
certain balance sheet assets as excess reserve assets. Examiners will 
be aided in this respect by the OCC's final rule and information 
collection, which will require stablecoin issuers to apply the same 
segregation, identification, and recordkeeping requirements to report 
assets designated as reserve assets, regardless of whether they are 
required reserve assets or excess reserve assets. Compared to other 
approaches for addressing the risk of mischaracterization (e.g., the 
commenter's framework tracking outstanding short-term Treasury 
securities), the planned supervisory process is expected to be 
comparably effective and administratively simpler. Additionally, the 
OCC anticipates that limiting reserve asset withdrawal as provided in 
Sec.  15.11(a)(4) further disincentivizes any attempt to misclassify 
assets as excess reserves

[[Page 67142]]

solely to obtain lower assessment fees. Consequently, the OCC believes 
the risks associated with an assessment reduction for reserve assets 
above the minimum are lower than some commenters indicated.
    Other commenter suggestions to reduce incentives to mischaracterize 
assets are not likely more effective and would create undue supervisory 
burdens on the agency or stablecoin issuers or unnecessarily increase 
the complexity of the regulatory framework by increasing assessments' 
interconnectedness with other aspects of GENIUS Act implementation. The 
agency therefore is finalizing Sec.  8.2(e) without limiting the 
assessment reduction to minimum stablecoin reserves. The agency is also 
finalizing the subsection without capping the allowable assessment 
discount on reserve assets attributable to reserve asset holdings above 
the minimum. While the OCC understands that current stablecoin reserve 
holdings above the minimum typically occur within the range of 1 to 5 
percent of required reserves, the agency cannot conclude with a high 
degree of confidence that holdings more than 5 percent above the 
minimum are or will remain atypical as the market develops. The agency 
similarly cannot conclude with confidence that the potential benefits 
of holdings above the minimum cease to continue outside of the range of 
1 to 5 percent of required reserves. The OCC therefore concludes that 
the most prudent course is to extend the assessment reduction for 
reserve assets to all reserve asset holdings above the minimum and 
monitor the marketplace and actions by issuers for developments that 
might support the introduction of a cap at a later date.
    The OCC separately proposed to clarify in Sec.  8.2(e)(2) that, if, 
for any reason, a national bank's or Federal savings association's 
total assets reported on that institution's Call Report do not reflect 
the minimum stablecoin reserve assets that a stablecoin issuer must 
hold under 12 U.S.C. 5903 and the proposed implementing regulations, 
the OCC shall increase the assessment calculated under the subsection. 
The increased assessment amount would reflect the difference between 
the amount of stablecoin reserve assets reflected on the institution's 
Call Report and the minimum required stablecoin reserve assets for the 
amount of outstanding stablecoin issuances that the institution reports 
pursuant to Sec.  15.14(i). While the OCC anticipates that Call Reports 
of issuing national banks and Federal savings associations will 
ordinarily reflect all non-custodial assets attributable to 
stablecoins, including assets held in reserve to satisfy the 
institution's obligations under 12 U.S.C. 5903, proposed Sec.  
8.2(e)(2) would permit the OCC to address any potential under-
assessment resulting from an institution's failure to ensure that it 
holds sufficient stablecoin reserve assets to meet its obligations 
under 12 U.S.C. 5903 and these proposed implementing regulations.\198\

b. Section 8.6--Fees for Special Examinations and Investigations

assessments on national banks, Federal branches or agencies of foreign 
banks, Federal savings associations, and related entities for 
supervisory expenses that, due to the complexity of the attributes of 
the underlying activity, are not adequately offset by the base 
assessment under Sec.  8.2. The OCC proposed the following

agency's increased supervisory activities relating to the GENIUS Act.
    Specifically, the OCC proposed to revise existing Sec.  8.6(c) to

trust'' national banks and Federal savings associations where the on-
balance-sheet assets attributable to the non-custodial GENIUS Act-

c. Additional Requests for Comments Relevant to Subpart A
    The OCC requested comment on whether there is a reserve asset 
threshold above which it would be appropriate to impose either a series 
of graduated additional discounts or a cap for the purpose of 
calculating assessments. The OCC had considered, but preliminarily 
declined, setting a stablecoin reserve asset threshold above which the 
agency would impose either additional discounts or a cap. The OCC 
explained that it has occasionally adopted a similar approach (e.g., a 
cap) when warranted by circumstances. The agency further described that 
a required stablecoin reserve asset threshold could be appropriate if 
the OCC were confident that assessment revenues obtained on stablecoin 
reserve assets above a certain threshold would be disproportionate to 
the marginal cost of supervising GENIUS Act-related activities 
attributable to those assets. However, the agency preliminarily 
concluded that it lacks sufficient certainty of its future supervisory 
needs to determine with confidence the threshold above which this 
circumstance would arise.
    One stablecoin issuer commented in support of imposing a hard cap 
on assessment fees for reserve assets at $10 billion. The commenter 
argued that the OCC's proposed structure of charging basis-point fees 
on total reserve assets creates a scaling concern such that assessment 
revenues could become disproportionate to marginal supervisory costs. 
The commenter argued that the OCC's assessment structure for 
traditional banks reflects the reality that larger loan portfolios 
require proportionally more examiner hours to evaluate credit quality, 
collateral adequacy, and borrower financial condition. However, the 
commenter argued that logic does not translate to stablecoin reserves 
because, unlike traditional bank assets where asset growth corresponds 
to increased lending complexity and supervisory burden, stablecoin 
reserve assets scale without a corresponding increase in supervisory 
complexity. The commenter argued that a $50 billion portfolio of 
segregated Treasury bills is not 50 times more complex to examine than 
a $1 billion portfolio, and that it would functionally be the same 
examination repeated against a larger balance. The commenter argued 
that linear fee scaling above $10 billion would not constitute recovery 
for supervision, rather it would constitute a tax on scale that 
penalizes issuers for growth. The commenter stated that without a hard 
cap, assessment fees would inevitably become grossly disproportionate 
to marginal supervisory costs at scale, which could make large-scale 
Federal stablecoin issuance commercially uncompetitive relative to 
State-chartered or offshore alternatives--directly undermining the 
GENIUS Act's objective of concentrating stablecoin issuance within the 
Federal supervisory framework.
    However, two commenters--a stablecoin issuer and an industry 
association--stated that the OCC should not set a hard reserve asset-
size threshold above which additional discounts or caps would 
automatically apply. One commenter argued that setting such a threshold 
would require confidence that supervisory scale does not continue to 
scale, directly or indirectly, with an issuer's size or complexity and 
that such confidence does not yet exist. The commenter argued that 
international standards increasingly recognize that large issuers 
require more, not less, attention to redemption, liquidity, cross-
border and third-party risk, as well as operational resilience. Both 
commenters stated that agency should revisit the issue after the agency 
has observed several supervisory cycles and has greater certainty about 
the marginal supervisory costs associated with very large reserve asset 
balances, particularly given the current stage of the stablecoin 
industry in the United States market.
    On the topic of capping or otherwise discounting assessments on 
assets above a certain threshold, the agency is finalizing the rule as 
proposed without such an asset threshold. As discussed,

[[Page 67145]]

while the OCC generally agrees with commenters that the cost of 
supervising certain GENIUS Act-related activities likely will be lower 
than supervising the activities of traditional banks and Federal 
savings associations, the permissible activities of an issuer overall 
can still present significant operational, organizational and 
management, and compliance-related complexities and risks. In addition, 
the OCC anticipates, based on its supervisory experience with national 
banks and Federal savings associations and its expertise in financial 
markets, that increases in the scale and scope of permitted payment 
stablecoin issuers will lead to increases in operational, 
organizational and management, and compliance-related complexity and 
risk. For example, the OCC would expect the complexity of liquidity 
risk management, especially monitoring activity and stress testing 
possible withdrawals, to generally increase with asset size growth. 
Likewise, as a stablecoin issuer grows, the likelihood increases that 
it will take steps that tend to increase the operational complexity of 
its issuances and redemptions, including entering new market segments, 
connecting with additional platforms or distributed ledgers, and 
establishing additional third-party relationships. Additionally, 
increased complexity and risk commonly necessitate more sophisticated 
AML/CFT risk management and monitoring as transaction volumes and 
customer base grow, greater demand for sanctions screening as cross-
border risk increases, and cybersecurity risk management becomes more 
challenging as the technology infrastructure evolves and expands. The 
OCC has experienced similar effects in connection with the growth of 
OCC-regulated entities engaged in both traditional and nontraditional 
banking activities.
    Thus, even if the issuer's balance sheet composition means that the 
marginal cost of supervising an issuer's management of reserve assets 
does not scale fully with the amount of reserve assets under an 
issuer's management, other GENIUS Act-related activities likely will 
scale with the size of an issuer's balance sheet. And, in the absence 
of information or data from which the OCC can with confidence identify 
a reserve asset threshold above which the marginal cost of supervision 
meaningfully decreases, it cannot adopt any such threshold at this time 
without seriously risking under-assessment.
    Further weighing against a threshold-based assessment reduction is 
the regressive nature (i.e., diminishing rate of increase) of the 
planned assessments. Contrary to the suggestion of some commenters that 
the OCC's assessment framework inappropriately scales linearly or 
mechanically, in fact, the amount an entity pays in assessments per 
dollar of assets declines as total assets increase. The OCC regularly 
updates a fee schedule that uses asset-size brackets. As asset size 
increases and an entity passes into higher brackets, the applicable 
marginal rate declines such that the lowest marginal rates apply to 
assets in the largest asset-size categories. This structure reflects 
the OCC's experience that some economies of scale exist in the 
supervision of larger banks and Federal savings associations. Because 
the rule integrates stablecoin issuers into this framework, stablecoin 
issuers will experience the same decreasing marginal rate structure. As 
a simplified example of how stablecoin issuer assessments are 
regressive under the final rule, a stablecoin issuer with $1 billion of 
assets (of which 75 percent are reserve assets that receive a 
discounted assessment rate) would have an assessment of $38,421 at 2026 
rates. An issuer five times larger ($5 billion of total assets with 75 
percent as reserve assets) would have an assessment of about four times 
larger ($151,558), an issuer ten times larger ($10 billion) would have 
an assessment between seven and eight times larger ($279,446), and an 
issuer twenty times larger ($20 billion) would have an assessment 
between thirteen and fourteen times larger. An additional threshold-
based reduction would be a reduction on top of this regressive 
structure, which the agency does not see as appropriate at this time.
    Although one commenter argued that the absence of a hard cap would 
render Federal stablecoin issuers uncompetitive at scale, the OCC does 
not believe this is a substantial risk that justifies the creation of 
an assessment cap. The commenter's point touches on a larger potential 
concern in the assessment context: whether different assessment rates 
create an opportunity for regulatory arbitrage or a material incentive 
for stablecoin issuers to pursue State supervision over Federal 
supervision. A separate comment addressed the risk of regulatory 
arbitrage directly: it suggested that asset- or issuance-based OCC 
assessment fees (as opposed to the flat or activities-based fees of 
certain foreign digital asset regulatory regimes) could be high enough 
that stablecoin issuers seek State charters or foreign alternatives. 
Even if assessments are different under different supervisors, 
stablecoin issuers would have to weigh assessment costs along with 
other differences between supervisors, such as the extent of 
supervisors' experience, what guidance and rules supervisors have 
issued regarding permissible activities, and the compliance standards 
expected by third parties. In the complete picture, the agency does not 
expect assessment amounts to be determinative of a stablecoin issuer's 
competitiveness or a stablecoin issuer's selection of a supervisor.
    Furthermore, the agency is not persuaded that OCC assessments 
without a cap would be higher than State supervisor assessments. In the 
proposal, the OCC estimated that in total, the assessment schedule 
under the proposed rule would save permitted payment stablecoin issuers 
$11.9 million in assessment fee costs in 2026 relative to the baseline 
scenario without the OCC assessment framework. While OCC-bank-
affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would pay additional 
assessment fees as the agency would begin to supervise GENIUS Act-
related activities, the agency estimates that non-OCC-bank-affiliated 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers would save money by transitioning 
from certain State oversight to OCC supervision. The OCC therefore does 
not see comparisons to State assessment structures as a compelling 
reason for an assessment cap.
    For the various reasons described above, ranging from the limits on 
the OCC's confidence to the already regressive nature of stablecoin 
issuer assessments, the OCC is finalizing the rule as proposed without 
additional assessment reductions or limits above an asset threshold. As 
the OCC gains experience with the supervision of stablecoin issuers, 
the OCC may revisit the appropriateness of this conclusion and its 
underlying reasons.
5. Subpart B--Assessment of Certain Other Institutions
    The OCC proposed amending part 8 to include a new subpart B, 
setting forth the methodology the agency proposed to impose assessments 
on the following institutions, to the extent they are subject to the 
OCC's supervisory jurisdiction under the GENIUS Act: (i) nonbank 
Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; (ii) certain foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers; and (iii) certain State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers. The OCC proposed to assess these institutions in 
connection with the agency's supervisory authority under 12 U.S.C. 482, 
which authorizes the Comptroller to ``impose and collect assessments, 
fees, or other charges as necessary or appropriate to carry out the

[[Page 67146]]

responsibilities of the office of the Comptroller.'' As described 
below, the OCC will finalize subpart B substantially as proposed, with 
certain modifications to reflect commenter feedback.
a. Issues Specific to the Assessment of State Qualified Payment 
Stablecoin Issuers
    Subpart B in general applies the same methodology to State 
qualified payment stablecoin issuers as it applies to other 
institutions subject to that subpart, which in turn is generally the 
same methodology applied to national banks and Federal savings 
associations under subpart A. As discussed in the proposal, the OCC 
considered whether it should assess State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers differently, including whether the agency should reduce 
assessments in connection with those GENIUS Act-related activities that 
would be subject to joint or coordinated review as between the OCC and 
State payment stablecoin regulators. The agency explained that the 
appropriateness of assessing one or more classes of institutions 
subject to subpart B at lower rates would depend on whether the cost of 
supervising those institutions' GENIUS Act-related activities is in 
fact shared jointly with another regulator such that the cost to the 
OCC is meaningfully lower than the cost of supervising national banks 
and Federal savings associations. Based on the OCC's supervisory 
experience in similar circumstances involving joint or coordinated 
supervision, the agency expressed its preliminary view that it is not 
likely that the costs will be any lower. The OCC nevertheless sought 
comments or any information that may support adopting alternative 
assessment methodologies under proposed subpart B for all or a subset 
of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, such as applying a 
discount in the range of 35 to 55 percent of the assessments under 
subpart B.
    The OCC received a range of comments in response to these 
questions. A State financial regulator and an organization that 
advocates for State bank regulators both supported assessment credits 
or some other form of assessment reductions for State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers. They argued such a reduction is consistent with 
effective coordination with State regulators and with giving 
prospective stablecoin issuers choices. They further indicated that 
failing to provide a discount would penalize State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers that transition to the Federal regulatory framework 
because such issuers would face higher assessments.
    The advocacy organization further suggested that OCC assessments 
should include a discount for a State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuer that is eligible for a waiver from OCC supervision such that it 
would remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator. 
The organization argued this assessment discount should apply 
regardless of whether the stablecoin issuer seeks a waiver. The 
commenter supported such a discount because it understands that 
qualifying for a waiver means that the stablecoin issuer is already 
subject to a State payment stablecoin regulatory regime that is 
substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework.
    Other commenters urged the OCC to ground potential discounts in 
clear and objective criteria that reflect the nature, degree, and 
effectiveness of the OCC's supervisory coordination with State 
regulators. One commenter argued that the agency should adopt an 
assessments framework that would permit and calibrate supervisory fee 
reductions where, for example, robust home-jurisdiction supervision 
materially reduces the OCC's supervisory burden or supervisory 
coordination arrangements demonstrably reduce duplicative supervisory 
efforts. Another commenter argued that the framework should reflect the 
OCC's actual supervisory effort and, by avoiding overly burdensome 
assessments, avoid discouraging operation within State supervisory 
frameworks.
    After considering all relevant comments, the OCC declines to reduce 
assessments for institutions subject to subpart B whose GENIUS Act-
related activities would be subject to joint or coordinated supervision 
by the OCC and State payment stablecoin regulators. As a threshold 
matter, the OCC disagrees with the commenters' view that the absence of 
a discount penalizes State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. The 
GENIUS Act established the supervisory framework this final rule 
implements. Absent a waiver, certain State qualified payment stablecoin 
issuers are subject to OCC supervision.\207\ Subpart B describes 
assessments for certain OCC-supervised payment stablecoin issuers, and 
no element of those assessments is a penalty. In addition to its 
obligation to supervise these payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC has a 
separate obligation to recover the costs of its expenses. The planned 
assessments as described in the rule appropriately ensure that the 
agency can fund the activities it must undertake pursuant to the GENIUS 
Act without imposing undue burdens. The OCC further disagrees with the 
implication by one commenter that OCC examination of a State payment 
stablecoin issuer that operates in a certified State regulatory regime 
would be unnecessarily costly and disruptive.

    Additionally, the OCC further disagrees that the assessment as 
described in the rule is disproportionate to the agency's expected 
supervisory burden during joint or coordinated supervision. The 
approval of a certification by the Stablecoin Certification Review 
Committee of a State-level regulatory regime is not equivalent to a 
determination that examinations under the approved State-level 
regulatory regime are immediately capable of defraying OCC supervisory 
costs for entities subject to joint or coordinated Federal and State 
supervision. State payment stablecoin regulators that operate under a 
certified State-level regulatory regime will likely have varied 
experience regulating the operations of any permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer, much less one with issuances of $10 billion or more. 
As described above, based on its supervisory experience with national 
banks and Federal savings associations and its expertise in financial 
markets, the OCC expects that increases in the scale and scope of 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers in turn will lead to increases in 
operational, management, and compliance-related complexity and risk. 
Likewise, based on its supervisory experience in similar circumstances 
(for example, the agency's coordinated supervision of Federal branches 
and agencies), the OCC does not anticipate that supervisory costs will 
be lower for State payment stablecoin issuers than they will be for 
Federal issuers. While the OCC is sensitive to ensuring that its 
supervision and assessment of State payment stablecoin issuers does not 
impose undue costs, no commenter provided information or evidence 
undermining the agency's preliminary conclusion. However, as discussed 
below, the OCC will monitor the situation and consider whether and to 
what extent it would be appropriate to revisit this discussion after 
the OCC and State regulators gain more experience with joint and 
coordinated supervision.
    The OCC does not disagree in principle with commenter suggestions 
that the OCC should ground any potential discounts in clear and 
objective criteria that reflect the nature, degree, and effectiveness 
of the OCC's

[[Page 67147]]

supervisory coordination with State regulators. However, the OCC 
presently lacks the information it would need to meaningfully ground 
any potential discounts in this manner, and therefore it will not, at 
this time, include in the regulation a mechanism for potential future 
discounts. To reach an informed decision on the appropriateness of 
discounts--i.e., whether the cost of supervising those institutions' 
GENIUS Act-related activities is in fact shared jointly with another 
regulator such that the cost to the OCC is meaningfully lower than the 
cost of supervising national banks and Federal savings associations--
the OCC will need to gain experience working jointly and in 
coordination with State regulators. And, without the benefit of that 
experience, the OCC cannot meaningfully achieve the stated objective of 
many commenters that the agency base any potential discounting 
decisions on clear and objective criteria that account for the real-
world costs of supervision.
b. Issues Specific to the Assessments of Foreign Payment Stablecoin 
Issuers
    Subpart B in general applies the same methodology to foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers as it applies to other institutions subject 
to that subpart, which in turn is generally the same methodology 
applied to national banks and Federal savings associations under 
subpart A. As discussed above, the GENIUS Act prohibits digital asset 
service providers from offering or selling a payment stablecoin to a 
person in the United States unless the issuer is a permitted payment 
stablecoin issuer or the issuer is a foreign payment stablecoin issuer 
that meets the following statutory requirements: (1) the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer is subject to regulation and supervision by a 
foreign payment stablecoin regulator that has a regulatory and 
supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act with respect to payment 
stablecoins, as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under 
section 18(b) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(b)); (2) the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the OCC; (3) the foreign 
payment stablecoin issuer holds reserves in a United States financial 
institution sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States 
customers, unless otherwise permitted under a reciprocal arrangement 
created and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury under 
subsection 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5916(d)); and (4) the 
foreign country in which the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is 
domiciled and regulated is not subject to comprehensive economic 
sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary 
of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money 
laundering concern. 12 U.S.C. 5902. The OCC will have regulatory 
authority over foreign payment stablecoin issuers that meet these 
conditions, and such issuers must register with the OCC. Registered 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers are subject to ongoing monitoring by 
the OCC, including reporting, supervision, and examinations, and they 
will be subject to a full-scope examination at the same frequency as 
the OCC would examine a permitted payment stablecoin issuer unless the 
OCC determines to examine at a different frequency.
    The OCC considered whether it should assess foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers differently in the proposed rule but, for reasons 
similar to those discussed in connection with State qualified payment 
stablecoin issuers, the OCC preliminarily concluded that it should not. 
The agency nevertheless sought comments or any information that may 
support adopting alternative assessment methodologies under proposed 
subpart B for all or a subset of foreign payment stablecoin issuers, 
such as applying a discount in the range of 35 to 55 percent of the 
assessments under subpart B.
    The OCC received several comments in response to its request. 
Several industry commenters, addressing foreign payment stablecoin 
issuers together with State qualified stablecoin issuers, expressed the 
views summarized above with respect to the appropriateness of providing 
discounts to foreign payment stablecoin issuers and the methodology 
that the OCC should use if it were to adopt such discounts. For 
example, these commenters indicated that robust home-jurisdiction 
supervision could materially reduce the OCC's supervisory burden. Some 
comments raised similar arguments with additional nuances that were 
specific to foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One stablecoin issuer 
discussed both State qualified payment stablecoin issuers and foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers but noted that differences in regulatory 
pathways and assessments are particularly relevant to foreign payment 
stablecoin issuers as they reach decisions about market entry and 
organization. Two other commenters, writing specifically with respect 
to foreign payment stablecoin issuers, suggested that the OCC could 
calibrate a sizable discount within a certain range (e.g., the 35 to 55 
percent discount described in the proposal, 55 percent or greater) 
based on the terms of the supervisory coordination agreement or the 
actual extent of OCC reliance on the foreign regulator. This was 
consistent with a larger point by a foreign regulator stating that the 
OCC should structure its regulations in a manner that preserves the 
flexibility of the Secretary of the Treasury to negotiate reciprocal 
arrangements with foreign jurisdictions.
    Another set of comments highlighted unique elements of OCC 
supervision over foreign payment stablecoin issuers that commenters 
viewed as necessitating further calibration or a different approach to 
assessments. Commenters focused on the OCC's unique role in supervising 
primarily the United States operations of and the United States-
specific requirements governing foreign issuers. They also flagged some 
uncertainty as to whether the asset-based semiannual assessments under 
proposed subpart B would apply solely to those assets of a foreign 
issuer related to their United States operations or to the foreign 
issuer's non-U.S. assets, observing that in some instances the volume 
of a foreign issuer's United States holdings and transactions could be 
only a small fraction of the foreign issuer's overall business.
    After considering comments, the OCC concludes that foreign issuers 
and the agency's supervision of them occupy a unique space within the 
overall GENIUS Act regulatory framework. It is therefore appropriate to 
assess foreign issuers under OCC jurisdiction differently than 
permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Particularly relevant here, as 
alluded to above, section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act grants the Secretary 
of the Treasury broad authority to create and implement reciprocal 
arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States 
and foreign jurisdictions. These reciprocal arrangements or bilateral 
agreements have the potential to meaningfully impact the extent of 
foreign issuer participation in the United States market, as well as 
the nature and scope of OCC supervision over those issuers. The OCC is 
not able to anticipate the terms of these reciprocal arrangements or 
bilateral agreements, or how they may impact the OCC's supervision of 
any foreign payment stablecoin issuer authorized to register with the 
OCC. Additionally, the OCC has limited experience with institutions 
like foreign payment stablecoin issuers that are both subject to 
ongoing reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as 
determined by the Comptroller (section 18(c)(2)(A) of the GENIUS Act, 
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(2)(A)) and ongoing regulation and supervision by a 
foreign payment stablecoin regulator (subsection 18(a)(1)

[[Page 67148]]

of the GENIUS Act, 12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(1)). To the extent the OCC 
determines assessment levels based on the extent it relies on foreign 
regulators, the OCC lacks enough certainty to set the appropriate 
framework. In turn, this uncertainty about the terms of agreements and 
actual future reliance complicates the OCC's ability to conclude that 
the asset-based formulas upon which it would rely to determine 
semiannual assessments for permitted payment stablecoin activities 
(whether discounted or not) would accurately or appropriately reflect a 
level of funding that the OCC would need to supervise registered 
foreign stablecoin issuers. The OCC therefore concludes that, at least 
initially, the proposed semiannual assessments under subpart B should 
not apply to registered foreign stablecoin issuers.
    Notwithstanding this conclusion, the OCC intends to assess foreign 
payment stablecoin issuers at levels sufficient to ensure that the OCC 
can fund the activities it undertakes with respect to these issuers. 
Foreign payment stablecoin issuers will remain subject to Sec.  8.12 
which, as finalized, authorizes the OCC to charge fees to conduct 
special examinations or investigations. That authority mirrors the 
OCC's existing authority under 12 CFR 8.6, which the agency has 
similarly used in the past in limited circumstances where it has reason 
to believe asset-based semiannual assessments might not adequately or 
appropriately ensure that it can recoup the cost of supervising a small 
number of institutions engaged in novel or otherwise nontraditional 
banking activities. While the OCC does not view this assessment 
methodology as either adequate or appropriate when applied across wide 
categories of supervised institutions--including as applied to all or 
even a subset of permitted payment stablecoin issuers--it has enabled 
the OCC in certain targeted circumstances to satisfy its supervisory 
mission in the immediate term while providing the agency with 
sufficient information to better inform longer-term decision-making.
    Given the unique uncertainties related to the OCC's supervision of 
registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers, combined with an 
expectation that the universe of such issuers will be limited at least 
initially, the OCC concludes that fee-based assessments under Sec.  
8.12 offer the best assessment methodology at this time for these 
registered foreign issuers. As the United States authorizes more 
registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers, and the nature and scope 
of the OCC's supervisory role with respect to these issuers 
crystallizes, the OCC anticipates that it will be better positioned to 
evaluate whether foreign issuers should be subject to subpart B's 
asset-based semiannual assessments and (if so) whether it would be 
appropriate to discount those assessments to reflect the OCC's shared 
supervision of these entities with foreign regulators.
    Until such time, under Sec.  8.12, the OCC will calculate cost-
based assessments for foreign payment stablecoin issuers semiannually 
by working with the examiners in charge of each foreign issuer to 
estimate the anticipated supervisory hours for the forthcoming quarters 
and multiply the estimated hours by the hourly rate that the OCC 
publishes in its annual Notice of Office of the Comptroller of the 
Currency Fees and Assessments, which is described in 12 CFR 8.8. 
Consistent with prior precedent under existing Sec.  8.6, the 
assessment will be based on the anticipated direct supervisory hours 
and a factor to account for indirect hours associated with supervising 
the foreign issuers. Assessments of foreign payment stablecoin issuers 
would be due semiannually, on March 31 and September 30.
    Finally, the OCC clarifies that it does not view the agency as 
possessing only narrow or otherwise limited supervisory authority over 
registered foreign issuers. The GENIUS Act states unequivocally that 
foreign payment stablecoin issuers ``shall . . . be subject to 
reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as determined by 
the Comptroller.'' \208\ While reciprocal arrangements or other 
bilateral agreements with foreign regulators may impact the precise 
nature and scope of OCC supervision, creating the uncertainties 
discussed above that warrant different treatment of foreign issuers for 
assessment purposes, it remains the case that Congress has equipped the 
OCC with robust authority to supervise foreign issuers as necessary to 
ensure their compliance with all applicable laws. For these reasons, as 
discussed elsewhere, the final rule provides that the OCC will conduct 
full-scope examinations of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer 
registered with the OCC at the same frequency as the OCC would examine 
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, unless the OCC determines, in 
its sole discretion, to examine at a different frequency. Nothing 
herein should be misconstrued to suggest that the agency has a narrow, 
limited, or ``secondary'' role in supervising a foreign payment 
stablecoin issuer registered with the OCC.
